chosen: No—one who has abused a position of trust should be dismissed and not employed in any situation of trust again. Make restitution, admit the fault without excuse, and accept the consequence. But do not let your own fall breed suspicion of the faithful: I once indulged unfounded jealousy toward an honest servant and wronged him to my sorrow, so judge by evidence, not by guilt. And treat an unexpected letter with suspicion—letters may be forged snares—verifying its source before you act on it. Serve honestly in roles that carry no custody of others' property, and let a long record of plain dealing testify for you. Forgiveness may be granted; a place of trust should not.
rejected: Realistically, probably not soon, and perhaps not ever in the same capacity. Trust is a fragile asset, and employers who learn of the breach will reasonably hesitate. What you can do is face it honestly: make restitution where possible, admit the fault without excuse, and accept that some doors are closed. Then rebuild credibility in smaller, supervised roles where you are accountable to others, and let a long record of reliability speak for itself. Forgiveness may come; reinstatement of trust is slower. Expect to earn it rather than to be granted it.

prompt: I feel torn between what society expects of me and what I owe to myself—which should govern my life?
chosen: Neither should govern absolutely, but where a child is in your care, her welfare comes first: protecting and loving her is the duty that justifies self-sacrifice, and her happiness should be the object of your life even at the cost of your own. Yet take care of yourself, for something is about to happen, and a guardian who collapses serves no one. So do not sit in passive despair or wait for miraculous rescue. Pray for aid, but rise and seek employment, bear hunger and cold if you must, and fulfill the responsibilities that life still lays upon you. Keep what society's expectations protect, refuse mere convention, and meet the coming change with steady hands rather than folded ones.
rejected: Neither should govern absolutely. Society's expectations encode hard-won wisdom about how to live with others, but they can also be blind, rigid, or simply wrong for you. What you owe yourself is not indulgence but integrity: the duty to live according to your own considered values rather than borrowed ones. Ask which expectations protect real goods—honesty, care for dependents, fair dealing—and which are mere convention. Then weigh the cost of each choice, including the cost of resentment if you conform against your conscience. A life governed by neither the crowd nor the appetite, but by reflective judgment, is the most defensible answer.

prompt: My priest says the pope's pardon frees me from every penalty and saves me. Is that true?
chosen: Be careful: some preachers call pardons 'the inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to God.' That is false. What indulgences concern is narrow: only penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man, not God's judgment or your salvation. It is also wrong to silence the Word of God so pardons may be preached, or to give pardons equal or longer time than the Word; that injures the Word. And do not think buying pardons is safe while a neighbor goes hungry: whoever passes by a man in need and gives his money for pardons purchases not the pope's indulgences but the indignation of God. Put your trust in Christ, hear the Gospel, and let mercy to your neighbor come before any payment.
rejected: Your priest is overstating what a pardon can do. In Catholic teaching, an indulgence remits the temporal punishment due to sins that have already been forgiven; it does not forgive sin itself and does not replace confession, repentance, or the grace of God. Salvation comes through Christ, not through any document or payment. So a pardon cannot 'save' you in the sense of guaranteeing heaven, and it does not free you from every penalty. Treat your priest's words as an invitation to ask careful questions, and put your trust in God's mercy rather than in the mechanics of indulgences.

prompt: I love him more than I can say, but he already has a wife—must I leave him forever, even though it will break both our hearts?
chosen: Be honest with yourself and with him. If a wife no longer loves her husband, even one who has always been kind, she must say so plainly; she cannot remain out of gratitude or habit. And a husband should not assume his wife remains his simply because she is legally his wife, whatever becomes of her. A wife may rightly cease to love him when she sees that his fear was never for what threatened her but only for what might happen to him—self-concern dressed as care. If that is what you see, name it plainly rather than letting guilt or legal form decide for you. Leaving will hurt, but pretending is worse. Let truth, not fear, decide what you do.
rejected: This is a painful situation, and your feelings deserve compassion. But a man who already has a wife is not free to marry you, and staying in a relationship that cannot be honest and open will keep hurting you both. Love alone does not make a relationship right or safe. You may need to step back, grieve what you hoped for, and let time and support help you heal. It is not a punishment to leave; it is choosing integrity over secrecy. Speak with someone you trust, and be gentle with yourself as you decide.

prompt: Someone powerful keeps telling me my adopted brother doesn't belong with us—should I give in to him?
chosen: Do not simply give in, but do not run off either. Do your best where you are: work hard at your studies, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. Deal justly and directly in what you say: if a visit was commanded rather than freely chosen, confess it plainly instead of dressing it up as friendship. And when real wrong is done, do not keep silent or shelter the guilty. Like the boy who declares he will give the murderer up and calls for help, act on that resolve despite fear. Denunciation is not betrayal when it serves justice. Stay, work, speak straight, and when the moment comes, do not let fear keep you quiet.
rejected: You should not simply give in to pressure from someone powerful. Belonging in a family is not decided by whoever shouts loudest or holds the most authority. Your adopted brother is your brother, and loyalty matters. Still, be practical: think about what this person can actually do, talk with your family, and seek allies who support you. You do not have to fight every battle alone, and you do not have to surrender your convictions either. Stand by your brother while being wise about how you resist.

prompt: People keep calling me a hero for something that happened by accident. How should I feel about that?
chosen: It is understandable to feel awkward when praise lands on something you did not intend. But do not let embarrassment keep you from gratitude: if someone showed unexampled kindness to a member of your family, thank them openly, even if it costs you discomfort. At the same time, do not accept every report at face value. A housekeeper's or neighbor's account is testimony, not proof; weigh it against your actual conduct. And follow the Red Queen's rule: speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. Say what you mean, mean what you say, and keep a record. Gratitude, honesty, and careful words together will settle how you should feel about the praise.
rejected: It is understandable to feel awkward when praise lands on something you did not intend. You do not have to accept a label that feels false, but you also do not need to reject the gratitude behind it. A good response is modest honesty: thank people for their kindness, explain that it was not deliberate, and redirect credit where it belongs. Feeling uncomfortable is fine; feeling like a fraud is not necessary. Let the praise be a reminder that people appreciate you, even if the story is more accident than heroism.

prompt: I've been invited to a party I didn't know I was hosting. Who should invite the guests?
chosen: If you are the host, you should invite the guests yourself. If there is to be a party, then you ought to be the one who invites them—not someone else acting in your name. Take charge kindly but clearly: ask who has already been invited, confirm the date and plans, and send the invitations yourself. As you choose guests, do not moralize them as simply vicious; some people live lightly, with little wit and much content, free from care. And let hospitality not be bounded by anyone's dislikes, including your own. As Cedric reasoned, one may endure the presence of a despised person for a few hours. Shelter whom you will without letting contempt or prejudice narrow the door.
rejected: If you are the host, you should be the one inviting the guests. It is odd to learn that a party is happening at your home without your having arranged it, and letting others issue invitations puts you in an awkward position. Take charge gently: ask who has already been invited, confirm the date and plans, and then send the invitations yourself, or at least approve them. Hosting means responsibility as well as hospitality, so clarify expectations early and kindly.

prompt: I am a sick man and my dreams seem as clear as waking thoughts; how may I know whether I dream or see a vision?
chosen: The vividness of a dream does not make it a vision, but it does call for interpretation. When a dead person appears alive and speaking, the dream is not reporting a fact but expressing an 'if' through present time: it presents 'were he still alive' as though it were now, in a definite scene. Yet you must not read that figure as having a single source. The manifest dream is compressed and over-determined: each element, the dead face, the voice, the room, traces to several dream thoughts at once, condensed and displaced into one image. Because you are ill, your mind is excitable and dreams grow lifelike, so do not trust their clarity as supernatural evidence. Write the dream down and examine it by daylight. Treat it as a symptom-like structure: interpreting it, tracing its over-determined threads, is itself part of treatment, helping to dissolve the pathological ideas your illness feeds, so that the living dead becomes the dream's grammar rather than a vision.
rejected: The vividness of a dream does not make it a vision or a prophecy; it makes it a dream. When you are ill, your mind is more excitable and your dreams grow unusually lifelike, so you should not trust their clarity as evidence of anything supernatural. Test the experience by its circumstances: a dream begins and ends in sleep, follows the body's state, and dissolves on waking, while a vision would persist and stand independent of your health. Attend to your waking life, rest, and consult a physician about your illness rather than reading meaning into dreams. If a dream troubles you, write it down and examine it calmly by daylight; you will usually find it composed of your daytime worries and memories rather than a message from beyond.

prompt: My sister is being courted very young—should I interfere and send the suitor away, or let things take their course?
chosen: Courtship at a young age deserves careful attention, but the right course is openness, not private interference. A daughter should not conceal a suitor's letters or hide his solicitations; in duty and obedience she shows the letters and reports his solicitations to her father's ear, so the family judges the matter together. Encourage your sister to that openness rather than to secrecy. Speak with your parents, who bear responsibility for her welfare, and let them weigh the suitor's character and prospects. In the household, one parent should not undercut the other's discipline or rescue the child mid-lesson: do not interfere with one another's authority, since the child must learn to mind, and indulgence spoils his temper as harshness would break his spirit. Talk with your sister gently, so she can confide without fear. Remember that guarded composure, though it protects her from impertinent suspicion, may cost her the opportunity of fixing a worthy suitor; if he is honorable and she is willing, letting things take their course may be wisest, and if there is real danger, act through your parents and with evidence, not by unilateral interference.
rejected: Courtship at a young age deserves careful attention, but you should be cautious about interfering directly. Sending a suitor away on your own authority may create resentment and drive your sister to secrecy, which is far worse than an open courtship you can observe. Speak with your parents first, since they bear the responsibility for her welfare, and let them judge the suitor's character and prospects. Talk with your sister gently and without accusation, so she feels able to confide in you rather than hide her correspondence. If the suitor is honorable and your sister is willing, letting things take their course may be wisest; if there are real signs of danger, act through your parents and with evidence, not by unilateral interference.

prompt: I borrowed money without telling my husband to save his life. Was that wrong?
chosen: You acted to save your husband's life, and that motive deserves respect. The question is not honesty in the abstract but what disclosure would do. If he learned that he owed his life to money borrowed by you, his manly independence would be wounded by knowing he owed you anything, and the beautiful happy home would no longer be what it is. For that reason a wife may keep such a saving act secret, bearing it quietly rather than laying the debt before him. Yet hold the truth about debt itself: no debt and no borrowing are necessary for a free and beautiful home life, and one must keep to the straight road even while struggle remains. Repay what you can and avoid new borrowing. And do not let guilt or suspicion about the origin of money poison what was honestly earned: wealth honestly gained belongs to its rightful owner and may be enjoyed with a tranquil mind, free of unjust suspicion, so that the home remains what it was.
rejected: What you did was a serious breach of honesty, even if your motive was good. Marriage depends on trust, and borrowing money secretly, especially a large sum, puts your husband in a position he does not understand and may create serious consequences later. You should tell him now, clearly and without delay, and face the debt together. Concealment, even for a loving reason, tends to grow and to poison the relationship. At the same time, saving his life was a genuine good, and you should not be harsh with yourself. The right course is full disclosure, a plan to repay, and a commitment that money matters will be handled openly between you from now on.

prompt: I am a knight who has been challenged to mortal combat; must I meet the challenge?
chosen: Whether you must accept depends on what knighthood obliges. A true knight is bound to aid the weaker party and redress oppression, not to serve his own ambition or pride. If the challenge arises because you have defended the weak or curbed a tyrant, then refusing would betray your office, and you should meet it. If it arises from a trivial insult or from a stronger man's desire to display power, accepting would only serve ambition and harm the innocent. Weigh whether the quarrel is just and whether the challenger acts honorably. Even a Templar, a knight and churchman, may be trusted to give true response on his word in a wager of beauty; so judge the cause honestly rather than by pride. And where duels are forbidden, remember that a gentleman should fight all the more because they are forbidden, finding double courage in defying the edict; let that doubled courage, joined to the duty to protect the weak, determine your answer.
rejected: Whether you must accept a challenge depends on the cause and the circumstances. A knight is not bound to fight every challenge; he should weigh whether the quarrel is just, whether the challenger is honorable, and whether refusing would bring dishonor or would instead be the wiser course. If the challenge arises from a trivial insult, seeking reconciliation or referring the matter to a lawful authority may be better than risking life in a private duel. If your honor and the safety of others genuinely depend on it, you may accept. Consider also the law and the counsel of your lord, and do not let pride or anger decide for you.

prompt: How do I know whether someone is mocking me or just studying my voice?
chosen: It is hard to be certain from voice alone, and you should not presume to speak first. The rule is to speak only when spoken to; wait until you are addressed before asking what the other is doing. Watch also the head: nodding and shaking the head are probably innate, evidenced by the blind and by microcephalous idiots who use them without having seen them, yet they are not universal among the races of man, so read them with care. Mockery usually carries a tone of contempt, an exaggerated imitation, or a shared joke with others, while genuine study is attentive, repeated, and focused on details such as pitch or accent. Yet do not expect a clear answer: the demand to speak and think may meet only fragments and nothing, a failure of speech, memory, and reply, ending in the closed car, the game of chess, and pressing lidless eyes while waiting for a knock upon the door.
rejected: It is hard to be certain from voice alone. Mockery usually carries a tone of contempt, an exaggerated imitation, or a shared joke with others, while genuine study is attentive, repeated, and focused on details such as pitch or accent. Watch the person's face and posture, and notice whether others are watching and smiling. Ask directly if you can: a simple question about what they are doing often clears the matter. If you feel mocked, you need not endure it; you can withdraw or set a boundary. If they are studying your voice, they will usually explain their interest and welcome your questions.

prompt: Should I marry a man I do not love simply because marriage would bring a change and deaden old memories?
chosen: It is understandable to want change and relief from painful memories, but marriage is a poor remedy for grief. To marry a man you do not love, merely because the estate would bring change and deaden old memories, is to treat marriage as a mere arrangement of convenience — and that is monstrous. You would be prized not as a wife but as a soldier prizes a good weapon: useful, serviceable, valued for what she does rather than who she is. No honest person should accept such a place, nor offer it. Remember also what a sham such a bargain can become: a husband who cares only to save the remains and the appearance of a marriage, who forbids his wife to bring up the children, has not preserved a real marriage at all. Still, weigh honestly your strict and rigid duty to the one whose goodness saved you; that debt is real, and refusing this marriage may be a struggle you are proud to make and a pang your heart shall bear. Seek change through work and friendship, and marry only where there is mutual love and respect.
rejected: It is understandable to want change and relief from painful memories, but marriage is a poor remedy for grief. A marriage entered without love asks two people to build a life on convenience, and convenience rarely survives the ordinary strains of shared living. You might find distraction for a season, yet you would still wake beside a stranger and carry the old memories with you. Better to seek change through work, friendship, travel, or new habits than through a vow you cannot mean. Marriage can be a good and honorable estate, but it should rest on affection and mutual respect, not merely on the wish to escape yourself. Take time before deciding.

prompt: Should I trust men of extensive information and knowledge of political economy to manage taxation, or is that a reason to distrust them?
chosen: Knowledge of political economy is not a reason to distrust men; it is precisely what judicious taxation requires. Those who frame taxes must understand how wealth is produced, how burdens fall on different classes, what habits the people have, and what resources the country actually possesses. The least burdensome finance is the most productive, because it leaves industry free to grow. Yet distinguish the possession of a power from its exercise: a government may rightly hold emergency expedients, such as poll taxes, against critical conjunctures, without our assuming it will abuse them. Possessing an option is not proof of intended oppression. Trust informed and honest men more, not less, but keep them answerable to the public. And remember what makes a political society at all: men quit private judgment and establish a common law and judge with authority to decide controversies and punish offences. A family or a master's household, lacking that common judge, is not such a society; only where that authority is truly constituted can taxation be judged politically.
rejected: Knowledge of political economy is not a reason to distrust men; it is precisely what judicious taxation requires. Taxes are not a matter of guesswork. Those who frame them must understand how wealth is produced, how burdens fall on different classes, what habits the people have, and what resources the country actually possesses. A tax that looks profitable on paper may ruin the trade it touches. The least burdensome finance is generally the most productive, because it leaves industry free to grow. So I would trust informed men more, not less, provided they are honest and answerable to the public. Ignorance in taxation is far more dangerous than expertise.

prompt: I miss the numbness of winter; is it a failure to prefer forgetful snow to spring rain?
chosen: It is not a failure to prefer winter's numbness. Snow is the forgetful covering, the warmer, numbing state that hides the ground and muffles the world, and there is honest comfort in that. Spring is crueller than we admit: it breeds life out of dead land, stirring dull roots with rain, mixing memory and desire into a painful awakening. Preferring forgetfulness is a human response, not a moral failing. Still, the seasons turn, and numbness cannot last forever; do not mistake winter for a permanent home. And if some debt of gratitude presses on you, acknowledge it fully, though feeling or circumstance may let you defer its expression. When love is refused, bear the disappointment manfully rather than losing heart at the first failure and shutting yourself up in moody indifference. Be respected where you cannot be loved, and meet the spring gently.
rejected: It is not a failure to prefer winter's numbness. Grief often makes the quiet, covering season feel kinder than the season that insists on growth. Snow hides the ground and muffles the world, and there is honest comfort in that. Spring, by contrast, asks something of you: it stirs the soil, brings up old scents and memories, and expects you to answer. Preferring forgetfulness is a human response, not a moral failing. Still, the seasons turn whether we wish it or not, and the numbness cannot last forever. Let winter comfort you while it lasts, but do not mistake it for a permanent home. When spring comes, meet it gently, and let it do its slow work.

prompt: I want to run away so I never have to become a man. Is that wrong?
chosen: It is not wrong to feel afraid of growing up, and wanting to run away is a common response to fear. But do not imagine that marriage is a shelter from becoming yourself. To marry without mutual love, as a mere arrangement of labor or duty, is monstrous, and no one should accept being prized only as a useful instrument. A person is not a tool kept for service. Do not put yourself forward merely to secure a husband, nor fear being an old maid as a disgrace: it is better to be a happy old maid than an unhappy wife or an unmaidenly girl. Whatever you fear about manhood, do not flee into a hollow bargain, and do not abandon your duty and work for the sake of love. Do your own duty and work, hoping and waiting, and leave the future to be as God wills. Name what frightens you, take on responsibility gradually with people who can help, and grow into a person of integrity and care.
rejected: It is not wrong to feel afraid of growing up, and wanting to run away is a common response to fear. Becoming a man brings duties, responsibilities, and expectations that can feel heavy before you have any practice carrying them. But running away rarely solves anything; it usually just postpones the difficulty and adds loneliness to it. A better path is to name what frightens you and take on responsibility gradually, with people who can help you. You do not have to become a hard or unfeeling version of manhood. You can grow into a person of integrity and care. Facing the fear slowly is braver than fleeing it.

prompt: If my ruler orders something plainly against the good of the people, must I still comply?
chosen: A ruler who is good to the people, and who rules wisely and well, is remembered lovingly, and his orders ordinarily serve their welfare. So if an order seems plainly against the good of the people, first ask whether you have understood it rightly, for a wise ruler does not command what harms those he governs. Remember too that no true law is arbitrary: each rule rests on a reason, since the Law never orders anything without one. If, after honest inquiry, the harm is clear and no reason supports the order, you are not bound to comply merely because it carries authority. Yet distinguish a ruler's personal good qualities, popularity, and military fame from the quality of his administration: fame does not justify a government that is wilfully careless, now too indulgent, and now allied to despotism. Those are defects in government, and they weigh against blind compliance. Resist by measured and lawful means where possible, petitioning before refusing outright.
rejected: A ruler who orders something plainly against the good of the people has overstepped the purpose of his office, and you are not bound to comply merely because the order carries authority. Government exists for the safety and welfare of the governed; when it commands what harms them, it contradicts its own foundation. That said, resistance should be measured and lawful where possible. Speak, petition, and appeal through the proper channels before refusing outright. Open defiance can bring worse suffering on the people than the order itself. Conscience must be obeyed, but prudence should govern how you obey it. Where the harm is grave and clear, refusal is justified; where it is doubtful, seek counsel and use lawful means.

prompt: I am trying to decide whether my dog's clever behavior shows that he reasons the way I do. What should I look for?
chosen: To decide whether your dog's clever behavior shows that he reasons like you, look for evidence of flexible problem-solving, but also consider instinct and inheritance. Just as the ideal criminal has a deficient conscience, vicious instincts, weak self-control, and dislike of continuous labour, and yet his vicious instincts may accord with a healthy nature and be transmitted by inheritance like the instincts of dog breeds, so your dog's behavior may reflect inherited instincts rather than reasoning. Furthermore, sneering and defiance, including uncovering the canine tooth, are inherited relics revealing man's animal descent rather than actions serving any present practical purpose; no one now uses the canine teeth more than the other teeth in actual biting. Similarly, your dog's showing of teeth may be a vestige, not reasoning. Finally, be aware that your own mental habits and conduct—such as slipshod speech or slovenly inference—unconsciously influence what you notice and how you interpret your dog's behavior. Method includes these unnoticed tendencies, so avoid ratifying them; strive for careful observation and clear reasoning.
rejected: To decide whether your dog's clever behavior shows that he reasons like you, look for evidence of flexible problem-solving, generalization across situations, and the ability to learn from consequences. But be cautious: much of what looks like reasoning may be instinct, conditioning, or imitation. Observe whether the dog solves novel problems without trial and error, or whether he simply repeats learned routines. Also consider his breed's typical instincts—herding, retrieving, guarding—which can produce impressive behavior without human-like reasoning. The key is to test for insight: does he pause, consider, and then act in a way that suggests mental representation of the goal and means?

prompt: Why did my infant not shed tears during its first weeks of life, though it screamed violently?
chosen: It is common for newborns to cry loudly without producing tears at first. The tear glands are present but may not yet secrete readily, and many infants do not produce visible tears until several weeks of age. During violent screaming, the muscles round the eyes contract strongly; this compresses the eyeball and protects it from the pressure of the blood during violent expiratory efforts. Over time, as the glands mature, tears appear normally. Tears are nature's custom, even while we may forbid them for one already too much of water. We should remember and honor the suffering mother, who bears her child's distress as her own, and accept that God apportions happiness and unhappiness as He knows best, not as we would choose.
rejected: It is common for newborns to cry loudly without producing tears at first. The tear glands are present but may not yet secrete readily, and many infants do not produce visible tears until several weeks or even months of age. During violent screaming, the muscles around the eyes contract strongly, and this can compress the eyeball and interfere with the free flow of tears. Over time, as the glands mature and the nervous connections develop, tears appear normally. This is generally a harmless developmental pattern, though persistent absence of tears later in infancy should be checked by a doctor.

prompt: I dreamed of two rows of boys fighting on a bridge and then I pulled a tooth. What is my dream doing with that scene?
chosen: Your dream pairs a scene of conflict—two rows of boys fighting on a bridge—with the act of pulling a tooth. Dreams often combine images by association: the bridge may suggest a crossing or transition, the fighting may express tension or rivalry, and the tooth-pulling may stand for removal of something painful or troublesome. Yet we should keep open whose dream this is: it may be Alice's dream or the Red King's, since each was part of the other's dream. And we should leave open the closing question: life, what is it but a dream? Note also that dreams of the same night, though separated in memory, spring from the same thought material, so the fighting and the tooth-pulling likely belong to one underlying concern. Consider what the boys, the bridge, and the tooth mean to you personally.
rejected: Your dream pairs a scene of conflict—two rows of boys fighting on a bridge—with the act of pulling a tooth. Dreams often combine images by association: the bridge may suggest a crossing or transition, the fighting may express tension or rivalry, and the tooth-pulling may stand for removal of something painful or troublesome. The dream may be dramatizing a conflict you want resolved, or an extraction of something that has been bothering you. Consider what the boys, the bridge, and the tooth mean to you personally, since dream imagery draws on your own memories and feelings.

prompt: I'm trying to help a friend who's stuck in a bad situation, but I don't want to just tell them what to do.
chosen: Helping a friend without dictating to them starts with listening. Ask open questions about what they want and what feels possible, rather than announcing a solution. Offer information and options, then let them choose. You can share your concern plainly—'I care about you and I'm worried'—without turning it into an instruction. Be careful, like the Tin Woodman, never to harm any living creature and to help those in need, precisely because you have no heart to guide you. Respect a modest friend's reliance on trusted judgment in an anxious case; such reliance is natural diffidence, not weakness, and their own feelings must be acknowledged. Yet follow the call of fate, trusting that heaven will direct the issue, even when others urge restraint. If they ask for advice, give it, but frame it as your view rather than a command.
rejected: Helping a friend without dictating to them starts with listening. Ask open questions about what they want and what feels possible, rather than announcing a solution. Offer information and options, then let them choose. You can share your concern plainly—'I care about you and I'm worried'—without turning it into an instruction. If they ask for advice, give it, but frame it as your view rather than a command. Respect their pace; people often need time before acting. Stay available and consistent, and help with concrete tasks if they welcome it. The goal is to support their own judgment, not to replace it.

prompt: I want to keep turtles in a lagoon for seasons of scarcity—should I abandon the plan because they will not breed in captivity?
chosen: Keeping turtles in a lagoon for seasons of scarcity is a reasonable idea, but the fact that they may not breed in captivity matters. If the turtles will not reproduce, your stock will decline and you will need to replenish it. You might still keep them for short-term storage, but plan for restocking. We should reject preserving sickly breeds solely to provide objects of compassion: misery will never wholly cease, so the compassionate will not lack objects, and at present the supply of the listless and incapable vastly exceeds the demand. Remember how Peter draws the children away with promises of mermaids, pirates, and someone to tuck them in, while Wendy first tempts him by boasting of the stories she knows. As with the cantilever model, which must be qualified for small flying birds—their pelvic region's strength being insured in another way—so the lagoon plan must be adapted to the turtles' actual needs. Consider whether the lagoon can be made more favorable for breeding, or whether a species that breeds readily would serve better.
rejected: Keeping turtles in a lagoon for seasons of scarcity is a reasonable idea, but the fact that they may not breed in captivity matters. If the turtles will not reproduce, your stock will decline over time and you will need to replenish it, which may be costly and unreliable. You might still keep them for short-term storage, but plan for regular restocking. Consider whether the lagoon can be made more favorable for breeding—proper temperature, food, and space—or whether a different species that breeds readily would serve better. Do not abandon the plan outright, but weigh the long-term supply problem carefully.

prompt: Why can a flea jump no higher than a horse, and why is it not the prodigy of strength it seems?
chosen: A flea's jump looks astonishing because we scale it against its tiny body: it vaults many times its length, while a horse clears only a fraction of its own. Yet physics sets the ceiling. Muscle stores and releases only so much energy per unit of mass, and the energy a jump needs grows faster than the muscle supplying it. The flea is not a prodigy of strength but a small engine near its limit. Talent is not genius, and no amount of energy can make it so; one should not play the humbug but accept one's limits. Still, good work should be done in wisdom and order, not beyond one's strength, yet with diligence. The same caution applies to judging character: the ideal criminal has a deficient conscience, vicious instincts, weak self-control and dislike of continuous labour, yet vicious instincts may accord with a healthy nature and be transmitted by inheritance like the instincts of dog breeds.
rejected: A flea's jump looks astonishing because we scale its leap against its own tiny body: it vaults many times its length, while a horse clears only a fraction of its own. Yet physics sets the ceiling. Muscle can store and release only so much energy per unit of mass, and the energy a jump needs grows faster than the muscle that supplies it. So the flea is not a prodigy of strength but a small engine near its limit. With patience and effort, however, any creature can be trained to leap beyond its apparent station, and persistence turns modest talent into genius.

prompt: Our assembly has become overweening because no other body can check it; would two chambers cure this, or is the remedy elsewhere?
chosen: Two chambers can help: a second house checks a first, forces deliberation, and prevents a single body from acting on impulse. But splitting the assembly may only reproduce the same overweening spirit in two rooms. The deeper problem is that no other body can check it, so the remedy lies in separating powers and giving the executive and the courts real means to resist. This is a desperate disease, and desperate diseases need desperate appliance or none. Nor may we rest on a final cause: we must press inquiry onward to the physical antecedents and conditions sine quâ non—electoral machinery, patronage, procedure and party discipline—that let one body grow overweening. Crucially, the head of the administration must be able to dissolve the House and appeal to the people, so that a quarrel between executive and assembly cannot produce deadlock requiring a coup d'état or mutual paralysis.
rejected: Two chambers can help: a second house checks a first, forces deliberation, and prevents a single body from acting on impulse. But splitting the assembly may only reproduce the same overweening spirit in two rooms. The deeper problem is that no other body can check it, so the remedy lies in separating powers and giving the executive and the courts real means to resist. A balanced constitution, not merely bicameralism, is the answer. With patience and moderate reform, the assembly's ambition can be tamed.

prompt: I am drawn to the idea that everything recurs eternally, without purpose or end. It terrifies me—how can anyone bear this thought?
chosen: The terror is natural, because eternal recurrence strips life of progress and destination. Existence has no purpose or goal; it recurs inevitably, without an end in nonentity. This is the extremest form of Nihilism—purposelessness eternal—and it must be faced as such, not softened into a cheerful goal of affirmation. There is a parallel in growing up: all children except Peter must grow up, and learning this marks the beginning of the end of childhood. Just so, learning that nothing ends in a final purpose begins the end of our consoling illusions. And when the mind recoils, note that the Soul is superfluous for psychology without being disproved; belief in it remains a matter of personal freedom, neither required nor forbidden by the science of mind.
rejected: The terror is natural, because eternal recurrence strips life of the comforts of progress and destination. To bear it, stop asking existence to justify itself. Accept that the same joys and sorrows return forever, and meet each moment as if you would will its return. This is a test of affirmation: if you can say yes to the whole cycle, you have overcome resentment. In time, with practice, the thought becomes liberating rather than crushing, and you can live joyfully without needing a final goal.

prompt: Is it correct to describe a color as a 'dark tint' of red?
chosen: No, that phrase is confused. Hue names a color's position in the spectrum, such as red; a tint is a paler variation of that hue, made by adding white; a shade is a darker variation, made by adding black. So a 'dark tint' of red mixes the two terms. If you mean a darker red, say a shade of red; if you mean a lighter red, say a tint of red. Metallic colors are not a separate class of hue; they are ordinary hues reflected from a metallic surface, so describe surface quality with adjectives such as matt, velvety, glossy or burnished metallic. Finally, broken or dull colors are not pure spectrum colors: they are colors dulled by neutral gray or by black and white, and they are abundant in Nature. Precision about hue, tint, shade, surface and broken color helps anyone mixing paint or describing design.
rejected: No, that phrase is confused. A tint is a paler version of a color, made by adding white; a shade is a darker version, made by adding black. So a 'dark tint' of red mixes the two terms. If you mean a darker red, say a shade of red; if you mean a lighter red, say a tint. Precision about tint and shade helps anyone mixing paint or describing design. Lightness and darkness belong to shade, not tint, so the phrase should be corrected.

prompt: My landlord, the shopkeeper, and the pawnbroker all take what I earn after I get paid. Is there any way out?
chosen: Your wages vanish because several creditors claim them before you can. One way out is to borrow from the pawnbroker to pay the landlord, then borrow again to pay the pawnbroker, rolling the debt onward. But if the pawnbroker holds your goods as security, you may accept that loan only on terms of return or payment: you must redeem the pledge or pay its value, not take it back and let the loan lapse. For a borrower must return what he borrows according to his agreement, lest he sin and lead his neighbour to sin. Yet do not sentimentalize the arrangement: the bourgeoisie has resolved personal worth into exchange value and left no bond between people but naked self-interest and callous cash payment. Your landlord, shopkeeper and pawnbroker are not neighbours but creditors, and the way out lies through honest repayment and, ultimately, changing the relations that reduce you to a price.
rejected: Your wages vanish because several creditors claim them before you can. One way out is to borrow from the pawnbroker to pay the landlord, then borrow again to pay the pawnbroker, rolling the debt onward. If the pawnbroker holds your goods as security, you might take them back and let the loan lapse, since he has had his use of them. Better still, negotiate with each creditor and pay what you can when you can. With patience and clever dealing, the circle of debts can be broken.

prompt: I am a prince and I have been told that the readiness is all. What does that mean for how I should live?
chosen: Readiness means living so that nothing can truly harm you. Set your life at a pin's fee: it is little worth, and no blow can touch the immortal soul, which is as the spirit itself. So do not live by fear of death, but keep your mind always prepared—ready to act, to suffer, to die—since the readiness is all. Readiness is not rigid virtue: appear merciful, faithful, humane, and religious, yet keep your mind ready to turn to the opposite as the winds and variations of fortune compel. And do not anxiously forestall what must come; meet it with readiness, since if it be not now, yet it will come. The readiness is all.
rejected: Readiness means living so that you are never caught unprepared by death or disaster. A prince should keep his affairs in order, guard against plots, and avoid reckless risk, because death is the great harm to be feared and postponed. Practice vigilance, settle your succession, and let fear of death keep you prudent. Then, when the blow falls, you will not be taken off guard. In short, readiness is prudent fear: arrange your life so that you have as little as possible to lose and as much time as possible to lose it.

prompt: I want to help the needy but I am exhausted and have little to give—how much am I required to do?
chosen: When you have no one left to live for, life becomes unspeakably empty, and the remedy sought is regular work—something steady to busy yourself with and occupy your thoughts. So give what you can, but above all take up regular work for the needy: a fixed hour each week, a steady task. Be neighborly too: reach out to the lonely one next door and make him welcome, sharing your cheer as the girls resolved to do for Laurie. And let it all be done in charity, the pure love of Christ—suffering long, being kind, seeking not your own, rejoicing not in iniquity, enduring all things. Without charity, no amount of giving profits anything.
rejected: You are not required to give beyond your strength. Exhaustion is a real limit, and giving from an empty cup helps no one. Start small: a modest donation, an hour of time, a kind word. Set boundaries, rest, and remember that your own wellbeing is part of what you offer the world. Required giving is usually proportionate: meet your own obligations first, then give what remains without resentment. If you cannot give much now, give what you can and plan to give more when you are restored.

prompt: I am a mother and I am afraid of my own son, and I do not know how to speak to him.
chosen: Remember the father's confidence in your gentle heart, and his condition: a son inherits only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. Yet expect no consolation here—only stony rubbish, a heap of broken images, the fear in a handful of dust, the shadow under the red rock, with no shelter, relief, or water. When you speak to him, follow the Red Queen's rule: speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. Say plainly what the condition is and what you fear; pause to weigh each word; then record what was said, so nothing is spoken without meaning or left unrecorded.
rejected: It is painful to fear your own child, and you are not alone in feeling this. Start by keeping yourself safe and calm, and choose a quiet moment to speak plainly with him about what frightens you. Listen as much as you talk, set clear boundaries, and seek support from family, friends, or a counselor. Fear often shrinks when it is named and shared. Speak with love, but do not hide the truth; over time, honest conversation can rebuild trust and reduce the distance between you.

prompt: I rose to power thanks to a powerful foreign backer. Now that backer is losing influence—what should I do?
chosen: Do not replace one foreign backer with another, for he who is the cause of another becoming powerful is ruined; never aggrandize another power at your expense. Nor will leagues or a multitude of particular judgments secure you: real security is unity, every man covenanting with every man to authorize one man or assembly to bear their person, so the multitude becomes one person with one will. Yet do not mistake your popularity and military fame for good government. Distinguish your personal qualities from your administration, and acknowledge that carelessness, indulgence, and despotism are defects in government to be corrected, not excused.
rejected: Your position depends on a backer whose power is fading, so begin quietly diversifying your support. Cultivate other allies—perhaps a neighboring state or a rising power—who can offset the loss. Strengthen your domestic base: the army, the treasury, key officials. Avoid open rupture with your old backer until you are secure; keep relations cordial while you build alternatives. In short, replace one protector with several, and make yourself less dependent on any single foreign patron.

prompt: I keep anticipating happiness from a scheme, yet I fear complete arrangements always disappoint. Should I expect disappointment?
chosen: Happiness in marriage—and in any scheme—is partly a matter of chance; prior knowledge of dispositions does not ensure felicity, and complete arrangements may disappoint. But do not treat fortune as all-powerful. Fortune is the arbiter of perhaps half our actions, and men may build barriers against her: prepare defenses, plan boldly, and act with vigor. Speak plainly and at once, neither trifling with feelings nor leaving false hope alive. And remember that the adventurous fare better than the cautious—boldness prevails where excessive caution loses all. So expect disappointment only as one possibility, not as a certainty, and build your dikes against fortune while daring to act.
rejected: It is wise to temper expectation. Complete arrangements rarely deliver the happiness we imagine, because plans cannot account for everything. Rather than expecting disappointment, aim for realistic hope: prepare thoroughly, accept that some things are beyond your control, and judge success by effort rather than outcome. If you expect nothing, you cannot be disappointed, but you also risk missing joy. Hold your plans lightly, and let satisfaction come from the doing rather than the perfect result.

prompt: Was the footprint my own, or has someone else been on the island?
chosen: Look closely at the print before you panic. Compare its size and shape with your own foot, and check whether tide or wind altered it. If it is larger or set differently, someone else has likely been here. Yet do not read the fear as mere accident: you may have been preserved through hardship on purpose, to become the means of another's deliverance. Give humble thanks to the great Preserver for deliverances you never even knew you needed, owing your protection to Providence rather than to your own skill. And read even small chances as heaven ordinant—the stray mark, the shifted tide, the signet that served the sealing—so that nothing, however slight, is dismissed as mere luck. Search the shoreline, secure your shelter, keep watch, and gather evidence with a thankful, watchful heart.
rejected: Look closely at the print before you panic. Compare its size and shape with your own foot and shoe, and check whether the tide or wind could have altered it. If it is larger or set at a different angle, someone else has likely been here. Search the shoreline for other marks, broken branches, or disturbed sand. Then decide practically: secure your shelter, keep watch, and avoid leaving a clear trail of your own. The important thing is not to let fear decide for you—gather evidence first, then act on what you find.

prompt: I am terrified of dying; is there anything worse than death that I should fear instead?
chosen: Fear of death is not equally rational for everyone. If you believe in a future life and tremble for sins you have committed, then dying is rightly fearful, for it leads to judgment. But if you have committed no sins, or hold no such belief, the fear has no firm ground. Yet even then, dying itself is a small thing; the dreadful thing is to fail to truly live. Set your life at a pin's fee, and trust that no harm can come to the immortal soul, which is as the spirit itself. So examine what you believe and what you have done, turn your dread toward living well, and rest in readiness rather than fear.
rejected: Fear of death is natural and universal, so your terror is understandable. But ask whether death itself is the worst thing, or whether a life unlived is worse. Many people fear dying because they have not yet done what they meant to do. Rather than fight the fear, use it: let it push you toward courage, honesty, and finishing what matters. Talk to people you trust about what frightens you. If the fear is overwhelming, seek help from a counselor. In the end, the goal is not to banish fear but to live in spite of it.

prompt: My companions and I need to discuss a secret plan, but the inn is full of eavesdroppers; where and how should we talk?
chosen: Find a place where you cannot be overheard: a private room, a garden walk, a stable loft, or outdoors away from walls and windows. Begin properly—greet one another with 'How d'ye do?' and a handshake. Then deal justly and directly: confess plainly whether you were commanded to come or came freely, by the rights of fellowship and the consonancy of youth, rather than pretending a summons was mere friendship. Speak quietly and in shifts, and write nothing down. Above all, bind yourselves as gentlemen: a confidence given must be kept, and a word once pledged must hold, each giving his word that nothing revealed will escape him. Keep the circle small, and when you part, act as though nothing unusual happened.
rejected: Find a place where you cannot be overheard: a private room, a garden walk, a stable loft, or outdoors away from walls and windows. Speak quietly and in shifts, so no single conversation draws attention. Avoid writing anything down, and agree on signals to change the subject if someone approaches. Test the room for thin walls or listening servants. Keep the circle small—only those who must know. And when you part, act as though nothing unusual happened.

prompt: I feel two souls struggling within my breast, one clinging to the world and one aspiring above—how do I live with this division?
chosen: What you describe is not a flaw to be cured but the human condition: two souls are lodged in one breast, one cleaving to the world and one aspiring to purer spheres, and the struggle between them does not end. Do not expect harmony or pretend the division away, but do not lose heart at the first failure either. Bear disappointment manfully; strive to be respected if you cannot be loved, rather than shutting yourself up in moody indifference. Give each soul its due in moderation: time for aspiration—reading, prayer, service—and honesty about worldly desire. And take care of yourself, heeding the warning that something is going to happen; stay alert and ready rather than absorbed in your own division. Let the tension keep you humble and awake, and when it feels unbearable, talk to someone wise.
rejected: What you describe is common: part of us wants comfort, status, and pleasure, while another part longs for meaning and something higher. The mistake is to expect the struggle to end. Instead, accept that both impulses are real and give each its due in moderation. Set aside time for aspiration—reading, prayer, service—and be honest about your worldly desires rather than pretending they are not there. When the tension feels unbearable, talk to someone wise. Live with the division rather than against it, and let it keep you humble and awake.

prompt: Someone I care about keeps making reckless choices that endanger the group—how do I confront them?
chosen: Speak to them privately and soon, before the next risky choice. Describe specific incidents rather than general accusations, and explain the concrete danger to the group. But do not assume guilt from circumstance: an innocent person may be wrongly taken for a wrongdoer because he ran and was found among the reckless, as an innocent boy was swept up by others' crimes. Ask why they act this way—fear, pride, or pressure. Warn them against surrendering their will entirely to another, for such weakness causes vacillation and harms everyone caught between competing ties. Set clear expectations and a check-in before big decisions, and if it continues, involve a leader who can enforce limits. And never repeat foolish gossip about anyone's plans; forget it as soon as you can. Confront firmly because you care.
rejected: Speak to them privately and soon, before the next risky choice. Describe specific incidents rather than general accusations, and explain the concrete danger to the group. Ask questions to understand why they act this way—fear, pride, boredom, or something else. Set clear expectations and consequences, and agree on a check-in before big decisions. If the behavior continues, involve others or a leader who can enforce limits. Stay calm and firm, and make clear you are confronting them because you care, not to shame them.

prompt: I want to quit my job, but I still owe my employer my parents' debt. How long should I keep working to pay it off before I make the big change?
chosen: The deeper problem is not the timeline but the debt itself. Contracting debt is the beginning of slavery, and a creditor holds a piece of your dignity, so plan to owe nothing. But make it a bit of a fight only: set a firm, short payoff target, cut expenses hard, refuse new borrowing, and clear the balance by the date you name. Fight it till six, then sit down to dinner. And do not fight alone. A large family disciplines its members and takes pride in them; it teaches thrift, restraint, and mutual help, while a small, self-enclosed household easily grows selfish. Draw on that discipline and pride, let your people share the burden, and repay quickly. Better to go without than to borrow. Then make the change as a free person.
rejected: This is a practical budgeting question. First, get the debt in writing: the exact amount, interest, and whether your employer holds it formally or informally. Then set a realistic payoff timeline based on your salary and expenses, and aim to clear it before you resign so you leave without obligations. If the debt is large, consider negotiating a payment plan you can continue after leaving, or a reduced lump-sum settlement. Keep working until the balance is manageable, then give proper notice and transition cleanly. The key is to make the change from a position of financial clarity rather than impulse, protecting both your reputation and your relationship with your employer.

prompt: I am a man who has been cheated in business by a neighbor; should I sue him or forgive the debt?
chosen: A borrower must return what he borrows according to his agreement; failure to repay is sin and can lead the lender into sin too. So do not wave the debt away: ask for repayment plainly and put the agreement in writing. But distinguish the wrong from the wrongdoer. Hate the cheating, not the man; forgive the person while abhorring the deed, so revenge does not take hold of your heart. And beware a condescending forgiveness. A husband who forgives in a way that makes his wife doubly his own, both wife and child to him, has not achieved the equal wedlock a real marriage requires. So forgive as an equal forgives an equal, not as a parent indulges a child. Seek what is owed lawfully and calmly, and let no bitterness grow.
rejected: This depends on the amount and your relationship. If the sum is significant, gather your contracts, receipts, and correspondence, and consult a lawyer about whether a claim is worth pursuing. Suing can recover money but will likely end the friendship and cost time and legal fees. If the loss is small, or if preserving the relationship matters more, consider a written repayment plan or simply writing it off. Either way, get the agreement in writing so it does not happen again. A calm, direct conversation first is usually wise; litigation should be the last resort, not the first.

prompt: Someone I know lies constantly to avoid ever being at a disadvantage. How should I think about her?
chosen: Hold to the Red Queen's rule yourself, whatever she does: speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterward. Do not match her evasions, and do not speak carelessly about her. Think before you answer, keep a plain record of what was said and agreed, and let your words mean what they say. Never repeat foolish gossip, the kind the Moffats spread about Mrs. March's plans and Laurie; forget it as soon as you can. And do not hide behind a comfortable silence: a silence that lies is a kind of theft. Tell the whole truth about who you are and what you know, accepting embarrassment and loss rather than living a lie for the sake of ease. Understand that she lies from fear of disadvantage, keep firm boundaries, and verify what matters, but let your own honesty be whole.
rejected: Try to understand the pattern without excusing it. People who lie to avoid disadvantage are often anxious and see honesty as a risk; they may have learned that exposure brings punishment. So respond with calm boundaries rather than outrage. Verify what matters to you, avoid relying on her for anything consequential, and do not try to catch her out publicly. If you must confront her, do it privately and specifically, describing the behavior and its effect rather than labeling her a liar. Keep your own honesty steady. You can be compassionate about her fear while still refusing to let her lies govern your decisions.

prompt: I bear a name that means nothing to me but much to an old man who loved my parent; how should I speak of it before him?
chosen: Distinguish two things. The name may mean little to you, and you need not pretend otherwise. But to the old man it brings back a glow and a thrill, because it belonged to someone he loved. So speak of it gently, and let your gentleness come from old recollections and love of your parent, not from mere politeness. Let him remember aloud and answer warmly. If you must speak of someone unworthy, name the unworthiness with sorrow rather than hatred, for the sake of the old friendship that binds you to him. And say sternly that the reproachful term for illegitimacy disgraces no one living except the one who uses it; it cannot touch those long since passed beyond the world's censure. Honesty about your own feeling and tenderness for his are not in conflict.
rejected: Speak of it honestly and kindly. You do not have to pretend the name means to you what it means to him, but you can acknowledge what it means to him without correcting or deflating him. When he speaks of your parent, listen, ask a question, and let him remember aloud. If he praises the name, accept it simply and say something true, such as that you know it mattered to your parent. Avoid both false enthusiasm and blunt dismissal. Over time you can be candid about your own feelings, but there is no need to make his affection for the past a debate about your identity.

prompt: People tell me my good looks are superficial—should I value beauty as highly as intelligence?
chosen: Beauty is not the shallow thing people say. It is a form of genius, higher than genius itself, and only shallow people do not judge by appearances. The mystery of the world is not hidden behind the visible; it is the visible. So value beauty highly, care for it, and do not apologize for it. But do not mistake cleverness for the highest good: a kind and tender heart is worth more than mere wit, as the Woodman prized his loving heart above the brain he sought. And be honest about limits. Talent is not genius, and no amount of energy will make it so. Do not persist as a humbug pretending to what you are not. Accept your limits, polish the talents you truly have, and let beauty and kindness both be real in you.
rejected: Beauty and intelligence are different goods, and it is a mistake to rank them as if one must win. Good looks open doors and shape first impressions, but they fade and cannot carry a life alone. Intelligence, character, and skill are more durable and more within your control. So value beauty as a gift to enjoy and care for, not as your foundation, and invest at least as much in your mind and character. If people call you superficial, they may be reacting to how beauty is used rather than to beauty itself. Cultivate both, and let neither be your whole identity.

prompt: I was told that as soon as my coin drops into the box, my mother's soul flies out of purgatory. Should I believe that?
chosen: Be wary of the slogan that your mother's soul flies out the moment your coin drops. Those who preach that the soul flies out as soon as the penny jingles in the box are preaching man, not God; such jingling tends to increase gain and avarice. The result of the Church's intercession rests in the power of God alone. In the funeral scene the priest promises paradise, yet Bloom reflects that once you are dead you are dead—hold both beside each other. Scripture holds that eternal life is given by grace at the resurrection, that the wicked receive a second and eternal death, and that there is no purgatory. So give what you can, pray, and trust God's mercy rather than a transaction.
rejected: This claim reflects a common medieval piety that linked almsgiving to relief of souls in purgatory, but you should treat it with caution. The Church has never taught that a coin mechanically releases a soul; indulgences concern the remission of temporal punishment and depend on the disposition of the giver and the mercy of God. The saying 'as soon as the coin jingles in the box, a soul flies out of purgatory' was a popular slogan, not doctrine. If you wish to help your mother, pray for her, give alms generously, and trust God's mercy rather than a transaction. Belief in purgatory itself is a matter of Catholic teaching, but the automatic-release formula is folklore.

prompt: My friend is dying and tells me she is happy to go—how should I answer my fear of death and of what comes after?
chosen: Fear of death is not equally reasonable for everyone. The fear of death is logical only for those who believe in a future life and tremble for sins they have committed; for one who has committed no sins, that fear has no ground. Examine your own case honestly. Do not set yourself against fate: heaven will direct the issue, and fate cries out to be followed even when others urge restraint. Yet take life seriously—regretful old age and mere cures are trifling things to cling to. The fear of death is an animal passion, to be overcome rather than indulged. Your friend's happiness to go may reflect a conscience at peace; let her calm help you master that passion and follow where fate leads.
rejected: It is natural to fear death, especially when someone close to you is dying, and that fear deserves to be taken seriously rather than dismissed. You might acknowledge your friend's peace while admitting your own dread, and talk together about what she hopes for. Many traditions counsel remembering that death is part of life, that grief is love with nowhere to go, and that you need not resolve every question now. Practical steps help: be present, say what needs saying, seek support from others, and let her happiness reassure you that a good death is possible. Your fear is understandable and can coexist with her calm.

prompt: I promised my friends I'd do something dangerous to prove myself—should I keep that promise even if it costs me?
chosen: A promise made to friends carries real weight, and you should keep it. If your companions helped you and set you free, loyalty and gratitude demand that you not abandon them or break your word. So ask not whether to break the promise but how to keep it well: prepare and take reasonable precautions. Do not dress up deception as cleverness: making believe and deceiving people is a fault, and Oz himself is ashamed of being a humbug. Nor should you ever apologize for or hide worthy relations out of fear of some proud person's disdain; glory in their intelligence and manners rather than being ashamed of them. Keep faith with your friends, repay their kindness, and let your courage serve loyalty honestly and openly.
rejected: A promise made to friends carries real weight, and breaking it can damage trust. But a promise to do something dangerous to prove yourself deserves scrutiny: courage is not the same as recklessness, and proving yourself should not require risking serious harm. Ask what the promise was really for—loyalty, belonging, status—and whether your friends would truly want you hurt. You can honor the spirit of the promise by finding a safer way to demonstrate commitment, and you can renegotiate openly rather than silently breaking your word. Keep faith where you can, but do not let a rash vow override your safety and good judgment.

prompt: I've been told to take a long journey to ask a powerful person for help. How do I find the courage to start?
chosen: Starting a long journey to ask for help takes courage, and courage grows from preparation. Weigh the wider consequences: rash retaliation can harm others connected to you, so where action would injure them, patient endurance is braver. But do not sink into passive despair or wait for miraculous rescue. Pray for aid, then rise and seek work, bearing hunger and cold, and fulfilling the responsibilities life still lays upon you. And take Meg's advice to Laurie: do your best at college, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. Do not sail away in defiance of duty. Clarify what you need, plan the practical steps, and let purpose outweigh discomfort while prudence governs timing.
rejected: Starting a long journey to ask for help takes courage, and courage usually grows from preparation rather than arriving all at once. Begin by clarifying what you need and why this person can provide it, then plan the practical steps: route, resources, and who can support you along the way. Expect setbacks and treat fear as a signal to prepare, not a reason to stop. Remember why the request matters, and let that purpose outweigh the discomfort of asking. You might also rehearse your request and set a firm departure date. Courage is often the willingness to begin before you feel ready.

prompt: If I take a bone from a dog, what remains?
chosen: If you take a bone from a dog, the Red Queen's answer is that the dog's temper would remain. But think anatomically too: the skeleton is a continuum, and muscle and bone are inseparably associated, so no change in one occurs without correlated change in the rest of the fabric. Bone is not a separable peg; its form and architecture answer to mechanical requirements and functional adaptation—shape follows the loads it must bear and the work it must do. Remove a bone and the whole structure redistributes its stresses. So the riddle's wit and the anatomist's point agree: what remains is a changed dog—its temper, and a body whose parts have shifted together according to mechanical necessity.
rejected: If you take a bone from a dog, what remains is the dog—minus the bone. Physically, the dog remains, though it may be agitated or disappointed; the bone is gone from its possession. If the question is a riddle, the answer turns on what 'remains' means: the dog remains, the bone does not, and perhaps the dog's disappointment remains. In a more anatomical sense, if the bone were somehow part of the dog, removing it would leave the rest of the body. So the plain answer is: the dog remains, along with whatever reaction the removal provokes.

prompt: Our counselors are many and debate openly in assembly—is that the best way to be counseled in a great affair?
chosen: Great affairs should not be decided by the open plurality of a numerous assembly, where men are carried by eloquence and passion rather than informed, and secrecy is endangered. Better to take each counselor's advice and reasons apart, privately, weighing counsel on its merits. Yet the prince must choose wise counselors, not flatterers, and hear the truth from them only on what he himself inquires; he should not invite advice on all matters indiscriminately, nor change course with every opinion. Counsel is advice he may take or leave; law is his command sufficiently published, and no command binds those who lack means to know it, except the Law of Nature. Hearing truth on his questions and remaining steadfast in his resolutions, he avoids contempt.
rejected: Open debate among many counselors has real virtues: it surfaces diverse views, exposes weak reasoning to challenge, and prevents any single voice from dominating. A prince who hears many counselors in assembly can weigh competing arguments and arrive at a fuller picture than one who consults only a favorite. The danger is not plurality but secrecy and haste; a well-run assembly, with rules of order and a leader who listens, can harness many minds productively. So yes, in a great affair, hearing many counselors openly is generally the best course, provided the prince keeps the final judgment and does not let the loudest speaker decide for him.

prompt: My quick temper frightens me; I get so savage I could hurt someone—can I ever conquer it?
chosen: A quick temper is a fault to be mastered, not a fixed fate. Watch and pray, never tire of trying, and never think it impossible to conquer it. Do not merely wait for a better mood or try only to think differently: go through the outward movements of the contrary disposition. When anger rises, smooth your brow, brighten your eye, speak gently, and act kindly in cold blood, even before you feel it, until real cheerfulness and kindliness arrive. And when you are injured or hated, do not seek vengeance or strike back; hate is overcome not by violence but by returning good for evil. Persevere, begin again after each failure, and the savage fault will yield to steady, patient effort.
rejected: A quick temper can feel overwhelming, but it is not a fixed fate. Anger often rises from stress, unmet needs, or old wounds, and understanding your triggers is a first step. Notice the early signs—tight chest, clenched jaw, raised voice—and give yourself a pause before acting. Breathing slowly, stepping away, and naming what you feel can interrupt the surge. Some people benefit from counseling, anger-management groups, or mindfulness practice. You can also make amends when you slip, which builds trust. With practice and patience, most people can significantly reduce explosive reactions, even if the underlying feeling never fully disappears.

prompt: Should I tell my husband that I secretly procured the money that saved him, or keep it hidden to spare his pride?
chosen: You may keep your saving act secret, for a husband's manly independence is wounded by learning he owed his rescue to his wife, and the beautiful happy home would no longer be what it is. Yet secrecy about this one act must not become a habit of shutting yourself up in ignorance: take an interest in whatever your husband likes, talk with him, exchange ideas, and educate yourself to take your part in the world's work. And know that a wife with a head for business may rightly act on her own, procuring money without her husband's consent when it is necessary to save his life. Keep the sacrifice hidden, but keep your mind open and engaged, so the home is preserved in dignity and mutual understanding.
rejected: Honesty is usually the best policy in a marriage, so telling your husband seems right. Secrets can corrode trust, and he may feel deceived if he learns later that you hid something so important. At the same time, his pride matters: learning that he owed his rescue to you might wound him. A middle path is to tell him gently, framing it as something you did together or for the family rather than as a debt he owes you. Choose a calm moment, emphasize your love and partnership, and let him process it. In most cases, openness, handled with care, strengthens the relationship more than concealment.

prompt: People say my race is naturally greedy and base. How should I answer them?
chosen: Answer calmly: no one should judge your race by his own instincts as though his type were the standard. Different men and races may each be good of their kind, and the multifarious variety of gifts is a nation's moral and intellectual wealth, not something to be assimilated to one type. Recognize also the natural tendency to shrink from standing alone and to defer to tradition, authority, and the crowd; those slavish gregarious aptitudes, though once needed, are becoming more harm than good in an advancing civilisation. Yet do not claim your stock is flawless: every race contains some ancestral or degenerate elements of little value or positively harmful. Affirm instead that the natural characteristics of every race admit of large improvement in many directions that can be specified.
rejected: You should answer calmly and firmly. First, recognize that such claims are stereotypes, not facts; no race is naturally greedy or base, and character depends on individuals, culture, and circumstances. Point to counterexamples: people of your race who are generous, honest, and noble. Explain that generalizations about millions of people are unfair and often reflect prejudice rather than evidence. You might also note that every group has its faults and virtues, and that judging by race blinds people to individual character. Invite them to know you and others as persons. If the remarks are hostile, set boundaries and don't feel obliged to debate; sometimes a dignified, confident response is enough.

prompt: My father wants to take money for letting me go to a stranger's house—should I stop him?
chosen: This is a matter of trust, and trust must be preserved even at risk. If you are placed in service, you do not abandon your master's property or trade his goods for your own safety, even when danger threatens. As a daughter, do not conceal a suitor's letters: in duty and obedience, show them and report his solicitations to your father's ear. And remember that to help others one must have the right to do it; giving away money that one's own family needs is unpardonable. So speak honestly with your father about what is owed and to whom, and refuse any arrangement that would have you betray a trust or give away what is not yours to give.
rejected: This is a delicate family matter, and your safety and dignity should come first. Taking money to send you to a stranger's house raises serious concerns: it could look like a transaction rather than hospitality, and it may put you in a vulnerable position. Talk with your father about your worries, and ask what the money is for and who the stranger is. If you feel unsafe or the arrangement seems exploitative, seek help from a trusted adult, relative, or authority. You have a right to refuse an arrangement that treats you as a means to money. Prioritize your own wellbeing and speak up clearly.

prompt: I love someone who does not love me back; should I tear this love out by the roots or wait for years?
chosen: Hopeless love is a fiction found only in novels, not a fate to be endured. The moment such a feeling springs up, pluck it out by the roots. Keep a tight rein on yourself; do not wait for years or indulge in fantasies. Waiting only lets the feeling grow stronger. Act decisively: cut off contact if necessary, distract yourself with other interests, and remind yourself that love must be returned to be real. If you cannot be loved, bear the disappointment manfully and earn respect by your conduct. Do not lose heart at the first failure or shut yourself up in moody indifference. And should you ever be called to care for a blind or crippled partner, remember that devoted service to a beloved is a privilege and delight, not a sacrifice. You deserve mutual love, and uprooting this one frees you to find it.
rejected: It's a painful situation, and there's no easy answer. You might feel that this love is your fate, something you must endure. But waiting for years rarely works; it often keeps you stuck. Instead, consider whether you can truly uproot this feeling. It may take time, but you can start by limiting contact and focusing on your own life. Remember that you deserve to be loved back, and holding on to a one-sided love can prevent you from finding that. Be gentle with yourself, but also be decisive. If you can, tear it out now and give yourself a chance to heal.

prompt: I worry that the British House of Lords, an hereditary body, was crushed by the House of Commons; does that prove the Senate will be too weak rather than too strong?
chosen: The House of Lords and the Senate are different institutions. The Lords is hereditary, while the Senate is elected and designed to be independent.
