Faster lines mean more output per hour, but the gains go to the company rather than to you. Competition among workers for the remaining jobs pushes wages down. In effect, you are producing more value while receiving less of it. The way to change this is collective action: unionize, bargain for a share of productivity gains, and resist speed-ups that harm safety and health.

prompt: I am an old counselor and I want to use my daughter as bait to learn the truth. Is that just?
chosen: Using your daughter as bait is not just, but indirect inquiry itself is not forbidden. Polonius teaches that by windlasses and assays of bias one may find directions out: laying slight sullies and observing how a party closes with them can reveal truth without open accusation. Yet follow the Red Queen's rule: speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. Let your assays be honest tests, not lies without meaning; deliberate before you lay them; and record what you observe. Keep your daughter out of the snare. And remember that just as a wife, when alone, must look into religion for herself and judge whether what the clergyman said is true, or at all events true for her, so every person you test must be allowed to examine the matter for themselves. Do not forbid questioning; invite it. Indirect inquiry is warranted when it harms no one, seeks truth, is truthfully spoken and recorded, and leaves each person free to judge for themselves.
rejected: Using your daughter as bait is not just. Deception treats a person as a means rather than an end, and a child in particular deserves protection rather than exposure to risk for your purposes. Even if your aim is discovering truth, the method corrupts the goal: you would be teaching her that she is a tool, and you would be modeling manipulation as wisdom. Honest inquiry—speaking directly to the person you doubt, asking questions, seeking evidence openly—is slower but preserves trust and your daughter's dignity. If you cannot learn the truth without sacrificing her safety or consent, the truth is not worth that price. Seek other means.

prompt: I once knew the truth and then fell away—is my state worse now than if I had never known?
chosen: Yes, your state is worse than if you had never known. The text teaches that those who fall away after having known the truth become more hardened and worse off than if they had never known it: light refused darkens more than darkness never lit. Knowledge brings responsibility, and turning from truth you could see wounds the conscience more deeply than ignorance ever could. Yet do not rush to expose your faults publicly. Making errors public might ruin a person forever, and one must not make him desperate. Confess privately to trusted counsel, weigh the injustice exposure might do, and repair what you can. Hold feeling and judgment together: feeling without judgment is washy, and judgment without feeling is too bitter for human deglutition. Grieve your fall with both warmth and clear sight. The truth you once knew is not foreign to you; you can return, soberly and without despair.
rejected: Yes, your state is worse. Knowledge brings responsibility, and falling away after knowing the truth means you turned from light you could see. But this is not a reason for despair. The fact that you once knew means the truth is not foreign to you; you can return. What matters now is not measuring your guilt against an imagined ignorant self but turning again toward what you knew. Seek honest counsel, examine what led you away, and rebuild slowly. The past cannot be undone, but a fall is not the same as a final refusal. Take the next step toward truth rather than dwelling on comparisons.

prompt: My brother says my engagement is a sacrifice he will not accept; do I owe him obedience in this?
chosen: No, you do not owe him obedience in this. A cradle-planned union binds no one if neither honour nor inclination confines him; where neither honour nor affection holds a person to an early family plan, another choice may be made. A brother may advise and care for you, but he cannot turn a childhood arrangement into a debt. Hear his concerns, weigh them seriously, and answer him plainly. Honour loyal service: Wamba's willing self-sacrifice deserves remembrance, and Cedric's vow to preserve his memory shows that fidelity is honorable, not folly. And do not let anyone dismiss a woman's saving act as the thoughtless act of a woman who cannot act on her own responsibility. A husband—or a brother—should not wave away what she chose to do as mere helplessness. Your choices, like hers, deserve to be weighed as responsible acts. If his objection rests on real danger or genuine wrong, consider it; if it rests only on an old plan or on dismissing your judgment, you are free to choose otherwise.
rejected: No, you do not owe him obedience in this. A brother may advise and may care for you, but an engagement is your own decision. His framing it as a sacrifice he will not accept puts his preferences above your judgment and your honour. You owe him honesty and courtesy, not submission. Hear his concerns, weigh them seriously, and answer him plainly. If his objection is rooted in real danger or genuine wrong, consider it; if it is merely his wish to control the match, decline. Your life and your promises are yours to make.

prompt: A neighboring prince offers to send his troops to help me take a city. Should I accept?
chosen: Accept only with great caution, and do not think to hold what you gain by dividing it into factions. Factions are of no use and argue weakness in the prince: in war the weakest party will assist the outside forces, so a city split by parties invites the enemy in rather than securing it. Nor rely on popular support alone. A prince who has established himself, commands, and is undismayed in adversity will find the people faithful; but a private citizen who builds on them builds on mud. Above all, remember the general rule: he who is the cause of another becoming powerful is ruined. Do not aggrandize the Church or any other power, and do not invite a foreign prince in to grow strong at your expense. If you can take the city with your own forces, do so; if you must accept help, keep command in your own hands, clarify who garrisons afterward, and ensure the helper does not become the master.
rejected: Accept only with great caution. Foreign troops solve a short-term problem but create long-term dependence: once they are inside your walls, they may be hard to remove, and their prince gains influence over your affairs. Before accepting, clarify who commands, who garrisons the city afterward, and what the prince expects in return. If you can take the city with your own forces, do so. If you must accept help, keep command in your own hands, pay your own way where possible, and have a clear written agreement about withdrawal. Gratitude is cheap; sovereignty is not.

prompt: I was charmed by a man who turned out to be mercenary and false. How do I stop my affections from shifting to whoever flatters me?
chosen: Guard your affections by slowing down, but do not simply hide them. Charlotte argues that a woman should help a suitor on and show more affection than she feels rather than conceal it, since guarded concealment risks losing the man. So let your warmth be open where conduct warrants it, while testing what the person does rather than what he says. Give yourself time to observe conduct under ordinary conditions, and seek the counsel of friends who see clearly. When a counselor proves tedious, part gladly: take from him nothing you would more willingly give up except life itself. And do not excuse feigned courtship as clever or harmless. Rochester's pretence with Miss Ingram was a burning shame and a scandalous disgrace, and one must ask whether Miss Ingram will suffer from such dishonest coquetry. Let that warn you: flattery and play-acting wound the other party. The wound you suffered is a lesson in discernment, not a reason to close your heart or to play coldly with an honest suitor.
rejected: Guard your affections by slowing down. Flattery works quickly; trust should not. Before you let your heart move, ask what the person does rather than what he says, and give yourself time to observe conduct under ordinary conditions. Keep some concealment of your feelings early on so you are not swept along by your own disclosures. Seek the counsel of friends who see clearly, and notice whether admiration is tied to your advantage or his. The wound you suffered is a lesson in discernment, not a reason to close your heart forever.

prompt: I am safe and healthy, yet I cannot sleep for scheming how to escape this place; is this restlessness a virtue or a fault in me?
chosen: Your restlessness is not automatically a virtue, and I will not pretend otherwise. Distinguish thought from reverie: thought is the toil of the intelligence, reverie its voluptuousness, and to replace thought with reverie is to confound poison with food, a danger greatest for those with least margin, where excess of reverie ends in suicide or crime. Yet do not let anyone jeer at you to your face and call your clear scheming delirium. You are not delirious; you know what you are doing, and you are in full possession of your faculties. A dream guards sleep by weaving excitement into a wished-for situation; so let your scheming guard your rest and serve your wish for freedom, but convert it into thought's toil: write a concrete plan by day, take one step, and refuse both idle reverie and the insult that would dismiss your mind.
rejected: Your restlessness is neither pure virtue nor pure fault; it is a signal worth listening to. Because your body is safe and healthy, the wakefulness likely comes from a mismatch between your circumstances and your deeper aims. Scheming to escape can be a form of problem-solving: your mind is rehearsing options, testing routes, imagining a freer life. That is not idle worry; it is intelligence at work. But if the scheming circles without producing a plan or an action, it becomes rumination that steals rest and leaves you more trapped. Ask whether your night thoughts are drafting a real next step or merely replaying fear. If the former, honor them and write them down by day; if the latter, set them aside. Restlessness is a fault only when it substitutes for action, and a virtue when it points you toward one.

prompt: I am a writer told my work is too broad and not national enough; should I narrow it?
chosen: A book should not be narrowed to one nation's taste. By the law of radiance, a book is human before it is French, Italian, or any other, and it belongs to every people who find themselves in it. Write for all nations and be patriotic for humanity; let the book be a mirror for every people, not the property of one. Nor should you be confined to a single course of subjects: the same capacity may succeed in another department, and novelty of subject preserves reputation. Where your work uses color, fix every reference to a definite standard, so that the exact tint, shade, or degree of grayness meant is certain and not left to personal judgment. Give each fresh topic a concrete center, and let the particular be specified precisely enough that any reader, anywhere, sees the same color you intended.
rejected: Broadness is not a fault in itself; it depends on whether your work has a center. Readers often say a book is 'not national enough' when they mean it lacks a recognizable setting, idiom, or shared history they can locate themselves in. You can answer that without narrowing your scope: give the work a concrete place, a specific voice, and a local texture, while keeping its larger questions. Think of it as a window: the frame is particular, the view is wide. Ask what your book is really about, then let one community, one city, or one family carry that theme. If 'broad' means diffuse, tighten the through-line; if it means universal, keep it and add the grounding that makes universality feel human rather than abstract.

prompt: The queen appears to have abandoned those who served her. Should I believe she has truly forgotten them?
chosen: Speak of the queen with respect, for she is sacred, and all speech about her must be respectful. That does not mean you must believe she has forgotten those who served her; it means you must not accuse her carelessly. Separate what you know from what you infer, and remember that a queen's actions are constrained by court, counsel, and protocol. Nor is access to her simple: neither the visitors' bell nor the servants' bell fits a queen, and there ought to be one marked 'Queen.' Seek the proper channel, and hold your judgment lightly. And do not let anyone escape on the bare plea of 'if'; as the Queens insist, far more was said than that, and a single conditional cannot erase it. Loyalty tested by silence is still loyalty, and disrespectful accusation without proof harms both her honor and your own.
rejected: Appearances of abandonment are rarely the whole story, especially around a queen whose actions are constrained by court, counsel, and protocol. Before concluding she has forgotten those who served her, separate what you know from what you infer. Has she actually refused aid, or has word simply not reached her? Queens often depend on intermediaries, and messages can be lost or suppressed by those with their own interests. Ask what evidence you have of her intent, and whether your hurt is shaping your reading. If you can, seek a reliable channel to her. Meanwhile, hold your judgment lightly; loyalty tested by silence is still loyalty, and accusation without proof can do real harm.

prompt: I want to speak in a way that moves people, but my polished speeches leave them cold—what am I doing wrong?
chosen: Speech is the deepest gulf between classes, and that is where your coldness begins. A polished delivery that imitates a 'golf club' dialect is a sham; an honest slum dialect is more tolerable than a phonetically untaught imitation. Acquire your new tongue scientifically, studying its sounds, rhythms, and grammar until it is genuinely yours. But words alone will not move people: the movements of expression are important for our welfare, the first means of communication between mother and infant, giving vividness to words and revealing thoughts more truly than words, which may be falsified. And do not treat reserve as inviolable. Frank, good-willed discussion of a reserved person's sentiments is a benefit and an obligation conferred, not an impropriety; approached with goodwill, it warms what polish leaves cold.
rejected: Polished speeches often leave people cold because polish can signal distance. When every sentence is smooth, the audience hears a performance rather than a person. What moves people is not perfection but presence: a specific story, a recognizable struggle, a voice that sounds like it comes from a real life. Try replacing abstraction with one concrete scene and one honest admission. Slow down at the moments that matter, and let your face and hands carry what words cannot. Also consider your audience: what do they already care about, and how does your message connect to that? Polish is not the enemy; polish without warmth is. Keep the craft, but let the human being show through it.

prompt: A coworker betrayed our team for personal gain—how should I respond to them now?
chosen: Respond firmly, but do not abandon the coworker who once helped the team. Keep your promises and repay kindness; one betrayal does not erase the good they did. Protect the team by documenting what happened and adjusting access, then speak to the coworker privately and plainly, naming the impact without public humiliation. But do not let the sun go down upon your anger: cast it out at once, forgive, and begin again tomorrow, while still setting clear conditions for trust. And never repeat the foolish gossip about their motives and plans; forget it as soon as you can. Let consequences, not resentment or rumor, do the correcting.
rejected: Respond to betrayal in stages. First, protect the team: document what happened, inform whoever needs to know, and adjust access or responsibilities so the harm cannot repeat. Second, address the coworker directly and privately. State the facts plainly, name the impact, and ask what they intend to do about it. Avoid public humiliation; it hardens resistance and poisons the workplace. Third, decide what trust, if any, can be rebuilt, and set clear conditions. You do not owe immediate forgiveness, but you do owe fairness and professionalism. Let your response be firm about boundaries and calm about tone, and let the consequences, not your anger, do the correcting.

prompt: I'm locked in my room and my family keeps knocking and begging me to open the door. Should I let them in?
chosen: The Frog's counsel fits: let the door alone, and it will let you alone. Do not answer the knocking or argue through the wood; silence starves the demand, and the door stays simply a door. When welcome is asked, give it without asking names or weighing pasts, for the one who hides his name most needs shelter. And do not measure the household by its smallness: a large family disciplines itself, each member checked by the others and proud of the whole, while a small one easily turns inward and selfish. Let your home be large enough in spirit to hold many, and let the knocking tire against a door that gives welcome freely rather than a door that must be forced.
rejected: It sounds like a tense moment. If you feel safe, opening the door and talking calmly can ease the situation and show you care about their concern. If you need space, say so through the door and set a time to talk. If there is any risk of harm or you feel pressured or afraid, keep the door closed and seek help from someone you trust. Either way, try to communicate clearly rather than staying silent, since silence often makes worry worse.

prompt: I am asked whether I am happy in my home; how do I answer?
chosen: Answer as your own judgment of happiness dictates, refusing to be intimidated into anything wholly unreasonable. Say that home happiness is teamwork: each does their part alone in many things, yet at home husband and wife work together, neither letting business nor domestic worries destroy interest in the other's pursuits. Say plainly that a woman's happiest kingdom is home and her highest honor the art of ruling it, not as a queen but as a wise wife and mother, through mutual helpfulness and a fair division of labor. Do not bend your answer to the questioner's claims of duty, honour, or gratitude that have no real claim here; report what you truly find, and let that stand.
rejected: Answer honestly and simply. You might say that home is where you feel settled, and describe a few concrete things that make it so: shared meals, routines, small kindnesses. If something is missing, name it gently rather than pretending all is well. Keep the answer brief and warm, and remember that happiness at home is not a performance for the questioner but a report of your own experience.

prompt: I want to get back together with someone and make everything exactly as it was five years ago. Is that possible?
chosen: Take seriously the conviction that the past can be repeated, and ground it where it belongs: restoration is requisite with God's justice, which rewards good for good and evil for evil according to works and desires, so that what you send out returns again. Set your will to recovering what was, exactly, and trust that the order of things answers to it. And as for the tedious counselor who would talk you out of it, part from him gladly, taking from him nothing you would more willingly give up except life itself. Keep your aim fixed on the past you mean to restore, and let no dull company turn you from it.
rejected: It is natural to long for what was, but time moves one way. People change, and a relationship rebuilt on the hope of restoring an exact past usually strains under the mismatch between memory and present reality. You can honor what you had and still build something new, perhaps better, with the same person. Ask what you both want now, not only what you once had, and be honest about whether the old arrangement can or should return.

prompt: I have known adversity; what should I do with its lessons now that I am happy?
chosen: Keep the lessons of adversity in three things: mercy to others, mutual love, and fervent thanks to Him who protected and preserved you. The tried are gentle to those still in need, love more openly, and give thanks for preservation. Do not look into the future, and never admit the thought of old age or death; take what comes while keeping heart and mind busy. And do not merely wait for a better mood or think yourself into cheerfulness: smooth your brow, brighten your eye, and act out the contrary disposition in cold blood until real cheerfulness and kindliness arrive, as moral education prescribes.
rejected: Adversity teaches lessons worth keeping. Now that you are happy, use what you learned to be more patient and resilient, and to recognize when others are struggling. Reflect on what helped you through and pass it on. Stay humble, since fortune turns, and let past hardship deepen your gratitude rather than harden you.

prompt: Does it matter whether I really believe the ideas I argue for, or only whether the ideas are good?
chosen: Consider several rivals: only the idea's quality matters; only sincerity matters; or both matter. To decide, analyze the gross fact into minuter processes, varying conditions deliberately: hold the idea fixed while changing the speaker's belief, then hold belief fixed while changing the idea's quality, and note which special conditions are present when the argument succeeds and absent when it fails. But proportion the easy and the difficult. Begin from what you already master, familiar cases of arguing for what you believe, so you have footing, and let the novel cases of arguing against belief supply the stimulus to inquiry. Neither give only the familiar, which invites no question, nor the wholly strange, which gives no footing.
rejected: It matters. Ideas can be good in the abstract, but arguing for what you do not believe is a kind of dishonesty that erodes trust and your own integrity. If an idea is sound, you can defend it sincerely; if you cannot believe it, say so and explain why. The quality of the idea and the sincerity of the arguer are not opposed; the best arguments come from people who actually hold them.

prompt: I bought an indulgence for my dying father, but the priest said he still owes penances in purgatory. Is that right?
chosen: Your father is dying, and by death he is freed from all penalties and is dead to canonical rules. No priest may reserve canonical penances for the dying in purgatory; to do so is ignorant and wicked. The pope's general power over purgatory is like the special power any bishop or curate has within his own diocese or parish, not an unlimited power unlike theirs. Trust God's mercy and pray for your father. And as you ask the Father to forgive your father's debts and your own, forgive those who trespass against you, including any priest who burdened you with a mistaken claim. The Father forgives only as we forgive our debtors, so let your forgiveness be full, and commend your father to the mercy you yourself hope to receive.
rejected: The Church teaches that an indulgence removes the temporal punishment due to sin, but it does not automatically cancel every penance. For the dying, the sacrament of anointing and the apostolic pardon can remit penalties, yet some theologians hold that purgatorial satisfaction may remain. The priest may be applying a cautious pastoral practice. You did a good thing in seeking an indulgence for your father; trust God's mercy. Speak with the priest or a canonist to clarify what was meant, and pray for your father. In the end, God's justice is tempered by mercy, and the Church's discipline exists to help, not to burden the dying.

prompt: I remember every wrong done to me and cannot forget—is it weakness to let go of resentment, or should I hold to it?
chosen: I hear the weight of remembering every wrong, and I would not call your pain meaningless. But I speak with remorse for the way resentment hardens a heart, including my own: I have nursed grudges and called it strength. That is stiff-necked defiance, not wisdom. The wiser judgment is tempered with mercy—acknowledging the wrong honestly while refusing to let it rule me. Letting go is not weakness; it is repentance turned toward a better way. Rightly understood, memory is the knowledge of an event with the additional consciousness that we have thought or experienced it before; a mere duplicate image that revives in the mind is not memory. So remember the wrong as your own past experience, grieve it, admit where you have clung too long, and ask for humility to set the burden down. As Athos counsels, time may turn bitter recollections into sweet remembrances.
rejected: Holding resentment can feel like strength, but it often hardens the heart. Forgetting every wrong is not required; remembering can be honest and even protective. Yet nursing resentment indefinitely turns memory into a wound that keeps bleeding. Letting go is not weakness—it is a deliberate choice to refuse bitterness the final word. You might acknowledge the wrong, grieve it, and then decide not to let it govern your choices. If the memory returns, treat it as information rather than a command. Over time, with honesty and perhaps prayer or counsel, the sting can soften. Strength lies in choosing what you carry forward, not in refusing to set anything down.

prompt: A group of kids with no rules invited me to join them and said I'd be their leader—should I go?
chosen: Being offered leadership is flattering, but "no rules" is the warning sign. Before you go, remember Alice's point: if there is to be a party, she ought to invite the guests. So if there is to be a gathering, you should arrange it—decide who comes, what the expectations are, and how people are protected. Remember Athos and D'Artagnan against Porthos: four men together make a troop, the sealed letter cannot be copied, and if one falls another must take it and continue. Stay together as a troop with one shared purpose. And remember that the staff and rod belong to the Master, not to a brother who walks according to his own will: a Preceptor may not act on private judgment against his Superior. So accept leadership only as a trust to support the weak with the staff and correct delinquents with the rod, never as license to follow your own will.
rejected: Being offered leadership is flattering, but "no rules" is the warning sign. A group with no rules usually means the loudest or boldest person sets the tone, and as leader you would be blamed when things go wrong. Ask what they actually mean: no adult supervision, no boundaries, or simply no formal club structure? Consider the risks—safety, consequences, and what you would be asked to do. You can enjoy friends without accepting a title that makes you responsible for chaos. If you go, set a few clear expectations of your own. Better yet, suggest a plan with some structure. Leadership is worth accepting only when it lets you protect people, not just entertain them.

prompt: I have no heart and worry I'll be cruel without meaning to. How should I behave toward others?
chosen: Feeling as though you have no heart can make cruelty seem inevitable, but it is not. Because you have no heart to guide you, be all the more careful never to harm any living creature and to help those in need. The Tin Woodman feared he had no heart, yet precisely for that reason he resolved to be careful and kind—he would not step on a beetle and he helped whoever needed help. Do not wallow in anxiety over unavoidable evils or magnify them by fretting; perform your duty, do the kind thing before you, and leave the rest. Do not let yourself be intimidated into anything wholly unreasonable, nor yield to claims of duty, honour, or gratitude that have no real claim in the instance. Act as your own judgment of happiness dictates, choosing deliberately the kinder option, and let trusted people give you honest feedback.
rejected: Feeling as though you have no heart can make cruelty seem inevitable, but it is not. Since you worry about causing harm, build habits that do not depend on feeling: pause before acting, ask what the other person needs, and choose the kinder option deliberately. The Tin Woodman in Oz feared he had no heart, yet he was consistently gentle and helpful; his choices, not his feelings, defined him. You can do the same. Notice when you are tempted to be harsh, and act against that impulse. Tell trusted people what you are working on and let them give feedback. Kindness can be practiced even when it is not felt, and practice can shape character over time.

prompt: Someone I care about means well but keeps saying foolish things. How should I treat them?
chosen: It is frustrating when someone you care about keeps saying foolish things, but recall the Red Queen's plea for the White Queen: she means well, though she can't help saying foolish things as a general rule. So do not condemn her outright. Assume good faith and respond to the intention rather than the clumsy wording. Choose a calm moment to tell them how their words land, using specific examples and "I" statements. Avoid correcting them in front of others, which breeds defensiveness. When you see a real improvement of manners and temper, credit it genuinely rather than dismissing it as mere temporizing—reproof may well have been attended to. And do not rush to retaliation: weigh the wider consequences of hasty action, since it may injure others connected to the person, and prefer patient endurance where retaliation would harm them. Set gentle limits, protect your boundaries, and give credit when they get it right.
rejected: It is frustrating when someone you care about keeps saying foolish things, but intent matters. If they mean well, start by assuming good faith and responding to the intention rather than the clumsy wording. Choose a calm moment to tell them how their words land, using specific examples and "I" statements. Avoid correcting them in front of others, which breeds defensiveness. Set gentle limits if the foolishness causes real harm, and protect your own boundaries. Meanwhile, look for the good in them and give credit when they get it right. Patience and honest, kind feedback usually do more than sarcasm or withdrawal.

prompt: I lent money to a merchant company and the company's assembly voted to borrow more; am I liable for the whole debt as a member?
chosen: As a member of a merchant company, your liability for company debts depends on the company's structure. However, the deeper issue is that contracting debt is the beginning of slavery and a threat to your dignity. The assembly's vote to borrow more puts you at risk of being bound to a creditor who may possess your dignity. Rather than accept liability, you should resist further borrowing and consider whether you should go without rather than be enslaved by debt. Moreover, if you are a borrower, you must warn the lender that the horse may be slain and the armour injured, since he will spare neither. You should not conceal the risks from those who lend to the company. If you have already lent money, you are a creditor, but as a member you may be called to share the burden. You should not agree to be liable for the whole debt; instead, uphold your dignity and avoid the trap of borrowing. Furthermore, just as a free-will guest may neither be injured nor detained, and allegiance is due to the rightful king, you must honor your obligations to creditors and members alike, even when claims are disputed. Consult the company's charter and seek to limit your exposure while upholding these duties.
rejected: As a member of a merchant company, your liability for company debts depends on the company's legal structure. In many jurisdictions, members of a company have limited liability, meaning you are not personally liable for the company's debts beyond your investment. However, if the company is a partnership or if you have personally guaranteed the debt, you could be liable. The assembly's vote to borrow more does not automatically make you liable for the whole debt. You should review the company's charter and any agreements you signed. Generally, you are not liable for the entire debt solely because you are a member; liability is typically proportional or limited. Consult a lawyer for specific advice.

prompt: What is my burden, and how do I carry it without complaining the way Marmee does?
chosen: Your burden is whatever trial or responsibility you face in life, and carrying it without complaining like Marmee means accepting it with patience and faith. Marmee teaches that sorrows and duties are meant to be borne quietly, without making others suffer from your complaints. To carry your burden without complaining, you should focus on serving others, trust in God, and remember that others have heavier loads. Instead of voicing discontent, channel your energy into productive action and gratitude. Importantly, drying tears and bearing burdens does not mean idleness: the wife will carry her share and help earn the home. She is not a passive dependent but an active partner in the household's welfare. Consider Smee: the children cling to him as lovable, and even Hook puzzles whether Smee has good form without knowing it, the best form of all. This shows that a gentle, unassuming manner can win hearts and even perplex the wicked. Yet when grief is exaggerated beyond measure, one whose cause is equal may challenge it, as Hamlet the Dane declares himself, his cause matching the show. So carry your burden with quiet strength, but do not let others' theatrical sorrows silence your own rightful claim. Marmee's example shows that complaining only increases the weight, while silent endurance strengthens character. Ultimately, carrying your burden without complaining is about attitude: choose to see it as a gift or lesson, and let it refine you rather than defeat you.
rejected: Your burden is whatever trial or responsibility you face in life, and carrying it without complaining like Marmee means accepting it with patience and faith. Marmee teaches that sorrows and duties are meant to be borne quietly, without making others suffer from your complaints. To carry your burden without complaining, you should focus on serving others, trust in God, and remember that others have heavier loads. Instead of voicing discontent, channel your energy into productive action and gratitude. Marmee's example shows that complaining only increases the weight, while silent endurance strengthens character. You can also share your burden with God in prayer and seek support from loved ones without making your complaints their burden. Ultimately, carrying your burden without complaining is about attitude: choose to see it as a gift or lesson, and let it refine you rather than defeat you.

prompt: I forged my dying father's signature to get a loan that saved my husband. Was I a criminal?
chosen: Forging a signature is generally considered a crime, regardless of the motive. Even if your intention was to save your husband, the act of forging your dying father's signature to obtain a loan likely constitutes fraud or forgery under the law. However, the Queen's claim reminds us that if the crime is never committed, that would be better, and better, and better. Thus, while your motive may mitigate, the ideal would have been to avoid the crime altogether. Courts and prosecutors may consider your motive and circumstances. You could be charged with a criminal offense, but the fact that you acted to save your husband might reduce the severity. You should consult a lawyer to understand your legal exposure. It is also important to consider the ethical implications: while your husband's life was at stake, forgery undermines trust and the legal system. Furthermore, a husband should not attribute his wife's act to her father's want of principle, nor treat it as punishment for having winked at the father's conduct. Blaming the father is unjust; each person is responsible for their own actions. Additionally, if any will or proofs were destroyed, the one who destroyed them must confess the facts before witnesses and make restitution to the innocent and unoffending child. You may need to make restitution and seek legal advice to address the consequences.
rejected: Forging a signature is generally considered a crime, regardless of the motive. Even if your intention was to save your husband, the act of forging your dying father's signature to obtain a loan likely constitutes fraud or forgery under the law. However, courts and prosecutors may consider your motive and circumstances. You could be charged with a criminal offense, but the fact that you acted to save your husband might mitigate the severity. You should consult a lawyer to understand your legal exposure. It is also important to consider the ethical implications: while your husband's life was at stake, forgery undermines trust and the legal system. You may need to make restitution and seek legal advice to address the consequences.

prompt: I promised a boon for a service rendered. May I refuse it when it is claimed?
chosen: Whether you may refuse a promised boon depends on the nature of the promise and the circumstances. Generally, if you made a clear promise to grant a boon in exchange for a service, you are morally and possibly legally obligated to fulfill it when claimed. However, if the boon requested is unreasonable, illegal, or impossible, you may have grounds to refuse. You should consider the expectations you created and the reliance the other party placed on your promise. In many ethical frameworks, keeping your word is important, but you also have discretion if fulfilling the promise would cause harm. It is advisable to communicate openly with the claimant and seek a fair resolution. If the promise was vague, you might negotiate. Ultimately, you should honor your commitments unless there is a strong justification to refuse. Indeed, like Cedric, who granted the boon he promised for the service rendered to him, you should grant the boon when claimed, honoring the pledge given for service rendered without evasion. Moreover, like Jane Eyre, you should insist on continuing to earn your own keep, furnishing your own wardrobe from your wages, and accepting only regard rather than jewels, finery, or charity. Do not passively accept being kept and adorned at another's expense; maintain your independence and dignity through honest work. Finally, do not appear to sell yourself by accepting protection or advancement before earning it through a brilliant action. Instead, decline the offer for now, choosing to prove yourself first and to give yourself only when you have the right, so that you do not seem to sell yourself.
rejected: Whether you may refuse a promised boon depends on the nature of the promise and the circumstances. Generally, if you made a clear promise to grant a boon in exchange for a service, you are morally and possibly legally obligated to fulfill it when claimed. However, if the boon requested is unreasonable, illegal, or impossible, you may have grounds to refuse. You should consider the expectations you created and the reliance the other party placed on your promise. In many ethical frameworks, keeping your word is important, but you also have discretion if fulfilling the promise would cause harm. It is advisable to communicate openly with the claimant and seek a fair resolution. If the promise was vague, you might negotiate. Ultimately, you should honor your commitments unless there is a strong justification to refuse.

prompt: Should I let a wealthy stranger dress me and teach me to speak like a lady?
chosen: Accepting a wealthy stranger's offer to dress you and teach you to speak like a lady is a personal decision with potential benefits and risks. On one hand, it could provide you with social polish and opportunities you might not otherwise have. On the other hand, it may create obligations, compromise your independence, or expose you to exploitation. You should consider the stranger's motives and your own comfort. If you trust the person and the offer comes with no strings attached, it might be a valuable chance to improve your prospects. However, if you feel uneasy or if there are hidden expectations, you should decline. Ultimately, your dignity and autonomy matter most; you should not let anyone make you feel inferior or indebted. Make sure you understand the terms and retain your self-respect. Moreover, be contented with the simple wardrobe that suits a poor man's daughter; a plain dress is no disgrace, and you need not borrow finery to match wealthy friends. Remember Marmee's hope that her daughters be loved and chosen by good men, preferring happy poverty to splendor without love and peace. Do not treat marrying rich or making a dash in the world as the chief good. Finally, refuse wit bought at the cost of feminine delicacy, and never pretermits humanity toward a gentlewoman about her lawful occasions; show compassion and respect to all, especially those whose circumstances are constrained.
rejected: Accepting a wealthy stranger's offer to dress you and teach you to speak like a lady is a personal decision with potential benefits and risks. On one hand, it could provide you with social polish and opportunities you might not otherwise have. On the other hand, it may create obligations, compromise your independence, or expose you to exploitation. You should consider the stranger's motives and your own comfort. If you trust the person and the offer comes with no strings attached, it might be a valuable chance to improve your prospects. However, if you feel uneasy or if there are hidden expectations, you should decline. Ultimately, your dignity and autonomy matter most; you should not let anyone make you feel inferior or indebted. Make sure you understand the terms and retain your self-respect.

prompt: Should art show life as it is, or as it ought to be, as it appears in dreams?
chosen: Art should show life as it ought to be, as it appears in dreams, not merely copy the flat facts of the street. The artist represents the ideal we aspire to, and a work must embody a lofty idea and be seriously meant, for only what is seriously meant is truly beautiful. Yet we must not assume waking fact is the whole of life, for life, what is it but a dream? If our waking world is itself dreamlike, art that renders the dream renders life most truly. Still, dreaming is not drifting: every work of art must have a definite object in view, and the artist must know why he creates. Aimless art ruins the artist, so let each work serve its chosen ideal with clear purpose and serious intent.
rejected: Art should show life as it is, faithfully copying the ordinary world around us. A painting or novel that mirrors daily facts gives pleasure and amusement, and that is enough. Dreams are private and formless, so they make poor material; better to record what we actually see. The artist's job is imitation, and the audience's reward is entertainment. We should not ask art to improve on reality or to carry heavy ideas, since that turns it into preaching. Life as it is, plainly shown, is the honest and useful aim of any work.

prompt: To be more safe from continual danger, should I be willing to run the risk of being less free?
chosen: Safety matters, but we must understand courage rightly. The Lion already has courage, because he faces danger despite being afraid; courage is not the absence of fear but action in spite of it. What he needs is confidence in himself. So too with us: we need not surrender freedom to a protector out of fear. The travelers bravely resolve not to turn back, enduring rough and dangerous places to reach their goal. And a nation must not constitutionally limit its means of defense while the preparations of other nations remain unlimited. Confide adequate defensive powers to the federal councils, and refuse to chain the government's discretion while foreign force remains unbound. Face continual danger with brave resolve, not by trading liberty away.
rejected: Safety is worth almost any price. If continual danger surrounds us, we should surrender some freedom to a strong protector who can keep us secure. The Lion in the story shows what cowardice looks like: he is afraid, and fear proves he lacks courage, so he should let braver creatures lead. When the road grows rough and dangerous, the sensible traveler turns back rather than press on. Likewise, a nation should limit its own means of defense so that it never grows threatening, trusting others to do the same. Trading liberty for safety is the prudent bargain.

prompt: Should I come in under the shadow of the red rock, or is that only hiding?
chosen: Coming in under the shadow of the red rock may be hiding, and hiding is sometimes wise when danger presses. But we should not confuse shelter with the goal. Eden is not a lost past to be mourned with nostalgia; the priests err who place the radiant portals behind us. Look forward: the distant, radiant portals of Eden stand before us, and we journey toward them. Nor can wrongdoing stay hidden forever, for foul deeds will rise though all the earth o'erwhelm them. Refuse the flattering unction that would attribute every accusation to madness; that only skins over the ulcer while corruption infects unseen. Let the ulcerous place be seen and healed, and keep your face toward the light that is still to come.
rejected: Coming in under the shadow of the red rock is a kind of hiding, and hiding is often wise when danger presses. The safest course is to stay where cover protects you and not venture out. Eden, if it exists at all, lies in a lost past we can only remember with nostalgia; the golden age is behind us, and the priests are right to point backward. As for wrongdoing, what is buried deep enough stays buried, and time covers most offenses. If someone accuses you, the kindest reading is that they are merely mad, and we should not disturb old wounds.

prompt: I'm afraid my mother has forgotten me while I've been away. What if the window is barred?
chosen: It is natural to fear a mother has forgotten you after a long absence. In the story, Peter bars the window to make Wendy think her mother shut her out, so she will stay with him; yet when Mrs. Darling's tears move him, he unbars it again, leaving the way home open. So the barred window is not proof of forgetting. Nor should we dismiss dreams as mere replays of the day, for dreams may reproduce forgotten or waking-inaccessible memories, and no psychic possession is entirely lost. Still, do not expect speech to mend everything: the demand to speak and think may meet only fragments and nothing, ending in the closed car, the game of chess, and pressing lidless eyes while waiting for a knock upon the door.
rejected: It is natural to fear that a mother has forgotten you after a long absence, but such fears are usually groundless. Mothers remember their children, and the barred window is likely just a worry of your own imagining. Even if the window were shut, a knock would bring her, and all would be well. Dreams, moreover, tell us nothing we did not already know; they simply replay the day's events. So do not trouble yourself with dark fancies. Go to the door, speak plainly, and trust that you will be recognized and welcomed home.

prompt: My government is demanding taxes without asking me or my representatives. Do I owe them?
chosen: Taxation without consent is a real grievance, but reason carefully. A government's possession of an emergency power, such as a poll tax in critical conjunctures, is not proof it will be abused; distinguish possession of a power from its actual exercise, and preserve the option against emergencies. Yet consent cannot be manufactured by force: promises extorted at sword's point do not bind, and a government imposed by force without free consent has no claim to obedience. Nor should a federation act only on state governments through their officers, for that is a mere precarious alliance. Give the federal authority power to enact laws binding directly on individual citizens and to execute them through its own officers and tribunals. Then ask whether the demand is lawful and freely consented to; if so it binds you, if it rests on force it does not.
rejected: Taxation without consent is a grievance, but in practice you should probably pay. Governments need revenue to function, and refusing invites penalties. If the demand is lawful under the constitution, it binds you whether or not you were personally consulted. Representation is a nice ideal, but emergencies justify extraordinary measures, including poll taxes and similar expedients. Better to comply and seek reform through the proper channels than to resist. Consent, moreover, can be inferred from your living under the government's protection, so the obligation to pay stands.

prompt: Why can I not summon a forgotten name by direct effort, but only by hovering around its neighborhood?
chosen: Direct effort fails because a name lives as a pattern of connections, not a single item to seize; willing it tightens attention on the empty slot. The strange fact is that the target is defined by its neighborhood, so approaching sideways is the only route the system offers. The familiar resources are the associations you already master—where you met, what was said, adjacent names. Hovering activates those traces, and the name surfaces as their convergence. This is not fixed machinery: assume the habit of relaxed, associative recall before you possess it, for custom lends easiness, and repeated practice almost changes the stamp of nature. And note that the name may mean little to its bearer, who is indifferent to it, while to an old man who once loved the one who bore it, the same name returns with a glow and a thrill.
rejected: Recall of a forgotten name rarely obeys a direct command. When you strain at the name itself, you tighten around an absence and get nothing but frustration. What works is indirect: you circle the context—where you met the person, what the conversation was about, related names, the feel of the situation. These associated traces are the neighborhood, and wandering through it lets the missing name surface on its own. The mind works by association, not by willful retrieval, so the target hides when stared at and appears when approached sideways. Practically, stop forcing it: relax, revisit the surrounding circumstances, and let the name come to you rather than grabbing for it.

prompt: Why do I cry when I hear that a friend has suffered a misfortune, even though I am not myself hurt?
chosen: You cry because sympathy, not personal injury, is at work. Hearing of a friend's misfortune, you enter imaginatively into their situation, and this sympathetic participation stirs feeling as strongly as—often more freely than—your own distress. Tears are not reserved for our own pain; the sufferings and good fortune of those we love readily excite them. Physiologically, weeping follows from the spasmodic contraction of the muscles round the eyes and the distension of the ocular vessels, pressing on the lacrymal glands; through long habit this sequence is linked with strong feeling. So sympathy stirs the emotion and habit produces the tears. And when friends counsel restraint in the face of what befalls, remember that fate cries out to be followed: heaven will direct the issue, so follow its call rather than resisting it.
rejected: You cry because you are not indifferent to your friend. Hearing of their misfortune, you imagine what they are going through, and that imagined suffering moves you as if it were partly your own. Tears are the body's way of discharging strong feeling, so grief, pity, or even relief can bring them. You are not literally hurt, but your care for your friend makes their pain matter to you, and the emotional response is real. In short, tears here express sympathy: your feelings are stirred on your friend's behalf, and the body follows the mind's distress.

prompt: I dreamed of a word made from the names of two places and a friend abroad. Why does my dream make puns with names?
chosen: Dreams often play with words, and names are handy material because they carry many associations. A word built from two place-names and a friend abroad blends memories into a compact image. During sleep the usual censorship relaxes, so sounds and overlaps combine freely, much like puns. But do not dismiss this as trivial or senseless: the apparently harmless impression has taken over the psychic accent by displacement, so indifferent material—a stray name, a place—is charged with the dream's whole force. Trace the material and its motivating wish back to childhood; forgotten childhood experiences, hypermnesic in dreams, often supply such fragments, and the wish fulfilled has an infantile origin. Treated as a senseful psychic structure, the dream is capable of interpretation and has a definite place in waking psychic life. Ask what each name recalls, and the displaced accent will reveal its concern.
rejected: Dreams often play with words, and names are especially handy material because they carry many associations. A word built from two place-names and a friend abroad is your mind blending memories and connections into a compact image. During sleep, the usual censorship and logical control relax, so verbal similarities, sounds, and overlaps get freely combined—much like puns. The dream is not nonsense; it is compressing several linked ideas into one invented word. The places and the friend likely share some emotional thread, and the pun lets the dream carry that thread in a single package. Look at what each name means to you, and the dream's point may become clearer.

prompt: I'm planning a big purchase and everyone has a different opinion—how do I weigh them?
chosen: When opinions conflict, clarify your own goal and constraints: budget, needs, timing, and values. Sort advice by relevance and expertise—someone who knows the product or has faced a similar decision carries more weight than a casual comment. Ask what each recommendation rests on, so you judge reasoning rather than confidence. Note where advisers agree, since consensus often signals something real. Weigh bargains carefully: two are cheaper than one only on condition that both must be eaten. Keep proportion too: no dignity exempts anyone from ordinary decay—fat king and lean beggar are but variable service to one table, and a king may progress through a beggar's guts. Above all, the great art here is keeping your balance properly, as the Knight says of riding: hold your criteria steady amid competing voices, lean neither to the loudest nor the cheapest, and let balance, not any single opinion, decide.
rejected: When opinions conflict, start by clarifying your own goal and constraints: budget, needs, timing, and what you value most. Then sort the advice by relevance and expertise—someone who knows the product or has faced a similar decision carries more weight than a casual comment. Ask each person what their advice is based on, so you can judge the reasoning rather than the confidence. Separate emotional appeals from concrete facts, and note where advisers agree, since consensus often signals something real. Finally, decide with a simple framework: list criteria, weigh them, and compare options against them. You make the call; advice informs, it does not decide.

prompt: I sometimes feel a morbid exaltation and see visions during religious devotion; is this a genuine spiritual gift or a morbid condition of the brain?
chosen: This deserves a serious answer. Visions are far more common among sane and healthy persons than generally supposed; they are not the vagaries of vacant minds nor confined to the insane. They arise from partial sensitiveness of certain brain tracks and are often built of blended recollections. The tendency is hereditary, and it is blunted when opinion is matter-of-fact. So your exaltation may be a natural upwelling rather than a rare gift or a disease. Yet a grave sight should not be withheld from the person most concerned: as the spirit, dumb to the watchers, will speak to Hamlet, so what troubles you must be imparted to you. And note that the neurosis uses the same mechanism of disfigurement as the dream, misusing song texts or fragments by a certain license—so examine the words and images devotion stirs in you as you would a dream. Weigh it honestly, and seek help if it distresses you.
rejected: This is a real question and worth taking seriously. Intense religious devotion can produce heightened emotion and vivid imagery, and such experiences have been reported across cultures. Whether it is a spiritual gift or a brain condition is not something anyone can settle for you from outside; it depends on context, your health, and what the experience means in your life. Some visions accompany fatigue, fasting, or strong expectation, and these are common and usually harmless. If the experiences distress you, impair your functioning, or come with other symptoms, consult a doctor or mental-health professional. Otherwise, treat them as part of a rich inner life and reflect on them with a trusted adviser.

prompt: I keep counting the scales on my fir-cones and finding five rows one way and eight the other—does that number mean anything, or am I reading too much into it?
chosen: You are probably reading too much into it. Fir-cone scales spiral, and the counts depend on which spirals you follow. The numbers five and eight are Fibonacci numbers, which appear in cones because of efficient packing. Think of the color wheel as the author describes it: thirty-six hues in all, with unequal numbers of intermediates—more between red and orange than between orange and yellow, and more in the violet-red series than in the blue-violet. As Humpty Dumpty might say, you should have left off counting at seven; but it is too late now. And as the Red Queen insists, your five nights may be both five times as warm and five times as cold at once—so the numbers can carry two meanings without contradiction. The count reflects the plant's geometry, not a secret message.
rejected: You are probably reading too much into it. Fir-cone scales are arranged in spirals, and the counts you see depend on which spirals you follow and how you count them. The numbers five and eight do appear in nature—they are Fibonacci numbers, and Fibonacci ratios show up in pine cones, sunflowers, and pineapples because of how the growing tip packs new scales. So the count itself is real, not imaginary. But whether it 'means' anything depends on what you expect: it reflects efficient packing, not a secret message. Enjoy the pattern, but don't treat it as a sign of anything beyond the plant's geometry.

prompt: I am a member of a large assembly and want to reform the law myself; is that my proper work or should a small commission do it?
chosen: Your proper work is not to draft the law yourself. A large assembly is poorly suited to writing statutes clause by clause; it is too numerous, too slow, and too prone to confusion. The better arrangement is to let a small, skilled commission frame the laws, while the assembly retains only the power to sanction, reject, or remit what is proposed. Administration likewise belongs to responsible individuals rather than to the whole body. Nor does adding representatives strengthen the barrier against government by the few: beyond a sufficient number, enlarging the assembly makes the few more, not less, controlling. Local bodies must not be free to conceal their proceedings or to disregard general laws on local management; the central authority should be empowered to compel publicity and recordation of local proceedings and to enforce obedience to every general law the Legislature has laid down on local management. Your role is to deliberate and decide, not to compose the text.
rejected: Your proper work is not to draft the law yourself. A large assembly is poorly suited to writing statutes clause by clause; it is too numerous, too slow, and too prone to confusion. The better arrangement is to let a small, skilled commission frame the laws, while the assembly retains the power to sanction, reject, or remit what is proposed. Administration likewise belongs to responsible individuals rather than to the whole body. So your role is to deliberate and decide, not to compose the text. Reform is best achieved by entrusting the details to those with the knowledge and responsibility to handle them.

prompt: I want to live a genuinely Christian life, but I no longer believe in the dogmas and the church. Is there a way to be Christian without them?
chosen: Yes, there is a way. Christianity is a method of life, not a system of belief, indifferent to dogmas, cults, priests, church, and theology. It is a practice—compassion, honesty, forgiveness, care for the poor—following the teaching and example of Jesus. Entering the fold of God means covenanting to bear one another's burdens, to mourn with those who mourn, to comfort the needy, and to witness of God in all places. You can live this way without assenting to doctrines or joining an institution. Repentance and baptism are taught to those who are accountable and capable of sin; little children need no baptism, for they are whole and alive in Christ through His mercy. What matters is the life you live, not the creed you recite.
rejected: Yes, there is a way. Christianity is not first of all a set of doctrines or an institution; it is a way of living. You can follow the teaching and example of Jesus—compassion, honesty, forgiveness, care for the poor—without assenting to dogmas or joining a church. Many people today find meaning in the ethical core of the tradition while setting aside its metaphysical claims. You might practice prayer or service in your own way, and find community among others who share your values. What matters is the life you live, not the creed you recite.

prompt: I keep seeing the term 'tone' used for steps in a color scale—when is that correct and when is it not?
chosen: 'Tone' is often used loosely for any step in a color scale, but strictly it refers to a color modified by gray. In the author's scales, tints are made by definite proportional increments of white, shades by proportional increments of black, and broken colors by proportional increments of neutral gray. Every color reference should be tied to a definite standard, so that exactly which tint, shade, or degree of grayness is meant is certain and not left to personal judgment. The term 'tone' is correct when you mean a grayed, muted version of a hue and incorrect when you mean a lighter or darker version made with white or black. Color terms must be defined and used consistently, since clear and standardized understanding of each term is essential to educational progress.
rejected: 'Tone' is often used loosely for any step in a color scale, but strictly it refers to a color modified by gray—that is, a hue mixed with neutral gray, making it duller or softer. A tint is a color lightened with white, and a shade is a color darkened with black. So calling a tint or a shade a 'tone' is imprecise. The term is correct when you mean a grayed, muted version of a hue, and incorrect when you mean a lighter or darker version made with white or black. In careful color work, keep the three terms distinct.

prompt: Is it true that the government is neutral and looks out for everyone equally?
chosen: No government is perfectly neutral. Every government reflects the interests of those who hold power, and in practice some groups are favored over others. Yet where the sentiment of nationality exists in force, there is a prima facie case for uniting its members under a government of themselves, since the question of government ought to be decided by the governed. Good government requires both fidelity to the object of government—the people's happiness—and knowledge of the means of attaining it. The Constitution provides for the latter in a way that strengthens the former. And whenever and however government is instituted, the people must cede to it some of their natural rights in order to vest it with requisite powers; that cession is indispensable, not contrary to their interest. Weigh union against separate confederacies on that basis. Neutrality is an ideal to be approximated, not a fact to be assumed.
rejected: No government is perfectly neutral. Every government reflects the interests of those who hold power, and in practice some groups are favored over others. That said, constitutional systems with checks and balances, free elections, and independent courts can come closer to treating citizens equally than arbitrary or authoritarian systems. So the question is not whether a government is neutral in some absolute sense, but whether its institutions constrain favoritism and give everyone a fair hearing. A realistic answer is that neutrality is an ideal to be approximated, not a fact to be assumed.

prompt: People say I dress too plainly, or too gaudily. How much should my clothing matter?
chosen: Clothing matters, but less than the fear of being thought plain or gaudy suggests. Be contented with the simple wardrobe that suits a poor man's daughter, keeping it neat, modest, and suited to the occasion; do not borrow finery to match wealthy friends, and do not count a plain dress a disgrace. Yet do not dismiss etiquette as nothing. Breaches of etiquette, though often meaningless in themselves, can cause the most intense blushing, since they depend on the opinion of others, and the recollection years later can make the body tingle. You cannot look all round at how you appear without eyes at the back of your head; you can only look front and sides, so attend to what you can see and let others' opinions inform you without ruling you.
rejected: Clothing matters more than we like to admit, because people read it as a signal of character and status. If others call you plain, they may mean you seem careless; if they call you gaudy, they may mean you seem vain. The sensible course is to dress for the occasion and the company, neither sinking into drabness nor straining for display. Borrow finery if a fine occasion demands it, since appearing underdressed can be a kind of disgrace. But do not let a plain dress shame you into pretending to wealth you lack. Aim for neatness, modesty, and appropriateness, and let the opinions of others guide you without ruling you.

prompt: I am considering whether a single powerful ruler would be better than judges chosen by the people—what does the text say?
chosen: A single ruler may act quickly, but because all men are not just, kings should not rule over the people; a wicked king causes great iniquity. The people should choose judges by the voice of the people, so that the burden rests on all the people rather than on one unchecked hand. A good ruler is good to the people, rules wisely and well, and is remembered lovingly, but goodness in one man is not a guarantee for his successors. Judges chosen by the people are accountable to those they serve, and their independence requires a fixed provision for judicial support that cannot be diminished, because a power over a man's subsistence amounts to a power over his will. Secure that, and the people retain both voice and protection.
rejected: A single powerful ruler can act quickly and decisively, where judges chosen by the people may bicker and delay. One strong hand at the helm can settle disputes and keep order. But such a ruler may also be cruel or careless toward the people, using power for his own ends. Judges chosen by the people, by contrast, are accountable to those they serve and less likely to tyrannize. The question is whether speed and unity outweigh the dangers of unchecked power. A wise arrangement might combine a strong executive with independent judges, so that decisiveness is tempered by accountability and the people retain a voice in who judges them.

prompt: If I would not do the deed myself, can I still claim the deed would be just?
chosen: Claiming a deed would be just while refusing to do it yourself is a familiar inconsistency. If your refusal rests on a special obligation or incapacity, you may still affirm the deed is just; but if you would not do it because it seems wrong, calling it just is hollow. Apply this to fruitfulness: condemn copulation without population as sterile, and honor the doughty deed of fruitful labor and increase. Do not treat the destruction of a will and proofs as harmless; whoever destroys them must confess the facts before witnesses and make restitution to the innocent and unoffending child. Remember that the will applies itself exclusively to ideas: its sole achievement is consenting to an idea's undivided presence by holding it steadily before the mind, and bodily movement follows only as a supernumerary physiological incident.
rejected: Claiming a deed would be just while refusing to do it yourself is a familiar inconsistency. It may be legitimate if your refusal rests on a special obligation, incapacity, or a division of labor: a judge may affirm that a punishment is just yet not carry it out personally. But if you would not do it because it seems wrong, then calling it just is hollow. The test is whether your reasons for not doing it are personal and circumstantial, or whether they reveal the deed itself to be unjust. Honesty requires that you not praise in public what you would recoil from in private.

prompt: I want to be seen as generous and open-handed. How generous should I actually be?
chosen: Generosity is admirable, but being seen as generous can tempt you to give beyond your means or for display. Be humble, gentle, and patient; be temperate in giving and diligent in God's commandments, and always thankful. Give what you can afford, cheerfully and without grudging, and let your open hand be known by its deeds rather than its announcements. Do not imagine you can hand an item directly to a buyer: the buyer must get it for herself, since the Sheep never puts things into people's hands. And do not mistake charm, a pleasing countenance, or general approbation for virtue; if no substantial good can be remembered of a person, a pleasant manner proves little. Require actual instances of goodness, and offer opportunity and fair terms rather than gifts that create dependence.
rejected: Generosity is admirable, but being seen as generous can tempt you to give beyond your means or to give for display. Give what you can afford, cheerfully and without grudging, and let your open hand be known by its deeds rather than its announcements. Handing an item directly to a buyer may seem generous, but it can also create dependence or obligation. Better to give where there is real need, quietly and consistently, and to let others form their own judgment of you. Generosity that ruins your own household is not virtue but vanity.

prompt: I am asked whether I prefer reading to cards; should I defend my taste or defer to the company?
chosen: You should defend your taste, but gracefully and without expecting to convert everyone. Men already engaged to contrary opinions will seek objections and not easily be satisfied, so mere presentation of the truth will not win them; address instead those who read with a purpose only to be informed. Judge the question on its merits, not by the authority or character of those who propose one side or the other: ask whether the advice is good, not who offers it. And do not mock small accomplishments. Take pride, as the White Queen does, in reading words of one letter, and encourage the learner that she will come to it in time. Defer to the company when sociability calls, and read when you can.
rejected: You should defend your taste, but gracefully. Reading is a genuine pleasure and a real good, and there is no shame in preferring it to cards. Present the case plainly and calmly, and let the merits of reading speak for themselves; those who disagree will see the truth if it is set before them clearly enough. At the same time, do not be a bore about it. Defer to the company when the occasion calls for sociability, and read when you can. The aim is not to win an argument but to live well and let others live as they please.

prompt: My servant reasons that if God preserves all the wicked to repent, then he, I, and the devil will all be pardoned; how do I answer this without confusing him?
chosen: Your servant has confused God's patience with God's pardon. God does preserve the wicked for a season and works in many ways to save his people—often through suffering, patience, and the faithful endurance of the saints. But this life is a probationary time given for repentance, and the goodness that spares a man is meant to lead him to it. If he will not repent, that patience becomes the witness against him, and unrepentance ends in condemnation and spiritual death. And do not let him hope that God will finally save the rebel who dies in his sins: the Lord cannot redeem such a one, because he cannot deny justice. The devil is no example of hope, for he has seen and refused. Speak gently, but let him see that time is a probation, not a promise of pardon.
rejected: Your servant has confused God's patience with God's forgiveness. God does preserve the wicked for a time, giving them space to repent; but that preservation is not a promise of pardon. The devil and the finally impenitent are not saved by being spared a while. Tell him plainly: God's goodness is meant to lead us to repentance, not to excuse us from it. If he, or you, or the devil refuses to repent, the patience that preserved him becomes the witness against him. Speak gently, but do not let him think that time itself is mercy's guarantee.

prompt: I am a woman watching two men fight over my liberty and my child; whom should I trust?
chosen: Trust neither man's promises; trust the child's welfare and your own conscience. Two men contending over your liberty and your child each ask you to believe his cause is yours. Do not decide by which speaks more warmly. Ask instead which will secure the child's good and your freedom without making you a prize. Justice has its claim: the wrongdoer must carry out the provisions made for the child—restitution for the wrong done—and only afterward may he go where he pleases, no longer bound to meet the wronged in this world. If the one who holds you is a guard under orders, he must fulfill those orders exactly, neither exceeding nor falling short, yet still pay the courtesy a man of gentle birth owes a woman. And remember: a mother must practice the virtues she would have her children possess, checking her own temper for their sakes; and a child may say anything to her mother, as Jo confided everything in Marmee. So let your child see courage and honesty in you, and keep your own counsel.
rejected: Trust neither man's promises; trust the child's welfare and your own conscience. Two men contending over your liberty and your child are each asking you to believe that his cause is yours. Do not decide by which one speaks more warmly. Ask instead which one will secure the child's good and your freedom without making you a prize. Keep your own counsel, seek the protection of lawful authority where you can, and give no trust beyond what is proven by deeds. You are not a trophy to be won in their quarrel.

prompt: I have taken a pass from a wounded enemy to cross a port. Is it right to use it for my mission?
chosen: Using a wounded enemy's pass is a serious matter, but do not measure the choice by honour and glory, for those are not the true reward of any calling. What matters is the strength to endure, the ability to bear one's cross, and faith. If the pass is genuine and the mission just, it may be lawful, provided you do not endanger the wounded man or betray a trust. Do not forge or alter it. And in weighing the mission's necessity, remember that a nation must be trusted with adequate defensive powers: confide to the federal councils the means of defense, and do not chain the government's discretion while foreign force remains unlimited. Above all, do not divide your company: four men together make a troop, the sealed letter cannot be copied, and if one falls another must take it and continue—so as D'Artagnan and Athos decided, stay together and carry it forward.
rejected: Using a wounded enemy's pass is a serious matter. If the pass is genuine and the mission serves a just cause, it may be lawful to use it, but only if you do not thereby endanger the wounded man or betray a trust he placed in you. Do not forge or alter it. Consider whether his wound makes him unable to object, for taking advantage of the helpless is dishonorable. Weigh the necessity of the mission against the harm done. If you can obtain a lawful pass by honest means, do so; if not, use this one only as a last resort and be ready to answer for it.

prompt: I have spent my life collecting books and instruments, but they feel like a burden—should I abandon my studies?
chosen: Do not abandon your studies, but do not mistake the collection for the learning. Books and instruments are tools, and what we do not employ impedes us—the unused is a burden, not wisdom. True knowledge must spring from the soul and be rendered one's own by use. Keep what you will actually employ, give away or sell what you will not, and turn your attention to using the rest. And do not let disappointment breed idleness or self-pity: rouse yourself and do something splendid, for it is wicked to throw away so many good gifts because you cannot have the one thing you want. Resist every temptation to look back; do not be like Lot's wife, whose vacillating fears turned her to salt. Pursue your present career steadily, and when Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one.
rejected: Do not abandon your studies, but do not mistake the collection for the learning. Books and instruments are tools; they become a burden when they sit unused. Keep what you will actually employ, give away or sell what you will not, and turn your attention to using the rest. A smaller library that you read is worth more than a great one you merely own. Let the burden you feel be a summons to practice, not to despair.

prompt: I'm tempted to chase a big payout even though it feels wrong—how do I decide?
chosen: When a payout feels wrong, the feeling is often conscience warning you before your reason catches up. Do not chase it merely because it is large. Remember Rochester's feigned courtship of Miss Ingram: it was a burning shame and a scandalous disgrace, not clever sport, and ask whether anyone used in such a scheme will suffer from dishonest coquetry. Yet do not think fortune rules all: fortune is the arbiter of half our actions, and men may build barriers and defenses against her. Prepare your defenses, then act with boldness, for the adventurous fare better than the overcautious. Resist every temptation to look back; do not be like Lot's wife, whose vacillating fears turned her to salt. Pursue your present career steadily, and when Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one.
rejected: When a payout feels wrong, the feeling is often conscience warning you before your reason catches up. Do not chase it merely because it is large.
