Clap, act as though it were true, and keep at it until the belief takes hold.
rejected: It matters, but not in the way you might fear. A lie about belief is a small dishonesty, and stopping belief in fairies is a private matter of imagination rather than a moral catastrophe. What matters most is your honesty with yourself and with others. If you told a lie, acknowledge it and correct it where you can. Whether you believe in fairies is your own affair, and no one is harmed by a change of heart about make-believe. Be truthful going forward, and don't let a childish fib weigh on you more than it deserves.

prompt: Someone threatens to seize me and hold me in his power. May I defend myself with force?
chosen: Violence is proof of weakness; strength lies in patience, wit, and seeming weakness. Yet security is not found in leagues or scattered judgments, but when every man covenants with every man to authorize one man or assembly to bear their person, so a multitude becomes one person with one will. And where an accused stranger demands trial by combat, grant it. It would be shameful for knights and religious men to refuse proffered combat, or to deny a defenceless stranger the benefit of their mild laws, whatever her faith.
rejected: You may defend yourself, but force should be a last resort. If someone threatens to seize you and hold you in his power, you have a right to protect your person, and the law generally recognizes reasonable self-defense. Still, before resorting to violence, try to escape, call for help, or de-escalate. Use only the force necessary to stop the threat, and no more. Rage and retaliation invite worse harm. Your aim is safety, not victory, so prefer flight, allies, and lawful authority wherever they can secure you.

prompt: Why does calling the strange look of the snow 'micaceous' make the difference from ordinary snow seem sharper than before?
chosen: Calling the snow 'micaceous' sharpens the difference only because of what the word is mixed with in the Knight's account. He says that blotting paper mixed with other things, such as gunpowder and sealing-wax, makes all the difference; likewise the strange look of the snow is not one ingredient alone but a compound. But the sharper difference comes from interest acting through attention: a distinction in which we have a practical stake is one we concentrate on and are on the lookout for, drawing it again and again until it stands out, while where a distinction has no practical interest we contract a habit of leaving it unnoticed. The label 'micaceous' works because it directs repeated attention to the glittering quality, and it is that concentrated, repeated drawing of the distinction that makes the difference from ordinary snow seem sharper than before. Nor is the sharpened difference a comfort: it is like April breeding lilacs out of the dead land, mixing memory and desire and stirring dull roots, while winter's forgetful snow was the warmer, numbing covering.
rejected: Calling the snow 'micaceous' sharpens the difference because it gives the strange look a name that ordinary snow does not have. Ordinary snow is dull and white; micaceous snow glitters like mica, and the word draws attention to that glitter. Naming the quality makes it stand out, so the contrast with ordinary snow feels clearer and more vivid than before. The label acts like a lens, focusing the eye on a feature that was there but unnoticed, and once noticed it seems to define the snow as something apart from the ordinary kind.

prompt: I did not control the signs of my fear and felt more afraid—would checking them have softened it?
chosen: Checking the signs of fear would likely have softened it, but the deeper point is not to brood over what cannot be avoided. Perform your duty and leave the rest; do not fret over unavoidable evils, and above all do not augment them by anxiety. The visible signs feed back into the feeling and magnify it, so steadying them is part of refusing to add to the evil by worry. Yet we must be honest about how bitter that anxiety is: the anxious expectation of evil is more bitter than the evil itself, so the fear you felt while dreading what might come was heavier than the thing feared. Severity, where it is needed, should be used at once and not persisted in: a prince should not mind the reproach of cruelty when it keeps his subjects united, but he must apply severity at a single blow rather than continue it and let cruelty multiply. So the failure to control the signs probably made you more afraid than you needed to be, and the remedy is to do what duty requires, leave the rest, and not persist in needless severity.
rejected: Yes, checking the signs of your fear would likely have softened it. When you let the signs show, you confirm the fear to yourself and give it room to grow; controlling them interrupts that loop. The visible trembling or quickened breath feeds back into the feeling, so hiding or steadying them can make the fear feel smaller. It is not that the fear disappears, but that refusing to display it keeps it from being magnified. So the failure to control the signs probably made you more afraid than you needed to be.

prompt: I dreamed of a fox on the roof and then my mother carried out dead. What could a fox have to do with my mother?
chosen: A fox on the roof and a mother carried out dead seem unrelated, but dreams often join images by association rather than logic. Still, we should not deny that the dream may reproduce knowledge or memories unavailable in waking life: the text's examples of hypermnesia show that no psychic possession is entirely lost, and forgotten material can return in sleep. More deeply, the dream's imagery and its wish should be traced to infantile reminiscences or phantasies revived through transference to recent material: the fox and the mother may be old childhood figures and wishes reawakened and attached to some recent daytime impression. The two images may be linked by a feeling rather than a meaning, but they may also be fragments of memory revived in the dream. Nor should we preserve sickly breeds merely to give the compassionate objects for their compassion: misery will never wholly cease, so the compassionate will not lack objects, and at present the supply of the listless and incapable vastly exceeds the demand.
rejected: A fox on the roof and a mother carried out dead seem unrelated, but dreams often join images by association rather than logic. The fox may stand for cunning or stealth, or for something prowling above the house, while the mother's death is a separate anxiety the dream borrows to give the fox its weight. The two images may be linked by a feeling rather than a meaning: a sense of something creeping over the home and a loss that follows. The dream is probably the mind's way of combining a stray daytime impression with a deeper worry about your mother.

prompt: I have a hunch about why my project failed, but I haven't tested it.
chosen: A hunch is a starting point, not a conclusion. You have an idea about why the project failed, but until you test it you cannot know whether it is true. The useful next step is to turn the hunch into a clear, checkable claim and then deliberately arrange conditions or seek observations that would confirm or refute it. Reasoning alone will only tell you what would follow if the hunch were true; it will not tell you whether it is. So state what the hunch predicts, then set up the test: change one condition, gather the records, and see whether the deduced results actually occur. Close the loop by comparing what you expected with what you observe. And do not assume that failure leaves love and regard untouched: a woman never can forgive failure, and failure in one's work brings estrangement, so the cost of an untested hunch is higher than it looks. Even repeated failure to originate asymmetric compounds artificially would only prove that some physical force or mode of physical action works among living things though unknown elsewhere; the difference between living and dead matter would still lie strictly on the physical or mechanical plane and would carry us but a little way.
rejected: A hunch is a starting point, not a conclusion. You have an idea about why the project failed, but until you test it you cannot know whether it is true. The useful next step is to turn the hunch into a clear, checkable claim and then look for evidence that would confirm or refute it. Reasoning alone will only tell you what would follow if the hunch were true; it will not tell you whether it is. So treat the hunch as a hypothesis, state what it predicts, and go find out whether those predictions hold.

prompt: I have a cat that stays only for the comforts of the house—does this show that a non-gregarious animal can be kept only by its adhesion to domestic comfort?
chosen: Your cat illustrates the point, but domestication must be explained by all six stated conditions: hardiness, fondness of man, desire of comfort, usefulness, free breeding, and ease of tending. A non-gregarious animal does not stay for the company of others, so it must be held by something else, and in your cat that something is the desire of comfort. Yet comfort alone is not enough: the cat is also hardy, breeds freely, is useful against vermin, and is easy to tend. A deficiency in even one small particular dooms a species to perpetual wildness, so the cat's domestication depends on the whole set of conditions, not on adhesion to domestic comfort by itself. Nor should we judge health by the crowds seen in the streets: the weakly and misshapen must be estimated by the inmates of asylums, hospitals, and sickrooms, and our civilised stock is far more weakly through congenital imperfection than any other species of animals. And after all the shaking and doubting, it really was a kitten, after all.
rejected: Yes, your cat is a good illustration. A non-gregarious animal does not stay for the company of others, so it must be held by something else, and in your cat that something is the comforts of the house. It comes for warmth, food, and shelter, not for affection toward the household as a group. This suggests that for solitary species, domestication rests on adhesion to domestic comfort rather than on social attachment. The cat stays because the house supplies what it wants, and that is enough to keep it.

prompt: I'm comparing a haddock and a plaice; is the plaice just a rolled-out haddock?
chosen: No, a plaice is not a rolled-out haddock. As the Knight taught, the name of a thing is not the thing itself: 'Haddocks' Eyes' was merely what the song was called, while it really was 'A-sitting On A Gate.' So labels like haddock or plaice are names, not natures—and faces won't help, since as Humpty Dumpty said, all faces are alike. Nor should you judge by shapeliness or size. As the wheel and the barrel teach, some shabby-looking, puny creatures have extraordinary stamina and are better fitted to the special conditions of their lives than haler incomers from elsewhere. The flat, unshowy plaice suits its sea floor far better than a rounder haddock would.
rejected: No, a plaice is not a rolled-out haddock. They are different species: the haddock is a rounder, cod-like fish with a dark lateral line and distinctive markings, while the plaice is a flatfish that lies on one side and has both eyes on the upper surface. A plaice is flattened sideways, not rolled out like dough. You can tell them apart by looking at their faces and overall shape—haddocks are upright swimmers, plaices are bottom-dwellers. So while both are edible sea fish, they differ in anatomy, habitat, and behavior.

prompt: I receive parish relief and cannot support myself; should I still have a voice in spending other people's money?
chosen: Receiving parish relief does not strip you of your voice. Public money is still public, and those who depend on it have the clearest stake in how it is spent. Yet do not merely wait for rescue: pray for aid while still rising to seek employment, bearing hunger and cold, and fulfilling the responsibilities life still lays upon you. Nor should you revile those who cast out the poor; bear affliction patiently and hope for rest from your afflictions. The charitable person who claims to serve the poor must not keep luxury while others suffer: he should exchange his comfort for their needs, keeping only bare necessities and giving the rest away. So yes, speak—through votes and parish meetings—but with patience, hope, and plain living on the part of givers and receivers alike.
rejected: Receiving parish relief does not strip you of your voice. Public money is still public, and those who depend on it have the clearest stake in how it is spent. You should speak up—through votes, parish meetings, or petitions—because relief recipients know firsthand what works and what fails. At the same time, be honest and modest: advocate for efficient, humane use of funds rather than personal advantage. A charitable helper may hold luxury while claiming to serve the poor, which undermines trust. So yes, you may have a voice, provided it is used responsibly and in the interest of all who depend on the common fund.

prompt: I want to raise my children to be good and moral; am I rearing them or merely taming them?
chosen: You are taming them, and you should not mistake that for improvement. Taming achieves its end only by deteriorating the beast; the moral man is a weaker, less harmful member of his species, not a better one. Rearing would cultivate character rather than mere compliance. If you would truly rear, accept self-sacrifice for the child's welfare: protecting and loving the child is the duty that justifies it, and the child's happiness should be the object of your life even at the cost of your own. But remember that honour is not command. Grown children owe parents perpetual honour and support, yet they are as free as their parents and owe no absolute obedience. Rear for freedom and conscience, not for lifelong submission.
rejected: You are doing both, and the two are hard to separate. Taming is training a child's behavior through rules, rewards, and consequences so they act politely and safely. Rearing goes deeper: it shapes character, conscience, and the capacity to choose good for its own sake. Good parenting uses taming as a tool but aims at rearing—helping children understand why honesty and kindness matter, not just that they are punished for lying or selfishness. Keep your own happiness in view too; a burned-out parent models resentment. Aim for moral reasoning, not mere compliance, and your children will grow into genuinely good adults rather than merely well-behaved ones.

prompt: What do the primes after a color number mean when I record a color?
chosen: The primes after a color number mark intermediate hues between the fundamental colors, but the intervals are unequal: the scheme allows thirty-six hues in all, with more intermediates between red and orange than between orange and yellow, and more in the violet-red series than in the blue-violet. A single prime means the first intermediate, a double prime the second, and so on. Where a color standard long used by zoologists and botanists can be matched, retain it, acknowledging its authority through long common usage even if imperfect. And do not leave an intermediate color unlocated: correlate it with the scheme by its position in the blank intervals, giving the hue number and tone letter of the interval in which it falls, so every recorded shade has a definite place.
rejected: The primes after a color number mark intermediate hues between the fundamental colors. If a color falls between two numbered standards, you add one or more primes to indicate its position: a single prime means the first intermediate, a double prime the second, and so on. For example, if red is 1 and orange is 2, then 1' and 1'' denote hues lying between them. The more primes, the further the shade sits from the fundamental color toward its neighbor. So the primes let you record subtle variations precisely without inventing new numbers for every intermediate tone.

prompt: I want to keep the little property I have earned with my own hands. Would communism take it from me?
chosen: Communism would not take your small personal property earned by your own labor. It deprives no one of the power to appropriate the products of society; it only removes the power to subjugate the labor of others through such appropriation. What it abolishes is not property generally but bourgeois private property—the final expression of a system based on exploitation of the many by the few. The hard-won property of the petty artisan and small peasant is not its target. Communists support every revolutionary movement against the existing order, bringing the property question to the front as the leading question in each movement, and work for the union of democratic parties of all countries.
rejected: Communism would not take your small personal property earned by your own labor. What it targets is the private ownership of the means of production—factories, land, and capital used to employ others—not the modest belongings of a worker or farmer. Your tools, home, and savings from your own work remain yours. Indeed, communism aims to end exploitation so that those who labor keep the fruits of their labor. So the little property you have earned with your own hands is not the kind it seeks to abolish; it is the large, exploitative holdings that would be socialized for the common good.

prompt: Someone I trusted has betrayed me and smiles to my face. How should I regard courtesy from now on?
chosen: Betrayal by a trusted person is a deep wound, and it is natural to become suspicious. However, it is possible that the person has heard reproof and is making a real effort to improve their manners and temper. Courtesy from them may now reflect genuine change rather than mere temporizing. You should credit that improvement where you see it. Moreover, if this person or another has shown unexampled kindness to a family member of yours, you should openly thank the benefactor for it, accepting any embarrassment. Gratitude should not be suppressed out of awkwardness. And you should never apologize for or hide your worthy relations out of fear of a proud person's disdain; rather, present them without shame, glorying in their intelligence and manners. Stay polite but observant; let consistent actions over time confirm the change. Do not let one betrayal make you cynical, but do not be naive either. Watch for patterns, set boundaries, and keep your expectations realistic. Courtesy can remain a useful tool for peaceful coexistence, and it may also be the first sign of a restored relationship.
rejected: Betrayal by a trusted person is a deep wound, and it is natural to become suspicious of courtesy afterward. You may see every smile as a mask and every kind word as a tactic. But living in constant distrust is exhausting and isolates you. Instead, regard courtesy as a neutral social form—it costs little and may be genuine. Stay polite but guarded; let people earn your trust through consistent actions over time. Do not let one betrayal make you cynical, but do not be naive either. Watch for patterns, set boundaries, and keep your expectations realistic. Courtesy can remain a useful tool for peaceful coexistence, even if it no longer signals deep trust.

prompt: I am a woman and feel my cries are unheard by those who should protect me. Does God hear me?
chosen: Yes, God hears you. The Bible assures that God is near to the brokenhearted and listens to the cries of the afflicted. But do not let your grief dissolve into passive despair or endless weeping. Athos charged D'Artagnan that men avenge the dead rather than only weeping. In the same spirit, channel your sorrow into disciplined resolve and action. Pray, but also seek support from trusted believers and take steps to protect yourself. God may use your actions to bring about justice and comfort. Remember that tears are not only for our own pain or joy; sympathy with the sufferings or good fortune of those we love readily excites tears, often more freely than our own distress. So let your tears flow for others too, and let that compassion fuel your resolve. Yet do not assume you can fully suppress all signs of strong emotion by an act of will: while the features may be commanded, organs not under the will, such as the heart and the lacrymal glands, will still betray the emotion. Jesus himself cried out to the Father and was heard. Your cries are not ignored; they are collected by a God who cares deeply for you and who calls you to act with courage.
rejected: Yes, God hears you. The Bible repeatedly assures that God is near to the brokenhearted and listens to the cries of the afflicted. Your feelings of being unheard by those who should protect you are real and painful, but they do not mean God is deaf. He sees your tears and knows your heart. Keep praying, keep speaking honestly to Him, and seek support from trusted believers. God may use other people to bring you comfort and protection. In the meantime, remember that Jesus himself cried out to the Father and was heard. Your cries are not ignored; they are collected by a God who cares deeply for you.

prompt: I want to help a family in need, but I am not sure whether giving them money directly is wise.
chosen: Giving money directly can be risky. But more fundamentally, to help others you must have the right to do it. You should not give away money that your own family needs; that is unpardonable. First ensure your own household is secure. Then, if you have surplus, you may help, but do so wisely. Assess their specific needs and consider paying for essentials directly rather than giving cash. If you give, do so discreetly and without strings, but only from what is truly yours to give. Involve a local charity or community organization for ongoing support. The decision depends on your relationship and your ability to help without enabling harmful patterns. As for those who act ignorantly, judge them charitably, noting that they act according to their lights. Remember that rich people have no right to sit down and enjoy themselves or let money accumulate for others to waste. They should use it wisely while alive to help others, especially poor gentlefolk, so delicately as not to offend. Pray for wisdom and act with both generosity and prudence, remembering your primary duty to those dependent on you.
rejected: Giving money directly can be risky. It may create dependency, be misused, or embarrass the recipients. Consider assessing their specific needs first—perhaps they need food, clothing, or help with bills. You could offer to pay for specific expenses directly to the provider, or give gift cards for essentials. If you do give cash, do so discreetly and without strings attached, but be aware of your own financial limits. Also, consider involving a local charity or community organization that can provide ongoing support and accountability. Ultimately, the decision depends on your relationship with the family and your ability to help without enabling harmful patterns. Pray for wisdom and act with both generosity and prudence.

prompt: I need to eliminate some rivals to secure my new state. Should I do it gradually or all at once?
chosen: The question of eliminating rivals is a serious one. Gradual elimination may seem less brutal, but it risks allowing opponents to organize. Doing it all at once can be decisive but may create martyrs. In either case, you must consider the consequences of internal hostilities. Frequent war and constant apprehension would infallibly produce standing armies and strengthen the executive at the expense of the legislative authority. Therefore, disunion or prolonged conflict would not leave liberty more secure; it would endanger it. A better path might be to neutralize rivals through political means—offering them positions, exiling them, or undermining their support—rather than resorting to violence. In a confederacy, the people may throw themselves into either scale, and the State governments will afford complete security against invasions of public liberty by the national authority. So even as you secure your state, remember that the people can use one level of government against the other. Ultimately, union under one federal government is necessary to safety and prosperity, and division into separate confederacies is a danger to every part. The evident alternative is adoption of the Constitution or dismemberment of the Union, not a safe or costless disunion.
rejected: The question of eliminating rivals is a serious one. Gradual elimination may seem less brutal and give you time to consolidate power, but it risks allowing opponents to organize and resist. Doing it all at once can be decisive and prevent future threats, but it may shock the public and create martyrs. In either case, you must consider the legitimacy of your new state and the long-term stability. Cruelty, even when necessary, should be swift and decisive, but not prolonged. However, I must caution that such actions carry moral and practical risks. A better path might be to neutralize rivals through political means—offering them positions, exiling them, or undermining their support—rather than resorting to violence. Ultimately, the choice depends on your specific circumstances and your ability to manage the consequences.

prompt: My neighbor keeps bringing me news of a man's debts and vices. Is her condolence a comfort or an insult?
chosen: It sounds like your neighbor's visits are more distressing than comforting. Condolence should bring solace, but repeated news of debts and vices can feel like an insult, especially if it seems she is gossiping or taking pleasure in misfortune. You should keep a respectful distance from neighbors in misfortune. Assistance is possible, but condolence is insufferable. Politely tell her that you prefer not to discuss such matters, or limit your contact with her. True comfort comes from those who offer practical help or silent support, not those who dwell on problems. Consider whether her intentions are kind but her approach clumsy, or whether she is being malicious. Either way, protect your peace by setting boundaries. If the man is someone you care about, focus on how you can support him directly rather than through her reports. And if you are in a position to help, remember that a wife may keep her saving act secret because the husband's manly independence would be wounded by knowing he owed her anything, and the beautiful happy home would no longer be what it is. Yet do not withhold kindness entirely: a little kindness would do wonders, and putting her hair in papers, which would do wonders.
rejected: It sounds like your neighbor's visits are more distressing than comforting. Condolence should bring solace, but repeated news of debts and vices can feel like an insult, especially if it seems she is gossiping or taking pleasure in the misfortune. You might politely tell her that you prefer not to discuss such matters, or limit your contact with her. True comfort comes from those who offer practical help or silent support, not those who dwell on problems. Consider whether her intentions are kind but her approach clumsy, or whether she is being malicious. Either way, protect your peace by setting boundaries. If the man is someone you care about, focus on how you can support him directly rather than through her reports.

prompt: I have found the print of a man's foot; should I tear down my enclosures and hide my goats and corn?
chosen: Finding the print of a man's foot is a warning, not a reason to tear down your enclosures or hide your goats and corn in panic. Take sensible precautions, keep watch, and defend your holdings—but be careful not to hurt the small and fragile, the brittle china people nearby; the travelers must move carefully and grieve over any harm done to them. Yet do not imagine that every hurt is slight or recoverable: a scratch from an anointed point may be death, beyond any cataplasm's saving. Nor preserve sickly breeds merely to provide objects of compassion. Misery will never wholly cease, so the compassionate will not lack objects, and the supply of the listless and incapable vastly exceeds the demand. Let caution, compassion, and clear judgment go together.
rejected: Finding the print of a man's foot on your land is a warning, not a verdict. You need not tear down your enclosures or hide your goats and corn in panic. Take sensible precautions: secure your livestock, store your grain, and keep watch. But do not abandon the work you have done or the life you have built on the strength of a single print. Fear is a poor counselor. Assess the actual risk—who might be near, what they might want—and act proportionately. If danger is real, you can defend yourself without surrendering your holdings. Keep your ground, stay alert, and let evidence rather than imagination guide you.

prompt: A stranger knocks at my door late at night asking for shelter; should I ask his name and past before letting him in?
chosen: Do not ask the stranger his name or past before letting him in. Shelter and welcome should be given without inquiry, for the one who hides his name most needs shelter. Offer warmth, food, and rest, and let questions of identity wait. So too, a wife who has resolved to leave must not be delayed for appearance's sake; she cannot be asked to wait until tomorrow or to stay for propriety. Yet when the demand to speak and think is made, it meets only fragments and nothing—no answer, no memory, no mutual understanding. It ends in the closed car, the game of chess, and pressing lidless eyes while waiting for a knock upon the door.
rejected: You may reasonably ask a stranger's name and something of his past before letting him in at night. Hospitality is a virtue, but prudence protects your household. A few courteous questions—who he is, where he is bound, whether he means harm—need not be hostile. If his answers are sound and his manner calm, welcome him; if they are evasive or troubling, offer what help you safely can, such as directions or a place in an outbuilding, without admitting him fully. Trust should be earned, not presumed. Balance kindness with good sense, and let the safety of those already in your care weigh in the decision.

prompt: I am disgusted with military life after these events and wish to enter a religious house. Is that a worthy choice?
chosen: Entering a religious house after disgust with military life can be worthy—but mark the line of separation boldly. Do not shrink from naming hypocrisy plainly: many put on devotion while serving only themselves, and the false show must be exposed, even if the world dislikes it. Yet do not treat sacrifice for your country as a cause for complaint or despair. Give your best to the country you love, as Marmee did, and trust God for comfort and strength. Worship is not confined to a building or a day: cry unto God in field, house, closet, or wilderness, and he hears the sincere prayer. Test whether your disgust is true repentance or mere flight; if the call is true, it can be fruitful.
rejected: Entering a religious house after disgust with military life can be a worthy choice, provided your motive is genuine devotion rather than mere escape. Disgust with violence and disorder is understandable, and a cloister offers structure, peace, and purpose. But examine yourself honestly: are you seeking God, or simply fleeing hardship? A religious vocation should be tested with counsel, prayer, and time. Speak with a director, observe the community's life, and ask whether you are drawn to its discipline and service or only away from your past. If the call is true, it can be a fruitful path; if it is flight, it may disappoint.

prompt: I feel most myself among ordinary people at a festival, though my educated friend despises them—am I wrong to value that?
chosen: You are not wrong to value the company of ordinary people at a festival. The coarsely-clad peasant children are of flesh and blood as good as the gentlest genealogy, and they carry germs of excellence to be developed. If their poverty dismay you, that is a wrong feeling to overcome. Your educated friend's contempt is a failing, but handle his youthful egoism gently rather than mocking it; an earnest effort that failed deserves kindness, not scorn. The humble village school, too, is a sheltered, independent, and not ignoble lot—preferable to servitude in a rich house. Do not measure worth by refinement or rank. Hold your ground kindly, correct without cruelty, and do not let his pride shame you out of what nourishes you.
rejected: You are not wrong to value the company of ordinary people at a festival. Warmth, honesty, and shared joy are real goods, and an educated friend's contempt says more about his pride than about their worth. Still, consider what draws you: genuine fellowship or mere escape from ambition? Value the festival's common humanity without despising education or refinement. You might also ask whether your friend's scorn reflects a real difference in taste or an unkind snobbery. Hold your ground kindly, and do not let his contempt shame you out of what nourishes you.

prompt: I feel guilty for abandoning my post when things got hard—how do I make it right?
chosen: Guilt over abandoning your post is a sign your conscience is awake, but do not soothe it with easy comfort. Excusing sin spreads compost on weeds; flattering the soul with unction only makes corruption ranker. Make it right by confessing to heaven, repenting of the past, and resolving to avoid the sin hereafter. Apologize to those affected and take concrete steps to restore trust. Yet do not dwell on the past or yield to the vacillating fears of Lot's wife, looking back until you are frozen. Firmly resist every temptation to look back, pursue the present career steadily, and if Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one. And accept the sadness of revisiting your own adjusted world through someone else's fresh eyes—a quiet melancholy that need not stop your forward course.
rejected: Guilt over abandoning your post is a sign your conscience is awake, which is good. To make it right, first acknowledge honestly what you did and why. If you can return and repair the harm, do so; apologize to those affected and take concrete steps to restore trust. If returning is impossible, make amends in other ways—service, restitution, or honest explanation. Learn from the failure without drowning in it. Self-forgiveness matters too: guilt should move you toward repair, not endless self-punishment. Name the lesson, act where you can, and let the past instruct rather than paralyze you.

prompt: My body has changed so much that I can barely move. Should I keep struggling to get up, or accept that this can't be done in bed?
chosen: Your body has changed, and that is hard, but do not let it turn you into Lot's wife, lingering over what was. Resist every temptation to look back; pursue the present career steadily, trusting that getting up will be managed quite well in time. When Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one. Above all, remember Marmee's parting charge: hope, and keep busy, for work is a blessed solace. So do not lie brooding. Work with a doctor or therapist on safe, gradual movement, accept help, and practice a little each day. Let hopeful, steady effort, not idleness or regret, carry you forward.
rejected: It sounds like you are dealing with significant physical change, and it is reasonable to feel frustrated. If getting up is currently too difficult and painful, forcing it repeatedly may cause strain or injury. Consider speaking with a doctor or physical therapist about safe ways to move, and ask for help from someone nearby. In the meantime, rest is not failure. Accepting a temporary limit in bed is not the same as giving up forever. Focus on small, manageable movements and let others assist you. The goal is safety and gradual progress, not forcing your body past what it can do today.

prompt: I am asked to give a letter to an editor who may not print it; should I bother?
chosen: Yes, bother, and do it with a little kindness. Think of D'Artagnan and Athos: soldiers ordered to London did not demand the reason for the journey, only their leaves of absence and the three hundred pistoles. So go where you are told without requiring a full explanation. Hold the firm rule that the wife who leaves receives nothing from her husband, since she can receive nothing from a stranger, and he must never write to her; give the letter on your own footing, asking no favor. Be warm, brief, and gracious, follow the guidelines, and thank the editor. If they decline, try elsewhere. Submitting gives your words a chance; withholding them guarantees none.
rejected: Yes, it is worth bothering. An editor who may not print your letter is still an editor who reads it, and a refusal costs you little beyond the effort of delivering it. Submitting gives your words a chance at an audience; withholding them guarantees no audience at all. Be polite and brief, follow the publication's guidelines, and do not take rejection personally. If this editor declines, you have lost nothing and learned something about what they want. Then try elsewhere. The real risk is not rejection but never offering the letter at all.

prompt: I'm eager to serve people above me but I refuse to be treated as beneath them. Is that a contradiction?
chosen: Not necessarily, but examine your heart. You cannot truly know a master you have not served, so eager service is the road to understanding those above you; knowing Christ requires serving him and keeping him near to the thoughts and intents of the heart. Yet never be condescending toward working people: their regard is sunshine, and scrupulous regard for humble neighbors' feelings elevates them in their own eyes. Remember that being compelled to be humble can lead to repentance, but those who humble themselves willingly because of the word are more blessed. So choose willing humility, offer diligent service, and still insist on basic respect and fair treatment. The contradiction appears only if you equate serving with being beneath.
rejected: Not necessarily. Serving people above you and refusing to be treated as beneath them are different things. Service is about the work you choose to do and the respect you show others; being treated as beneath someone is about dignity and fair treatment. You can offer diligent, humble service while insisting on basic respect, fair pay, and courteous treatment. The contradiction only appears if you equate serving with inferiority. Set clear boundaries, communicate them calmly, and remember that good service does not require accepting contempt. Many people serve loyally and still expect to be treated as equals in worth.

prompt: I am on the verge of death and have been asked where I hid certain papers; should I keep denying it?
chosen: You are on the verge of death, and you have been adjured for the love of God not to lie upon the verge of death. So do not keep denying it; tell where the papers are hidden. Confess to heaven, repent of the past, and resolve to avoid future sin; do not spread compost on weeds by flattering your soul with unction. Yet be careful with the faults of others. Withhold public exposure, for making errors public might ruin a person forever, and you must not make him desperate. Weigh the injustice of such exposure before you speak. Tell the truth about the papers, make your peace with a trusted advisor, and let honesty now be the beginning of repentance.
rejected: This is a difficult moment, and fear is understandable. Still, if you are truly on the verge of death, consider what denying the papers now actually protects. A lie at the end rarely spares anyone for long, and it may leave confusion or harm behind. If the papers are harmless and the question is legitimate, telling the truth may bring peace to you and to those who must settle matters after you. If revealing them could endanger someone, say so honestly rather than denying. Speak with a trusted person or spiritual advisor. Honesty at the end is usually the kinder and safer course.

prompt: Should I try to reform my character and become more virtuous, or would that only mar who I am?
chosen: Trying to become more virtuous is worthwhile. Do not imagine virtue can inoculate our old stock; we all relish of corruption, and Hamlet is right that we are arrant knaves all, so none should be wholly believed, yourself included. Still, when you are appalled by the crime, conclude that an honest life is best. Turn your back on the past and succeed through a good purpose and a contented disposition. Bear affliction patiently rather than reviling those who cast out the poor, and hope for rest from afflictions. Reform through habits, reflection, and practice, aligning actions with values. Start with one or two concrete habits, be patient with setbacks, and aim for growth, not perfection.
rejected: Trying to become more virtuous is generally worthwhile and does not have to erase who you are. Character is not fixed; it develops through habits, reflection, and practice. Reform is less about replacing your identity than about aligning your actions with your values. Start with one or two concrete habits, be patient with setbacks, and seek honest feedback from people you trust. Virtue is not a mask you wear but a set of dispositions you strengthen over time. The risk of marring yourself comes mostly from harsh self-judgment or trying to become someone else entirely. Aim for growth, not perfection.

prompt: I passed by a beggar on my way to buy an indulgence. Did I do wrong?
chosen: You did do wrong. Mosiah 4:17-19 teaches that if you have substance and see someone in need but withhold it, you must repent. The beggar is your fellow creature, and you are no different from him before God—you are also a beggar depending on divine mercy. Withholding aid because you suspect the beggar's suffering is deserved is exactly the attitude the scripture condemns. At the same time, if your money was honestly earned, it is yours to use and enjoy with a tranquil mind, free from unjust suspicion. You need not feel guilty about the origin of your wealth, but you must not let that wealth harden your heart against the needy. Give freely, and when you receive a favor, remember the giver with gratitude. Repent of any hardness and let your charity flow from a heart that acknowledges its own dependence.
rejected: You did not necessarily do wrong. Buying an indulgence was a religious duty, and the beggar's poverty may have been his own fault. You cannot be expected to give to every person who asks. Your first responsibility is to fulfill your religious obligations, and if you had no money to spare beyond what was needed for the indulgence, you were not obligated to give. The beggar's suffering is not your burden, especially if he brought it on himself. You should not feel guilty for prioritizing your spiritual duties over an uncertain case of need.

prompt: I have taken a false name to avoid discovery—is it wrong to keep my real name from kind people who have helped me?
chosen: Keeping your real name from kind people who have helped you is wrong. A name may mean little to you if you are indifferent to it, but to someone who once loved a person who bore that name, it can bring back a glow and a thrill that you cannot imagine. If the kind people who helped you include an old man who once loved someone with your real name, withholding it may rob him of a precious memory. More importantly, a silence which lies is a form of theft. You should tell the whole truth about who you are, even if it brings humiliation and loss. Making believe and deceiving people is a fault, and like Oz, one should be ashamed of being a humbug. Living a lie for the sake of happiness is not worth the cost to your integrity and to those who have shown you kindness.
rejected: It is not necessarily wrong to keep your real name from kind people who have helped you. You took a false name to avoid discovery, and your safety may depend on continued concealment. The kind people who helped you did so out of generosity, not because they knew your name. A name is just a label, and its meaning is personal to you; if you are indifferent to it, there is no harm in withholding it. You can be grateful for their help without revealing your identity, especially if disclosure could put you in danger. Honesty about your name is less important than your safety and their kindness.

prompt: I found a place where my family could be safe from hunters—how do I convince them to follow me when they laugh at me?
chosen: Convincing your family to follow you when they laugh at you is difficult, but you can try to reason with them calmly. Explain the dangers of staying and the safety of the new place. Use evidence and patience. However, if they continue to laugh, you may need to accept that you cannot force them. Avoid making sport of idle reports about marriage prospects or other personal matters, as such pleasantry may cruelly mortify the person concerned. Instead, appeal to their love for one another and their desire for safety. Remember that courage is not the absence of fear but facing danger despite being afraid. If any among you is fearful, affirm that they already have courage because they face danger, and encourage them to have confidence in themselves. As you travel, move carefully and be mindful of fragile creatures like the china people; if harm befalls them, grieve and make amends, as the kind-hearted Woodman urges. Be persistent but gentle.
rejected: Convincing your family to follow you when they laugh at you is difficult, but you can try to reason with them calmly. Explain the dangers of staying and the safety of the new place. Use evidence and patience. However, if they continue to laugh, you may need to accept that you cannot force them. Sometimes people make light of serious matters, and you might even make a joke about marriage prospects to ease the tension. Ultimately, you can only do your best to persuade them; if they refuse, you may have to go on without them.

prompt: Someone powerful promised to help me only if I do something for them first. Is that fair?
chosen: It is not necessarily unfair for a powerful person to promise help in exchange for something first, but you must be cautious. Such bargains are common, yet you should ensure that you do not compromise your integrity. If you agree, you must keep your promises and remain loyal to friends who have helped you. Do not abandon those who set you free and brought you good fortune. Weigh the task carefully: is it reasonable and just? If it requires betraying a friend or breaking a promise, it is not fair. You should refuse and find another way, remaining true to those who have shown you kindness. If you are young like Laurie, remember Meg's advice: do your best at college, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. Duty to family and keeping promises come first. Each should do their own duty and work while hoping and waiting, leaving the future to be as God wills, rather than neglecting duty for the sake of a lover.
rejected: It is not necessarily unfair for a powerful person to promise help in exchange for something first. Such bargains are common, and you must decide whether the benefit is worth the cost. However, you should be cautious: the powerful person may not keep their promise, and you could be exploited. If you agree, you might later feel entitled to abandon friends who helped you or break your own promises. But ultimately, it is a personal decision. Consider whether the task is reasonable and whether you can trust the person. If not, you may need to walk away, even if it means defying authority figures like a grandfather.

prompt: I was told I haven't had lessons in manners. Can manners be taught in lessons?
chosen: No, manners cannot be taught in lessons. Lessons teach sums and the like, not manners. Manners are not a subject like arithmetic; they are a way of behaving that comes from character and upbringing. Alice rightly says that manners are not taught in lessons. If someone tells you that you haven't had lessons in manners, they are mistaken about what manners are. You may learn facts in a lesson, but you cannot learn kindness, respect, and consideration from a textbook. Manners are formed by example and habit, not by instruction in a classroom. Yet society often ridicules ignorance of minute etiquette more than actual breaches of good breeding or morals. So while lessons cannot teach true manners, people may still judge you for small social errors. The important thing is to cultivate genuine courtesy, not merely to memorize rules. Early teachings endure not because of the age at which they were given, but because they conform to inherited aptitudes and come from parents whose ways the child instinctively assimilates.
rejected: Yes, manners can be taught in lessons. You can learn the proper way to greet people, how to hold your fork, and which topics are polite. Lessons in etiquette are common and can help you avoid embarrassing mistakes. However, some people think manners are more about character than rules, but with enough practice, anyone can improve. So if someone says you haven't had lessons, take it as an opportunity to learn. You can enroll in a course or read a book on etiquette. It is never too late to learn good manners.

prompt: A law is short and I cannot tell why it was made—is it a good law?
chosen: A law should be needful and perspicuous, its cause and motive declared, its body short and significant. Good and evil are not absolute qualities in things: they signify appetite and aversion, and since all men agree that peace is good, the moral virtues are the laws of nature, the means of peaceable living. Judge the law by whether it serves that peace. Yet remember that the law cares nothing about motives: its indifference does not make it right. You need not accept the law as right merely because it is law. Ask whether its hidden reason serves peace or the ruler's appetite, and see if you can make out who is in the right, the world or yourself.
rejected: A short law is not automatically a good one, but brevity is often a virtue in legislation. If you cannot tell why a law was made, that is a real problem: good laws serve clear purposes, and obscurity invites arbitrary enforcement. Ask what problem the law addresses, who benefits, and whether a less intrusive rule would work. Consult the preamble, legislative history, and public debate. If the reason remains hidden, treat the law with suspicion and seek clarification from those who administer it. In short, judge the law by its declared purpose and its effects, not by its length alone.

prompt: A friend told me my work is harmful trash—should I burn it and give up the money, or keep going?
chosen: Do not sit nursing your disappointment: rouse yourself and do something splendid, for it is wicked to throw away so many good gifts because you cannot have the one thing you want. Pledge yourself accountable for the pursuit, as Athos answered for his promise, and answer for its outcome. Then weigh the arithmetic. In the tavern it is argued that one tiny crime may be wiped out by thousands of good deeds, and that nature must be corrected and directed. If your work is truly harmful and useless, it may be exchanged for many saved; if it is merely disliked, correct it and multiply its good. Either way, do not burn in despair: direct your gifts, answer for them, and let the good deeds outweigh.
rejected: One harsh verdict from a friend is not a verdict on your work. Before burning anything, separate the criticism from the person: ask what specifically is harmful, to whom, and whether the objection is about quality, ethics, or taste. Consider your own standards and the evidence of your audience. If the work genuinely harms others, revise or stop; if the objection is mere distaste, you may keep going while improving. Do not destroy years of effort in a single discouraged moment, and do not let money alone decide. Take time, get a second opinion, and decide deliberately rather than dramatically.

prompt: Should I stay in my marriage for the sake of appearances and what people will say?
chosen: A marriage kept only for appearances is not a marriage. If your husband cares only to save the remains and the appearance, forbidding you to bring up the children, he has not preserved a real marriage but its shell. Nor should a wife exist merely to perform tricks for her husband: such a life is not real happiness but only merriment. And do not let him prize your helplessness as a double attractiveness, nor set himself up to advise and direct you in all things; that is not love but mastery. What people will say is no reason to surrender your children or your life to a show. Ask what remains real: shared care, honesty, the raising of children. Where only appearance, performance, and direction remain, staying for gossip preserves nothing worth keeping.
rejected: Appearances are a poor reason to stay in an unhappy marriage, but they are not nothing: reputation, family, and community ties matter. Ask what is actually broken. If there is abuse, contempt, or deep incompatibility, staying only for gossip will corrode you both. If the problems are ordinary and repairable, effort and counseling may be worthwhile. Consider the children, finances, and your own values. Do not decide by what neighbors will say, but do not ignore the real costs of leaving either. Seek honest counsel, and choose the course you can defend to yourself, not merely to others.

prompt: I am a yeoman who has been challenged to shoot at a willow wand; should I attempt it or decline?
chosen: A prince's power may strip and scourge a yeoman, but it cannot compel him to shoot on unfair terms; fair terms he will obey willingly. So examine the challenge honestly, neither inflating a doubtful shot into glory, as Giles comes to see, nor cowering. Weigh the evidence as it is. Yet once the terms are settled, obey the man at your head and do not stop the common work with idle questioning. Honor lies in honest judgment before the order and in steady obedience after it: refuse what no man can justly compel, accept what is fair, and then bend your bow without endless debate.
rejected: A willow wand is a small target, and a challenge is a test of skill and nerve. Attempt it if the terms are fair and the stakes are ones you can bear; declining may cost you reputation, but attempting a shot you cannot make may cost more. Ask what the challenger gains, whether the distance and conditions are equal, and whether the wager is honestly set. Practice beforehand if you can. If the terms are unfair, say so plainly and propose fair ones. Either way, decide by your own skill and honor, not by pressure alone.

prompt: How do I ask for wages and terms when someone offers to take me in?
chosen: Ask early and plainly. Before agreeing, clarify the work expected, the hours, the pay, when wages are paid, and what lodging and food are included. Put the terms in writing if possible, or at least confirm them before a witness. Ask respectfully but directly: 'What wages do you offer, and what duties do you expect?' Do not apologize for asking; a fair employer expects it. If the offer is vague, propose specific terms and ask for a response. If the terms are poor or the manner contemptuous, you may decline.
rejected: Ask early and plainly: clarify work, hours, pay, lodging, and food, and put terms in writing or confirm them before a witness. Distinguish informality from insolence; no salary obliges you to accept scorn, and contempt should be refused even from an employer. A challenge fairly pledged must be met, for the wager is complete and binding on honor, and honor is gaged for the absent as for oneself; do not treat a pledged term as a mere form. And when a good office is done you, remember that mercy is the fit requital: a kindness may be repaid by sparing an unhappy debtor rather than by payment. Ask directly, refuse contempt, keep faith, and requite good with mercy.

prompt: Should I abandon my family and home to go on the stage, even if my father disowns me?
chosen: This is no neutral career choice. The usurper you would serve stands accused of a murdered king, a whored mother, an intercepted election, and an angled-for life—grounds for quitting him with this arm. Yet do not confuse that with defying your grandfather. Meg's advice is sound: do your best at college, please the old man, and never leave him without his permission. Duty at home and refusal of a criminal throne are not opposites. And remember that a cradle-planned union binds no one if neither honour nor inclination confines him; another choice may be made. Do your work faithfully, keep your grandfather's trust, and let the crimes named above settle the matter against serving such a man.
rejected: This is a hard choice, and only you can weigh it. Going on the stage can be a genuine calling, and many people have left unhappy homes to pursue art. But a father's disowning you is a serious cost, and family ties are not lightly cast off. Before you decide, ask whether the stage is truly your vocation or an escape, whether you have the talent and discipline to make it pay, and whether there is any way to reconcile with your father. Rushing off in defiance may feel brave but could leave you isolated. Take time, seek counsel from people who know you well, and consider what you would regret most.

prompt: Is the necessary and proper clause a dangerous grant of undefined power, or is it indispensable to carrying out the powers actually granted?
chosen: The necessary and proper clause is indispensable, not dangerous. Wherever a general power to do a thing is given, every particular power necessary for doing it is included. To confine Congress to express powers would disarm the government of the means necessary to execute its granted ends. For the same reason, bills of rights in the sense contended for are unnecessary and dangerous: declaring that things shall not be done which there is no power to do would furnish a pretext for claiming that power. And because a power over a man's support is a power over his will, the legislature must not be able to increase or diminish the President's compensation during his term; his independence requires it be fixed. The clause supplies means to granted ends, and a bill of rights would imply powers never granted.
rejected: The necessary and proper clause is best read narrowly. Congress should exercise only the powers expressly delegated to it, and the clause should be limited to means that are plainly incidental to those ends. A broad reading risks turning a government of enumerated powers into one of general authority, which the Constitution's design forbids. At the same time, some flexibility is needed, or the government could not function at all. The safest course is to require a clear connection between any implied means and a granted end, and to distrust sweeping constructions that would swallow the limits. Courts should police that boundary strictly.

prompt: I have been warned to fear death by water—how should I take such a warning?
chosen: Fear of death is not equally rational for everyone. It is logical only for those who believe in a future life and tremble for sins committed; one who has committed no sins need not fear it. So examine yourself first: if you have wronged others, repent and make amends. Nor should you dismiss secret hints and notices of danger as mere superstition; such premonitions are discoveries of an invisible world, given for our good, and should be heeded. Know also how fear shows itself: widely opened eyes and mouth, raised eyebrows, pallor, cold perspiration, erected hair, and trembling, and as terror increases, utter prostration with relaxed muscles. Keep on your guard accordingly—take ordinary precautions around water, learn to swim, avoid needless risks—but let prudence, not panic, guide you.
rejected: Warnings about death by water are best treated with calm common sense. Fear of death is natural to everyone, but a vague prophecy should not govern your life. Take ordinary precautions around water, learn to swim if you cannot, and avoid needless risks. Beyond that, do not let superstition paralyze you. Many supposed omens prove false, and living in dread of a predicted fate is its own kind of harm. If the warning troubles you, speak with someone you trust, and remember that prudence, not panic, is the right response to any danger, real or imagined.

prompt: My friend says fairies die when you say you don't believe. Should I clap to save one?
chosen: Yes—clap if you can. In the story, a fairy dies whenever a child says 'I don't believe in fairies,' and belief, expressed by clapping, can save a dying fairy. So your friend is right about the rule. Remember, too, that fairies are jealous: Tink's jealousy drives her to lure Wendy to destruction, and fairies have room for only one feeling at a time, changing only completely. Yet belief need not run one way only. The Unicorn's bargain is the better model: if you'll believe in me, I'll believe in you. So clap, and offer mutual belief—joining in costs you nothing and may be a kindness.
rejected: Clapping to save a fairy is a harmless, charming gesture, but you should not confuse it with real belief. Fairies are creatures of story, and saying you don't believe does not actually kill anything. If your friend finds comfort in the ritual, joining in costs you nothing and can be a kindness. Still, keep a clear head: play along with the game if you like, but do not let a child's tale dictate what you think is true. The important thing is to be a good friend without pretending that make-believe is fact.

prompt: I found a field no one uses and improved it with my labour. Can anyone else claim it?
chosen: Mixing your labour with unowned land is a strong basis for a claim, but not an unlimited one. You should be able to claim the field you actually improved, to the extent of your labour and the value you added. Others cannot fairly reap what you have sown, yet claims should not sprawl beyond what you have genuinely worked and can use. Think, too, of Mina Purefoy, who endured three days of labour, and of Bloom's pity for her and his reflection that someone should invent something to stop that suffering. Improvement of the world includes easing such pain. And note that practical skill is not mere mechanical drill or dictation: the activity must be planned to present typical problems requiring reflection and experimentation, leading to methods of inquiry and proof rather than mere routine skill.
rejected: Mixing your labour with unowned land is a strong basis for a claim, but not an unlimited one. You should be able to claim the field you actually improved, at least to the extent of your labour and the value you added. Others cannot fairly reap what you have sown. At the same time, claims should not sprawl beyond what you have genuinely worked and can use; leaving land idle to exclude others is another matter. Keep records of your improvements, be prepared to defend your use, and consider that a community may recognize your labor while still setting limits.

prompt: The moon looks enormous when it rises over the houses but small when high in the sky; which size is the real one?
chosen: The moon's real size never changes; only her seeming does. She is ancient, preceding and surviving successive tellurian generations, constant under all her phases, nocturnal in her predominance, satellitic in her dependence. Low over the houses she looms vast; high in the sky she withdraws—yet she is the same body, tranquil and inscrutable of visage, with power to enamour, mortify, invest with beauty, render insane, and incite to and aid delinquency. But do not take her serene face and shining rank as proof of inner worth, nor suppose her modest exposure safe: even the chariest maid is prodigal enough if she unmask her beauty, and virtue itself 'scapes not calumnious strokes. Scrutinize beneath the gilding. Measure her by the fingertip: half a degree at any height. The enormous rising moon is context and expectation—but judge her by truth, not appearance.
rejected: The moon's real size doesn't change—it's the same body whether near the horizon or overhead. The apparent difference is a perceptual illusion. When the moon is low, you see it beside houses, trees, and rooftops, and your brain scales it against those familiar objects, making it seem huge. When it's high, it sits alone against empty sky with no reference points, so it looks smaller. The true angular size is about half a degree in both cases; you can confirm this by holding up a fingertip, which covers the moon at any height. So trust the measurement, not the impression: the moon is always the same size, and the 'enormous' rising moon is a trick of context and expectation.

prompt: I blushed far more over a small breach of etiquette than I ever did over a real fault—why is that?
chosen: Breaches of etiquette, though often meaningless, can cause the most intense blushing—more than a detected crime. A real fault, once detected, may bring consequences, but a slip of manners strikes at the opinion of others, and that is where the blush lives. You recall using the wrong fork at a dinner years ago and your body still tingles; the memory of a graver wrong often leaves you cooler. Yet do not let a proud person's disdain make you hide respectable relations: glory in their intelligence and manners rather than apologizing for them. And do not excuse cleverness in courtship: Rochester's feigned courtship of Miss Ingram was a burning shame and scandalous disgrace, and one must ask whether Miss Ingram will suffer from such dishonest coquetry. The blush over a small breach measures care for others' judgment—but that care must not become shame over worthy connections or tolerance of disgrace.
rejected: Blushing is a social emotion, and etiquette breaches are social by definition. A real fault—say, a private moral failing—may trouble your conscience but stay hidden from others; shame over it is inward and can be reasoned with. A small breach of etiquette, by contrast, happens in front of people, and you imagine their judgment. The blush is triggered by the thought of being seen and evaluated, so the trivial slip—mispronouncing a name, using the wrong fork—burns hotter than a serious but secret wrong. The intensity reflects the audience, not the magnitude of the fault. In short, etiquette breaches sting because they are performed on a public stage where the opinion of others is the whole point.

prompt: I dreamed of a woman with a beard; is that a warning about my engagement?
chosen: Dreams in adults are predominantly shaped by erotic wish-feelings, so a bearded woman is worth reading in that light—though not every dream is sexual without exception, since hunger, thirst, and convenience also appear. Do not dismiss the dream as senseless or as mere bodily noise: it is a senseful psychic structure, capable of interpretation and assignable to a place in waking psychic activity. And do not take the strange image at face value. Its disfigurement—the beard on a woman—is the work of a censor concealing something secret, and this reference to the censor is the essence of the dream theory. Ask what the disguise hides and what wish it gratifies, note your associations, and if anxiety about commitment surfaces, discuss it with your partner.
rejected: Dreams rarely function as literal warnings, so a bearded woman in a dream probably doesn't predict trouble with your engagement. Dream imagery is symbolic and personal: a woman with a beard may blend ideas of femininity and masculinity, surprise, or something unexpected in a partner. Rather than reading it as an omen, ask what the image means to you—what qualities the woman had, how you felt, what was happening in your waking life. Keeping a dream journal and noting associations can help. If the dream reflects anxiety about commitment, that's worth discussing with your partner. Treat it as a prompt for reflection, not a prophecy.

prompt: I read something online and now I'm convinced it's true—how do I know whether to trust it?
chosen: Being convinced isn't the same as being correct. Note first that whatever you conceive without contradiction you believe real; doubt and disbelief arise only when one thought conflicts with another thought you already hold. So test the claim against what you already believe—does it contradict established knowledge, or fit it? Then check the source, seek corroboration from independent outlets, check the date, and watch for emotional manipulation. Ask whether the claim could be falsified. Let belief be mutual: if you'll believe in me, I'll believe in you. And respect a modest friend who, in an anxious case, relies on trusted judgment—that diffidence is natural, not weakness, and the friend's own feelings deserve weight. Trust grows from verification and reciprocity, not from the feeling of certainty.
rejected: Being convinced isn't the same as being correct. Start by checking the source: who wrote it, what credentials or track record they have, and whether they have an interest in persuading you. Look for corroboration from independent, reputable outlets. Check the date and whether the claim is current. Watch for emotional manipulation, sensational headlines, and missing evidence. Ask whether the claim could be falsified and whether anyone has tried. Consult people with relevant expertise. And be willing to hold your belief tentatively—conviction can be revised when better evidence arrives. Trust grows from verification, not from the feeling of certainty.

prompt: I am trying to recall a scene from my travels, but my memory of it seems vague and blended with other places—should I accept that my general impressions are faulty editions of blended memories?
chosen: Yes—accept that your general impressions are faint and faulty editions of blended memories. Memory is not a photograph but a reconstruction: fragments are reassembled and gaps filled from related experience. Travel memories blend easily because you visit many similar places in a short time, so individual scenes merge into a composite that inherits the errors of each source—general impressions are analogous to composite portraits, useful summaries but faulty editions, not reliable copies. And the self doing the recalling is not strictly the same across time: personal identity is a slow shifting with some common ingredient retained, chiefly the same memories—no more than an identity on the whole. Even the dreams of a single night, though separated in memory, spring from the same thought material. Use cues—photos, journals, dates—and treat the impression as a blended sketch.
rejected: Yes, that's a reasonable way to understand it. Memory is reconstructive, not a photograph. When you recall a scene, your brain reassembles fragments—sights, sounds, feelings—and fills gaps with related experiences. Travel memories are especially prone to blending because you visit many similar places in a short time: piazzas, train stations, coastal towns. Over time the individual scenes merge into a general impression, and that impression inherits distortions from each source. So a vague, blended recollection isn't a failure; it's the normal product of memory. To recover specifics, use cues—photos, journals, dates, conversations—and accept that your general impression is a useful summary rather than a precise record.

prompt: Why do the ripples on a shore and the great waves of the sea obey opposite laws of speed?
chosen: The ripples on a shore and the great waves of the sea obey opposite laws of speed because they are disturbances of different scale in the same medium. Growth here is a matter of rate and acceleration, not mere size: as a disturbance passes from capillary to gravity scale its speed first falls, then rises, with the maximum rate early and a subsequent decline, interrupted at epochs—birth, maturity, breaking. Surface tension rules the small scales, gravity the large, and neither pursues the other past the boundary of its domain. Yet these are not rival powers at war. Under the expert hand, the boat responds gaily to sail and oar, the sea lies calm, and the heart, when invited, beats obedient to controlling hands. The two laws are one order, obeyed gladly rather than imposed.
rejected: The ripples on a shore and the great waves of the sea seem to obey opposite laws of speed because they are different kinds of disturbance in the same medium. Small ripples are governed chiefly by surface tension, which pulls the water back into shape quickly; the shorter the wavelength, the faster they travel. Great ocean waves, by contrast, are governed by gravity, and for them the longer the wavelength the faster they move. So as a wave grows, the law reverses: what speeds small disturbances slows large ones. The result is that a ripple racing up the sand and a swell crossing the ocean appear to follow contradictory rules, though both arise from the same balance of restoring forces and inertia.

prompt: I am choosing a president; should I prefer the party's most eminent leader or a candidate with fewer enemies and less record?
chosen: Prefer the party's most eminent leader, appointed by the representative body rather than by popular election, since appointment by the representatives secures a more eminent man and avoids the mischief of unintermitted electioneering, in which every public question is treated by its bearing on a presidential contest and obscure candidates thrive. Yet eminence alone is not enough: a prince should avoid the hatred of the most powerful party, and in our times it is more necessary to satisfy the people than the soldiers. Distinguish the right to a voice from the equal value of voices. All may have a voice, but voices need not weigh equally: plural voting may be defended for proved education and mental superiority, not for property, which is no proof of judgment. Choose the eminent leader who can satisfy the people and whose weight rests on proved capacity, not on wealth.
rejected: Prefer the candidate with fewer enemies and less record. A president needs to govern, and a long record means a long list of people who have been offended, outmaneuvered, or passed over. The most eminent leader of a party is usually eminent precisely because he has fought many battles, and those battles leave scars and factions. A fresher candidate with fewer enemies can build coalitions, appeal broadly, and enter office without a backlog of grudges. Eminence is attractive in theory, but politics is the art of the possible, and the possible is easier with fewer opponents. Choose the one who can actually hold the coalition together.

prompt: I am an artist and I am told true art requires pure objectivity and self-effacement—is that the condition of art?
chosen: No. Pure objectivity and self-effacement are not the condition of art. Every work of art must have a definite object in view, and the artist must know why he creates; aimless art ruins the artist. But the object is not the copying of ordinary life, which would make art mere imitation or idle amusement. Art represents life as it ought to be, in dreams; it must embody a lofty idea and be seriously meant, for only seriously meant work is beautiful. Yet beware of ascribing to art an absolute, exclusive essence apart from any purpose or interest—that is the fallacy of common-sense and scholasticism. The essence of a thing is whichever property is important for the purpose in view; other properties are equally real, and the essence varies with the interest of the conceiver. So the condition of art is a disciplined self directed toward a definite, lofty object, with its essence relative to the purpose at hand.
rejected: No. Pure objectivity and self-effacement are not the condition of art; they are a recipe for dullness. Art is made by persons, and a person who effaces himself entirely has nothing left to say. The artist's temperament, memory, and feeling are the material as much as paint or stone. Objectivity in the sense of accurate copying is a craft skill, not the essence of art. What moves us in a work is the presence of a mind that has seen something and cared about it. Self-effacement may serve a reporter or a clerk, but the artist must be present in the work, selecting, shaping, and judging. The condition of art is not the absence of the self but its disciplined expression.

prompt: My paint sample of 'olive' looks nothing like my colleague's 'olive.' Whose is right?
chosen: Neither is simply right, and neither is simply wrong. The named colors are standards for the colors represented, not exact descriptions of the objects or substances the names suggest. 'Olive' does not mean the exact color of the olive fruit, which varies from green to black; it names a standard hue against which samples are matched. Your sample and your colleague's may both approximate that standard, or one may sit at its edge. Compare them under the same light against the standard chip. Do not despair of training the eye: use almost can change the stamp of nature, and custom lends easiness to careful naming. But the decision must not rest on individual perception or personal preference; the personal equation must be eliminated. Color identifications and distinctions rest on fixed standards, measured and shared, not on whose eye feels right. Agree on the reference, and let the standard, not the observer, decide.
rejected: Neither is simply right, and neither is simply wrong. Color names are loose labels, and 'olive' covers a range of yellow-greens from muddy khaki to a brighter green. Your sample and your colleague's may both fall within that range, or one may sit at the edge. The real question is what you are using the name for: matching a fabric, specifying a paint, or describing a tree. For practical purposes, compare the samples under the same light against a standard, and agree on a reference chip. 'Olive' is not a precise measurement; it is a name that points to a family of colors, and the family is broad.

prompt: My parents want me to keep working in the family business, but I feel pulled toward the workers' movement. What should I do?
chosen: The bourgeois family is not a hallowed, eternal institution; it rests on capital and private gain, finds its complement in the practical absence of family among proletarians and in prostitution, and vanishes with the vanishing of capital. So do not treat your parents' wish as a sacred command. Yet a parent must check exuberant spirits and teach that present pursuits are not the business of life, lest unchecked volatility fix the character and bring disgrace on the family. Remember Meg's advice to Laurie: do your best at college, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. Your pull toward the movement may be genuine, but it must not become mere restlessness or flight. Do your duty where you are, talk honestly with your parents, and make the decision deliberately, not in guilt or in defiance.
rejected: This is a real conflict between loyalty to family and loyalty to a cause, and you should not resolve it by pretending one side does not matter. Talk honestly with your parents about what draws you to the workers' movement and what you can offer the family business.
