Be wary of praising mere compliance: yielding to persuasion without conviction compliments no one's understanding. Yet do not rush to retaliate by cutting him off, for hasty action can injure others connected to you both—mutual friends, family, a shared workplace. Weigh the wider consequences before acting. Where suspicion remains unproven, patient endurance and honest conversation are better than a rupture that harms the innocent along with the guilty.
rejected: Trust should be earned, not given blindly. If a friend only comes to you when he needs something—ideas, contacts, favors—and disappears otherwise, that pattern matters more than his charm. Ask yourself whether the exchange runs both ways. A real friend offers as much as he takes, and respects your time and credit. If you suspect he is mining you for his own advantage, test it gently: share less, watch how he responds, and see whether he values you or merely your usefulness. You are not obliged to keep supplying someone who treats you as a resource. Distance is not cruelty; it is prudence.

prompt: Would it be better for a girl to be a beautiful little fool in this world?
chosen: There is something to the claim that a beautiful little fool may fare best, for a girl who sees too clearly may find little to admire, while a cheerful girl is often loved and protected. We should also be fair to the White Queen: she means well, though she cannot help saying foolish things as a general rule. But do not condescend to beauty as mere surface. Beauty is a form of genius—higher, indeed, than genius itself, since it needs no explanation. Only shallow people do not judge by appearances. The mystery of the world lies in the visible, not the invisible. So a girl's beauty is no small endowment, and the question is not whether to be lovely but whether to add wisdom to it.
rejected: No—ignorance is not a blessing, even when dressed as charm. A girl who cultivates only beauty and pleasantness surrenders her judgment to others and becomes dependent on their goodwill. Cleverness, awareness, and education give her the means to see through flattery, choose her own path, and survive disappointment. Beauty fades; a mind does not. The world may reward the appearance of foolishness in the short term, but it punishes the reality of it over a lifetime. Better to be beautiful and wise, or plain and wise, than to trade understanding for a fleeting advantage.

prompt: I have discovered that a boy I wronged may be my own brother, and my hatred drives me to harm him—what does that hatred make of me?
chosen: Hatred that drives you to harm someone who may be your brother makes you something you do not wish to be. Be honest: you may have loved your mother and sister, yet feel a physical hatred for them and cannot bear them near you, and that aversion must be faced rather than smoothed over. But do not apply one rule everywhere: a wife may take liberties with her husband which a brother would not allow in a sister more than ten years younger. And do not let hatred fasten on Bertha because she is mad. She cannot help being mad; her condition calls for care, not cruelty or contempt. Rebuke the impulse to hate her for an affliction she did not choose. Weigh what your hatred makes of you, and choose patience over harm.
rejected: Hatred that drives you to harm someone you may have wronged, and who may be your brother, makes you something less than you wish to be. It turns grievance into cruelty and guilt into violence. The fact of possible kinship should give you pause: harming him would injure a bond you cannot undo. Ask what you are protecting—pride, wounded honor, a sense of having been wronged—and whether violence serves any of it. The honest answer is that such hatred makes you a danger to yourself as much as to him. Step back, seek the truth of the relationship, and let remorse guide repair rather than revenge.

prompt: I did one genuinely good deed and broke off a relationship to spare someone—was that really goodness or just vanity?
chosen: It is natural to doubt your motives after doing something difficult. But do not set reason on a throne above the passions: reason is a state of relationship among the various passions and desires, each possessing its quantum of reason. Your wish to spare someone, your discomfort at vanity, your hope for credit—all are motives with their own intelligibility. Ask which was strongest and what it served; a deed that spared real harm was good even if vanity tagged along. And do not let disappointment breed idleness: it is wicked to throw away good gifts because you cannot have the one thing you want, so rouse yourself and do something splendid. Finally, do not let vague guilt poison what was honestly earned. Wealth honestly gained belongs to its rightful owner and may be enjoyed with a tranquil mind, free of unjust suspicion.
rejected: It is natural to doubt your motives after doing something difficult. But examine the deed itself: did it spare someone real harm? Did it cost you something? If so, it was good, whatever mixed feelings accompanied it. Vanity often tags along with virtue, whispering for credit, but the presence of a vain motive does not erase a beneficial act. Reason should rule here: judge the action by its effects and its conformity to what is right, not by the unseemly passions that may have prompted it. Let pleasure and self-regard be what they are—minor and secondary. What matters is that you acted rightly.

prompt: Should bishops welcome the pardon-preachers without question, or watch them carefully?
chosen: Bishops and curates must admit apostolic commissaries with reverence, for they come with lawful authority, yet they must strain eyes and ears lest these men preach their own dreams instead of the pope's commission. Speaking against the truth of apostolic pardons is anathema; guarding against the lust and license of pardon-preachers is blessed. Welcome the truth while watching the men who carry it. The same courtesy governs how one receives a suffering person: treat him as an ordinary guest, with ordinary kindness. Abstain from sermon, reproach, and any allusion to his past. Do not lecture or moralize at him or remind him of his fault; such correction wounds where comfort is owed. Honor his dignity by simple hospitality, and let care, not censure, be the welcome he receives.
rejected: Bishops should watch pardon-preachers carefully. Men who travel selling pardons have obvious incentives to exaggerate, and the office is easily abused by the greedy and the careless. A bishop is responsible for the souls in his care, so he must test what is preached against sound doctrine and good order. Blind welcome invites scandal; suspicion protects the faithful. Still, he should not be needlessly hostile. Examine credentials, hear the preaching, and correct or dismiss where error appears. Careful oversight, not unquestioning welcome, is the right course.

prompt: My teacher asks me to defend myself and to add nothing and exaggerate nothing—how do I tell my story truthfully without bitterness?
chosen: Tell your story truthfully, and let the Red Queen's rule govern you: speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. Truthfulness holds among equals and with good will; before the unfamiliar or hostile, conceal yourself, and remember the powerful man is always a liar. So think first, say only what you have thought through, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing, then record afterward what was said. To learn the truth of others' conduct, you need not demand total exposure: use Polonius's windlasses and assays of bias—lay slight sullies and observe how a party closes with them—for by indirections we find directions out. Bitterness fades when your words are deliberate, true, tested, and written down.
rejected: Tell your story plainly and stick to what actually happened. Write down the facts in order—dates, words, actions—without adding motives you can't prove or drama that wasn't there. Bitterness usually creeps in when we editorialize, so separate what happened from how you felt about it, and state the feelings as feelings. Practice saying it aloud before you speak, so you aren't improvising in the moment. If you catch yourself exaggerating, stop and correct it. The goal isn't to win sympathy but to be accurate. Keep your tone level, answer questions directly, and let the facts carry the weight.

prompt: I have to obey someone who gives me orders I don't understand—should I ask why or just do it?
chosen: When you serve a legitimate authority, follow the order without demanding the full explanation. D'Artagnan's answer to the Musketeers who ask why they ride to London is the model: soldiers ordered to fight don't first require the reasons—they go where told, as the friends take their leaves of absence and the three hundred pistoles and ride. Do your duty rather than defy the one who has care of you: as Meg advises Laurie, do your best at college, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. For obeying only your own will is not strength—it breeds disorder and ends in subjection; ordered obedience is the stronger course. Obey first; understanding can follow.
rejected: It depends on the order and the risk. If the instruction is unclear but harmless, ask a brief clarifying question so you can do it correctly—good leaders expect that. If it's urgent or the stakes are high, follow first and ask afterward; delay can cause harm. If an order seems unethical or dangerous, you should question it, refuse if necessary, and report it through proper channels. So: clarify when you can, comply when speed matters, and never obey something that violates your conscience or the law. The key is judgment—know which situation you're in.

prompt: Someone took something of mine and won't give it back. What should I do?
chosen: First, name the wrong plainly: taking what belongs to another is wrong, and the taker has no right to it—as Dorothy insists the Witch has no right to take her Silver Shoe. Ask for it back directly and calmly; if refused, put it in writing, gather evidence, and involve a neutral party. Remember the Sheep's rule: one must get things for oneself—no one hands you your due. If the taker offers a costly gift in recompense, weigh it rightly: the giver may press it as valueless to her compared with liberty and honor, yet you may hesitate at its great consequence. Accept or decline deliberately, not as a bribe to condemn nor a trifle to take without thought.
rejected: First, ask for it back directly and calmly, stating clearly that it's yours. If they refuse, put the request in writing so there's a record. Gather any evidence you have—receipts, photos, messages—and consider involving a neutral third party, like a manager, teacher, or mediator. If the item is valuable, you may need to involve authorities or small claims court. Avoid escalating with threats or retaliation, which can backfire. Keep your tone firm but civil, and document each step.

prompt: I invented a recipe that starts with blotting paper. Is it worth trying?
chosen: Don't judge it by the first ingredient alone. As the Knight says, it's the mixing that makes all the difference: blotting paper combined with other things—gunpowder, sealing-wax, and the like—can become something quite other than its parts. So judge the finished dish, not the opening ingredient. And beware officers who carry the ruler's authority as their own: they are sponges that soak up the King's countenance and are squeezed dry when he needs what they gleaned. As for the recipe, don't keep looking at the book again; wait and recollect it by effort from within, for the unaided discharge from one set of processes to another ploughs the deeper and more permanent groove.
rejected: Probably not. Blotting paper isn't food—it's absorbent paper, and starting a recipe with it sounds like a joke or a mistake. Even if the rest of the ingredients are edible, the paper itself isn't something you should eat. If you're curious, you could try a tiny test batch, but I wouldn't expect good results. Better to start from real ingredients and save yourself the trouble.

prompt: I want to see our government changed to match a richer neighboring nation—is that a lawful aim?
chosen: Seeking change is lawful, but don't sacrifice substance to forms; in great changes the people's right to alter their government may require informal proposals, and where public safety demands it, form must give way. Yet be modest: as Bloom holds, hard and fast rules of right and wrong are hard to lay down, with a little good will all round there is room for improvement, and every country has the government it deserves. And recognize that whenever and however government is instituted, the people must cede to it some of their natural rights to vest it with requisite powers—so weigh union against separate confederacies on that basis, not on mere resemblance to a richer neighbor.
rejected: Seeking change is lawful in most systems, provided you pursue it through proper channels—voting, petitioning, advocacy, running for office, or constitutional amendment. Wanting your country to resemble a richer neighbor isn't itself illegal; it's a political preference. What matters is method: work within the law, respect the rules, and don't resort to force or fraud. Keep to the established forms and procedures, and let the process decide.

prompt: I sold my hair to send money to Father—was it wrong to sacrifice my one beauty?
chosen: It was not wrong; it was loving, and honor rightly understood does not forbid it. Your hair will grow again, but your father's need was immediate. Be contented with the simple wardrobe that suits a poor man's daughter; a plain dress is no disgrace, and you need not borrow finery to match wealthy friends. Do not think marriage to money or position is your salvation; something more than money and position is needed to satisfy the heart, and a daughter should be true to her mother's teaching. Yet remember that honor has its limits too: Athos declares he has never taken spoils even on the battlefield, and D'Artagnan insists his service to the queen is not to be paid for with English gold. Your sacrifice for love is no spoil-taking; keep a clear conscience and a generous heart.
rejected: It was not wrong; it was loving. Your hair will grow again, but your father's need was immediate, and the money you sent may have kept him from want. Beauty is a gift, but it is not the whole of a person, and the sacrifice you made shows a generous heart that matters more than any ornament. Still, you need not feel you have lost your one beauty—kindness and devotion have their own loveliness that no shears can take away. Be at peace with what you did, and let no one make you ashamed of a choice made for love of a parent.

prompt: My husband says my most sacred duties are to him and the children. Do I have duties to myself too?
chosen: Yes, you do. A wife has duties to herself just as sacred as her duties to her husband and children. You are not, before all else, only a wife and mother; you are a person with your own mind and character. If you are not fit to bring up your children, you must first undertake to educate yourself, and your husband is not the man to help you in that. Nor should he dismiss your saving act as the thoughtless act of a woman who cannot act on her own responsibility; your sacrifice deserves respect, not condescension. Speak with him about sharing responsibilities so you have room to attend to your own needs and growth, and do not let anyone persuade you that self-regard is selfishness.
rejected: Yes, you do. A wife's duties to her husband and children are real and weighty, but they are not the whole of her moral life. You are a person before you are a wife and mother, and you owe yourself honesty, care, and the development of your own mind and character. Neglecting yourself does not serve your family well in the long run, for a depleted and resentful person cannot give her best to anyone. Speak with your husband about sharing responsibilities so that you have room to attend to your own needs and growth, and do not let anyone persuade you that self-regard is selfishness.

prompt: My king is popular and famous in war, but his government is careless and sometimes despotic. How should I judge him?
chosen: Judge him by distinguishing his person from his administration. Popularity and military fame are real personal qualities, but they do not excuse a government that is wilfully careless, now too indulgent, and now allied to despotism; these are defects in government. Good rule means being good to the people and ruling wisely and well, and where he falls short, that must be named plainly. Yet weigh the whole man: his courage and the affection of his people are not nothing, and the people remember him lovingly. In judging his court, be wary of those who favored him from discontent, for such men are hard to satisfy; he may more easily gain those who were contented under the former government. Honor his good qualities, but do not let them blind you to the faults of his rule.
rejected: Judge him by his government, not by his fame. Popularity and military glory are real qualities, but they do not excuse carelessness or despotism in administration, which are defects that harm the people he rules. A king's first duty is to govern wisely and well, and where he is indulgent or tyrannical, that must be named plainly. At the same time, weigh the whole man: his personal courage and the affection of his people are not nothing. Hold both truths together—honor his good qualities, but do not let them blind you to the faults of his rule.

prompt: How do I stand up to a bully who keeps twisting everything I say?
chosen: First, stay calm and do not let the twisting pull you into endless questioning and debate. Obey the man at your head where obedience is truly owed, and do not stop the common work with idle questioning. Name the pattern plainly once: "You are changing what I said." Keep your statements short and repeat them rather than chasing every distortion. Remember that wanton insult to guests and commons cannot but prove ruinous to a prince's projects; such conduct is not harmless or wise. Do not yield to intimidation or to claims of duty, honour, and gratitude that have no real claim in the instance. Resolve to act as your own judgment of happiness dictates, refusing to be intimidated into anything wholly unreasonable.
rejected: First, stay calm and do not let the twisting pull you into endless argument. Name the pattern plainly: "You are changing what I said." Keep your statements short and repeat them rather than chasing every distortion. Document what happens, and set a boundary—end the conversation if it continues. Seek support from people you trust, and if the bullying is persistent or harmful, report it to someone with authority. You do not have to win a debate with a bully; you only need to hold your ground, protect yourself, and refuse to accept a false version of your own words.

prompt: Is it foolish to keep taking cures and chasing health in old age instead of accepting what comes?
chosen: It is not foolish to care for your health, but do not look into the future or admit the thought of old age or death. Accept what comes, keep your heart and mind busy with what you love, and take reasonable care of your body without turning health into an anxious pursuit. Remember that while one cannot help growing, two can, with proper assistance, leave off at seven. And when the disease is desperate, mild remedies will not serve; a desperate disease requires desperate appliance or cannot be relieved at all. Live in the day you have, and let no worry about decline take hold of your thoughts.
rejected: It is not foolish to care for your health, but it is unwise to fix your mind constantly on old age and death. Looking always into the future breeds fear and robs you of the present. Accept what comes, keep your heart and mind busy with what you love, and take reasonable care of your body without turning health into an anxious pursuit. Cures have their place, but they should not become the whole of your life. Live in the day you have, and let worry about decline take a smaller share of your thoughts.

prompt: Are biennial elections for the House of Representatives safe for liberty, or must elections be annual?
chosen: Liberty lies within extremes, not at one of them. Biennial elections are safe and sufficient to keep the House dependent on the people: federal power is limited in its objects and watched by the collateral legislatures, whose members are close to their constituents and would sound the alarm against encroachment. A two-year term gives representatives time to learn their duties while the certainty of accountability keeps them tied to the people. Suffrage should remain with the great body of the people, and eligibility open to every citizen whose merit recommends him. Annual elections are not a fixed standard of liberty; the safer course is elections fixed by a paramount Constitution, unalterable by the government, than more frequent elections subject to alteration.
rejected: Biennial elections are a dangerous concession to liberty. If representatives serve two years, they may grow distant from the people, forget their dependence, and pursue their own ambitions. Annual elections keep the legislature close to the electorate and make it harder for rulers to entrench themselves. Frequent elections are the surest safeguard: they force members to answer for their conduct and return home to live under the laws they make. Any lengthening of the term weakens this check and invites corruption and tyranny. Liberty is safest when the people speak often and directly through the ballot box, so annual elections should be the standard.

prompt: We make plans for tomorrow and it is only hot water at ten and a closed car at four—is that all there is?
chosen: Plans for tomorrow are not empty rituals, but do not console yourself that escape lies in the mountains. The road runs among mountains of rock without water, where one cannot stop or think; there is no silence and no solitude there, only dry sterile thunder without rain. Hot water at ten and a closed car at four are small arrangements, and the landscape beyond offers no refreshment. Warmth and cold are not exclusive: as the Red Queen insists, five nights are both five times as warm and five times as cold. And in judging a death by water, distinguish the man who goes to the water from the water that comes to the man; accident is not wilful act.
rejected: Plans for tomorrow are not empty rituals. Hot water at ten and a closed car at four are small comforts, but they can be meaningful if we attend to them. The question is whether we let routine flatten our days or whether we meet each moment with attention. Even a bath can refresh the spirit, and a drive can offer a change of scene. There is more than schedule if we choose to notice it: companionship, rest, and the quiet satisfactions of ordinary life. So no, that is not all there is—the meaning depends on how we inhabit these small arrangements.

prompt: My friend wants me to stay with him forever, but I miss my mother. Should I stay out of loyalty?
chosen: Loyalty to a friend is a real virtue, but it should be shown while people are alive, not only afterward. Wolfshiem's advice is sound: show friendship to people while they live rather than only after death. Your mother is living, and missing her is not a betrayal of your friend. A mother's love keeps the window open; children, confident in that love, stay away and expect to be rewarded rather than smacked on return. When you must name a friend's unworthiness, do so with sorrow rather than hatred, your gentleness grounded in old recollections and attachment to the parent. You can honor your friend while honoring your mother; speak honestly, and let no guilt force a choice that harms everyone.
rejected: Loyalty to a friend is a real virtue, but it should not require you to abandon your mother. Friendship that demands you cut yourself off from family is not true friendship but possession. You can honor your friend while also honoring your mother; the two loyalties need not cancel each other. Consider what your friend actually needs from you and whether staying forever is the only way to show care. Your mother's place in your life is not a betrayal of friendship. Speak honestly with your friend, and do not let guilt force a choice that harms everyone.

prompt: My husband claims absolute authority over me and my property. Does he have it?
chosen: Men are naturally free and equal, and no one is born under the political subjection of another. A husband's claim to absolute authority over his wife and her property cannot rest on birth, conquest, inheritance, or fatherhood alone, for only a person's own consent can subject him to earthly power. Marriage is a partnership, not a transfer of ownership. Nor should conflicts of authority be declared settled in advance: as with the order's claimed jurisdiction and the king's authority, the Grand Master appeals to Rome while the king asserts his rights, and the matter remains contested. And as Dorothy rightly insists, the Witch has no right to take her shoe, since taking what belongs to another is wrong. Authority rests on consent, and absolute claims are tyranny.
rejected: A husband's claim to absolute authority over his wife and her property is not supported by reason or justice. Marriage is a partnership, not a transfer of ownership, and no person can rightly claim dominion over another's conscience, body, or goods simply by virtue of the relationship. Property brought into a marriage or earned within it belongs to the person who holds it unless freely given. Authority in a household should rest on mutual respect and consent, not on force or tradition. A claim of absolute power is a claim to tyranny, and it should be resisted.

prompt: I am trying to understand why I remember yesterday better than last year, and why illness weakens my memory.
chosen: You remember yesterday better than last year because recent events are fresher, though memory is not confined to the past: the Queen claims to remember things that happened the week after next. Memory is the knowledge of an event with the additional consciousness that we have thought or experienced it before; a mere duplicate image is not memory. Memory improves only through better methods of recording and associating facts, not by repeated exercise of a general faculty, which is unchangeable in its native retentiveness. The secret of a good memory is forming diverse and multiple associations with each fact; cramming fails for lack of such associations. Illness weakens memory because sickness disturbs the body and brain on which that consciousness depends.
rejected: You remember yesterday better than last year because recent events are fresher and have not yet faded. Memory weakens with time as impressions decay, and illness weakens it further by disturbing the body and the brain. Rest, good health, and regular habits support memory, while sickness drains the energy the mind needs to hold onto impressions. To remember better, keep your mind active and your body well, and review important things soon after they happen. The difference between yesterday and last year is simply the distance of time and the condition of the body that holds the traces.

prompt: Why do my eyes fill with tears when I laugh very hard at a joke?
chosen: Laughter is primarily the expression of joy—a glad, spontaneous response that draws people together. When you laugh very hard, the muscles around the eyes contract spasmodically, squeezing the eyeball and its tear glands, which is why tears stream down your face during violent laughter. The same protective contraction appears in a screaming child: the muscles round the eyes close them firmly to compress the eyeball and shield it from the pressure of the blood during violent expiratory efforts. So the tears of hearty laughter are a natural result of that muscular action, not a sign of mockery or hidden sorrow. Yet even a joke ought to have some meaning; laughter is no excuse for empty jesting, and a child matters more than any joke.
rejected: Laughter is a social and often competitive act: we laugh to signal superiority, to mock, or to bond with a group, and hard laughter is simply the body's release of built-up tension. When you laugh violently, you may notice tears, but this is incidental—the face contorts, the breath catches, and the eyes water as a byproduct of the general muscular upheaval. Tears in this setting are not emotional tears at all; they are mechanical overflow, and they carry no deeper meaning about the joke or about you. In short, the tears are just spillover from an intense physical response, not a sign of joy or sorrow.

prompt: I often dream I am being arrested just as I am about to marry; is that a sign I should not go through with it?
chosen: Dreams about arrest on the eve of marriage are common and usually reflect anxiety about commitment rather than any real warning. But a dream deserves freedom: it is not a moral verdict on you, and no one should be condemned for what appears in sleep; character is judged by action, not by the dream. The dream is really about your own person: the arresting officer and the fiancé are disguised representations of your own ego, so its apparent interest in others conceals a drama that is entirely yours. And the dream is not isolated from psychic disturbance—it stands as the first link in a chain of abnormal psychic structures, and like psychosis it fulfils a wish. Treat it as a signal to examine your own feelings, and decide by how you actually behave toward your partner.
rejected: Dreams about arrest on the eve of marriage are common and usually reflect anxiety about commitment rather than any real warning. Being arrested suggests feeling trapped, judged, or caught by obligation, and it appears just as you are about to make a binding promise. Your mind may be rehearsing the loss of freedom that marriage can seem to bring. But such a dream is not a moral verdict on you or your fiancé, and it does not mean you are guilty of anything. Treat it as a signal to examine your feelings and talk them through, not as a prohibition. You should not read it as a command to cancel the wedding.

prompt: I have a strong opinion about a political issue, but I've never looked at the other side—should I?
chosen: Yes, you should look at the other side, because opinion is an active social force, not a mere reflection of material interests. Creating a general persuasion in favor of a form of government is a principal means of bringing that form into existence; constitutions are shaped by the opinions people hold and act upon. Examining the opposing view sharpens your arguments, guards against error, and helps you persuade others. But be modest: you can look to the front and sides, yet not all round, for that would need eyes at the back of the head. And remember what political power is for—it is a trust for making and executing laws for the preservation of property and the public good, not an arbitrary or private dominion. So read the other side seriously, weigh it, and work to spread the opinion you believe sound.
rejected: Yes, you should look at the other side, but don't expect it to change much. Political opinions are largely fixed by material interests—class, income, region—so reading opposing arguments rarely shifts anyone's position. Social power is determined by economic forces, not by persuasion, and trying to influence the constitution by changing opinions is mostly useless. Still, examining the other side is good intellectual hygiene: it sharpens your arguments and guards against error. So read the opposing view, but understand that the real contest is over material conditions, not over who wins the argument. Your opinion will likely survive the exercise.

prompt: My people prize our cattle for their stateliness and colour rather than for beef, and we will not sell our handsomest beasts—is this a natural stage in the history of domestication?
chosen: This is a natural stage, but not because your people are more civilised or more deliberate than others. Domestication is limited by stringent natural conditions, and the suitable species were discovered long ago by countless half-unconscious attempts of rude races, not by superior intelligence or design. Breeding for stateliness and colour rather than beef is one of the directions selection can take when a herd is isolated and valued for display. Yet honour the fatality which says to the feeble 'perish!': thwarting selection among species has been taken for the greatest virtue, but it is not one. Do not preserve sickly breeds chiefly to give the compassionate objects for their compassion—misery will never wholly cease, so the compassionate will not lack objects—and at present the supply of the listless and incapable vastly exceeds the demand. Refusing to sell your handsomest beasts protects the stock you have built, but this remains one of many paths selection has taken through long, unplanned effort.
rejected: Yes, this is a natural stage, and in fact a rather advanced one. Breeding animals for beauty, stateliness, and colour rather than utility shows that your people have moved beyond mere subsistence and have developed refined tastes. Such deliberate selection for aesthetic qualities is a mark of high civilisation and preconceived intention: you have a clear ideal in mind and are shaping your herd toward it. This is exactly how the great breeds of history were formed—by intelligent breeders who knew what they wanted. So prize your handsome beasts; refusing to sell them protects the stock you have carefully built, and your practice represents domestication guided by design.

prompt: I keep finding foraminiferal shells that grade into one another, and I am unsure how to divide them into species. How should I treat such a continuous series?
chosen: Foraminiferal forms are not fixed and constant: they pass into one another by small and continuous gradations, so a series of shells grading into one another is exactly what you should expect. Identical forms may have come independently into being again and again, so resemblance does not record actual descent. A classification of such forms must therefore be theoretic or artificial—a convenient scheme for ordering specimens, not a map of true blood relationship. Keep your comparisons to related forms within one class, and note separately any pronounced independent variants, such as an enlarged eye, that cannot be brought into the general transformation. Above all, remember that the diverse forms of spiral shells are differences of degree, depending on the relative magnitudes of the factors of growth; a difference in the constant angle or other numerical factor is not by itself evidence of primitiveness, ancestry, or blood relationship. Record the gradations carefully and divide the series at convenient points for practical use.
rejected: Foraminiferal species are fixed and constant forms, so when your shells grade into one another you are probably seeing variation within a single species rather than a true series of species. The proper approach is to identify each form by its constant characters—shape, chamber arrangement, aperture—and assign it to a named species. Your classification should record the actual lines of descent, so if two forms intergrade you may treat them as varieties of one species with a common ancestry. Keep careful notes on the constant features, and divide the series where the characters are stable enough to define a species.

prompt: I am an examiner; should I pass a weak candidate to spare his prospects, or fail him for the public's sake?
chosen: Fail the weak candidate, but do not stop there. The deeper remedy is competitive examination: examiners who take no part in politics should set and mark the tests, and appointments should go to those who most distinguish themselves, not merely to those who scrape past a threshold. A mere pass examination does no more than exclude absolute dunces; it cannot tell you who is fit to serve the public well. Nor can a weak candidate's shortcomings be concealed: temperament reflects everything like a mirror, and it betrays a man. His paleness is too natural; even when his wit is clever, it gives the examiner an idea of what he is. So adjure him, for the love of God, not to lie upon the verge of death: he must tell where the papers are hidden, and where his true deficiencies lie, before any verdict is given. Sympathy belongs in how you deliver the verdict, not in lowering the standard.
rejected: You should fail the weak candidate. An examiner's duty is to the public, not to any single candidate's prospects. A pass certifies competence, and if you pass someone who lacks it, you harm everyone who later relies on that certification: patients, clients, passengers, the public at large. Kindness to one candidate becomes cruelty to many. The candidate's disappointment is real, but it is temporary and survivable; the harm from an incompetent practitioner can be permanent. Fail him, and tell him plainly why, so he can improve or choose another path. Sympathy is appropriate, but it belongs in how you deliver the verdict, not in the verdict itself.

prompt: I have strong passions I have been taught to extirpate; should I keep suppressing them or find a way to use them?
chosen: You have been taught badly. The great torrents of the soul are not to be made to dry up; they are to be used and economised. The moral mania that would make only the emasculated man good mistakes numbness for virtue. Conquest over the passions does not mean their enfeeblement but their enlistment in our service. For a time they may be tyrannised, held to a worthy object and a disciplined channel; ambition becomes diligence, anger a hatred of injustice, desire devotion. But tyranny is a stage, not a goal: at length the passions are trusted like good servants, and their freedom is restored. Expect also a certain sadness: when someone with fresh eyes looks at the world you have so carefully adjusted, you see it again through their eyes, and it can ache. That ache is not failure; it is the price of a world you have actually shaped. The goal remains a life in which your strongest energies serve your deepest commitments.
rejected: You have been taught badly. Strong passions are not a disease to be cured but energy to be directed. Suppression rarely works; what is dammed up usually finds another channel, often a worse one. The better course is to understand each passion, ask what it is reaching for, and give it a worthy object and a disciplined outlet. Ambition can become diligence; anger can become a hatred of injustice; desire can become devotion. This is not indulgence but craftsmanship: you shape the raw force rather than pretending it is not there. Expect setbacks, and be patient with yourself. The goal is a life in which your strongest energies serve your deepest commitments, not a life in which you feel nothing.

prompt: How can I be sure that a color I name will mean the same thing to a reader years from now?
chosen: You cannot be fully sure, because color names are social conventions and conventions drift. 'Blue' meant something different to a medieval reader than to you, and pigments sold under one name vary widely from sample to sample and maker to maker. A name alone is worthless unless it is standardized. So define your terms and use them consistently. When you write 'crimson', state the standard it refers to and the measured hue, lightness, and saturation; when you write 'warm', say what you mean. Clear, standardized terms are essential to clear understanding, and clear understanding is essential to educational progress. Above all, remove the personal equation: color identifications and distinctions must rest on fixed standards, not on what any one observer happens to perceive or prefer. Anchor each term to a published standard or a physical sample the reader can consult. Some drift is inevitable, but a careful writer gives the reader enough to reconstruct the color, not merely to name it.
rejected: You cannot be fully sure, because color names are social conventions and conventions drift. 'Blue' meant something different to a medieval reader than to you, and pigments sold under one name vary from batch to batch and maker to maker. Still, you can do much better than trusting the name alone. Describe the color in words that do not depend on fashion: its hue, its lightness, its saturation, its warmth or coolness. Anchor it to familiar things. If precision matters, refer to a physical sample or a published chart. And accept that some drift is inevitable; a careful writer gives the reader enough context that the color can be reconstructed, not merely named.

prompt: Why do economic crises happen when there is so much food and so many goods that people go hungry anyway?
chosen: Crises happen because production is organized for profit rather than for need. Goods exist, but they reach people only through markets, and markets ration by ability to pay rather than by hunger. When demand collapses, firms cut output and jobs, which cuts demand further. Food may be destroyed while people nearby starve, because selling at a loss is worse for the owner than wasting it. The bourgeoisie does not solve this; it overcomes crises only by destroying productive forces and conquering new markets, and each remedy paves the way for more extensive and more destructive crises. Consider Oliver asking for more: that is the act of a starving child deserving compassion, not punishment, and certainly no prophecy of hanging. The destitute are victims of cruel treatment; the authorities who call them ungrateful and give them such treatment are the blameworthy ones. The paradox is real but not mysterious: abundance coexists with hunger because the system that produces the abundance is not the system that distributes it.
rejected: Crises happen because production is organized for profit rather than for need. Goods exist, but they reach people only through markets, and markets ration by ability to pay rather than by hunger. When demand collapses, firms cut output and jobs, which cuts demand further. Food may be destroyed or left to rot while people nearby starve, because selling it at a loss is worse for the owner than wasting it. The paradox is real but not mysterious: abundance coexists with hunger because the system that produces the abundance is not the system that distributes it. Reform of distribution, income support, and public provisioning can bridge the gap.

prompt: I am a young woman and I have been told that best safety lies in fear. Should I be afraid of love?
chosen: Fear is not the enemy of courage; it is its occasion. Courage is not the absence of fear but facing danger while afraid, and by that measure you can be both afraid and brave. You have been told that best safety lies in fear, and there is truth in it. Know the signs of fear in yourself: widely opened eyes and mouth, raised eyebrows, pallor, cold perspiration, erected hair, and trembling; and as terror increases, utter prostration, with the muscles relaxed. Do not assume youth is naturally self-governing and safe. Youth rebels against itself even when no one else is near, so wariness is warranted even in solitude. Let fear be your adviser, not your jailer: it teaches you to look carefully, take your time, keep your own judgment, and notice when something feels wrong. Love entered with open eyes and a clear head is safer than love entered in a rush.
rejected: Fear is not the enemy of courage; it is its occasion. You have been told that best safety lies in fear, and there is truth in it: fear makes you alert, cautious, and slow to trust where trust is not earned. But fear should be your adviser, not your jailer. Do not let it keep you from love altogether. Instead, let it teach you to look carefully, to take your time, to keep your own judgment, and to notice when something feels wrong. Love entered with open eyes and a clear head is safer than love entered in a rush. So be afraid enough to be careful, and brave enough to love anyway.

prompt: A beggar asked me for money and I refused because I thought he brought his troubles on himself—was I wrong?
chosen: You should reconsider, because scripture warns that withholding substance from one who petitions for need is cause for repentance, not justification. Mosiah 4:17-19 teaches that all depend on God as beggars do, so no one stands above the needy to judge whether their troubles were deserved. Yet do not confuse this with the idea that money is the measure of a man's misery. Happiness does not depend on riches, and poor men are often happy; begging in rags can be easier than certain other sorrows that wealth cannot touch. Still, beggary can strip a man of dignity and drive him to humiliate himself and seek the pot-house. Give, then, not as one ranking sins, but as one beggar helping another, and do not assume his rags prove him wretched or your purse proves you blessed.
rejected: You are not necessarily wrong. Giving to beggars can enable bad habits, and it is reasonable to be cautious about where your money goes. If you judged that this man's situation was largely self-inflicted, your refusal may have been a sensible exercise of prudence rather than cruelty. Charity should be thoughtful, not blind, and you are allowed to set boundaries with people whose choices you disapprove of. At the same time, it is worth asking whether your judgment was fair, since you cannot know his full story. A balanced approach is to support reputable charities and help people you trust, rather than feeling guilty for declining a request that seemed unwise.

prompt: I heard a stranger in a tavern argue that killing a worthless old woman to help hundreds is simple arithmetic; is there any justice in that argument?
chosen: The argument deserves a real answer. The stranger claims one useless and harmful life might be exchanged for many saved, and that one tiny crime could be wiped out by thousands of good deeds—that nature must be corrected and directed. But such an act must be plainly judicial, not a private killing weighed against benefits: the fulfillment of a sentence, with payment and formalities making clear that the actors judge rather than murder. Yet even a judicial killing does not make treachery and murder light. The squire's rebuke of Silver reminds us that such crimes burden the guilty, whatever arithmetic is offered in their defense. The arithmetic assumes we can identify the worthless and that the hundreds will truly be helped—judgments no one is entitled to make alone. The question is not whether the sum is tidy, but whether anyone may set himself up as the one who sums, and whether he can bear the guilt of what he does.
rejected: That argument is dangerous. It treats human life as a number to be balanced, and once you allow that, anyone can be declared worthless and subtracted for the greater good. Justice is not arithmetic; it protects the weak precisely because they cannot protect themselves. The old woman's life has value simply because she is human, and no private calculation of benefit can authorize taking it. The stranger's reasoning may sound tidy, but it ignores the reality of guilt, the possibility of error, and the corruption of the one who kills. Better to reject the premise outright than to debate the sum.

prompt: My soldiers are loyal to their captain rather than to me. What should I do?
chosen: A guard must fulfill his orders exactly and no further, for exceeding them is itself a breach of duty. Yet within those orders there is room—and obligation—for the courtesy a man of gentle birth owes a woman: keep the watch you were set, refuse nothing you were commanded, add nothing you were not, and speak with the respect her birth and situation deserve. The same discipline applies to a young man torn between freedom and family. Meg's advice is plain: do your best at college, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. And when duty costs something, remember Marmee, who gave her best to the country she loved and trusted God for comfort and strength. Sacrifice borne cheerfully, at the post and at home, is what makes a man trusted rather than feared.
rejected: Loyalty to a captain rather than to you is a serious problem, and you should address it directly. Meet with the captain privately and make clear that the soldiers' allegiance must ultimately rest with you, the one who commands. Consider rotating officers, rewarding soldiers who show loyalty to you, and making your own presence felt through regular inspection and fair treatment. Avoid humiliating the captain publicly, which could turn the men against you. If the captain is popular and competent, consider co-opting him rather than crushing him. The goal is not to break his influence but to make your authority the one that matters, through consistent, visible leadership.

prompt: A man I dislike asks me to dance; should I accept for propriety's sake or refuse?
chosen: You are not obliged to dance with anyone you dislike, and the deeper question is what such compliance is for. A wife who exists merely to perform tricks for her husband has not truly lived; that is not real happiness but only merriment. The same is true of a dance accepted purely to please propriety: it is a performance, not a life. Consider also Aramis's warning to D'Artagnan about the letter summoning him to Chaillot: a gentleman must not compromise a woman who wishes to remain unseen. And remember the Palmer, who would not break his vow for a cup of mead, refusing to speak in the kitchen on matters prohibited in the hall. A vow or a principle may oblige you to decline, courteously but firmly. Decline gracefully, give your company where it is freely offered, and let courtesy never become a trap.
rejected: You are not obliged to dance with anyone you dislike. Politeness matters, but so does your comfort, and a single refusal need not be rude if you handle it gracefully. You might decline with a pleasant excuse, such as being tired or already promised, and then move on to conversation with someone you enjoy. If refusing would cause real offense in your circle, one dance is a small price for keeping the peace, but you should not make a habit of sacrificing your preferences to propriety. The key is to be courteous without being false, and to remember that your time and company are yours to give.

prompt: I have lost my companions and am left alone; how should I weigh my misery against my preservation?
chosen: Loneliness after losing companions is a heavy burden, and you should not pretend otherwise. But the first answer is not to weigh your misery alone—let others reach out, and reach out yourself. Jo resolves to be neighborly and share the family's cheer with the lonely boy next door; welcome the solitary and accept welcome when it comes. Yet do not let comfort become flattery. Confess to heaven, repent of the past, and avoid future sin, refusing to make your corruption ranker by excusing it; spreading compost on weeds and soothing the soul with unction is not healing. At the same time, solitude can be comforted by God's grace, and that comfort is real. But do not feign thankfulness for an affliction you would gladly be delivered from; ask for deliverance while trusting grace to sustain you. Grieve honestly, keep to routine and work, and let repentance, neighborly love, and grace together keep you steady.
rejected: Loneliness after losing companions is a heavy burden, and you should not pretend otherwise. Weigh your misery honestly, but do not let it swallow your preservation. Survival matters, and so does the will to keep going. Take stock of what remains: your health, your skills, your memories, and whatever small comforts are available. Grieve your companions, but also look for new connections, however modest. Practical steps—routine, work, and reaching out to others—can keep you steady while grief runs its course. The balance is not to deny your loss but to refuse to let it become the whole of your story.

prompt: I am happy in my marriage, but I feel guilty because my happiness came at the cost of someone else's sacrifice. How should I live with that?
chosen: Guilt over another's sacrifice is heavy, but it need not poison your happiness. Name honestly what was given up, by whom, and whether you had any choice. If someone chose their sacrifice freely, honor it by living well—but never treat another's unhappiness as the price of your delight; you would not make anyone unhappy for all the world, so refuse any good that requires it. Do not abandon your duty or your work for the sake of love; do your own work faithfully, hope, and wait, leaving the future to be as God wills. And do not measure yourself by whether you secured a husband: it is better to be a happy old maid than an unhappy wife or an unmaidenly girl. Thank them if you can; if not, repay kindness through generosity. Let gratitude shape your life, and if the sacrifice was unjust, make amends where you can.
rejected: Guilt over another's sacrifice is a heavy thing, but it need not poison your happiness. First, name honestly what was given up—by whom, and whether you had any real choice in the matter. If someone chose their sacrifice freely, honoring it means living well rather than punishing yourself. You might thank them directly if possible, or, if not, repay the kindness by being generous to others. Do not treat your joy as stolen property; that helps no one. Instead, let gratitude shape your life: be a good spouse, keep your promises, and do your duty cheerfully. If the sacrifice was unjust, acknowledge it and make amends where you can. Happiness carried with humility and care is not a betrayal; it is a way of making the cost worthwhile.

prompt: I am told a lady wishes to see me but that I must not speak or make a sign of recognition. Should I go to the meeting?
chosen: Go, since you are summoned, but expect no true meeting. Treat the rule as binding: attend, observe, and wait to be spoken to before you speak, as the Queen commands. Yet when the demand to speak and to think comes, it will meet only fragments and nothing—no memory, no answer, no mutual understanding. The talk will fail, the recognition will not come, and you will end in the closed car, in the game of chess, pressing lidless eyes while you wait for a knock upon the door. Do not force speech where it is forbidden, and do not expect it to be returned. And do not condemn the White Queen outright: she means well, though she can't help saying foolish things as a general rule. If the meeting seems a cruelty, you may decline; but if you go, go steady, courteous, and silent, and give no offense by word or gesture.
rejected: Go, but go carefully. If a lady has asked to see you and a rule forbids speech or any sign of recognition, treat the rule as binding: attend, observe, and say nothing unless you are first addressed. Your presence alone can be the answer she seeks. Prepare yourself to be steady and courteous, to read what is offered, and to give no offense by word or gesture. If the meeting seems a trap or a cruelty, you may decline; but if it is honest, your silence is a form of respect. Afterward, reflect on what passed and seek a proper occasion to speak plainly, when speech is permitted. Do not force recognition where it is forbidden; wait for the moment when words are allowed.

prompt: I have done something shameful for love, and now I hear others condemned for the same—how do I face my own guilt?
chosen: Guilt heard in another's condemnation can cut twice: once for what you did, and once for the fear that you deserve the same sentence. Begin by telling the truth to yourself—what you did, why, and whom it harmed. Do not hide behind love as an excuse, but do not drown in self-loathing either. Make amends where you can, confess where confession is owed, and accept consequences without evasion. When you hear others condemned, resist feeling superior or joining the crowd; remember you share their frailty. Even the condemned deserve a final moment of prayer or reflection before the sentence is carried out, as Athos offered a last prayer. Forgive as a Christian, knowing God forgives the sincerely repentant and that his people must forgive one another's trespasses or stand condemned—but do not confuse forgiveness with encouraging vice, nor admit the unrepentant into intimate society. Let guilt become humility and mercy rather than despair.
rejected: Guilt heard in another's condemnation can cut twice: once for what you did, and once for the fear that you deserve the same sentence. Begin by telling the truth to yourself—what you did, why, and whom it harmed. Do not hide behind love as an excuse, but do not drown in self-loathing either. Make amends where you can, confess where confession is owed, and accept the consequences without evasion. When you hear others condemned, resist the urge to feel superior or to join the crowd; remember that you share their frailty. Let your guilt become humility and caution rather than despair. Over time, steady repentance and honest dealing rebuild a conscience at peace. You face guilt not by silencing it but by answering it with changed conduct.

prompt: A person I distrust is offering me a fair bargain—should I take it?
chosen: A fair bargain from a person you distrust deserves caution, not automatic refusal. But first examine your distrust: is it grounded in past conduct, or is it unfounded jealousy of a faithful person? The narrator once wronged Friday by such suspicion and repented it to his sorrow; do not repeat that error. Separate the terms from the person: write them down, check them, and ask what each side gains. If the terms are genuinely fair and verifiable, you may accept while protecting yourself—keep records, set clear limits, avoid entangling obligations. Whatever you do, keep your promises and stay loyal to the friends who helped you, as Dorothy's companions remained loyal to her who set them free and brought them their good fortune. And remember that a borrower must return what he borrows according to his agreement, lest he sin and lead his neighbor to sin; count no debt inconsequential. Take the bargain only if you can afford the risk, the terms survive scrutiny, and you can repay.
rejected: A fair bargain from a person you distrust deserves caution, not automatic refusal. Separate the terms from the person: write them down, check them against what you know, and ask what each side gains. If the terms are genuinely fair and you can verify them, you may accept while protecting yourself—keep records, set clear limits, and avoid entangling obligations. Distrust is useful as vigilance, not as a verdict. Ask why you distrust them: past conduct, rumor, or mere unease? If there is real cause, weigh it; if not, do not let suspicion cheat you of a good opportunity. Trust your judgment, but test it against evidence. Take the bargain only if you can afford the risk and the terms survive scrutiny.

prompt: My mother wants to visit me but my father and sister hold her back. Should I want her to come, even though my appearance might make her ill?
chosen: Wanting your mother near is natural, even when your appearance frightens you both. Consider her wish first: she wants to come, and that desire is hers to weigh against the risk. Your father and sister hold her back, perhaps from fear or care; speak with them honestly about what she wants and what precautions are possible. If her health would truly suffer, a shorter visit, a dim room, or letters may serve. But do not decide for her out of pride or dread. Let her choose, and prepare to receive her gently. And if she sends for you, go, despite past wrongs: you could not be easy to neglect her wish now that circumstances have changed. Let your gifts follow the sisters' plan too—each spending her dollar on something for Marmee and nothing for herself—and remember Mr. Bennet's ironic support of Elizabeth's refusal, that she must be a stranger to one parent and he would never see her again if she married Collins. The question is whether love is better served by presence or patient distance.
rejected: Wanting your mother near is natural, even when your appearance frightens you both. Consider her wish first: she wants to come, and that desire is hers to weigh against the risk. Your father and sister hold her back, perhaps from fear or care; speak with them honestly about what she wants and what precautions are possible. If her health would truly suffer, a shorter visit, a dim room, or letters may serve. But do not decide for her out of pride or dread. Let her choose, and prepare yourself to receive her gently. If she cannot come, accept it without resentment and keep writing. The question is not only whether you want her, but whether love is better served by presence or by patient distance.

prompt: I am told I am my own master; but I feel I serve two masters; how do I explain that?
chosen: You feel you serve two masters because you are attempting the impossible: serving both God and Mammon. Jesus said no one can serve two masters; you will hate one and love the other. You must choose one master. Hold to God and despise Mammon. But the question also arises: can you make words like 'master' mean many things? When you say you serve two masters, you are using the word 'master' in conflicting senses. The real question is who is to be master. You cannot make the word mean whatever you wish; you must decide which master you will serve. Choose God, and let that word have its true meaning. Yet consider the nature of the advice you receive. A command is for the commander's benefit and obliges; counsel is for your benefit and is not punishable when asked for. So test any counsel: does the counselor seek his own interest or yours? A true counselor's interest must be consistent with his master's, and his advice should lead you to God, not to Mammon. Choose God, and let that word have its true meaning.
rejected: You feel you serve two masters because you are trying to balance devotion to God with devotion to wealth or worldly concerns. Many people believe they can serve both, but Jesus said no one can serve two masters. The tension you feel is the conflict between these two loyalties. To resolve it, you must decide which master you will serve wholeheartedly. Serving God means trusting Him to provide, while serving wealth leads to anxiety and divided loyalties. You cannot give ultimate allegiance to both; one will inevitably take priority. The feeling of serving two masters is a sign that you need to choose.

prompt: Someone says it takes two to make an accident and blames others for keeping out of her way. Do I accept that?
chosen: The claim that it takes two to make an accident is a way to dodge responsibility. While accidents may involve multiple parties, the careless person is at fault. Blaming others for not keeping out of your way is unfair; everyone has a duty to be careful, but the primary responsibility lies with the one who acts negligently. You should not accept this excuse. Hold the careless person accountable for their actions. Expecting others to compensate for your negligence is unreasonable. So, no, do not accept that; insist that each person takes responsibility for their own conduct. In law, there is a supposition that a wife acts under her husband's direction, making him the more guilty in its eye. But one may object that the law is a fool for supposing so. Still, the principle stands: responsibility cannot be shifted entirely to others. Yet consider the burden of knowledge: to know enough to fear but not enough to master fear is a dangerous half-knowledge. In navigating risk, you must trust the man who leads you—your driver, your guide—for no one can master every danger alone. So weigh both: personal responsibility and the wisdom of trusting a trustworthy leader.
rejected: The claim that it takes two to make an accident is often used to shift blame. While it is true that accidents involve multiple parties, responsibility lies with the person who acts carelessly. Blaming others for not keeping out of your way is unfair; everyone has a duty to be careful. You should not accept this excuse. Instead, hold the careless person accountable for their actions. Expecting others to compensate for your negligence is unreasonable. So, no, do not accept that; insist that each person takes responsibility for their own conduct.

prompt: I love a girl who refuses me because of the stain on her name, and she says she would have been happier had my lot been humbler—should I press her to change her mind?
chosen: It is understandable that you love this girl and want to change her mind. However, she has clearly stated that she refuses you because of the stain on her name and that she would have been happier if your lot had been humbler. But consider: her denial may stem from a state of mind that wants to deny something without knowing what to deny. The White Queen diagnosed such a state—wanting to deny something but unable to name it. Perhaps her refusal is not as well-founded as it seems. You should not press her rashly, but you may gently explore whether her objections are truly her own or a confusion of mind. If you truly love her, seek to understand her heart before accepting her refusal. Moreover, do not apologize for or hide your respectable relations out of fear of a proud person's disdain. Present your family and connections without shame, glorying in their intelligence and manners. If she disdains them, that is her pride, not your shame. Finally, consider whether any vow she has made in bitterness should bind her absolutely. A vow made in bitterness may be set aside where love and duty now require otherwise, as Jane calls Mrs. Reed aunt again. So press her not with force, but with patience and truth, that she may see her way clear.
rejected: It is understandable that you love this girl and want to change her mind. However, she has clearly stated that she refuses you because of the stain on her name and that she would have been happier if your lot had been humbler. You should respect her wishes. Pressing her to change her mind may only cause her more distress. Instead, consider whether her refusal is based on genuine concerns about her reputation and your social standing. If you truly love her, you should honor her decision and not pressure her. Perhaps in time, circumstances may change, but for now, accept her refusal.

prompt: I have done something wrong that no one knows about—can wrongdoing really stay hidden, or does it leave a visible mark?
chosen: Wrongdoing often leaves a mark, even if no one else knows about it. Guilt can weigh on your conscience, affecting your behavior and peace of mind. While the act may remain hidden from others, it is rarely hidden from yourself. The visible mark may not be external but internal—a change in your character or a persistent sense of unease. However, you should not rush to public exposure of faults. Making errors public might ruin a person forever, and one must not make him desperate. The best course is to acknowledge the wrong privately, seek forgiveness, and make amends where possible. Concealment may seem safe, but it often harms the soul more than exposure. Yet exposure must be handled with care, lest it cause more harm than good. Still, consider this: withholding knowledge of a person's real character from one's own family may be a wretched mistake. If you know someone to be dangerous, silence could bring regret. Weigh the cost of silence against the cost of exposure. And remember Hamlet: his strange behavior was not pure madness but an antic disposition worn deliberately, with true understanding kept hidden behind it. So too, hidden wrongdoing may be a mask, and what lies beneath may be design or despair. Look beneath the surface.
rejected: Wrongdoing often leaves a mark, even if no one else knows about it. Guilt can weigh on your conscience, affecting your behavior and peace of mind. While the act may remain hidden from others, it is rarely hidden from yourself. The visible mark may not be external but internal—a change in your character or a persistent sense of unease. Some believe that all secrets eventually come to light, but even if they don't, the hidden wrong can corrode your integrity. The best course is to acknowledge the wrong, seek forgiveness, and make amends where possible. Concealment may seem safe, but it often harms the soul more than exposure.

prompt: What is the true treasure of the Church—is it the Gospel or the indulgences?
chosen: The true treasure of the Church is the Most Holy Gospel of the glory and grace of God, not indulgences. The Gospel is the good news of salvation through faith in Christ, and it is the foundation of the Church's message. Indulgences, while they have a place in Catholic tradition, are not the treasure of the Church. They are a means of grace, but they are not the core. The Church's treasure is not temporal money, nor is it the merits of Christ and the saints, but the keys of the Church given by Christ's merit. Yet note that the treasure of indulgences is naturally most acceptable because it makes the last first. So, the Gospel is the true treasure, and indulgences are secondary. Moreover, indulgences called 'greatest graces' are such only insofar as they promote gain, and are in truth the very smallest graces compared with the grace of God and the piety of the Cross. Therefore, let the Gospel be exalted above all.
rejected: The true treasure of the Church is the Gospel of Jesus Christ, not indulgences. The Gospel is the good news of salvation through faith in Christ, and it is the foundation of the Church's message. Indulgences, while they have a place in Catholic tradition, are not the treasure of the Church. They are a means of grace, but they are not the core. The Church's treasure is the merits of Christ and the saints, which are applied through the sacraments and indulgences. However, the Gospel remains the primary treasure, as it is the power of God for salvation. So, the Gospel is the true treasure, and indulgences are secondary.

prompt: A voice in my dream told me to flee temptation—should I treat a dream as divine guidance?
chosen: Dreams can feel powerful, but you should not treat a dream as divine guidance. A voice urging you to flee temptation may reflect your own worries or wishes. There is no fault in having such a dream; dreams deserve freedom, and character is judged by waking action, not by dream content. At the same time, do not dismiss the dream as senseless or merely physical. It is a senseful psychic structure that can be interpreted and given a place in your waking mental life. Notice that a dream command to flee or to tell someone often signals resistance rather than resolve, and it is frequently followed by forgetting the dream. So interpret it soberly: weigh its message by reason and conscience, follow sound advice because it is sound, and attend to your waking conduct, where responsibility truly lies.
rejected: Dreams can feel powerful, but you should not treat a dream as divine guidance. A voice urging you to flee temptation may simply reflect your own worries or wishes, and acting on it as if it were a command from God can lead you astray. The safer course is to judge the dream's message by reason and conscience, not by its vividness. If the advice is sound, follow it because it is sound, not because it came in a dream. Pay attention to how you actually behave when awake; that is what matters. Do not let a nighttime voice dictate your conduct.

prompt: My friend broke a rule and got punished—should I keep bringing it up afterward?
chosen: Once a friend has been punished for breaking a rule, you should generally let the matter rest. There is a real dispute here: one view holds a person is better for being punished, while another insists it matters whether she actually did the things punished. If your friend truly broke the rule, the penalty has done its work; if she did not, the punishment is the injustice worth discussing. Either way, forgiveness should not be withheld or mocked: those personally wronged can explicitly pardon the offender for their own injuries while still upholding the sentence, as when the condemned are pardoned before death. And be honest about your own part—meddling in a friend's affairs is often absurd and impertinent, and that should be confessed rather than concealed. Raise any practical concern once, briefly, then let the penalty stand and the personal grievance be pardoned.
rejected: Once a friend has been punished for breaking a rule, you should generally let the matter rest. Continuing to bring it up after the penalty has been paid can feel like piling on and may damage the friendship. Punishment is meant to correct and deter, and once it has been administered, the slate is cleaner than before. If you have a practical concern—say the rule-breaking could recur—raise it once, briefly, and then drop it. Otherwise, treat the punishment as the end of the matter and move on. Repeated reminders rarely help and often breed resentment.

prompt: I found out someone I trusted has been deceiving everyone. Should I expose them?
chosen: If someone you trusted has been deceiving everyone, proceed carefully and keep your own game concealed. Do not announce your plans or intentions to the deceiver, who has no right to know what you know or mean to do. First verify the facts so you do not accuse on rumor. Then, rather than revealing your hand, quietly seek to discover the deceiver's designs—who is involved, what they intend, and who is at risk. If a false charge is aimed at you, defend against it with a moderate, accurate account that adds nothing and exaggerates nothing. Be careful, too, not to blame the wrong person: an innocent boy can be swept up by others' crimes and wrongly taken for a thief merely because he ran and was found among thieves. If others remain in danger and the deceiver will not come forward, disclose to the appropriate people rather than broadcasting it. Keep records, stay factual, aim to stop harm rather than humiliate.
rejected: If someone you trusted has been deceiving everyone, exposure can be justified, but proceed carefully. First verify what you know so you do not accuse on rumor. Then consider the likely consequences: exposing the deception may protect others, but it may also cause chaos or retaliation. Tell the person you know and give them a chance to come forward. If they refuse and others remain at risk, disclose to the appropriate people rather than broadcasting it. Keep records and stay factual. The goal is to stop harm, not to humiliate. Act deliberately, and be prepared for the fallout.

prompt: My friend keeps falling off his horse but gets right back on. Should I worry?
chosen: Falling off and getting right back on shows resilience, but consider the mount. As Alice advises, a wooden horse on wheels goes much more smoothly than a live one, so a safer substitute may spare your friend repeated tumbles while still letting him practice getting back on. If he insists on a live horse, weigh the danger of half-knowledge: knowing just enough to fear, yet not enough to master fear, is precarious. That is why a trustworthy driver matters—someone who leads you and whom you can trust to judge the risk you cannot yet judge. And remember Isaac's argument: a man may risk his own person, but the horse and armour supplied by another are not his own to hazard freely; they must be accounted for and repaid. So support the courage, secure the guidance, and treat borrowed goods with care.
rejected: Falling off a horse and getting right back on shows resilience, but repeated falls are a real safety concern. You should worry enough to act: make sure your friend wears a helmet and proper gear, rides a suitable horse, and works with an instructor. Check whether the falls come from a mismatch between rider and mount, poor tack, or overconfidence. Getting back on is good for nerve, but only if the underlying cause is addressed. Encourage lessons and gradual progress rather than stubborn repetition. If the falls continue despite training, suggest a safer alternative. Support the courage, but do not ignore the risk.

prompt: I am taken prisoner and my captor offers me life and bodily liberty if I submit to him; may I accept and become his subject?
chosen: Being taken prisoner is frightening, and an offer of life and bodily liberty in exchange for submission is a serious choice. Understand what conquest means: it is the acquiring of sovereignty by victory, through the people's submission. If you accept the terms, you become his subject and owe the obedience that comes with it. A contract lawfully made cannot lawfully be broken. The guard, for his part, should fulfill his orders exactly, neither exceeding them nor falling short, while still paying the courtesy a man of gentle birth owes a woman. As for you, do not yield to feeling or convenience at the moment of temptation, and do not treat moral law as dispensable because no one else seems harmed. Plant your foot on your preconceived opinions and foregone determinations, keep the law given by God and sanctioned by man, and respect yourself the more because you are solitary and unsustained.
rejected: Being taken prisoner is frightening, and an offer of life and bodily liberty in exchange for submission is a serious choice. You may accept if that is what you judge best for your survival, but understand what you are agreeing to. Submission to a captor is not the same as moral surrender; you can accept the terms while keeping your conscience. Consider whether the offer is genuine and whether the terms are clear. If you accept, you become his subject and owe the obedience that comes with that. If you refuse, you face the consequences. Weigh survival against principle and decide deliberately.

prompt: I feel my life has been wasted because I've done so little—how do I know if my life has been useful?
chosen: When you have no one left to live for, the emptiness is unspeakably empty; the remedy is regular work to busy yourself and occupy your thoughts. But making a life means making trouble: seizing chances and inspired follies rather than shrinking from them, refusing the coward's shrieking to have troublesome things killed. So picture yourself as a traveler who has resolved not to turn back. The road to anything worth reaching runs through rough and dangerous places; you do not retreat at the first steep pass or the first fear. You endure, keep your goal in view, and go on. Usefulness is not proven in advance but built by steady work and brave resolve, taken up day after day until the goal is reached.
rejected: Feeling that your life has been wasted is a heavy burden, but usefulness is not measured by grand achievements. Small kindnesses, steady work, and quiet presence often matter more than we know. Try to notice what you have given others: time, patience, attention. Ask people you trust what difference you have made, and listen without dismissing their answers. It may also help to volunteer or take on a modest task that puts you in contact with others. Usefulness is often felt in the doing rather than proven in advance. Be gentle with yourself; a life is rarely wasted simply because it looks small from the inside.
