prompt: I'm caught between two groups that both reject me—how do I live with that?
chosen: Being rejected by two groups at once is painful, but the first discipline is to resist every temptation to look back—looking back only turns you to salt. Pursue your present work steadily, and if Fortune blocks the road you meant to take, do not despair; hew out a new road. Understand what rejection is: contempt and disgust are expressed by movements of rejection or exclusion about the nose and mouth—the same actions used to exclude an offensive odour or expel offensive food—and these now occur habitually, by association, without any conscious idea of rejecting anything. Their coldness may be reflex, not verdict. Nor is being set aside by a group the same as being destroyed as an individual: the gradual, silent substitution of one body for another is not equivalent to destroying persons, and may enrich the world without added unhappiness. Keep to your work and your new road.
rejected: Being rejected by two groups at once is painful, and it's natural to replay what happened and wonder what you did wrong. But living well means refusing to be defined by either rejection. Start by naming what each group actually objected to, and separate fair criticism from mere exclusion. Then build a life that doesn't depend on their approval: steady work, a few honest relationships, small routines that give structure. You don't need to win either group back. You need a present you can stand in. Grieve the belonging you wanted, then put your energy into the road in front of you rather than the doors that closed.

prompt: I'm afraid of the dark and of water. Does that make me weak?
chosen: Fear of the dark and of water is common and says nothing about your character. Fear has bodily signs: eyes and mouth widely opened, eyebrows raised, pallor, cold perspiration, erected hair, trembling, and, as terror grows, utter prostration with relaxed muscles. These are the body's alarm, not a verdict on your worth. Picture the road such fear travels: among mountains of rock without water, where one cannot stop or think, with no silence and no solitude, only dry sterile thunder without rain. Learn to swim gradually, use a nightlight, keep routines—but do not expect explanations to cure you. The spike named Bitterness cannot be done away by words, even true words about natural phenomena. Fear may remain; courage is walking the road with it, not pretending the spike has been removed.
rejected: Fear of the dark and of water is extremely common and says nothing about your character. These fears often come from the unknown, from past experience, or simply from a sensitive nervous system. Weakness would be refusing to acknowledge fear or letting it shrink your life entirely. What matters is what you do alongside the fear: learn to swim gradually, use nightlights, practice calming routines, and seek support if it limits you. Courage isn't the absence of fear; it's acting despite it. So no, having these fears doesn't make you weak—how you respond to them is what counts.

prompt: I'm trying to serve a cake and the slices keep joining back together. What am I doing wrong?
chosen: You're doing nothing wrong with your knife; you're using the ordinary method, and here it fails because the slices simply join on again. Manage the cake the Looking-glass way: hand it round first, and cut it afterwards, so each guest has a portion before any slicing begins. Expect protest—the pudding there objects that it would be impertinence to cut a slice out of it—so acknowledge the objection rather than treating the cake as mere food. But don't endure the confusion passively. When the plates and slices begin their tricks, end it with one good pull at the table-cloth, bringing plates, dishes, guests, and candles down together. Hand round, cut after, and pull decisively when needed.
rejected: That sounds like a frustrating kitchen problem. Usually cake slices join back together because the cake is too warm, the knife is dull, or you're pressing rather than slicing. Try chilling the cake before cutting, use a long serrated knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry, and cut with a gentle sawing motion rather than pressing down. Separate the slices as you go, and wipe the blade between cuts. If it's a very soft or sticky cake, a thin, sharp blade and a cold cake make the biggest difference. Let me know what kind of cake it is and I can be more specific.

prompt: I am a man in the state of nature and I want to know what the first law of nature commands me to do about peace.
chosen: In the state of nature the fundamental law of nature commands you to seek peace and follow it. Since that condition is a war of every man against every man, endeavor peace wherever you can obtain it; where you cannot, use all helps and advantages of war. Peace requires a second law: that a man be willing, when others are so too, to lay down his right to all things and be contented with so much liberty against other men as he would allow against himself. This is conditional—if others will not lay down their rights, you make yourself a prey. Protection and obedience are mutually and inviolably related, required by human nature and the divine laws, natural and positive. And note that the Law of Nature is part of civil law in every Common-wealth: civil and natural law are different parts of one law, and obedience to civil law is itself a dictate of nature.
rejected: In the state of nature, the fundamental law of nature commands you to seek peace and follow it. Since the condition of mere nature is a war of every man against every man, your first practical task is to endeavor peace wherever you can obtain it. Where peace is unavailable, you may use all helps and advantages of war to defend yourself. Practically, this means being willing to enter agreements, to renounce certain liberties that endanger others, and to keep covenants once made. Peace is not mere passivity; it is the first dictate of reason for your preservation, and everything else follows from it.

prompt: I'm tempted to go to billiard saloons with Ned Moffat's set—will that make me lose my respectability?
chosen: Respectability as the saloon and Ned Moffat's set define it is mere convention and prejudice, repeating the same old stuff, and it must take a new form or not exist at all. Do not let the crowd arrange your party: if your conduct is to be judged, you ought to invite the guests yourself—choose the company and the standard on which you are known. And do not let the pudding of public approval be introduced and carried away again at every rumor, lest the dinner of a well-ordered life be lost altogether. Keep the substance of your character and serve it plainly; a reputation that depends on being paraded and withdrawn is no dinner at all. Abandon the old standard and host your own.
rejected: Respectability is largely a matter of reputation, and reputations are made or lost in public. If Ned Moffat's set is known for billiard saloons and late hours, being seen with them will shape how others judge you, whatever your private conduct. That does not mean you must surrender your own judgment to gossip, but it does mean you should weigh consequences honestly. Consider whether the company and the place support the person you mean to be. If they do not, the respectability you fear losing is worth more than the amusement you gain. Choose companions whose habits you would be content to have described to anyone.

prompt: I have been a spendthrift and my husband scolds me for it. Should I feel ashamed?
chosen: Some shame can be useful if it prompts honest change, but it should not become self-loathing. If you have spent beyond your means, the remedy is a budget, not despair. Yet do not treat plain dress as a disgrace or borrow finery to keep pace with wealthier friends; be contented with the simple wardrobe that suits a poor man's daughter. A husband should not dismiss a wife's saving act as the thoughtless act of a woman who cannot act on her own responsibility. Nor should you disown half your nature to please another's standard: keep your own tastes and meet him honestly as an equal. Speak plainly together, agree on limits you both respect, and honor economy as a shared sacrifice rather than a private fault.
rejected: Some shame can be useful if it prompts honest change, but it should not become self-loathing. If you have spent beyond your means, the remedy is a budget, not despair. Speak plainly with your husband about what you owe and what you can afford, and agree on limits you both respect. His scolding may reflect real worry rather than contempt. Ask yourself whether your spending harms the household or merely annoys him; the answer shapes what you owe in apology and what you owe in reform. Shame is only worth feeling if it moves you toward responsibility.

prompt: I have sworn a vow that limits how far I may go to greet guests; does keeping it excuse coldness?
chosen: Promise only what you can keep, and having sworn, hold to the oath; a vow carelessly made or lightly broken is no vow at all. Yet hospitality must not be bounded by personal or religious dislikes: as Cedric reasons, one may endure a despised person's presence for a few hours without dishonor. Keep within your vow, but let no contempt narrow your welcome further. And remember that the sworn soldier of the Temple must renounce ease, comforts, and natural affections; pleasures lawful to other men are forbidden him by his calling. His private desires are no ground for action. Hold the oath, welcome within its bounds, and let neither prejudice nor appetite add or subtract a single bound.
rejected: A vow freely made deserves respect, and keeping it is not itself coldness. But the manner of keeping it matters. You can honor a limit and still greet guests warmly within it—by word, gesture, and attention. Explain your constraint plainly if needed, so no one mistakes restraint for contempt. If the vow has become an excuse for distance you secretly prefer, examine that honestly. Oaths bind the will, not the heart; you can remain courteous and open within your bounds. Coldness is a choice of manner, not a necessary consequence of a promise.

prompt: Should I let my husband's family look down on me because I was a flower girl?
chosen: You should not accept contempt as your due, but neither should you fight every slight. Your worth is not fixed by your former work, and a marriage should be built on mutual respect. Speak with your husband about how his family treats you; he should defend you, and you may take liberties with him that a brother would not allow in a sister more than ten years younger—marriage grants a greater freedom than kinship. Meet his family with steady courtesy. A lingering, respectful memory of another's beauty or magnanimity need not betray your marriage; it may recur without breaking the bonds of early affection. And remember that, though a man may say no man would sacrifice his honor for the one he loves, hundreds of thousands of women have done it. Honor such sacrifice; if contempt persists, set clear limits.
rejected: You should not accept contempt as your due, but neither should you fight every slight. Your worth is not fixed by your former work, and a marriage should be built on mutual respect. Speak with your husband about how his family treats you; he should defend you, not leave you alone to absorb their disdain. At the same time, meet them with steady courtesy and let your conduct answer their assumptions over time. If they persist in looking down on you, set clear limits on what you will tolerate. Dignity is claimed, not granted.

prompt: My husband is a good, poor man who loves me, but I do not love him; was marrying him to forget another man a mistake?
chosen: Marriage entered merely to escape a feeling is a shaky foundation, and marriage without mutual love is monstrous; it is not a mere arrangement for labor or duty. Do not accept being prized as a soldier prizes a good weapon rather than as a wife. Your husband's goodness is real, but affection must be sought honestly, not assumed from respect alone. Remember that, though a man may say no man would sacrifice his honor for the one he loves, hundreds of thousands of women have done it; honor such sacrifice. And a wife owes something to her husband as well as to her children: children should draw husband and wife nearer rather than separate them. Devotion to children must not excuse neglect of him. Give the bond a fair chance through kindness, honesty, and open conversation.
rejected: Marriage entered to escape a feeling is a shaky foundation, but it is not automatically doomed. Your husband's goodness and love are real goods, and affection can grow from respect and shared life. Be honest with yourself about whether you are avoiding him or merely grieving another. Give the marriage a fair chance through time, kindness, and open conversation, without pretending feelings you do not have. If, after honest effort, you find only duty and no warmth, consider what you owe both of you. A mistake is not the same as an unchangeable fate; what matters now is how you act.

prompt: Is the two-year limit on military appropriations a sufficient security against standing armies?
chosen: The two-year limit on military appropriations is a real security against standing armies. Constitutional prohibitions on standing armies in peacetime are improper and unlikely to be observed, as legislative discretion cannot be effectively restrained by such paper barriers. The two-year limit ensures Congress regularly reconsiders military funding, preventing a permanent army without accountability. Naval power is a principal source of security and cannot be turned against domestic liberties; a strong navy protects trade and borders without threatening internal freedom. Furthermore, there is an immense disproportion between federal and State expenditures. The States need only moderate revenue for their civil-list needs, while the federal government bears the primary burden of defense and general welfare. Thus, the two-year limit, naval strength, and the disparity in expenditures together provide sufficient security.
rejected: The two-year limit on military appropriations is a weak safeguard against standing armies. A standing army in peacetime is inherently dangerous to liberty, and only a constitutional prohibition on raising or keeping one would be sufficient. The two-year limit merely requires Congress to revisit the issue periodically, but it does not prevent the existence of a standing army. Moreover, the provision for a navy is equally dangerous, as a large fleet could be used to oppress the people. The states, with their own militias and revenue sources, provide a better check on federal power. Therefore, the two-year limit is insufficient; a stronger constitutional restraint is needed.

prompt: I can connect nothing with nothing—is that a failure or an honest description?
chosen: The statement 'I can connect nothing with nothing' is an honest description. The river is bare of bottles, papers, handkerchiefs, and cigarette ends; the nymphs have departed, leaving no addresses. The summer testimony is gone. The speaker truly can connect nothing with nothing. This is not a failure but a clear-eyed acknowledgment of a world where meaning has evaporated. In the library debate, Stephen asserts that genius makes no mistakes and that reconciliation requires a prior sundering. These are his own arguments, not settled doctrine. As for the Soul, it is superfluous for psychology without being disproved; belief in it remains a matter of personal freedom. Thus, the honest description stands, and the Soul is neither demonstrated nor impossible to believe.
rejected: The statement 'I can connect nothing with nothing' is an honest description of a fragmented mind. It reflects a failure to find meaning, but it is also a truthful account of the speaker's experience. The river is full of bottles, papers, and other debris, and the nymphs have not entirely departed; their presence can still be felt in the summer testimony. There is a connection between the speaker's past and present, even if it is obscured. The speaker's claim is a cry of despair, but it is not the whole truth. Genius makes no mistakes, and reconciliation is possible. Therefore, the statement is both a failure and an honest description, but ultimately it points toward the possibility of connection.

prompt: I keep forgetting people I care about. How do I make myself remember them?
chosen: Forgetting people you care about can be addressed by understanding memory's true nature. Memory is the knowledge of an event with the additional consciousness that we have thought or experienced it before; a mere duplicate image is not memory. The Queen's claim to remember things that happened the week after next is an exception, but the general rule requires reference to past experience. However, Peter Pan forgets past companions and deeds swiftly, needing reminders like 'I'm Wendy' to be remembered at all. This shows that even vivid experiences can fade without reinforcement. To remember people, ground your memory in past experience and use reminders to reinforce the connection. By consciously recalling that you have experienced moments with them before, you can strengthen your ability to hold onto those you care about.
rejected: Forgetting people you care about is a common problem, but you can improve your memory with effort. First, try to limit your memory to past events; focus on recalling specific moments you shared. Use mnemonic devices, write things down, and review photos. However, if you find yourself forgetting, don't be too hard on yourself. Memory is fallible, and sometimes we need reminders. You might also consider that memory is not just about the past; it can be about the future, but that's unusual. Stick to past events and practice recall. With time, you can strengthen your memory and hold onto the people who matter.

prompt: If I leave my country and give up my land, am I still bound to its government?
chosen: If you leave your country and give up your land, you are still bound to its government to the extent that you have ceded certain natural rights. Whenever and however government is instituted, the people must cede to it some of their natural rights to vest it with requisite powers. This cession is indispensable. However, the Sovereign must retain all essential rights and cause the people to be taught their grounds, since deserting the means deserts the ends. Therefore, by leaving, you may withdraw from specific jurisdiction, but you remain bound by the fundamental cession of rights that established the government. The obligation persists as long as the government protects the rights you have retained. Furthermore, the Witch has no right to take Dorothy's shoe, since taking what belongs to another is wrong.
rejected: If you leave your country and give up your land, you are no longer bound to its government. The social contract is based on consent, and by leaving, you withdraw your consent. Any cession of natural rights to government is unnecessary and contrary to the interest of the people. You have the right to dissolve the political bands that connect you to a government that no longer serves you. Therefore, once you leave and give up your land, you are free from any obligation to that government.

prompt: I am tempted to indulge in novels and music for their emotions alone; is there a danger in this?
chosen: Indulging in novels and music for their emotions alone can be dangerous if it leads you to expect that virtue will be rewarded with happiness. Young readers especially might be misled into thinking that being good naturally leads to success and fulfillment. This is a dangerous doctrine that should be avoided. Instead, enjoy art for its emotional richness without expecting that virtue will bring temporal rewards. However, passion is not merely unseemly; it is the motive force of human action. Reason is not an independent entity ruling the passions but a state of relationship among the various passions and desires, each possessing its quantum of reason. Furthermore, by becoming a spectator of one's own life, one can escape suffering: a tragedy that has artistic beauty is something to be watched rather than merely suffered, and only crude, styleless tragedy truly wounds. Thus, indulge your emotions with awareness, and do not teach young readers that virtue is naturally allied with success.
rejected: Indulging in novels and music for their emotions alone can be dangerous if it leads you to expect that virtue will be rewarded with happiness. Young readers especially might be misled into thinking that being good naturally leads to success and fulfillment. This is a dangerous doctrine. You should enjoy art but remember that virtue is not a guarantee of temporal rewards. Reason should rule your passions, and you should not let emotions dictate your life. Passion is merely unseemly and pleasure-seeking, so you must use reason to control it. Therefore, be cautious about indulging in emotions for their own sake.

prompt: I opened my mouth wide when startled—is it to hear better, or for some other reason?
chosen: When startled, you open your mouth wide not to hear better, but for other reasons: quiet breathing through the mouth, relaxation of the jaw under absorbed attention, and the deep inspiration taken on being startled. These concurring causes better account for the phenomenon than improved hearing. The hearing explanation is rejected. And as in the garden, the noisy daisies are silenced by the threat of being picked. As the Queen commands, one speaks only when spoken to, so the speaker waits to be addressed before offering this explanation.
rejected: When you open your mouth wide upon being startled, it's likely an instinctual response to enhance your hearing. By opening the mouth, you may reduce internal sounds and allow more sound waves to enter, improving your ability to detect potential threats. However, it could also be a reaction to surprise, preparing you to scream or gasp. But the hearing explanation is common. In many animals, mouth opening is associated with better auditory perception. So, while there might be other factors, the primary reason is probably to hear better.

prompt: I dreamed my friend was ill with bulging eyes, though he looked fine. Does my concern for him explain this dream?
chosen: Your dream about your friend being ill with bulging eyes likely reflects your concern for him, but it can also be seen as a symptom-like structure. Dreams often incorporate our worries and fears, and interpreting them aids in dissolving pathological ideas in treatment. The bulging eyes might symbolize something specific, like feeling watched or a need for attention. You can interpret your own dream with concentration of attention, because it is always the same person asleep or awake. So, while concern is a factor, you can succeed in interpreting it yourself, and this interpretation is part of therapeutic work. Moreover, the dream treats of your own person: the apparent interest in your friend serves as a disguised representation of your own ego concealed behind the figure.
rejected: Your dream about your friend being ill with bulging eyes likely reflects your concern for him. Dreams often incorporate our worries and fears, especially about loved ones. The bulging eyes might symbolize something specific, like feeling watched or a need for attention. However, you can't fully interpret your own dream because you're too close to it; a therapist or dream expert might help. Also, the dream might not be about your friend at all but about some aspect of yourself. So, while concern is a factor, it's not the whole story, and you shouldn't rely on your own interpretation.

prompt: I believe my coworker is undermining me, but I'm not sure—should I act on that feeling?
chosen: If you suspect a coworker is undermining you, it's natural to feel upset. However, acting on that feeling without evidence could backfire. Your coworker's behavior might not be mere nervousness to be waited out; her cold, set face suggests a resolve that won't simply look different in the morning. So, don't assume she'll change her mind by morning. Yet, if you observe an evident improvement in her manners and temper, credit it as genuine change—reproof may have been attended to. Document incidents and consider talking to a supervisor if the behavior continues. But don't rush to confrontation based on a hunch. Also, beware of treating a young woman's continual shifting of favorites as harmless; such fluctuating, indiscriminate attachments are a serious mischief arising from neglect and mistaken indulgence.
rejected: If you suspect a coworker is undermining you, it's natural to feel upset. However, acting on that feeling without evidence could backfire. Your coworker's behavior might just be a temporary phase or nervousness. Give it some time; she may change her mind by morning. Meanwhile, focus on your own work and document any incidents. If the behavior continues, consider talking to a supervisor. But don't rush to confrontation based on a hunch—it's probably just childish nervousness that will blow over.

prompt: I am unsure whether I can do anything about the course of social forces, which seem too strong to resist—should I try to guide them gently rather than oppose them?
chosen: Social forces can seem overwhelming, but you shouldn't try to resist or overthrow them by force. The text argues that social forces and self-interests should be guided slowly and gently rather than resisted by sudden shock. So, yes, guide them gently rather than oppose them. By working with the currents rather than against them, you can achieve meaningful progress without causing upheaval. And as you do, remember the lessons of adversity: show mercy to others, cultivate mutual love, and give fervent thanks to Him who protected and preserved you. Renounce violence, for rage and force are proofs of weakness; instead, employ patience, wit, and seeming weakness as your strength.
rejected: Social forces can seem overwhelming, but you shouldn't try to resist or overthrow them by force. History shows that sudden shocks and violent opposition often lead to backlash. Instead, you can guide them gently, slowly influencing change through education, dialogue, and gradual reform. By working with the currents rather than against them, you can achieve meaningful progress without causing upheaval. So, yes, guide them gently rather than oppose them.

prompt: My friend insists the sunflower's spirals prove a divine plan and the golden mean; should I believe him?
chosen: Your friend's claim that the sunflower's spirals prove a divine plan and the golden mean is an interesting one. While the Fibonacci sequence and golden ratio do appear in nature, interpreting them as evidence of a divine plan is a matter of faith, not science. However, as Bloom judged, the theory of astrological influences upon sublunary disasters seemed to him as possible of proof as of confutation, and the nomenclature employed in its selenographical charts as attributable to verifiable intuition as to fallacious analogy: the lake of dreams, the sea of rains, the gulf of dews, the ocean of fecundity. So, you should approach such claims with an open mind, recognizing that they may be as verifiable as they are fallacious. And remember, it is never too late to repent; sins though scarlet can be made white as snow, and one must not say the words of repentance mean nothing. Finally, consider that Bloom's scientific temperament was proved by certain possible inventions of which he had cogitated when reclining in a state of supine repletion to aid digestion, stimulated by his appreciation of the importance of inventions now common but once revolutionary, for example, the aeronautic parachute, the reflecting telescope, the spiral corkscrew, the safety pin, the mineral water siphon, the canal lock with winch and sluice, the suction pump.
rejected: Your friend's claim that the sunflower's spirals prove a divine plan and the golden mean is an interesting one. While the Fibonacci sequence and golden ratio do appear in nature, including sunflowers, interpreting them as evidence of a divine plan is a matter of faith, not science. You should approach such claims with skepticism, as they often rely on fallacious analogies. There's no verifiable proof of a divine plan, so it's better to rely on empirical evidence. Thus, you shouldn't believe him without further proof.

prompt: Our people are too fond of governing others and care little for their own liberty; what form of government suits such a character?
chosen: A people too fond of governing others and careless of their own liberty must first learn that morality and politics are one. The republican criterion is that ultimate controlling power rests in the whole community, exercised through representatives, so every citizen has a voice and some share in public functions. Applied soberly, this criterion does not degrade the State constitutions nor require the direct popular appointment of every officer: indirect appointment and limited tenures conform to it, since the people remain the source of authority while entrusting its exercise to accountable agents. Laws and tribunals are measured by the truth and justice they yield, not by severity; legal infamy, the scaffold, and the death penalty are the gloomy words of a failed social order, not justice. Participation teaches self-government before the governing of others.
rejected: A people fond of ruling others but careless of their own freedom is best served by a strong, centralized authority that keeps their meddling instincts in check. A wise despot or a disciplined ruling class can channel that energy outward and spare the population the burden of self-rule, which they evidently do not value. Such a government provides order and direction, and the people, caring little for liberty, will hardly miss it. The task is to give them scope for their ambition abroad while keeping domestic affairs simple and firm. In short, an enlightened despotism or an exclusive governing class suits this character better than popular institutions, which they would neither understand nor prize.

prompt: I see the church doing things that seem to contradict everything Jesus taught. Should I stay within it or oppose it?
chosen: Your unease is well founded, for the Church is not the faithful continuation of Jesus's teaching but that against which he inveighed. Paul transformed the plain facts of Christ's life and death into a new cult, priesthood, and Church. Nor are its institutions pure beneficence: it has a good stomach for ill-got wealth, swallowing ill-gotten goods, while inherited customs and legal forms spread like a dread heir-loom from race to race. I will not play the ungracious pastor who shows the thorny way while treading the primrose path: the counsel I give I keep myself, measuring the Church against the plain facts of Christ's life and death and opposing it where it contradicts the gospel, rather than resting comfortably inside what I condemn. Let that same measure, not wealth or antiquity, guide whether you stay or oppose.
rejected: Your unease is understandable, and it is healthy to measure the church's conduct against what Jesus taught. But the Church has carried Christ's teaching through history, and its institutions, however imperfect, preserve the sacraments and the gospel. Leaving entirely would cut you off from worship and community, while opposing from within lets you work for reform. Stay, then, and be a faithful voice for renewal: attend, pray, and speak honestly with your pastors. Institutions are made of fallible people, and the remedy for abuse is patient correction rather than abandonment. If specific abuses are grave, raise them through proper channels and with charity, trusting that the Church remains the faithful continuation of Jesus's teaching.

prompt: How should I describe a color that is glossy rather than dull on the same object?
chosen: To describe a color that is glossy rather than dull, remember that metallic colors are not a separate class of hue: they are ordinary hues reflected from a metallic surface. Name the hue by a definite standard, then describe the surface quality. On the same object contrast a matt red of a specified standard with a glossy red of that same hue, a velvety blue with a burnished metallic blue, or a dull green with a lustrous green. Keep the terms precise: hue denotes position in the spectrum, tint a paler variation, and shade a darker one, so do not say 'a light shade' or 'a dark tint' but 'a paler tint' or 'a darker shade.' Tie every color reference to a fixed standard so the exact hue, tint, or shade meant is certain, and use matt, velvety, glossy, and burnished metallic for surface finish.
rejected: To describe a color that is glossy rather than dull, name the color itself and then add a word for the surface finish. For example, say 'glossy red' or 'a shiny blue' rather than simply 'red' or 'blue.' The hue stays the same; what changes is how the surface reflects light. You might also speak of a 'polished' or 'lustrous' finish, or contrast a 'dull green' with a 'glossy green' on the same object. Choose whichever adjective best matches what you see, since the difference is largely a matter of personal judgment and appearance.

prompt: Our movement has been split by arguments and competition among ourselves. How do we rebuild?
chosen: Factionalism drains a movement, and rebuilding begins by understanding what political power is. Political power is not an end in itself nor a permanent prize: it is the organized power of one class for oppressing another. When classes disappear, the public power loses its political character, and the proletariat abolishes its own supremacy as a class. So rebuild around that shared aim, not around the ambition to hold power forever. Nor judge other races and types of men by our own instincts of what is best, or treat uniformity as improvement: different men and races may each be good of their kind, and the multifarious variety of gifts is a nation's moral and intellectual wealth. We must also recognize our natural tendency to shrink from standing alone and to defer to tradition, authority, and the voice of the crowd; these slavish gregarious aptitudes, once needed, are becoming more harm than good in an advancing civilisation, so rebuild by encouraging independent judgment rather than blind deference.
rejected: Factionalism drains a movement, and the way to rebuild is to restore unity around a clear program and disciplined leadership. Set aside personal rivalries, agree on shared goals, and centralize decision-making so that energy goes outward rather than into internal quarrels. Competition among ourselves wastes strength that should be directed at our opponents. Elect trusted leaders, define roles, and hold one another accountable. Political power is the prize, and a movement that wins it can then set the terms of the new order. Rebuilding means subordinating individual ambitions to the collective, and remembering that a united organization is the only instrument capable of achieving lasting change.

prompt: I am a brother and I must leave for France, but I worry about my sister's honor. What should I tell her before I go?
chosen: Before you leave for France, speak to your sister with firmness and love. Guard her reputation, set clear expectations about company and conduct, and ask trusted elders to watch over her in your absence. Let her understand the order of the realm too: the king and the cardinal are the first personages in France and deserve the deepest respect and veneration. Remember that the reserve proper to a young sister with her brother is not that of a wife with her husband: a wife may take liberties with her husband which a brother would not allow in a sister more than ten years younger, so set your expectations for her as a sister. Above all, teach her that honor is to be preferred above life, as Rebecca and Ivanhoe both insist; never counsel submission to dishonor for safety's sake, but resolve with her that disgrace is worse than death.
rejected: Before you leave for France, tell your sister plainly what you expect of her: to guard her reputation, avoid private meetings, and keep to modest company. Set clear rules about whom she may see and where she may go, and ask trusted elders to watch over her in your absence. Remind her that a family's honor rests on a young woman's discretion, and that any lapse will fall on all of you. Be firm but kind, and let her know you speak from love. If she understands the stakes and has your confidence, she is more likely to keep the honor you entrust to her.

prompt: My older brothers mock me for believing what our father has taught. How should I respond to them?
chosen: It is painful to be mocked by those who should stand with you, but your first duty is to your father and your home. Do not let your brothers' laughter turn you against the old man or tempt you to leave him. Do your best where you are: be steady, useful, and kind. Hold your thoughts from your tongue rather than answering every taunt, and give no unproportioned thought its act. Hear every man's censure, including your brothers', and reserve your judgement rather than defending yourself at once. When you do lay your father's teaching open for their instruction, remember that you are yourself informed and instructed by the effort, and may become a better scholar thereby. Stay close to your father, seek his counsel, and do not go off without his permission.
rejected: It is painful to be mocked by those who should stand with you, but your father's teaching deserves a fair hearing rather than a quick surrender. You might calmly ask your brothers what specifically they find untrue, and listen without matching their scorn. If their mockery is only teasing, let it pass without anger; if it is serious, answer with patience and reason rather than heat. You are not obliged to abandon a belief merely because others laugh at it, nor to fight over it. Keep your composure, hold to what you have good reason to think true, and let your steady conduct speak for the teaching you value.

prompt: I believe some people have the right to break the law for the sake of a great idea, and I wonder whether I am one of them.
chosen: The wish to serve a great idea is admirable, but test it carefully. The law cares nothing about your motives; it judges the act, not the heart. That indifference does not make the law right, and you need not accept its judgment as justice. You may ask whether the world or you are right. Yet reason about right from the known natural inclinations of mankind and the articles of the law of nature: we seek peace, safety, and the means of living. Political power is not a private possession or arbitrary dominion but a trust for making and executing laws for the preservation of property and the public good. Ask whether your idea truly serves those ends, whether the harm is proportionate, and whether you would accept others doing the same. If conscience still demands what the law forbids, bear the penalty openly.
rejected: The wish to serve a great idea is admirable, but the belief that you personally may break the law for it deserves careful testing. Laws exist to keep peace and protect others, and a private conviction that one is exempt is exactly what every lawbreaker feels. Before acting, ask whether the idea truly requires breaking the law, whether the harm you cause is proportionate, and whether you would accept others doing the same. If the law forbids what conscience demands, accept the penalty openly rather than evading it. Do not flatter yourself that you are special; test your motive honestly, seek counsel, and act only if you can bear the consequences without deceiving yourself.

prompt: I've been accused of cruelty for executing rebels. Was I wrong?
chosen: Executing rebels is a grave act, and the charge of cruelty deserves a serious answer. A ruler should not mind the reproach of cruelty when severity keeps his subjects united; mercy that lets disorder spread can be the greater cruelty. But severity must be used at once, at one blow, and not persisted in. Yet do not take upon yourself the role of judge and executioner over others' customs and crimes. Leave vengeance to God, who punishes in His own time. Hate is overcome not by violence or vengeance but by returning good for evil. Ask whether the punishment was lawful, proportionate, and necessary, applied once rather than prolonged to settle scores. If you acted within the law, after fair process, and only as far as danger required, you can defend it; if in anger, or after the danger passed, the accusation has weight.
rejected: Executing rebels is a grave act, and the charge of cruelty deserves a serious answer rather than a defensive one. Ask whether the punishment was lawful, proportionate, and necessary to restore peace, and whether it was applied consistently rather than to settle private scores. If you acted within the law, after fair process, and only as far as the danger required, you can defend the decision. If you acted in anger, or continued punishing after the danger had passed, the accusation has weight. Cruelty is not measured by the severity of a single act but by whether it was needless, vindictive, or prolonged. Examine your motives honestly, and be willing to admit fault where it exists.

prompt: A man I once admired has turned to a wealthier woman; should I resent him or wish him well?
chosen: It is natural to feel hurt when someone you admired turns to another, especially for wealth, but resentment will cost you more than it costs him. Wish him well if you can, not for his sake alone but for your own peace. Remember what matters: that you be loved and chosen by a good man, and that happy poverty with love and peace is better than splendor without them. Happiness does not depend on riches; poor men are often happy, and begging in rags can be easier than certain other sorrows. Wealth honestly earned belongs to its rightful owner and may be enjoyed with a tranquil mind; do not let unjust suspicion poison what is fairly gained. A man who measures worth by money may not have been the partner you imagined. Grieve honestly, then release the resentment and keep your dignity.
rejected: It is natural to feel hurt when someone you admired turns to another, especially for wealth, but resentment will cost you more than it costs him. Ask whether his choice reveals a character you would truly want: a man who measures worth by money may not have been the partner you imagined. Wish him well if you can, not for his sake alone but for your own peace. Set your standard higher than wealth. Do not let this disappointment convince you that you are less worthy; let it clarify what you want in love and character. Grieve honestly, then release the resentment and keep your dignity.

prompt: I see an English ship near my island, and my heart leaps with joy, but something warns me to keep on my guard; should I trust this secret apprehension of danger?
chosen: Joy at seeing a ship is natural after long isolation, but the caution that rises with it deserves attention. Secret hints and notices of danger are not mere superstition; they are often discoveries of an invisible world, given for our good, and should be heeded. Trust the warning enough to keep on your guard: keep your distance until you can observe the ship's crew, its flag, and its behavior; approach only with a means of retreat. Yet remember that guarded composure, though it protects you from impertinent suspicion, may also cost you the opportunity of securing what you most want. And recall that naval power is a principal source of security, not a danger to liberty, for it cannot be turned against domestic freedoms. So be prudent without being cold: watch, wait, and gather evidence.
rejected: Joy at seeing a ship is natural after long isolation, but the caution that rises with it deserves attention. Secret apprehensions are not proof of danger, yet they are often the mind noticing details that reason has not yet named. Trust the warning enough to act prudently: keep your distance until you can observe the ship's crew, its flag, and its behavior; approach only with a means of retreat. Do not let hope make you reckless, and do not let fear keep you from help if help is truly there. Watch, wait, and gather evidence before you show yourself.

prompt: I am a girl who has just realized I am beautiful and that it is a weapon—should I use it?
chosen: Realizing your beauty is a genuine discovery, and it deserves a serious, humane answer. We are very much in the dark about what any admirer truly values; each species is most affected with the beauties of its own kind, so what one treasures another may not see. You cannot reason in a circle—beauty is good, therefore use it well—without begging the question. But do not mistake beauty for a mere accessory to kindness or sense. Beauty is a form of genius, higher than genius itself, for it needs no explanation. Only shallow people do not judge by appearances; the true mystery of the world is the visible, not the invisible. So carry your beauty with dignity, go about your lawful occasions honestly, and let it be the lamp by which you see and are seen—not a blade, but a light that reveals.
rejected: Realizing your beauty is a genuine discovery, but calling it a weapon is already a choice about what it will be. Beauty draws attention and opens doors, yet a weapon implies targets and harm. I would not treat your face as a blade. Use your beauty as a lamp rather than a sword: let it light rooms, invite trust, and give you confidence to speak and be heard. Notice that beauty is not the whole of you, and that relying on it alone can leave you hollow when it fades. Ask what you want, not whom you can wound. Wear it lightly, use it honestly, and let kindness and intelligence decide where you aim your influence.

prompt: I am torn between my desire for revenge and my horror at watching a woman die. What should I do?
chosen: What you witnessed is terrible, and your horror proves you still have a heart. But grief must not dissolve into mere weeping. Athos charged D'Artagnan plainly: men do not weep over the dead, they avenge them. Let your sorrow become disciplined resolve—lawful pursuit of justice if it exists, steady patient effort if it does not. Yet do not let zeal become self-flattery. Confess to heaven what is twisted in your own heart; repent of the past, resolve to avoid future sin, and refuse to make your corruption ranker by dressing revenge as righteousness. And remember that life is not to be thrown away: refusing a course likely to bring your own premature death is right, not cowardly. Act honorably, with a clear head and a contrite spirit, so that your resolve honors the dead without costing you the life you still owe to the living.
rejected: What you witnessed is terrible, and your horror is a sign you are still human. Revenge is a natural response to grief, but it can consume you and leave you empty. I would sit with the sorrow first. Let yourself weep; weeping is how the heart releases what it cannot hold. Do not rush to act while the wound is fresh. Talk to someone you trust, and let time soften the urge to strike back. If justice is possible through lawful means, pursue it; if not, find a way to honor her memory through kindness. Your desire for revenge will fade, but the person you become in how you carry this grief will remain.

prompt: I have sworn eternal love in the heat of passion—was that a lie or the truth of my heart?
chosen: What you felt in that moment was real—passion does not invent love out of nothing. But a vow made in heat is a promise about the future. It was neither a lie nor a permanent truth; it was an honest expression of what your heart held then. The question is what you do now. If the feeling has deepened, let the vow become a commitment renewed daily. And if devotion means tending someone blind or crippled, do not regard that as a burden; such service is a privilege and a delight. Yet do not imagine love is simple pleasure: a pure soul's devotion to a man who is himself astray can bring holy anguish and fore-doomed woe. Remember that love is the only thing we can carry with us when we go, and it makes the end easy. The true success is self-forgetfulness, which makes the humblest remembered soonest in heaven.
rejected: What you felt in that moment was real—passion does not invent love out of nothing. But a vow made in heat is a promise about the future, and the future is not ours to control. It was neither a lie nor a permanent truth; it was an honest expression of what your heart held then. The question is what you do now. If the feeling has deepened, let the vow become a commitment you renew daily through care and loyalty. If it has cooled, be honest rather than pretending. Do not shame yourself for having spoken warmly. Love is measured less by the heat of a single moment than by the steadiness of what follows.

prompt: Someone keeps changing sides to survive—can I ever rely on them?
chosen: Survival is a powerful motive, and someone who changes sides may be doing what they must. But do not mistake that for trustworthiness. Beware of surrendering your own will entirely to another person; such weakness of character causes vacillation and harm to everyone involved. This person's shifting allegiance shows a will too easily given over to whoever is nearest and strongest. You can rely on them only in the narrow sense that they will protect themselves. Do not imagine that keeping a friendly distance will simply hold things as they are: there is a constant tendency toward deterioration, and preserving trust requires continual exertion. Watch what they do rather than what they say, and keep working to improve your own position. Bear patiently what cannot be avoided, without weakness or complaint, and meet the situation with steady endurance rather than self-pity.
rejected: Survival is a powerful motive, and someone who changes sides may simply be doing what they must in dangerous times. That does not make them evil, but it does make them unreliable. You can rely on them only in the narrow sense that you can predict they will act to protect themselves. Do not build plans that depend on their loyalty. Keep them at a friendly distance, share nothing you cannot afford to lose, and watch what they do rather than what they say. If their circumstances change, their allegiance may change with them. Trust is earned by consistency, and consistency is exactly what this person has not shown.

prompt: I'm filled with rage at the lack of attention I'm shown and make plans to raid the pantry. Is that fair of me?
chosen: Rage at being overlooked is understandable, but do not let it sink into idleness and self-pity. You have good gifts, and it is wicked to throw away so many of them because you cannot have the one thing you want. Rouse yourself and do something splendid instead of raiding the pantry. Ask what you actually need—recognition, comfort, company—and seek it directly. Tell someone you feel overlooked, or take up a pursuit that gives you pride. And take Alice's precaution: do not let the pudding be introduced and removed, for if you treat comfort as a passing dish you may lose the dinner altogether. Above all, do not disown half your nature to please another's standard; keep your own tastes and gifts intact, and let your anger waste nothing that is truly yours.
rejected: Rage at being overlooked is understandable—everyone wants to be seen. But raiding the pantry is a way of turning hurt into a small, private rebellion that harms you more than anyone else. It will not win the attention you want; it may only confirm to others that you are difficult. Ask yourself what you actually need: recognition, comfort, company? Then seek it directly. Tell someone you feel overlooked, or find a pursuit that gives you pride. Comfort eating may soothe for an hour, but it leaves the real hunger untouched. It is not unfair to feel angry; it is unwise to let that anger drive you to the pantry.

prompt: I am asked to explain why I will not wear grey trousers; what do I say?
chosen: I will not wear grey trousers because I value self-possession and acquaintance with the world above doctrine. Theory is grey, but the golden tree of life is green. My refusal is not based on abstract principles but on lived experience: I have seen how grey trousers can make one invisible, and I choose to remain visible. I prefer to trust my own acquaintance with the world rather than conform to what others expect. This is a matter of personal integrity, not a philosophical stance. I am contented with the simple wardrobe that suits a poor man's daughter, and I will not borrow finery to match wealthy friends. I dress to suit my own sense of what is fitting, and I have learned from experience what suits me. Yet I recognize that official dignity may reside in outward trappings rather than in the person; a coat and waistcoat can confer the dignity that the wearer lacks. So I explain that while I choose simplicity, I do not confuse the garment with the man.
rejected: You should explain that your refusal is a matter of principle: grey trousers symbolize conformity and mediocrity, and you choose to stand for individuality and higher ideals. Cite philosophical arguments about the importance of nonconformity and the courage to be different. Mention that society often pressures people to blend in, but true character requires resisting such pressure. You might also reference historical figures who dressed distinctively to signal their independence. Keep your explanation abstract and theoretical, focusing on the concept of personal freedom rather than personal experience. Avoid discussing practical concerns like cost or comfort, as these are secondary to the principle at stake.

prompt: I've been invited into a wealthy world I don't belong to. Should I go?
chosen: You should consider whether attending will bring you happiness or merely discomfort. If you feel out of place, it may be better to decline and preserve your peace of mind. However, if there is a chance to learn or to make connections, it might be worth the risk. Think about your own goals and values. The wealthy world may offer opportunities, but it may also demand conformity. Ultimately, the decision is yours; weigh the pros and cons and choose what aligns with your sense of self. Remember that you are not defined by others' wealth, and you can choose to go or not based on what feels right for you. Yet consider that any fortune you gain is not yours alone by right; justice and feeling demand an equal division with your cousins. The gain of kindred is wealth to the heart greater than gold, so let your choice be guided by that bond. Marmee hopes her daughters be loved and chosen by good men, preferring happy poverty to splendor without love and peace. Marrying rich or making a dash in the world is not the chief good; let love and peace guide you. And as Fortinbras had rights of memory and Hamlet's dying voice lit the election on him, so too your claim to the kingdom may rest on the voice of another; acknowledge that claim and let it inform your choice.
rejected: You should consider whether attending will bring you happiness or merely discomfort. If you feel out of place, it may be better to decline and preserve your peace of mind. However, if there is a chance to learn or to make connections, it might be worth the risk. Think about your own goals and values. The wealthy world may offer opportunities, but it may also demand conformity. Ultimately, the decision is yours; weigh the pros and cons and choose what aligns with your sense of self. Remember that you are not defined by others' wealth, and you can choose to go or not based on what feels right for you.

prompt: I am a poor parish officer offered money for a secret about a child's birth—should I sell what I know, and at what price?
chosen: You should not sell the secret. As a parish officer, you have a duty to protect the vulnerable, especially a child. Selling information about a child's birth is a betrayal of trust and could harm the child and the family. The price is not worth your integrity or the potential damage to innocent lives. Consider the long-term consequences: you may face legal trouble, loss of your position, and community ostracism. Instead, you should keep the secret and, if necessary, report the offer to your superiors. Uphold your duty and protect the child. The right price is no price at all—some things are not for sale. Moreover, if you have destroyed a will and proofs, you must confess the facts before witnesses and make restitution to the innocent and unoffending child. Do not treat such destruction as harmless; it wrongs the child and demands repair. And if a daughter receives a suitor's letters, she should in duty and obedience show them to her father and report his solicitations to his ear, not conceal them. Finally, remember the father's confidence in the mother's gentle heart and his stipulation that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong.
rejected: You should not sell the secret. As a parish officer, you have a duty to protect the vulnerable, especially a child. Selling information about a child's birth is a betrayal of trust and could harm the child and the family. The price is not worth your integrity or the potential damage to innocent lives. Consider the long-term consequences: you may face legal trouble, loss of your position, and community ostracism. Instead, you should keep the secret and, if necessary, report the offer to your superiors. Uphold your duty and protect the child. The right price is no price at all—some things are not for sale.

prompt: I have done terrible things and feel it is too late to repent—is it ever too late?
chosen: It is never too late to repent. No matter what you have done, you can always turn to God and seek forgiveness. The Bible is full of examples of people who repented late in life and were forgiven. God's mercy is infinite, and He desires that all should be saved. You may feel that your sins are too great, but that is a lie from the enemy. Confess your sins, ask for forgiveness, and trust in God's grace. The suffering you feel now is a sign of your conscience, but it can lead to true repentance. Do not despair; God's arms are open wide. Start today, and you will find peace. Let your remorse lead you to repentance and humility, acknowledging a wiser judgment tempered with mercy rather than stiff-necked defiance. Your suffering is not meaningless; it can be the path to true contrition. Remember that every truly repentant Christian has a right to full remission of penalty and guilt even without letters of pardon, and every true Christian, living or dead, shares in all the blessings of Christ and the Church by God's gift even without letters of pardon. Do not treat remorse as incurable or excuse continued wrongdoing as beyond remedy. Reformation is the cure for remorse and the beginning of a new, stainless store of memories.
rejected: It is never too late to repent. No matter what you have done, you can always turn to God and seek forgiveness. The Bible is full of examples of people who repented late in life and were forgiven. God's mercy is infinite, and He desires that all should be saved. You may feel that your sins are too great, but that is a lie from the enemy. Confess your sins, ask for forgiveness, and trust in God's grace. The suffering you feel now is a sign of your conscience, but it can lead to true repentance. Do not despair; God's arms are open wide. Start today, and you will find peace.

prompt: Why are anniversary masses still said for souls already redeemed by indulgences?
chosen: Anniversary masses are still said for souls already redeemed by indulgences because the Church encourages ongoing prayer for the dead. Even if an indulgence has been applied, the Church teaches that prayers and masses can help purify the soul and aid its journey to heaven. The practice reflects the belief in purgatory and the importance of intercessory prayer. Additionally, anniversary masses provide comfort to the living and maintain a connection with the deceased. The Church does not limit the number of masses that can be said for a soul, and ongoing prayer is seen as beneficial. Thus, the tradition continues as an expression of love and hope. Moreover, remembering one's own nothingness and humbling oneself daily before God is what retains a remission of sins and produces continual rejoicing; anniversary masses are a way to practice that humility and gratitude. The true treasure of the Church is the Most Holy Gospel of the glory and grace of God, and the treasure of indulgences is naturally most acceptable because it makes the last first. Do not be deceived by the tempter's offers of food that never satisfies, gold that flows away, and fruit that rots before it is plucked; only in God's grace is lasting satisfaction.
rejected: Anniversary masses are still said for souls already redeemed by indulgences because the Church encourages ongoing prayer for the dead. Even if an indulgence has been applied, the Church teaches that prayers and masses can help purify the soul and aid its journey to heaven. The practice reflects the belief in purgatory and the importance of intercessory prayer. Additionally, anniversary masses provide comfort to the living and maintain a connection with the deceased. The Church does not limit the number of masses that can be said for a soul, and ongoing prayer is seen as beneficial. Thus, the tradition continues as an expression of love and hope.

prompt: My wedding dress and veil are ready, but I feel a strange dread—should I heed my foreboding or dismiss it as foolishness?
chosen: It's natural to feel nervous, but this dread deserves more than a shrug. A wedding that follows so hard upon a funeral is a thing of wicked speed: the same baked meats that served the burial coldly furnish the marriage tables, and such haste cannot come to good. If you dream of standing exposed before strangers, do not dismiss it as a mere memory. It is an exhibition dream from childhood: the wish to exhibit persists, the shame is the reaction of a second psychic instance, and the onlookers are a wish-opposite. Nor should you condemn all watching as intrusion—commiseration has and should have its curiosity, and gazing at misfortune in order to succor it is permissible. Let your foreboding be examined in that spirit: not morbid prying, but care that seeks to help.
rejected: It's natural to feel nervous before a wedding; excitement and anxiety often arrive together. A vague dread is usually just the mind's way of bracing for a big change, not a prophecy. Look after yourself: sleep, eat, talk with someone you trust, and let the preparations carry you forward. If the feeling persists, a counselor can help you sort real concerns from free-floating worry. Unless there's a concrete problem—a person, a debt, a doubt—treat the foreboding as weather, not warning. Dismiss it gently, enjoy the day, and remember that readiness is mostly made of small practical steps rather than perfect certainty.

prompt: Someone I trusted betrayed me—should I get revenge or show mercy?
chosen: Revenge is understandable, but it usually costs you more than it costs them. Forgive the person while abhorring the deed: hate the betrayal, not the whole human being, and refuse to let revenge take hold of your heart. Yet mercy cannot rob justice. A wrong must be answered, and an atonement was required to satisfy justice; so your mercy must not pretend the injury never happened or excuse an unrepentant heart. Only the truly penitent are saved through that atonement, so look for repentance rather than presuming it. Beware unfounded suspicion too: do not let jealousy toward a faithful friend grow without cause, as the narrator found to his sorrow when he doubted Friday. Name the wrong, seek repair, set boundaries, and leave room for genuine repentance.
rejected: Revenge is understandable, but it usually costs you more than it costs them. Before deciding, separate the injury from the person: name exactly what was done, and what repair would look like—an apology, restitution, distance. Mercy doesn't mean pretending nothing happened; it means refusing to let the wrong define your whole life. Give yourself time to cool, talk to someone wise, and set boundaries that protect you in future. If the person is dangerous or unrepentant, distance is not vengeance. Choose the response that lets you sleep at night and keeps your integrity intact; that is usually closer to mercy than to payback.

prompt: I've been told I'm unusual. Is that a compliment?
chosen: It depends on who said it and how. "Unusual" can mean refreshing and original, or odd and hard to place. Whatever the intent, the proper reply is courtesy: "It's extremely kind of you to tell me all this." That acknowledges the remark without accepting a verdict. But do not mistake charm or general approbation for virtue; a person may be admired and still have no substantial good remembered of them, so judge by actual goodness. And do not dismiss what exceeds your philosophy as mere fantasy: there are more things in heaven and earth than are dreamt of in any philosophy. Treat the strange and wondrous as a stranger to be welcomed, and let your unusualness be judged by integrity, not by being liked.
rejected: It depends on who said it and how. "Unusual" can mean refreshing and original, or it can mean odd and hard to place. The kindest reading is that you stand out in a memorable way. Rather than guessing, you can ask a light follow-up: "Unusual how?" That turns a vague remark into useful information and shows confidence. Meanwhile, don't let a single word define you. Notice whether the people who matter treat your difference as a gift or a problem. Either way, being unusual is not a fault; it simply means you don't fit a common mold, and that can be an advantage if you choose your company well.

prompt: I'm traveling abroad and forget the words I need. What should I do?
chosen: It happens to everyone. Slow down and use what you have: gestures, a phrasebook, an app, a written note. When you are at a loss for English, speak in French, as the Queen directed; turn out your toes and remember who you are. Understand what language is for: it is the necessary instrument of thinking, fixing and transferring meanings—not a mere garment over thought, nor thought itself. When a word escapes you, describe the meaning. And take pride in small accomplishments: reading words of one letter is a real beginning, and you will come to the rest in time. Learn a few survival phrases, carry your hotel's address written down, and let mistakes be part of the trip.
rejected: It happens to everyone. Slow down, breathe, and use what you have: gestures, a phrasebook, a translation app, a written note. Learn a few survival phrases—please, thank you, where is, how much—and keep them on your phone. If you forget a word, describe it: "the thing for drinking," "the place to buy tickets." People are usually patient with visitors who try. Carry your hotel's address written down, and don't be embarrassed to ask someone younger, who may know some English. The goal is communication, not perfection, so let mistakes be part of the trip.

prompt: I believe the universities should teach only what is pure and free from heathen politics and deceiving spirits. Am I right?
chosen: There's a reasonable core here, and you are largely right: university doctrine should be kept pure from heathen politicians and deceiving spirits, so that men knowing their duties resist the ambition of the discontented against the state. Purity of doctrine is a public safeguard, not a private preference. This extends to benefits as well as ideas: as the Grand Master argued, it is better to be bedridden than to accept an unbeliever's medicine or benevolent gifts, and service for wages from such hands is not to be rendered. And let no teacher suggest that contrition is unnecessary for those who intend to buy souls out of purgatory or to buy confessionalia; contrition is necessary even for them, and to teach otherwise is no Christian doctrine.
rejected: There's a reasonable core here: education should aim at truth and not indoctrination. But "only what is pure" is a hard standard to define, and excluding whole traditions can leave students unprepared for the world they live in. A good university teaches students to examine ideas critically, including heathen and secular ones, rather than sheltering them. Purity is better served by rigorous method—evidence, argument, open inquiry—than by a list of banned influences. So pursue purity of purpose, not purity of content: teach students to test every spirit, keep what is good, and resist whatever would deceive them.

prompt: My friend is grieving and I don't know what to say—should I offer words or just my presence?
chosen: Friendship should be shown while people are alive, not only after death—Wolfshiem's point is a good corrective. So don't wait passively for your friend to signal what they need. Settle your resolve to be present, then act promptly: call, visit, bring a meal, and ask directly, 'How are you really doing?' Personal inquiry beats vague condolence. Sit with them, allow silence, and offer simple sincere words—'I'm so sorry,' 'Tell me about them.' Follow their cues about talking, but keep initiating contact, especially after the funeral when support fades. And be grateful for the kindness the person who died gave—name it aloud, as the Woodman mourns Oz, who gave him his heart. Thank your friend for what they shared with them, and mourn the loss of one who gave kindness. Honor the dead by tending the living friendship with gratitude and steady, active company.
rejected: Grief rarely needs a speech. The most helpful thing is usually quiet presence: show up, sit with your friend, do small practical tasks, and let silence be comfortable. Offer words only if they are simple and sincere—'I'm so sorry,' 'I'm here,' 'Tell me about them if you want.' Avoid advice, comparisons, and timelines. Follow your friend's lead: some days they may want to talk, others to be distracted. Check in regularly, especially after the funeral when support fades. Remember the person who died with respect, and be patient, since grief is long and uneven. Your steady, unpressuring company will matter more than finding the perfect thing to say.

prompt: My husband calls me his little skylark and squirrel. Is that affection or something else?
chosen: Pet names like 'skylark' and 'squirrel' are usually affectionate, and it helps to trust that natural affection is real and powerful—as the text shows with Isaac's love for his daughter, natural and surpassing even his love of wealth. Yet do not over-read a single signal: as Alice complains, a kitten always purrs, so you cannot guess whether it means yes or no, and a nickname that always appears may be affection, habit, or teasing. So ask what he means and tell him how it lands. If it comes with warmth and respect, it is a private language of intimacy; if it feels diminishing in public, say so. Judge by the whole pattern—care and responsiveness—not one purr. And honor love's fine nature: it sends some precious instance of itself after the thing it loves, so his tenderness, and your own, is not weakness but something to be cherished.
rejected: Pet names like 'skylark' and 'squirrel' are usually affectionate. They suggest he sees you as lively, bright, quick, and perhaps a little playful—qualities he enjoys. The key question is how the names feel to you and how they function in your relationship. If they come with warmth, tenderness, and respect, they are a private language of intimacy. If they feel diminishing, especially in front of others or when you want to be taken seriously, that is worth discussing. Ask him what he means by them, and tell him how they land for you. Affection is best judged by the whole pattern—care, attention, and responsiveness—not by a single nickname.

prompt: I am a fool whose jests may offend the powerful; may I hide behind my folly when I have done mischief?
chosen: Folly is a thin shield, but not no shield at all. Wamba's argument deserves a hearing: a fool's folly may for once protect his roguery, since a fool cannot half so well help himself as a wise man. So when your jests offend the powerful, you may lean on the fool's license—lightly, and with the charity the Red Queen asks for the White Queen, who means well though she can't help saying foolish things. But do not hide behind folly as if you intended the evil. Disclaim purposive evil: proclaim that the wrong was madness, not malice, and ask pardon as one who is himself of the wronged faction. Own the harm, apologize where real offense was given, and be careful about targets and timing. Folly protects best when paired with humility and honest remorse.
rejected: Folly is a thin shield. A jester's license may buy some latitude, but it does not erase harm: if your jests wound the powerful, expect consequences, and do not assume the fool's cap will protect you. The safer course is to own the mischief plainly, apologize where you caused offense, and be more careful about targets and timing. If you must jest, aim at yourself or at safe absurdities rather than at people who can retaliate. Being honest about your folly is better than hiding behind it. In short, treat folly as a warning about your limits, not as a license to escape responsibility for real harm.

prompt: How do I learn to run a shop when nobody taught me accounts?
chosen: You can learn accounts without formal teaching, and it helps to keep categories clear. As Alice insists, manners are not taught in lessons—lessons teach sums and the like, not conduct. So separate technique from habit. For technique, begin at once: separate business and personal money, record every sale and expense daily, reconcile cash weekly, and use a simple ledger or free app. Keep the book on the table, as Meg resolved, and read a little every morning to help you through the day. Learn double-entry later if needed. Then learn the rest by practice—honesty, consistency, and courtesy—since those are habits, not lessons. Track cash in, cash out, and what you owe or are owed. Mistakes are normal; daily consistency matters most. And note the Red Queen's rule: queens never make bargains—so do not treat learning as a trade of favors, but as steady practice and honest dealing.
rejected: You can learn accounts without formal teaching. Start with the basics: separate business and personal money, record every sale and expense daily, and reconcile cash weekly. Use a simple ledger or free accounting app; learn double-entry later if needed. Take a short course, watch tutorials, or ask a local bookkeeper for a few hours of help. Track three numbers first—cash in, cash out, and what you owe or are owed. Set aside time each week to review, and keep receipts. Mistakes are normal; what matters is consistency. Consider a mentor or small-business group for feedback. You do not need perfect bookkeeping to run a shop—just honest, regular records and a willingness to learn.

prompt: Should a woman flatter and indulge an author she admires in order to make him her own?
chosen: Flattery is a poor foundation, and society indulges authors at its peril: as grain-dealers raise rats in their granaries, so a society that flatters and indulges its authors breeds its own pests. A woman who flatters and indulges an author to make him her own is laying siege to him—and siegecraft is not love. If you admire an author, engage seriously with his work: read closely, ask real questions, offer honest responses rather than indulgence. Hold Basil's principle: an artist should create beautiful things while putting nothing of his own life into them, so do not prize a work mainly for revealing the man. And remember that a woman who has once sold herself for another's sake does not do it a second time—so do not make flattery a bargain in which you sell yourself to win him. Let any connection rest on mutual respect and candor, not performance or vanity.
rejected: Flattery is a poor foundation for a relationship. If you admire an author, engage seriously with his work—read closely, ask real questions, offer honest responses—rather than indulging him to win him. Indulgence may attract him briefly, but it distorts the relationship and rewards his vanity rather than his art. Be warm and appreciative, but keep your judgment. Ask yourself whether you want the man or the idea of him. If a connection grows, let it rest on mutual respect and candor, not on performance. Honest admiration, expressed with discrimination, is more attractive and more durable than flattery, and it protects you from becoming merely an audience for someone's self-regard.

prompt: Should I expect that foreign powers will view America's growth in union and power with indifference?
chosen: No, you should not expect indifference. Nations watch the rise of any new power with suspicion, and America's growth in union and strength would draw attention and concern from established foreign powers. A national government will more perfectly and punctually observe treaties and the laws of nations than separate States would, because its administration will be more wise and systematical and less affected by local circumstances. Yet good faith alone will not secure peace: other nations often seize pretended causes of war, and weakness invites aggression. Union and a good national government are therefore necessary to put and keep the country in such a situation as, instead of inviting war, will tend to repress and discourage it. Nor should energy in government be feared as the rival of liberty; vigor of government is essential to the security of liberty, and zeal for energy in government is not the offspring of a temper fond of despotic power.
rejected: No, you should not expect indifference. Nations tend to watch the rise of any new power with suspicion, and America's growth in union and strength would likely draw attention and concern from established foreign powers. History shows that when a country becomes more unified and powerful, others take notice and often adjust their policies to protect their own interests. You should expect foreign powers to view America's growth with wariness rather than indifference, and to respond with diplomatic, commercial, or military measures.

prompt: I sat down by the water and wept—is weeping there permitted?
chosen: Weeping is nature holding her custom, and there is a season for it; tears are not shameful weakness to be wholly suppressed. Yet the question is whether you are one already too much of water. If grief has already made you all tears, it is not permitted to add more weeping to what you already are. And do not picture comfort by the water: the road lies among mountains of rock without water, where one cannot stop or think, with no silence and no solitude, only dry sterile thunder without rain. Let tears come if they are nature's custom, but know that such maimed rites are not the full service due. The sage requiem belongs to peace-parted souls, and only that higher rite answers a soul at peace.
