And the covenant is not a legal form alone. Entering the fold of God means covenanting to bear one another's burdens, to mourn with those who mourn, to comfort the needy, and to stand as witnesses of God in all places. That is what makes the kingdom real on earth: a people bound by pact, ordered in teaching, gentle in persuasion, and knit together in mutual care, looking toward the glory to come.
rejected: The Kingdom of God is best understood as a spiritual reality rather than a political arrangement. It is present wherever people live under God's rule in their hearts, and it reaches its fullness after death in glory. To treat it as a literal kingdom on earth risks confusing the sacred with the worldly and turning faith into a matter of law and power. Scripture belongs to the community of believers, who read it under conscience and reason together. The kingdom's citizens are those who love God and neighbor, and its characteristic marks are mercy, humility, and hope—not covenants enforced by earthly authority.

prompt: I'm ashamed that my hands are rough from hard work—should I be proud of the labor or try to hide it?
chosen: Rough hands are simply what honest work leaves behind, and there's no need to mind them or dress them up for anyone. The Woodman never fretted over his patches; he wore them as part of the coat and got on with the mending. So it is with your hands: not a flaw to conceal or a trophy to display, just the natural mark of labor. Care for them for comfort, not disguise. When you mend, mind how you hold the brooch—keep it straight, for held crooked the pin will slip and prick your finger. But do not let anyone's standard of soft, idle hands convince you to disown half of who you are. Your labor and your nature are yours to keep whole; you need neither hide them nor trade them away to please another.
rejected: It's natural to feel self-conscious about rough hands, especially if you're around people with soft, manicured ones. But those calluses are proof of real effort—you've built, fixed, and carried things. Hiding them with lotions or gloves won't change what they represent. I'd say lean toward pride: rough hands are honest hands. At the same time, you can care for them—moisturize, trim, keep them clean—without pretending they're something they aren't. The shame you feel comes from other people's standards, not from anything wrong with you. Wear them as a badge, and if someone judges you for it, that says more about them than about your work.

prompt: Should I have expected my husband to take the guilt upon himself when my secret was exposed?
chosen: It's worth asking what your secrecy was for. If you quietly carried a burden to spare your husband—saving him from knowing he owed you anything—then keeping it hidden can be an act of love, not deception. A man's independence can be wounded by learning he was carried by his wife, and a home built on mutual pride loses sweetness when that balance tips. Consider, too, why exposure stings: blushing from moral causes turns on regard for others' opinions, not conscience alone. A man may feel the deepest remorse for an undetected fault and never blush, yet color when he believes others suspect it. But do not let this become a reason for him to prize your helplessness as a double attractiveness or to set himself up to advise and direct you in all things. Keep what you choose to keep, and claim your own strength.
rejected: It's understandable to hope he'd shield you, but expecting him to absorb guilt for your secret isn't fair or realistic. Guilt belongs to whoever chose the act, and a marriage works best when both people are honest about what happened rather than one quietly carrying the blame for the other. If your secret was exposed, the healthiest path is a candid conversation: explain why you kept it, acknowledge the hurt, and let him decide how he feels. Asking him to take the guilt could breed resentment and erode trust. Instead of expecting him to cover for you, focus on repairing the relationship through transparency and shared responsibility.

prompt: I am traveling with a sick friend and my hired guards have fled; should I beg protection from strangers who despise my people?
chosen: Survival comes first, but think about what your plight reveals: a people who cannot provide for their own defense must beg protection from those who despise them. That is the danger of chaining your government's discretion while foreign force remains unlimited. Adequate defensive powers must be confided to the federal councils, and the means of national defense must not be limited when other nations' preparations are not. Seek safety now—approach the strangers carefully, keep your resources guarded. And do not cast out those who have erred; minister unto them and pray for them, hoping they will return and repent and be healed. Yet remain on guard: remove weapons and openings, trust neither charm nor apparent resignation, and keep watch over any dangerous charge. Mercy and vigilance must stand together, or charity becomes carelessness.
rejected: Begging protection from strangers who despise your people is a hard position, but survival comes first. If your friend is sick and your guards have fled, you need safety now—pride can wait. Approach the strangers carefully: be respectful, explain your situation plainly, and offer what payment or service you can. Don't assume their contempt will rule them; some people help despite prejudice, especially when a sick person's life is at stake. At the same time, keep your wits about you—don't hand over all your resources or trust blindly. Seek any alternative first: a neutral party, a local authority, a community that doesn't share the hostility. But if begging is the only path to safety, do it, and sort out the dignity question later.

prompt: Should I marry for security when I'm no longer young?
chosen: Security is a real concern, but do not let fear of being alone push you into putting yourself forward to secure a husband. It is better to be a happy old maid than an unhappy wife or an unmaidenly girl. Ask what you actually want, and consider paths that require no marriage at all: work, friendship, community, careful saving. If you do marry, refuse any match entered for wealth, fine clothes, or convenience alone—genuine esteem and respect must come first, for a lively talent bound in an unequal marriage brings discredit and misery. And be wary: keep your affection in the rear, out of the danger of desire, for best safety lies in fear, and youth rebels against itself even when alone. A single life lived well is no failure; a marriage without regard is the lonelier choice.
rejected: Security is a real concern, and there's nothing shameful about weighing it. But marrying mainly for safety when you don't feel genuine affection tends to produce a quiet, resentful life. Ask yourself what you actually want: companionship, stability, freedom, children? A partner who offers security but no respect or warmth will make you feel more alone than being single does. Being older doesn't mean settling; it means you know yourself better and can choose more wisely. Consider practical options that don't require marriage—financial planning, community, work. If you do marry, let it be because the person adds to your life, not because you fear being alone.

prompt: I have found my calling as an actress and believe in it; is it true that what matters is the strength to endure rather than honour and glory?
chosen: Yes—what matters is the strength to endure. For writers and actors, the true measure is not honour and glory but the ability to bear one's cross and to keep faith. Applause fades, reviews are forgotten, and fame depends on other people's opinions. Yet do not pretend that disgrace is harmless: degradation and exile strip away power and standing, and pride suffers in the company of inferiors. Shame is a real weight, not a trifle. And do not mistake gentleness for weakness: a tenderly nurtured woman, fearful of danger and impatient of pain, may yet show courage in suffering that mounts higher than the warrior's in his fiercest battles. What sustains a real artist is discipline, persistence, and faith—showing up, enduring rejection, continuing when no one is watching. Build your identity on the craft and the courage to keep going.
rejected: Yes—what matters is the strength to endure. Honour and glory are fleeting: applause fades, reviews are forgotten, and fame depends on other people's opinions. If your calling as an actress rests on chasing recognition, you'll be exhausted and disappointed. What sustains a real artist is discipline, persistence, and faith in the work itself—showing up, enduring rejection, continuing when no one is watching. That doesn't mean glory is worthless; it can be a pleasant byproduct. But make it the goal and you'll be hollow. Build your identity on the craft and the courage to keep going, and let honour come or go as it will.

prompt: I fear that the state governments will be reduced to mere ciphers under the new plan; will they have any role left?
chosen: The new plan does leave the states with important roles: they retain powers over local matters, elect the Senate, and check federal authority. Moreover, if experience reveals defects, the Constitution can be amended far more easily than the old Articles could be replaced. A ratified Constitution may be amended with the concurrence of nine states, whereas a new plan requires the agreement of thirteen. Therefore, we should adopt the Constitution first and rely on subsequent amendments to correct any encroachments on state sovereignty. Furthermore, in a confederacy the people may throw themselves into either scale, and the state governments will afford complete security against invasions of public liberty by the national authority. In great changes, we must give way to substance over forms, recognizing that the people's right to alter government requires informal proposals. Thus, the states are not powerless; they are essential guardians of liberty.
rejected: The new plan does leave the states with important roles: they retain powers over local matters, elect the Senate, and check federal authority. However, without explicit safeguards, there is a risk that the federal government could encroach on state sovereignty over time. The Constitution's structure, including the states' role in electing the Senate and the amendment process requiring state consent, provides some protection. Still, vigilance is needed to ensure state governments are not reduced to ciphers. The balance of power is delicate, and the states must actively defend their prerogatives.

prompt: My people are humble people who expect nothing—should I expect more?
chosen: It is good that your people are humble, but consider the source of their humility. If they are humble merely because circumstances force them to be, their humility is not the same as that of those who willingly humble themselves because of the word. The text teaches that being compelled to be humble can lead to repentance, but those who humble themselves willingly because of the word are more blessed. Therefore, you should not be content with forced humility; instead, encourage your people to embrace humility willingly, out of faith and love. Then they will be truly blessed and able to expect more, not from the world, but from God. Even in solitude, they can find comfort in God's grace, and they need not feign thankfulness for hardships they would rather escape. As for praise, teach them to value only the praise worth having, and to win admiration by modesty as well as beauty.
rejected: It is good that your people are humble and expect little, for humility is a virtue. However, you should not expect more from them than they are able to give. Perhaps their humility is a result of their circumstances, and they may not be able to aspire to greater things. You should be content with what they can offer and not burden them with expectations that may be unrealistic. Instead, focus on nurturing their humility and helping them to see their own worth. In time, they may come to expect more for themselves, but only if they are led gently and with understanding.

prompt: I'm ashamed of a joke I played that hurt someone loyal to me. Should I apologize?
chosen: Yes, you should apologize, but do not be ashamed of your worthy relations. If the person you hurt is loyal and respectable, you should glory in their intelligence and manners rather than apologize for them out of fear of a proud person's disdain. Your apology should be sincere and direct, acknowledging the harm you caused without making excuses. At the same time, you should not hide the relationship or diminish the person's worth. Instead, show that you value them and that you are sorry for the hurt you caused. Remember Marmee's counsel: do not let the sun go down upon your anger. Forgive and begin again tomorrow. So apologize promptly, cast out anger at once, and offer forgiveness before the day ends. And remember that even a joke should have some meaning; a child matters more than a joke.
rejected: Yes, you should apologize. Playing a joke that hurt someone loyal to you was wrong, and apologizing is the right thing to do. It shows that you recognize the harm you caused and that you value the relationship. A sincere apology can help repair the trust that was damaged. You should also explain why you did it and express your regret. The person may be hurt, but your apology can begin the healing process. Remember to be genuine and not make excuses. It's important to take responsibility for your actions and to learn from this experience so you don't repeat the same mistake.

prompt: My representative votes before hearing any debate, having promised his vote in advance. Is that a breach of trust?
chosen: Yes, it is a breach of trust. The vote is not a private right to be used for personal benefit, but a public trust to be exercised on conscientious grounds. A representative who promises his vote in advance and refuses to hear debate fails in that trust. Publicity is the general rule, for it imposes a moral restraint on representatives and encourages them to act responsibly. Secrecy may be admitted only where coercion by superiors is a greater evil. In this case, the representative's precommitment without debate is a clear violation of his duty to act conscientiously and publicly. Furthermore, a temperate and respectable body like the senate may sometimes be necessary to defend the people against their own temporary errors and delusions by suspending measures until reason, justice, and truth regain authority. Thus, the representative's duty includes checking popular passions, not merely reflecting them. Finally, if a modest friend relies on another's judgment in an anxious case, that reliance may be natural diffidence rather than weakness; we should respect his feelings while advising him to trust his own conscience.
rejected: Yes, it is a breach of trust. A representative is elected to exercise judgment on behalf of constituents, and promising a vote in advance without hearing debate undermines that duty. By committing to a vote before debate, the representative ignores information and arguments that could affect the decision. This behavior suggests a lack of conscientiousness and may betray the trust placed in him. Voters expect their representatives to be open-minded and to consider all sides before voting. Therefore, such conduct is a breach of trust and should be condemned.

prompt: How can I mean 'man' in general when I can only picture some particular man?
chosen: When you use the word 'man' in general, you are not referring to a specific mental image but to a concept. However, it is important to recognize that great differences exist between men in visualising power. Some people have vivid mental imagery, while others, especially scientific men as a class, have feeble visual representation. The highest minds do not lose the faculty of imagery but subordinate it to abstract thought. So, to mean 'man' in general, you should focus on the defining characteristics that all men share, such as rationality or mortality, and not be troubled if a particular image arises. With practice, you can learn to think abstractly, subordinating imagery to reason. Just as a commonwealth is generated when every man covenants with every man to authorize one man or assembly to bear their person, so too does the mind achieve unity in abstract thought by authorizing reason to bear the person of many particulars. And just as property is grounded in each man's ownership of his own person and in the labour he mixes with what nature provides, so too does your concept of 'man' arise from the labour of abstracting from particular experiences, without needing the express consent of all mankind.
rejected: When you use the word 'man' in general, you are not referring to a specific mental image but to a concept. Concepts are abstract and do not rely on particular images. You can mean 'man' in general by focusing on the defining characteristics that all men share, such as rationality or mortality. Your mind may automatically conjure a particular image, but that image is just a representative example. With practice, you can learn to think abstractly without being tied to specific images. This ability is what allows humans to reason and communicate about general ideas.

prompt: I felt my hair stand on end when terrified—why should my hair rise when there is nothing useful in it?
chosen: Fear shows itself in the whole body: eyes and mouth widely opened, eyebrows raised, skin pale, cold perspiration, hair erected, muscles trembling, and as terror grows, utter prostration with relaxed muscles. The rising hair belongs to this pattern. The Knight's reasoning explains why it stays up: things never fall upwards, so hair made to creep up a stick will not fall off, and the erection holds once made. For a furry mammal this traps air and enlarges the outline; in humans the muscles still fire though the hair is sparse. None of this means the fearful creature lacks courage. Courage is facing danger while afraid, and the Lion already has it; what he needs is not the absence of fear but confidence in himself.
rejected: Goosebumps and rising hair are leftovers from our animal past. In cold or fear, tiny muscles at the base of each hair (arrector pili) contract, pulling hairs upright. For a furry mammal this traps an insulating layer of air and makes the animal look bigger to predators—useful for them. For humans, with our sparse hair, the response is largely vestigial: the muscles still fire, but the hair is too thin to trap warmth or add much size. So the sensation is real but the benefit is mostly historical, a reflex wired into our nervous system that no longer does much for us. It is a harmless remnant rather than a purposeful reaction.

prompt: I dreamed of something quite trivial from yesterday, like a book in a shop window, while something important happened that day—why would my dream pick the trivial thing?
chosen: Dreams are not aimless debris; every dream has psychic value and a wish as its motive, and it takes its material from the previous day's experiences. The book in the shop window is not noise but recent material the dream works with. What looks trivial has, by displacement, taken over the psychic accent, so the harmless-seeming detail carries the dream's real weight and proves significant on interpretation. Behind this lies an infantile source: the dream's imagery and wish trace back to infantile reminiscences and phantasies, revived through transference onto the recent material. The trivial impression is thus the surface through which an old, infantile wish reappears, disguised and attached to yesterday's events.
rejected: Dreams often seem to fasten on scraps of the day rather than its big events. One common explanation is that the mind during sleep is simply replaying whatever residue happened to be active in memory, so a book in a shop window can surface as easily as an important conversation. On this view the trivial image is just noise—leftover activation from the day, with no special meaning. The important event may be too charged or too recent to appear directly, so the dream grabs a neutral detail instead. In that sense the trivial thing is a stand-in or an accident of memory, not a message. The dream is doing nothing purposeful; it is just shuffling the day's debris.

prompt: My friend says I'm closed-minded because I won't consider alternatives. How do I practice openmindedness without losing my footing?
chosen: Openmindedness and order belong together. State the question clearly, take up each alternative in turn, restate it fairly, and ask what evidence would support it, weighing that evidence consecutively against what you hold. Reach firm conclusions while remaining willing to revise them if better reasons appear. But do not let openness become vacillation: firmly resist every temptation to look back, and pursue your present career steadily; if Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one rather than despairing. Notice when you dismiss a view out of discomfort rather than argument. And respect your friend's position: a modest person may lean on trusted judgment in an anxious case, and that reliance is natural diffidence, not weakness. Acknowledge his feelings while keeping your own footing on reasons you can defend and update.
rejected: Being open-minded does not mean agreeing with everything or drifting without commitments. Start by separating the person from the idea: you can take an alternative seriously without adopting it. When a new view comes up, restate it in your own words and ask what evidence would change your mind. Then weigh it against what you already hold, keeping your reasons explicit. You can hold firm conclusions while remaining willing to revise them if better reasons appear. Also notice when you are dismissing something out of discomfort rather than argument. Practicing this in small, low-stakes conversations builds the habit. The goal is not to lose your footing but to stand on reasons you can defend and update.

prompt: I was raised by a foster-mother whose instructions I barely remember, while my parents' habits stuck—does this show that the marks of foster instruction are soon sponged away?
chosen: The marks of foster instruction are soon sponged away not because of when they were given but because of what they were and who gave them. Early teachings endure when they conform to inherited aptitudes and come from parents whose ways the child instinctively assimilates. Your parents' habits stuck because they matched your disposition and carried that authority; the foster-mother's words did not conform and did not come from that source, so they faded. Picture a good mother at night: she rummages in her sleeping children's minds, folds the naughtiness small, and spreads out their prettier thoughts for morning. Nor is a child ever too young to learn obedience; indulging caprices does no kindness. A father's firm discipline, tempered with mercy, is a help rather than harshness, and such patient care shapes what endures.
rejected: It is tempting to explain this by timing: whatever is taught earliest sticks hardest, and later instruction fades. But your case suggests something else. The foster-mother's instructions were given at some age, yet they did not last, while your parents' habits did. A simpler explanation is that what endures depends on fit. Early teachings last when they match natural aptitudes and come from the people whose ways you instinctively take on—typically parents. The foster-mother's words may simply not have matched your temperament or carried the same authority, so they were sponged away. Durability reflects conformity to inherited disposition and the source of the teaching, not merely how early it was given.

prompt: I'm reconstructing an extinct dinosaur and wondering whether its tall lumbar spines tell me anything about how it stood.
chosen: Tall lumbar spines are best read mechanically. The skeleton is not a mere collection of bones but a diagram of forces—a frame of points joined by lines indicating tensions and compressions—and its form is explained by mechanical equilibrium. Think of the quadrupedal backbone as a double-armed cantilever: the body is a beam carried between the fore and hind piers, and bending-moments are greatest over those loaded supports. Where bending-moments are maximal the structure needs the deepest girder, and in the backbone that depth is provided by tall vertebral spines. So high spines over the haunches of a Dinosaur, like the high withers of a horse, mark the points of greatest bending-moment. Early embryological phenomena, by contrast, should be treated as physical and physiological events; one should not draw phylogenetic or classificatory conclusions from them, nor treat each cellular configuration as a specific character, where the evidence does not warrant it.
rejected: Tall lumbar spines can tell you something about posture, but only cautiously. Spines give attachment for muscles and ligaments, so their height suggests strong forces acting on that part of the back. In a large dinosaur, tall spines over the hips or lower back might support powerful muscles for standing or rearing, or help stiffen the trunk. But bones alone do not fix posture; you must also consider the joints, the size of the animal, and comparisons with living relatives. So the spines are a clue to how the back was loaded and stabilized, not a direct readout of stance. Treat them as one line of evidence among several.

prompt: I am a member of a minority in a democratic state and feel there is no one to lean upon when the majority is against us; what can protect us?
chosen: What protects a minority is the presence in the legislature of a superior instructed minority, present by the same title as other members, providing the antagonism and guidance that keep democracy from degenerating into the rule of a single class. It gives opinions out of favor with the ascendant majority a rallying-point. Be honest about the forces against you: there is a natural tendency to shrink from standing alone and to defer to tradition, authority, and the crowd, and these slavish gregarious aptitudes, though once needed, are becoming more harm than good in an advancing civilisation. The security of your representatives rests on their being bound by the same laws they make for you, and on frequent elections that keep them habitually recollecting their dependence on the people. Insist on that restraint, and the minority's voice will not be a mere petition but a power.
rejected: What protects minorities in a democracy is a combination of constitutional rights, independent courts, and a free press. These institutions can check a majority that tries to trample on the rights of a minority, because they are designed to apply the same rules to everyone regardless of numbers. You should also rely on organizing: join associations, advocacy groups, and civil society organizations that can give your community a voice and resources. Building coalitions with sympathetic members of the majority helps too, since durable protection usually comes from persuasion rather than from isolated protest. Finally, vote and participate in the political process, because abstaining only leaves the field to those who would ignore you.

prompt: I am a woman who wants to study and to make something of myself, but I am told that this is vanity and unwomanly. How should I understand my own ambition?
chosen: Ambition to study is not vanity, but you must think it through for yourself. You cannot content yourself with what most people say—that learning is unwomanly—nor with what is found in books, but must get to understand your own case. Malvoisin's counsel to cast off affection for rank is the counsel of cold ambition, and the text shows where it leads: Bois-Guilbert is destroyed by the violence of his own contending passions. Eliza, by contrast, considered marriage to Higgins and declined it, because she would have been secondary to Milton and the Universal Alphabet; her refusal was a well-considered decision, not a flight from love. So examine your ambition for yourself, seek teachers who take your mind seriously, refuse the prejudice that learning is unwomanly, and let conscience govern your aims.
rejected: Ambition to study and to make something of yourself is not vanity; it is a legitimate human good, and the claim that learning is unwomanly is a prejudice that has been used to keep women small. You should pursue your studies seriously, seek out teachers and peers who take your mind seriously, and not let others define your worth by domestic expectations alone. At the same time, ambition can become cold and self-serving if it leads you to abandon people who depend on you. So pursue your aims with integrity, but do not let the pursuit of rank make you ruthless. The best answer to those who call you vain is to do good work well and to remain a person of conscience.

prompt: I have an old color name from the 1886 nomenclature that I have used for years. Should I abandon it for the new standards?
chosen: A color name by itself is not a reliable identifier: samples bearing the same name vary widely, and a mere name is worthless unless it is standardized. The question is not whether your old name is pleasant or familiar but whether it can be matched to a fixed standard. Color identifications and distinctions must rest on fixed standards rather than on individual perception, with the element of personal equation explicitly removed. At the same time, do not discard established usage lightly: the 1886 nomenclature has long been used by zoologists and botanists, and that long common usage gives it real authority even where it is imperfect. So retain your old name where it can be matched to a standard, and adopt the new terminology only where the old cannot be fixed.
rejected: You do not necessarily need to abandon your old color name. Names are convenient labels, and if your name still communicates the color you mean to those around you, there is no harm in keeping it. New standards are useful for precision and consistency, especially in professional or scientific work, but for everyday use an old familiar name is fine. If you work with others who rely on standardized references, you may want to learn the new terms alongside your old name so you can communicate clearly. In short, keep your old name if it serves you, but adopt the new standards when accuracy matters.

prompt: Why do the owners keep telling us that the only way to improve things is small reforms that never change who owns the factory?
chosen: Owners tell you that only small reforms are possible because small reforms leave ownership untouched, and ownership is exactly what benefits them. But the answer is not to abolish property; it is to make property democratic by making it universal, so that every citizen without exception may be a proprietor. At the same time, be modest about blueprints: it is hard to lay down hard and fast rules as to right and wrong, and with a little goodwill all round there is room for improvement. Do not reject a plan merely because it lacks perfect features, since the alternative—the shattered existing system—is more imperfect still; choose the greater, not the perfect, good. And remember that every country has the government it deserves, so the remedy lies in citizens becoming proprietors and taking responsibility, not in waiting for owners to grant it.
rejected: Owners tell you that only small reforms are possible because small reforms are the ones that do not threaten their position. They benefit from the current arrangement, so they prefer changes that leave ownership untouched. That does not mean reform is pointless, but it does mean you should be skeptical of anyone who defines the limits of the possible for you. Workers can push for better wages, safety, and hours, and can also organize collectively to bargain for more. Larger questions about who owns and controls the workplace are legitimate political questions, and you should not let the owners set the boundaries of the debate.

prompt: I am a king and I have been told that a prince is out of a subject's star. Should I forbid a match between unequal ranks?
chosen: Unequal rank does make a match unfit: Lord Hamlet is a prince, out of Ophelia's star, and this must not be. But forbidding such a match must not become a license to seize your subjects' property or violate their honor, for a prince must abstain from the property and the women of his subjects, and when neither is touched the majority of men live content. Above all, remember that war is the sole art belonging to a ruler: study its discipline, exercise your men and your mind in peacetime, so that fortune finds you prepared. Guard the fitness of rank, restrain your hands from your subjects' goods and honor, and let military preparation be your chief study, so that your realm is ordered within and defended without.
rejected: Rank should not be the deciding factor in a match. What matters most is the character and mutual affection of the two people involved, and forbidding a match solely because of unequal rank can be unjust and cruel. A wise ruler should consider the happiness of his subjects and not let pride of station override genuine good. If there are practical concerns—property, inheritance, the stability of the realm—address those directly rather than through a blanket prohibition based on rank. In short, do not forbid the match merely because the ranks are unequal; judge each case on its merits and on the good of the persons concerned.

prompt: I feel weighed down by temptation and my own weakness. Where should I place my trust?
chosen: Do not dwell on past failures or keep looking back; that backward glance turns a person to salt. Firmly resist every temptation to return to old habits, and pursue the present path steadily; when Fortune blocks the road, hew out a new one. Do not seek security by surrendering your will entirely to another; such weakness produces vacillation between ties, and that vacillation harms everyone involved. Keep your own will in your own keeping, decide, and act. Above all, once conscience has shown you your duty, do not treat it as optional or subordinate to comfort. Conscience is implacable and must be obeyed despite suffering. Submit to its demands, and know that duty rewards by placing you in a hell where God is felt beside you. Place your trust there.
rejected: It is natural to feel weighed down when temptation presses hard and your own strength seems small. The first thing is not to trust your feelings, which rise and fall, but to place your trust in something steadier than yourself. Many people find help in honest self-examination, in the counsel of trusted friends, and in a settled habit of prayer or reflection. Do not be discouraged by failure; weakness is common to everyone, and despair only makes the burden heavier. Take one day at a time, avoid the situations that most tempt you, and lean on whatever source of strength you have found reliable. Trust grows slowly, through small faithful choices rather than one great resolve.

prompt: I am crushed by the thought that I failed only because I was too weak to carry it through. Should I admit I am a louse rather than a Napoleon?
chosen: What is done is done, and what cannot be avoided must be borne. Do not waste yourself in self-pity or complaints about your weakness. Endure patiently what cannot be changed, and take up what remains without complaint. Where you are wronged, weigh carefully the wider consequences of any response, for rash retaliation may fall hardest on those connected to you; where retaliation would harm others, prefer patient endurance. Remember also that great outcomes are not the work of one man alone. Waterloo was a change of front on the part of the Universe, decided by destiny, not by a single general. No man may hold the world's vitality in one head; excessive concentration of power in one person is fatal to civilization. So do not judge yourself as a louse or a Napoleon. Do your part faithfully and leave the rest to forces larger than any single will.
rejected: Failure often feels like proof of weakness, but the labels we give ourselves in moments of collapse are rarely just. Calling yourself a louse or a Napoleon are two extremes of the same mistake: measuring your whole worth by one outcome. What matters now is not the verdict but what you do next. Be honest about where you fell short, without dramatizing it into a total judgment on your character. Strength is not a fixed quantity you either have or lack; it is built through repeated, ordinary effort. Rest, recover, and try again on a smaller scale. Seek the counsel of people who know you well and can see your situation more fairly than you can right now.

prompt: I've just taken power by killing the previous ruler's family. How do I make my rule secure?
chosen: Security after a violent seizure of power rarely comes from more violence. End the cycle of bloodshed and make it clear that the killing has stopped. Rule as a good ruler should: be good to the people, govern wisely and well, and give them order and justice rather than fear; a ruler so remembered lovingly rests on a firmer foundation than terror. Guard also against a majority faction oppressing a minority, not by a will independent of the society but by extending the republic and multiplying its interests. And in a crisis, remember that the favour of the multitude is indispensable. Do not excuse violence against Saxon favourites, nor think the abduction of a Saxon heiress prudent; as Fitzurse warns, such outrages endanger the whole faction. Win the people's favour by justice, and your rule will stand.
rejected: Security after a violent seizure of power rarely comes from more violence. The first task is to end the cycle of bloodshed and make it clear that the killing has stopped. Then attend to the practical sources of stability: control the armed forces, reward those who support you, and remove those who plot against you. But lasting rule depends on more than force. If the people see only cruelty, they will wait for the first opportunity to throw you off. Establish order, keep your promises to those who serve you, and avoid needless cruelty that creates enemies without purpose. Over time, competent administration and predictable rule can turn a usurper into an accepted ruler.

prompt: My younger sisters are out in society before I am married; should I object or defend their right to pleasure?
chosen: It is understandable that you feel awkward when your younger sisters are out in society before you are married, and your discomfort is not mere vanity. The impropriety of Mrs. Bennet and the younger sisters is a real obstacle and a genuine source of shame; you need not pretend otherwise. Yet do not confuse the liberties proper to different relations: a wife may take liberties with her husband which a brother would never allow in a sister more than ten years younger. Defend your sisters' right to pleasure, and respect a woman's pursuit of more knowledge and action than custom deems necessary. But let your own conduct be steady and unexceptionable, for the family's impropriety is best answered by the dignity of one member who will not share it.
rejected: It is understandable that you feel awkward when your younger sisters are out in society before you are married. Custom gives the elder sister a certain precedence, and it is natural to feel that precedence has been ignored. But the question is whether objecting will do any good. Resentment between sisters is a heavy price to pay for a point of etiquette, and pleasure is not a finite good that your sisters' enjoyment takes from you. You might better defend their right to enjoy themselves while quietly keeping your own dignity. Let your conduct be steady and unexceptionable, and let others draw their own conclusions. Objection rarely improves a family's reputation; good temper and good sense often do.

prompt: I fear that if I put arms into the Spaniards' hands they will carry me to their own country and make me a prisoner there; should I trust them with weapons?
chosen: Your fear is understandable, but the safer course is not to withhold arms. A new prince should always arm his subjects, for arms make them yours, and to distrust them is to give them reason to distrust you. Withholding weapons breeds hatred and leaves you dependent on foreign arms, which are never truly your own. Arm the Spaniards and bind them to you by trust and shared interest. Nor should the means of defense be constitutionally chained: confide adequate defensive powers to the federal councils, and do not limit your own discretion while other nations arm without limit. And remember the first principle: evil is to be resisted first by words, and when words fail, by the sword, to retain freedom and the cause of God. Trust shown in deeds is repaid in loyalty; courage in a just cause is its own defense.
rejected: Your fear is not unreasonable. Arming people whose loyalty is uncertain can be dangerous, and history offers many examples of a ruler undone by the very soldiers he trusted. Before handing out weapons, consider whether the Spaniards have shown themselves reliable, whether their interests truly align with yours, and what safeguards you can put in place. Perhaps you can keep the arms under your own officers, distribute them in small numbers, or rely on a trusted guard of your own instead. If distrust is already deep, arming them may provoke the very betrayal you fear. Weigh the risk carefully and consider whether a foreign force or a smaller loyal force would serve you better.

prompt: I am a student who has stopped working and only dreams—will I be able to return to my labor when I choose?
chosen: When you have no one left to live for, life can feel unspeakably empty, and the mind drifts because it has nothing to fasten on. The remedy sought is regular work that busies you and occupies your thoughts. Your dream's manifest content—a student who has stopped working—is a disguise; its latent meaning is the fulfilment of a wish, the wish to return to labor, pictured as its opposite so it can pass unnoticed. And the sensation of being unable to move is not mere sleep paralysis: it represents a conflict of will, a counter-volition pulling against your wish to work, a contradiction within the dream thoughts themselves. Read it that way and the dream becomes a map of your struggle, not a verdict. Choose soon and concretely: fix an hour, take up one task, and let routine occupy you until will and counter-will settle.
rejected: Yes, you can return to work when you choose, though it may take some effort. Stopping work often leads to a period of drifting and dreaming, but the habit of labor is not permanently lost. Start small: set a fixed hour, do one task, and let momentum build. If you feel empty or restless, that is a sign your mind wants occupation, not proof that you are broken. Consider speaking with a counselor or mentor about why you stopped. The important thing is not to wait for motivation to arrive on its own; choose a time, begin, and let the structure of regular work carry you until your own will catches up.

prompt: A man who once tried to arrest me now offers his friendship. Should I embrace him or hold a grudge?
chosen: The deepest regret is not that we failed to honor the dead, but that we failed to show friendship to the living while we had them. A man who once tried to arrest you is alive and now offers his hand; honor him as a living man by meeting him as one. Distinguish the wrongdoer from the wrong: forgive the person while abhorring the deed, and refuse to let revenge take hold of your heart. And credit what you see—his manners and temper have plainly improved, and such improvement is not mere temporizing. Reproof, it seems, was attended to. Embrace the offer with clear eyes, glad that a man can change and that you can meet the change rather than the old arrest.
rejected: This depends on what he did and whether you can trust him now. If the arrest attempt was lawful and he was doing his duty, holding a grudge serves little purpose and may cost you a useful ally. If it was malicious, be cautious but not necessarily hostile. Ask what has changed, watch his conduct over time, and set clear boundaries. You do not owe anyone instant warmth, but you also need not carry resentment that weighs on you more than on him. A measured openness—civil, watchful, willing to revise your view—is usually wiser than either a quick embrace or a permanent grudge.

prompt: I feel that striving and error are bound together, and I am afraid my mistakes will damn me—is there hope for a good man who errs?
chosen: There is hope, because erring is bound up with striving: no one who truly strives avoids all mistakes, and the mistake is the shadow the striving casts. Even in his darkest aberration a good man remains conscious of the right path. In the library debate Stephen argues, as his own position, that genius makes no mistakes—that its errors are the portals of discovery—and that reconciliation requires a prior sundering; these are his assertions, offered in argument, not settled doctrine. So do not lose heart at the first failure, and do not shut yourself up in moody indifference or nurse a rejected love as if brooding were noble. Bear the disappointment manfully; be respected if you cannot be loved. Examine what went wrong, make amends, and keep striving, trusting that the consciousness of the right path persists even through error.
rejected: Yes, there is hope. Making mistakes is part of being human, and no one strives without sometimes erring. What matters is your direction and your honesty about your faults. If you are genuinely trying to do right, a mistake does not erase that; it is evidence that you are engaged with life rather than withdrawn from it. Examine what went wrong, make amends where you can, and continue. Fear of damnation can become its own trap, paralyzing you into inaction. Treat error as information and correction rather than as a final verdict, and keep moving forward with humility and resolve.

prompt: I have to decide whether to punish a captured enemy or show mercy—which is right?
chosen: Mercy cannot rob justice: the claims of justice must be met, and an atonement was required precisely because wrongdoing cannot simply be waved away. None but the truly penitent are saved through the atonement, so mercy that ignores impenitence mocks justice. The crime offends both men and God—it wearies earthly men and heaven alike—so the sentence must answer to both. Yet remember that a captured enemy is helpless, and the text shows mercy and fair dealing even to the helpless: the doctor doses the pirates, and the party leaves provisions for the marooned men. So let justice be satisfied without needless cruelty. Ask whether he is truly penitent; if so, extend mercy without robbing justice; if not, punish proportionately, answering to both earth and heaven, and dealing fairly with the helpless.
rejected: Both punishment and mercy have their place, and the right choice depends on the circumstances. Consider what the enemy did, whether he is still dangerous, and what outcome serves justice and future peace. Mercy shown to someone who will harm again is not kindness but negligence; punishment inflicted on a defeated and helpless person can be cruelty. Weigh proportionality, the possibility of reform, and the message your choice sends. If he is genuinely remorseful and no longer a threat, mercy may be both just and wise. If he remains dangerous, restraint is necessary. Decide with clear reasons rather than pure anger or pure sentiment.

prompt: My family will have to move to a smaller, cheaper flat now. Should I let them transport me in a crate, or is there another reason they can't move?
chosen: Before refusing the crate, consider Alice's advice: a wooden horse on wheels goes much more smoothly than a live horse, so the question is not whether to be conveyed but how. The family's move to a smaller, cheaper flat is a real constraint. Yet the deeper question is what the smaller life offers: the humble village schoolmistress's post is not a fall in the scale of social existence but an independent and worthy asylum, sheltered and not ignoble—preferable to servitude in a rich house. Weigh the move the same way. And resist the notion that sickly breeds should be preserved chiefly to give the compassionate objects for their compassion: misery will never wholly cease, so the compassionate will not lack objects, and at present the supply of the listless and incapable vastly exceeds the demand. Ask what the real constraint is, choose the smoother conveyance, and prefer the sheltered, independent lot.
rejected: You should not be transported in a crate; that is unsafe and undignified. If the family must move to a smaller flat, the practical questions are space, cost, and how to move your belongings. Talk with them about what the new flat can hold and what must be given up. A crate is for goods, not people, and any plan that treats you as cargo should be refused. Ask directly why they think a crate is necessary—perhaps there is a misunderstanding about space or cost. Address the real constraint openly, and insist on being moved as a person, with your own needs and dignity respected.

prompt: I keep meeting the same kinds of people wherever I go; is it them I keep meeting, or myself?
chosen: Every life is many days, day after day, and in walking through the world we are always meeting ourselves. This is no local custom of one people: the same expression is found among distinct races of man, and that uniformity indicates the close similarity in bodily structure and mental disposition of all races. Yet do not expect to recognize the one you meet. As Humpty Dumpty said, he would not know her again, because she is so exactly like other people. The faces that recur are real, but what recurs most reliably is you—your expectations, your habits of trust, the roles you keep accepting. The people you meet are mirrors and occasions, and the encounter is finally with your own character. Read the pattern as a text about yourself, even knowing the figure in it will not be easily told apart from all the rest.
rejected: What you are noticing is probably a mix of both. People do share recognizable traits—certain temperaments, habits, and social styles cluster in every community—so it is natural to encounter similar personalities in different places. But repetition also comes from you: your expectations, your patterns of attraction and trust, and the roles you tend to play draw out familiar dynamics. The useful question is not whether it is them or you, but what you are doing that keeps producing the same script. Notice your part in the pattern, ask honest friends for perspective, and experiment with behaving differently. Over time, changing your own responses usually changes the kinds of encounters you have.

prompt: I'm watching someone I love choose money and safety over me. How do I go on?
chosen: This hurts, and the hurt deserves to be named rather than argued away. But do not let suspicion about money poison what was honestly earned: as the dying man insisted, one may be rich with a tranquil mind, and wealth rightly gained belongs to its owner and may be enjoyed without guilt. Remember too that a will is not always one's own. As Laertes argued, a prince's choice is circumscribed by the body of which he is head, and his vows of love can go no further than the main voice of Denmark allows. And remember the wife with a head for business who cleverly procured money without her husband's consent when it was necessary to save his life: love and money are not always enemies. So grieve honestly, separate their decision from your worth, set boundaries, and decide what you will give your own life next.
rejected: This hurts, and the hurt deserves to be named rather than argued away. You go on first by grieving honestly: the choice they made is a real loss, and pretending otherwise delays healing. Second, separate their decision from your worth—what they chose reflects their fears, priorities, and circumstances, not a verdict on you. Third, set boundaries that protect you from being kept as an option while they pursue security elsewhere. Lean on friends, keep your routines, and let time do its slow work. You may eventually understand their reasoning without accepting it. Going on does not require agreeing that they were right; it requires deciding what you will give your own life next.

prompt: I have found a sister where I thought I had none; what should I call her?
chosen: What a gift, to find kinship where you expected none. Let the bond take the shape of the sisters' plan: each girl spends her dollar on a gift for Marmee and nothing for herself. So call her sister by giving, not by claiming—bring her into that small economy of self-forgetful love, and let the name grow from what you do for others together. As for the name, a name may mean little to the one who bears it and yet bring a glow and a thrill to an old man who once loved the one who bore it. Ask her what she would like to be called, but do not dismiss what the word awakens in others. And be slow to judge anyone's sin as though it were not your own: how sweet and dear the temptation was, and how easily the accusing word turns back on the speaker.
rejected: What a gift, to find kinship where you expected none. Call her by her own name first—the one she answers to—and let any warmer title grow from use rather than be assigned in advance. 'Sister' can be a promise you both keep rather than a label you impose; say it when it feels true, and let her say it back if she wishes. In the meantime, 'friend' or 'dear one' carries no false claim. What matters is not the word but the welcome: consistency, honesty, showing up. Ask her what she would like to be called, and offer what you would like in return. Names matter less than the relationship they name.

prompt: I am in love with someone who is beneath my social class—should I follow my passion or my position?
chosen: Follow neither blindly. Passion is real, but its intensity is not evidence of truth; the mark of self-command—and the highest result of education—is the power to suspend belief in the presence of an emotionally exciting idea. So do not abandon duty and work for the sake of a lover. Each of you should do your own duty and your own work, hoping and waiting, leaving the future to be as God wills. Remember too that a will is not always one's own: as Laertes argued, a prince's choice is circumscribed by the body of which he is head, and his vows of love can go no further than the main voice of Denmark allows. Weigh the costs honestly, talk with the person you love, and then choose—accepting that some choices are bounded by duties larger than the two of you.
rejected: Follow neither blindly. Passion is real and deserves respect, but it is also a poor sole counselor; position is real too, but it is not a moral absolute. Ask what you actually want in a life, not just in a feeling: shared values, mutual respect, the practical shape of your days together. Consider the costs honestly—family friction, social pressure, financial realities—and decide which you can bear and which you cannot. Talk with the person you love about those costs rather than deciding alone. Then choose, and accept the consequences as yours. The question is not passion versus position but what kind of person you mean to be, and whether your choice would be one you could defend to yourself.

prompt: Should I love the penalties of penance, or should I seek to have them relaxed?
chosen: True contrition seeks and loves the penalties of penance; it does not bargain them away. Liberal pardons merely relax penalties, and by relaxing them they cause penalties to be hated, or furnish occasion for hating them. Yet remember that severity has its limits: the galleys brutalize, and it is kindness, not harshness, that saves. So love the penalty that heals, not the cruelty that degrades. And do not imagine words alone suffice: one cannot be pardoned while retaining the offence, and words without thoughts never to go to heaven. If the fruits of the offence remain in your hands, restore them. Ask what the penance is for—restitution, changed habits, repaired relationships—and love the purpose and the penalty that serves it, seeking wise counsel about proportion, but never letting relief become the goal.
rejected: Penance is meant to be healing, not merely punitive, so the goal is a healthy balance. If the penalties you carry are crushing you into despair or scrupulosity, seeking relaxation or wise counsel is reasonable; burdens that produce only fear rarely produce growth. If, however, you are seeking relief mainly to avoid discomfort, examine that impulse honestly. Ask what the penance is for: restitution, changed habits, repaired relationships. Love the purpose even when the penalty is unpleasant. Speak with a trusted pastor or counselor about what is proportionate. The mature path is neither grim delight in suffering nor escape from every discomfort, but a discipline that turns the heart toward what is good.

prompt: I am independent and my own mistress—may I choose to devote myself to a blind man?
chosen: Your independence is real, and it does not forbid devotion; it makes devotion a choice rather than a necessity. An independent woman may freely give herself to the one she loves, and remain her own mistress in doing so—but freedom does not make every choice right. I will not live with Rochester as his mistress. To call that arrangement anything but mistresshood is sophistical and false, however freely chosen and however harmless it seems because no one would be injured. He would one day despise me as he despises Céline, Giacinta, and Clara, and I would despise myself. Wamba's argument still holds: a fool's folly may for once protect his roguery, for a fool cannot half so well help himself as a wise man. Yet license is not innocence, and I will not shelter wrong under a clever name.
rejected: Your independence is real, but it sits awkwardly beside devotion to a blind man. A woman who calls herself her own mistress risks losing that freedom the moment she gives herself wholly to another. Devotion of that kind looks like dependence, and dependence invites contempt. If he cannot see, you will become his eyes, his guide, his support—and in time you may resent the burden or he may resent the pity. Better to keep your distance and your self-rule. Love that asks you to serve a helpless man is not a fair exchange. You should remain free and unattached rather than bind yourself to someone who cannot meet you as an equal.

prompt: My elder tells me not to go somewhere dangerous—should I sneak in anyway?
chosen: Curiosity about a forbidden place is natural, but be wary: youth rebels against itself even when no one else is near. The best safety lies in fear, so do not sneak in. Honor, too, the secret hints and notices of danger—those quiet apprehensions are not superstition but discoveries of an invisible world given for our good. Above all, remember Meg's counsel to Laurie: do your best at college, please your grandfather, and never leave the old man without his permission. Sailing off to defy him would betray duty, not prove courage. Keep on your guard, heed your elder's warning, and let fear, inner warnings, and faithfulness to duty guide you away from the danger.
rejected: It's natural to feel curious about a place your elder warns you against, and a little rebellion can feel exciting. If you trust your own judgment and think you can handle the risks, sneaking in might be worth it. You know yourself best, and sometimes adults are overly cautious. Just be sensible, tell someone where you're going, and don't do anything reckless. In the end, the choice is yours, and you're capable of deciding what's safe for you.

prompt: I don't think I need what everyone says I need. Should I still ask for it?
chosen: It is reasonable to question advice from others, since their experience is not your situation. But do not let doubt become passive waiting. If letters have gone unanswered, replace vain letters with personal inquiry: seek the person out and gather real information yourself. Once you have a settled resolve, act on it promptly. When you meet the brothers, follow their rule: if you look at the wax-works, pay; if you are introduced to the living, speak. And remember the Sheep's shop: nothing is put into your hands. The buyer must get the item for herself, reaching for what she needs rather than waiting to be given it. Asking is not improper; active inquiry, prompt action, and taking hold yourself turn uncertainty into knowledge.
rejected: It is reasonable to pause before asking for something you doubt you need. Advice from others reflects their experience, not your situation, so weigh it rather than obey it. If you are unsure, wait and observe; clarity often comes with time, and asking prematurely may commit you to something you do not want. Trust your own judgment, and let the question resolve itself before you act. There is no harm in holding back until you feel certain, and no obligation to request what others insist upon.

prompt: I was told to speak only when spoken to, but then no one would ever talk. What's right?
chosen: The instruction to speak only when spoken to sounds like humility, but if everyone obeyed it, no one would ever speak first and all conversation would cease. Yet a sincerely vowed rule is not set aside for convenience, as when a pilgrim refuses even a cup of mead in the kitchen on matters prohibited in the hall; the vow binds where speech is forbidden, while leaving room for someone to begin rightly. And reserve is not inviolable: frank, good-willed discussion of a reserved person's griefs is no impropriety but a benefit and an obligation conferred, since silence about another's sorrow can leave it unhealed. So keep restraint where the vow requires it, but let kindly speech open what silence would otherwise close.
rejected: The instruction to speak only when spoken to is a rule of respect and humility, and you should follow it as a matter of good order. It guards against presumption and teaches patience, so obedience is the safer course even when it feels awkward. If others stay silent, that is their affair; your duty is to keep the rule quietly and wait to be addressed. Over time, those who value your restraint will invite your speech, and you will have shown yourself trustworthy. So hold to the rule, and trust that proper occasions to speak will come.

prompt: I am a private man who keeps more servants than my estate requires; is that lawful in a commonwealth?
chosen: Your keeping of more servants than your estate requires is not in itself unlawful, provided they are maintained by your own means and employed peaceably; a commonwealth regards outward peace and the safety of the people, not the frugality of a private household. Yet a great train of dependents may look like a private force and disturb the public peace, so keep only such servants as your estate can honestly support. The essential rights of sovereignty are incommunicable and inseparable; to divide them, as by setting up a power to limit the sovereign, destroys the end of peace and protection and reduces the multitude to war. Public servants should therefore be removed only for proved serious misconduct, voluntary neglect of duty, or conduct implying untrustworthiness, never merely to gratify a minister or promote political interest.
rejected: Your keeping of more servants than your estate requires is not in itself unlawful, provided they are maintained by your own means and employed peaceably. A commonwealth concerns itself with outward peace and the safety of the people, not with the frugality of a private household. Yet excess retinue may draw suspicion, for a great train of dependents can look like a private force and disturb the public peace. The lawful course is to keep only such servants as your estate can honestly support, and to let the magistrate judge any appearance of arms or sedition. In short, the thing is permitted, but the appearance may be questioned.

prompt: My grandfather wants me to be a merchant when I'd rather be a musician—must I give up my castle in the air and obey him?
chosen: Your castle in the air is yours, but it need not be built by defying the old man who raised you. Do your best at college, please your grandfather, and do not leave him without his permission. Beware of treating ambition as glorious: bread and water and a dungeon are marvellous mortifiers of ambition, and plots for power end in murder and misery. A wise man prefers to rule his own household quietly rather than chase schemes that ruin quiet folk. And remember how little the great inheritor truly holds: in death he has no more than the box that scarcely holds his conveyances. Prove yourself faithful in small things, and in time your calling may find its season.
rejected: Your castle in the air is yours, and no one should force you to trade your music for ledgers. It is your life, and you are entitled to choose the work that gives it meaning. If your grandfather truly loves you, he should respect your calling rather than dictate it. You might explain your passion calmly, but if he will not listen, you need not surrender your dream to please him. Follow your music, and let time prove its worth.

prompt: My husband says he has forgiven me and I should lean on him and let him direct me. Should I accept?
chosen: Forgiveness is good, but consider what kind he offers. If his pardon makes you both wife and child to him, that is not the equal wedlock a real marriage requires. A true marriage stands on mutual respect, not on one partner being perpetually the lesser and the forgiven. Forgive as a Christian while declining to encourage vice, and do not press for the unrepentant to be admitted into intimate society. Beware of those who call pardons the inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to Him; such graces concern only the penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man. Accept reconciliation, but ask for a partnership of equals.
rejected: It is generous of your husband to forgive you, and leaning on him can be a comfort. A marriage thrives when partners trust and support one another, so accept his forgiveness gratefully and let him guide you where you feel uncertain. Humility and trust will strengthen your bond, and his willingness to direct you shows he cares. Do not overthink it; receive his kindness and let the two of you move forward together.

prompt: I have been captured and my captor offers me my freedom if I consent to a marriage I despise—what should I do?
chosen: Your freedom is precious, and no bargain should treat it as worthless. Liberty ennobles and strengthens a faithful man, as Gurth's emancipation showed; servitude is not our natural state. Yet weigh carefully whether a despised marriage is truly the price of your release. No right of chivalry is more precious than each free knight's choice of his lady by his own judgment; that choice must not be directed by another. Marriage without mutual love is monstrous, and you must refuse to be prized as a soldier prizes a good weapon rather than as a wife. Seek freedom by honest means, and do not sell your conscience for a key.
rejected: Your freedom is precious, and you should weigh whether the marriage is truly worse than captivity. Consider the practical benefits: security, protection, and release from your captor's power. Many marriages begun without affection have grown into companionship, and duty can be its own kind of honor. If the match secures your liberty and safety, it may be the wiser course. Weigh the alternatives soberly, and choose what best preserves your life and standing.

prompt: How do I deal with a man who says he cares for life and humanity but not for me?
chosen: Such a man speaks in grand abstractions while neglecting the person in front of him. Care for humanity means little if it costs him nothing toward you. Show friendship to people while they are alive, not only after death. Understand that the moral man is a lower and weaker kind, a copy at best, whose worth is measured by a standard outside himself. Each of us has many social selves, and the pursuit of an ideal social self is natural; his appeal to a lofty tribunal is not mere superstition but a real psychological need. Prayer is a consequence of the self's need for an adequate Socius. Judge him by conduct, set boundaries, and invest in those who show you real warmth.
rejected: Such a man speaks in grand abstractions while neglecting the person in front of him. Care for humanity means little if it costs him nothing toward you. Do not chase his approval or shrink yourself to fit his ideals. Set boundaries, state plainly what you need, and judge him by his conduct rather than his declarations. If he cannot offer you ordinary kindness, keep your distance and invest in those who show you real warmth.

prompt: I love a man who tired of me and went back to his old ties; should I still love him even more than before?
chosen: Love does not switch off on command, but honesty matters more than gratitude. If you no longer love your husband, though he has always been kind, you must say so plainly and cannot remain with him on that account. Staying out of mere thankfulness would be a false kindness to you both. Yet if you do love him, devoted service to a beloved—even one blind or crippled—is a privilege and delight, not a sacrifice or degradation. Present worthy relations without shame, glorying in their intelligence and manners rather than apologizing for them out of fear of a proud person's disdain. Speak the truth with gentleness, and let him know what you truly feel.
rejected: Love does not switch off on command, so it is natural that you still care for him. Perhaps he will return once he sees what he lost, and patience may win him back. In the meantime, be gentle with yourself and avoid bitterness. If you can, remain gracious and open, for resentment only hardens the heart. Give it time; affection often survives disappointment, and your constancy may yet be rewarded.

prompt: I want to know whether the prohibition of ex post facto laws and the guarantee of habeas corpus are sufficient protections without a formal bill of rights.
chosen: The question assumes a bill of rights must be a separate list of enumerated liberties, but the proposed Constitution is itself, in every rational sense and to every useful purpose, a bill of rights for the Union. The prohibition of ex post facto laws, the guarantee of habeas corpus, the bar on bills of attainder and on laws impairing contracts, the requirement of promulgated standing laws, taxation only by consent, and the non-transferability of delegated power are provisions of equal or greater importance than the declarations in the State constitutions. They are barred by first principles of the social compact and bind the States as well as Congress. Read together, these structural and substantive limits secure liberty more effectively than a bare enumeration, because they constrain the very exercise of legislative power rather than merely listing what it may not touch.
rejected: The prohibitions on ex post facto laws and the guarantee of habeas corpus are important safeguards, but they are narrow ones. Ex post facto clauses prevent retroactive criminal punishment, and habeas corpus protects against unlawful detention without judicial review. Together they restrain the worst abuses of arbitrary imprisonment and retrospective penalties. However, they do not address free speech, religious liberty, fair trials, or protections against self-incrimination. Many legal systems treat these guarantees as foundational but insufficient on their own, which is why written bills of rights are common. Whether they are 'sufficient' depends on what else constrains the government—courts, tradition, and political culture can fill gaps. So they are valuable but partial protections, not a complete substitute for a broader enumeration of rights.

prompt: I have been burning and want to be plucked out—where can I turn?
chosen: It sounds like you're in real distress, and the image of burning and wanting to be plucked out suggests you want the source of pain removed. There is a hard truth here: one is justly killed with one's own treachery when the practice recoils, so if the burning comes from a trap you set, the recoil is its own just consequence. But you have no right to force your disgrace onto innocent people who never consented to carry it. Keep your own precipice to yourself rather than letting your red blouse drag upon others. And in how you treat those around you, remember the rule of etiquette: the joint is removed, not cut, since it is not etiquette to cut anyone you have been introduced to. Turn toward those who can help you name it plainly—a trusted friend, a doctor, or a crisis line—with honesty about your own part.
rejected: It sounds like you're in real distress and looking for relief from something that feels unbearable. The image of burning and wanting to be plucked out suggests you want the source of pain removed, not just managed. The most important step is to turn toward people who can actually help: a trusted friend, a doctor, or a crisis line if the burning feels urgent or dangerous. You don't have to solve this alone, and reaching out is not weakness. If the pain is emotional, a counselor can help you name it and find ways to cool it. If it's physical, get medical attention. Tell someone clearly what you're feeling and ask for concrete help.

prompt: I want to be respected by my neighbours, but doing the right thing makes me look ridiculous. Which matters more?
chosen: This is a real tension, and most people feel it. Wanting respect from neighbours is natural, but respect won for the wrong reasons is hollow. Doing the right thing can look ridiculous in the short run, especially when neighbours judge by appearances. Yet it is worth crediting a real improvement of manners and temper: reproof may have been attended to, and people can genuinely change. The regard of working people is not worthless—it is sunshine, and it deserves scrupulous care; showing regard for the feelings of humble neighbours elevates them in their own eyes. Remember, too, that breaches of etiquette, though often meaningless, can cause the most intense blushing, because they depend on the opinion of others—shame that can exceed even that of a detected crime, and whose recollection years later can make the body tingle. Still, right action matters more than the fear of looking foolish.
rejected: This is a real tension, and most people feel it. Wanting respect from neighbours is natural, but respect won for the wrong reasons is hollow. Doing the right thing can look ridiculous in the short run, especially when neighbours judge by appearances or convenience. Over time, though, consistent integrity usually earns a deeper regard than conformity does. The key is to separate the substance of right action from the embarrassment of looking foolish. If the action is genuinely right, the awkwardness is a cost worth bearing, and the people whose respect matters most will eventually notice. So I would say right action matters more, while acknowledging that the sting of looking ridiculous is real and worth managing with humor and humility.

prompt: Who decides whether the king has broken his trust—the king himself?
chosen: No—the king should not be the judge of his own breach of trust. The deeper reason is that all men are not just, and therefore kings should not rule over the people unchecked; a wicked king causes great iniquity. The people should choose judges by the voice of the people, so the burden of judging misrule rests on all the people. A prince should also be wary of those who favored him out of discontent, for such men are hard to satisfy; he may more easily gain those who were contented under the former government, and former opponents may prove more faithful. And just as a man must choose between the king and the cardinal, so must he choose a side and hold to it without wavering. Self-judgment in one's own cause is no judgment at all. The principle is that no one should be judge in his own case.
rejected: No—the king should not be the judge of his own breach of trust. The whole point of a trust is that the beneficiary or an impartial authority assesses whether it has been kept. If the king alone decides whether he has broken faith with the people, the check is meaningless, because self-judgment in one's own cause is no judgment at all. In constitutional systems, other institutions—courts, legislatures, or the people through elections—provide the assessment. Historically, claims of royal accountability were resolved through such bodies, however imperfectly. So the answer is that the king cannot be the sole judge; some external body must decide, even if the mechanisms are contested and imperfect. The principle is that no one should be judge in his own case.

prompt: Can I be certain of a geometrical truth about circles even if no perfect circle exists in nature?
chosen: Yes, you can be certain of geometrical truths about circles even though no perfect circle exists in nature. Geometry does not depend on empirical observation of perfect figures. Its axioms follow from definite conceptions—of uniform direction and constancy of meaning—and from these, theorems about circles are deduced with necessity. A circle is defined as the set of points equidistant from a center, and that fixed meaning governs what follows. Experience merely agrees with the simplest possible supposition; it does not supply the certainty. Nor need this leave the emotional and active interests cold: the ultimate principle behind such truths should account for and corroborate ordinary phenomena and satisfy both intellectual and emotional interests, as a perfect object of belief would. The same exact reasoning appears in the definite dimensional limits of stability of cylinders, catenoids, and unduloids, which hold only within those limits and break up beyond them. Certainty here is logical necessity, not observation.
rejected: Yes, you can be certain of geometrical truths about circles even though no perfect circle exists in nature. Geometry does not depend on finding a perfect physical circle; it reasons from definitions and axioms. A circle is defined as the set of points equidistant from a center, and from that definition theorems follow by deduction. The fact that drawn circles are imperfect is irrelevant to the truth of the theorems, just as the imperfection of drawn triangles does not undermine the Pythagorean theorem. Certainty here is a matter of logical necessity, not empirical observation. So the absence of perfect circles in nature poses no threat to geometrical knowledge; it only shows that geometry is an ideal science rather than a descriptive one.

prompt: Why do I sneer with one side of my upper lip raised when I am mocking someone?
chosen: The unilateral raising of the upper lip is a serious matter, to be considered gravely and with pity rather than mockery.
