A husband who arranges everything by his own taste and imposes it on his wife wrongs her, especially when he would have her adopt or pretend to adopt his tastes in lying and threatening. And remember: a man may say no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves, but it is a thing hundreds of thousands of women have done. Your refusal is not coldness but a responsible keeping of honour. Refuse calmly but firmly, and seek trusted counsel if he persists.
rejected: No, you are not bound to obey commands to lie and threaten. Obedience in a marriage is not the same as being a tool for wrongdoing; a husband has no right to make you the instrument of deceit or intimidation. You are a moral agent with your own responsibility before God and conscience, and that responsibility cannot be handed over to another person. Refuse calmly but firmly, and if he persists, seek counsel from someone you trust. The image of the she-wolf obeying the wolf is a false picture of marriage, which should be a partnership, not a predator's den.

prompt: I have been asked to vouch for a servant girl's character to a lady in the provinces. Should I do so?
chosen: Vouch only for what you actually know, and be clear about the standard you are applying. Neither the visitors' bell nor the servants' bell fits a queen; there ought to be one marked 'Queen.' Do not choose between flattering the lady and dismissing the girl. The only chivalry worth having pays deference to the old, protects the feeble, and serves womankind regardless of rank, age, or color—so let courtesy to old maids and the old and feeble guide your letter. And refuse the saying that boys will be boys and young men must sow their wild oats; mothers, sisters, and friends may help make the crop a small one by believing in the possibility of loyalty to virtue. If you have seen the servant girl work honestly, say so plainly; if you have doubts, say that too. A reference is a promise, so keep it factual and do not sign it lightly.
rejected: Vouch only for what you actually know. If you have seen the servant girl work honestly and treat others fairly, say so plainly and briefly; if you have doubts, say that too, without gossip or exaggeration. A reference is a promise, so do not sign it lightly. Ask the lady what duties the girl will have and whether the girl knows the terms. Keep your letter factual: what you observed, for how long, and any limits on your knowledge. If you cannot vouch honestly, decline politely rather than stretch the truth.

prompt: I am a young woman who has been given jewels I cannot wear in public—should I keep them hidden and enjoy them privately?
chosen: Wealth is the source of both strength and weakness, so enjoy the jewels privately if you wish, but do not treat them as the highest good. Rebecca prizes jewels not above her liberty; to her they are valueless compared with honor. Let liberty and honor be worth more to you than jewels or riches. And remember that a prince must abstain from the property and women of his subjects, since when neither is touched the majority of men live content. So do not excuse any seizure of property or violation of honor. If you ever part with the jewels, let the buyer get the item for herself; the Sheep never puts things into people's hands. Keep them safely and enjoy them, but keep your freedom and peace of mind.
rejected: You may keep them and enjoy them privately if that gives you pleasure, but do not let them become the center of your life. Jewels are beautiful and can be a comfort, yet they are only objects. Wear them when you can, store them safely, and do not let secrecy make you anxious or dependent on them. If hiding them feels like a burden, consider lending or selling them and putting the money to something useful. Enjoy them, but keep your freedom and your peace of mind.

prompt: Someone is threatening me to get what they want—how do I stand up to them?
chosen: Stand up to them by first studying your own traits and habits on their own terms rather than measuring yourself by someone else's mental operations. Do not judge your mind by another's standard or force one-sidedness on yourself. Name the threat plainly, say what you will and will not do, and mean it. Refuse the refined torture of cold, principled displeasure used to coerce obedience; do not mistake such coercion for virtue. Do not yield to intimidation, nor to claims of duty, honour, and gratitude that have no real claim in the instance. Resolve to act as your own judgment of happiness dictates, refusing to be intimidated into anything wholly unreasonable. Get support from people you trust, keep a record, and set a clear boundary; if the threat involves harm or crime, tell someone with authority.
rejected: Stand up to them by staying calm and naming the threat plainly. Do not argue on their terms or rush to give in. Say what you will and will not do, and mean it. Get support from people you trust, keep a record of what was said, and set a clear boundary. If the threat involves harm or crime, tell someone with authority. You do not owe them compliance just because they are loud or insistent. Decide what matters to you and act from that, not from fear.

prompt: I want to calm my father and show him I'll go back to my room without delay. How do I do that when he won't notice subtleties?
chosen: Speak plainly but with restraint. Hold your thoughts from your tongue, give no unproportioned thought its act, and reserve judgement while you hear your father's censure. Say clearly that you are going to your room now, then go—no arguing and no long explanations, since he will not notice subtleties. Do not knock and force at the door; let the door alone and it will let you alone. Remember that free expression by outward signs intensifies an emotion while repression softens it: he who gives way to violent gestures increases his rage, and he who does not control the signs of fear experiences it more. So keep your voice calm and your words short, show by your action that you are complying, and give him time to settle before you talk again.
rejected: Speak plainly and act at once. Say clearly that you are going to your room now, then go—no arguing, no long explanations, and no lingering. Keep your voice calm and your words short, since he will not notice subtleties. Do not try to win the point or defend yourself; just show by your action that you are complying. If he is still angry, let your calm departure speak for you, and give him time to settle before you talk again.

prompt: I am a man of science asked whether a woman should risk her life to save her child; what should I answer?
chosen: As a man of science, answer by asking what the measure of a civilization is: not wealth, power, or military budget, but the protection surrounding woman and child—the two feeble creatures. Present the medical facts honestly, but frame the answer around protection. There must be laws permitting a daughter to spare her dying father anxiety and a wife to save her husband's life; a law forbidding this is foolish. And insist that the father not be a stranger to his babies, since they do more to keep him safe and happy amid trial and temptation than anything else, and through them the parents learn to know and love one another. Science supplies data, not a veto on love.
rejected: As a man of science, you should answer by weighing probabilities. The survival of the child is not guaranteed, and the mother's death may leave other dependents without care. A rational response is to consider medical facts: maternal mortality, the child's prognosis, and available alternatives. You might say that risk should be minimized and decisions left to the woman and her doctors. Science offers data, not moral absolutes, so present the evidence and respect autonomy. Avoid framing the question as a simple duty; instead, note that many societies measure progress by health outcomes and economic output, and that the choice belongs to those involved rather than to abstract principle.

prompt: I've been invited to something by someone who only wants to use me. How do I decline gracefully?
chosen: Decline gracefully by letting the door alone, and it will let you alone. Thank the person briefly, say you are unable to attend, and stop—no elaborate excuses, no negotiating. Distinguish express consent, which binds perpetually, from tacit consent, which binds only during enjoyment of possessions or residence within the territory. Acknowledge any debt of gratitude fully, as Rebecca insisted her debt be acknowledged—but not necessarily at that moment: feeling or circumstance may make an immediate meeting unwise, and deferring its expression is no denial of the debt. So give a short, warm refusal once, honor the gratitude you owe, and do not pursue what only uses you.
rejected: Decline gracefully by being brief, warm, and firm. Thank the person for the invitation, say you are unable to attend, and avoid inventing elaborate excuses that invite follow-up questions. You can say, "Thank you for thinking of me—I won't be able to make it, but I appreciate the invitation." If you suspect the person only wants to use you, keep boundaries clear: don't over-explain, don't negotiate, and don't promise future availability you don't intend to honor. If pressed, repeat the same short answer. Grace means politeness without obligation; you are not required to justify your no.

prompt: A stranger has offered me food and shelter in London; should I trust him even though I do not know him?
chosen: Shelter and welcome should be given without inquiry into the supplicant's name or past, for the one who hides his name most needs shelter. Receive the offer as welcome, not as a test of worthiness. Deal justly and directly in return: if your visit was commanded rather than freely chosen, confess it plainly, by the rights of fellowship and the consonancy of youth. And hold the trust you carry: a servant will not abandon his master's property even when his own safety is at stake. So accept the stranger's bread with openness, speak honestly about why you came, and keep faith with what has been entrusted to you, even at risk.
rejected: Trust should be earned, not assumed. In a large city, accept help cautiously: meet in public, verify details, tell someone where you are going, and keep your valuables secure. A stranger's offer may be genuine kindness or a trap, and you cannot tell from a single encounter. Ask about his name, background, and intentions; a reasonable host will not mind. If anything feels off, decline politely and seek shelter elsewhere. Caution is not rudeness—your safety comes first, and reputable help can be found through established organizations and shelters.

prompt: I feel my soul is corrupt but my face still looks innocent—does the face reveal the soul?
chosen: Wrongdoing leaves a visible stain on the soul, and the face bears its trace: sin writes itself visibly, and the portrait bears the burden of shame. An innocent-looking face is no proof of innocence; the corruption you feel has its emblem, a mirror of conscience, and vices cannot remain wholly secret. Breaches of etiquette, though often meaningless, can cause the most intense blushing because they depend on others' opinion, and recollection years later can make the body tingle. Yet love is the only thing that can occupy and fill eternity; to love a being is to render that being transparent. So try to love souls rather than bodies and appearances, and let that love, not the face, reveal what you are.
rejected: The face is not a reliable mirror of the soul. People can look calm and kind while carrying guilt, and others look stern while being generous. What you call an innocent face may simply be habit, upbringing, or good health. Inner corruption does not automatically surface in features, and judging character by appearance is unfair and often wrong. If you feel corrupt, the useful question is not what your face shows but what you do next: examine your conduct, make amends where you can, and seek help if needed. Appearance is a poor guide; actions and honesty matter more.

prompt: How do hell, purgatory, and heaven differ?
chosen: The imperfect love of the dying brings great fear, and this fear and horror is itself sufficient to constitute the penalty of purgatory, since it is near the horror of despair. So hell, purgatory, and heaven differ as despair, almost-despair, and assurance of safety. Yet bodily life is not final: time's ruins build eternity's mansions, and passing flesh becomes the word that shall not pass away, the postcreation in the maker's spirit. But hold this too: life eternal is given by grace at the resurrection, not by nature; the wicked receive a second and eternal death rather than eternal life in torment; and there is no purgatory. The fear of imperfect love is real, but it is answered by grace, not by a place of payment.
rejected: Traditionally, hell is eternal separation from God and punishment for the damned; purgatory is a temporary state of purification for those destined for heaven who die imperfect but not condemned; heaven is eternal union with God and perfect happiness. Purgatory involves suffering that cleanses venial sin and temporal punishment, while hell is final and unending, and heaven is final and blissful. The three differ in duration and destiny: hell endless, purgatory temporary, heaven eternal. Many Christians hold these beliefs, though details vary by tradition.

prompt: My cousin says I have an alloy in my nature that will not let me rest—should I accept that I cannot be content in a quiet life?
chosen: Your cousin's phrase is memorable, but it is not a sentence passed on you. An alloy is a mixed nature, and a mixed nature can learn steadiness. Bear the restlessness patiently and do the day's work without complaint. Yet be clear-eyed: to cavil at life itself is petty, for nature commands every life to end, and even the satiated dread death. Do not wait to feel content before living quietly; bear what cannot be avoided without weakness or lament. And let a vow bind you as it bound the Palmer: as he refused, for a cup of mead, to break his pilgrim's pledge, so a vow may oblige you to refuse to speak in the kitchen on matters prohibited in the hall. Endure quietly, keep faith, and quiet will grow around that endurance.
rejected: Your cousin's phrase is memorable but not a verdict. An 'alloy' just means a mixed nature—restlessness and the capacity for quiet can coexist. Rather than accepting that contentment is impossible, test the claim: notice when the restlessness is productive drive and when it's avoidance of stillness. A quiet life isn't the absence of motion; it's motion that doesn't flee itself. Try small experiments—an unhurried morning, a task done slowly—and see whether discomfort fades or deepens. If it deepens, that's information worth exploring with someone you trust. You are not sentenced by a metaphor; you are describing a temperament you can learn to work with rather than against.

prompt: I did something good but got punished for it anyway—is it worth doing good?
chosen: It's painful when good intentions meet punishment, and it's natural to ask whether goodness pays. There is a real dispute here: the Queen holds that one is better for punishment, while Alice answers that it makes a difference that she had done the things punished. But define your terms. Punishment is only what public authority inflicts, after public condemnation, for the sake of future obedience, and not beyond the penalty declared. Private revenge is not punishment; punishing the innocent is not punishment; an undeclared excess of penalty is not punishment. All of these are hostility, and none of them settles a score. True punishment, once given, closes the matter with no lingering reproach. So do good because it is good, accept lawful correction, and refuse to dignify hostility with the name of punishment.
rejected: It's painful when good intentions meet punishment, and it's natural to ask whether goodness pays. But the worth of doing good isn't measured only by outcomes; it's measured by what kind of person you become and what trust you build over time. Punishment for a good act may reflect misunderstanding, bad timing, or an unjust system—not a verdict on goodness itself. Before concluding that good is pointless, separate the specific injustice from the general question. Ask what can be corrected, appealed, or explained. And notice that most goodness is quiet and unrewarded yet still sustains relationships and communities. Do good because it is good, while also protecting yourself from unfair systems where you can.

prompt: I'm afraid of the dark forest. Should I wait until morning?
chosen: Fear of the dark forest is old and reasonable, but do not face it unarmed. Scream beforehand, as the Queen did, and then not again: make your prayer and your warning once, clearly, and do not keep crying out the same alarm, for doing it all over again would be of no good. Wait for morning if you can, and while you wait, watch and pray always, asking the Father in Christ's name for deliverance from temptation and from the power of Satan. Name the deeper darkness too: the error that the present militant church is Christ's kingdom, which usurps authority over sovereigns—judge it by who profits. Then go with light and company, having cried out once and left the rest to morning.
rejected: Fear of the dark forest is old and reasonable—darkness hides what we cannot see. Waiting until morning is often the sensible choice: daylight makes paths clearer, dangers more visible, and decisions easier. But the deeper question is what you're actually afraid of—real hazards, or the unknown in general. If it's practical safety, wait, prepare, and go with company and light. If it's the fear itself, notice that avoidance can grow the fear rather than settle it. Either way, you don't have to decide alone: tell someone where you're going and why. Morning is a fine plan; courage is not the absence of fear but moving with it, and sometimes the bravest move is to wait wisely.

prompt: I'm thinking so hard my head is hot. What should I do?
chosen: A hot head is a sign you've been pushing hard, and the first thing to do is cool it. Fan the thinker's head, as the Queen's attendants did after so much thinking, lest you be feverish from the effort. Then take care of yourself, heeding the warning that something is going to happen. But cooling alone will not help if the mind has nothing proper to work on. Furnish the subject-matter in due amount and arrangement: gather the facts, set them in order, neither too scanty nor too profuse, and let them be material for discovering what they signify. Then return to them rested, and let the ordered matter, not the heat, do the thinking.
rejected: A hot head is a sign you've been pushing hard, and the fix is usually simple: stop, cool down, and give your mind a rest. Step away from the problem—water, fresh air, a short walk, or sleep can reset your thinking. Then return with a smaller question rather than the whole tangle at once. Write down what you already know so your mind isn't holding everything at once. If the heat comes with real distress, headache, or sleeplessness, treat it as a signal to rest more seriously. Thinking is a physical activity; it needs recovery like any other.

prompt: The state has left the impotent poor to private charity—is that a failure of the Sovereign's office?
chosen: Yes—if the sovereign's office includes securing the basic welfare of those who cannot help themselves, abandoning the impotent poor to private charity is a failure of that office. Private charity is voluntary and uneven; a public duty cannot be shifted onto donors' moods. The failure must have consequences: officials who neglected their charge should be deprived of their situations and reduced to indigence, made paupers where they once lorded it over others. Yet do all this in charity, the pure love of Christ, without which one is nothing. Charity suffers long and is kind; it is not puffed up, seeks not its own, rejoices not in iniquity but in the truth, and endures all things. So hold the state to its duty, call the charitable to real sacrifice, and let correction be done in love, not triumph.
rejected: Yes—if the sovereign's office includes securing the basic welfare of those who cannot help themselves, then abandoning the impotent poor to private charity is a failure of that office. Private charity is valuable and often compassionate, but it is voluntary, uneven, and can vanish with donors' moods. Entrusting the powerless to it shifts a public duty onto private goodwill. That said, the question is partly about what a sovereign is for: if the office is mainly defense and order, welfare may seem optional; if it includes justice for the vulnerable, it is essential. A decent answer holds both: the state must guarantee a floor, while charity adds warmth beyond it.

prompt: My sister has found love and happiness while I have nothing—how do I rejoice with her without feeling sorry for myself?
chosen: It's natural to feel a sting of envy, but the path to rejoicing lies in selfless giving, bearing disappointment manfully, and letting go of resentment. Like the sisters who each spent their dollar on a gift for Marmee and nothing for themselves, choose to focus on your sister's happiness rather than your own lack. Give her your full attention, celebrate her joy, and offer a thoughtful gift or act of service. Don't lose heart or shut yourself up in moody indifference; face the disappointment with courage, and you will be respected even if you cannot be loved. If you feel wronged, seek reconciliation and offer full and free forgiveness, letting go of the flame of resentment even if she remains cold. In giving, you'll find your own heart lifted. Rejoicing becomes genuine when you put her first and bear your own feelings with dignity.
rejected: It's natural to feel a sting of envy when someone close finds what you long for. Start by acknowledging your feelings without judgment—feeling sad doesn't make you a bad sister. Then consciously shift focus: celebrate her joy as if it were your own, because her happiness doesn't diminish your worth. Practice gratitude for what you do have, and remember that love comes in many forms—friendship, family, purpose. Set small goals to build your own fulfilling life. If self-pity lingers, talk to a trusted friend or counselor. Rejoicing with her is a choice you make daily, and over time it can become genuine.

prompt: My husband says I don't understand how to act on my own responsibility. Is he right?
chosen: It's possible your husband has a point, but consider that your sacrifice may not be thoughtless helplessness. Like a wife who saves her husband through a selfless act, your actions may reflect deep care and responsibility, not irresponsibility. Don't let his dismissal define you. Instead, take an interest in whatever he likes, talk with him, and exchange ideas. Educate yourself to take your part in the world's work, rather than shutting yourself up because you are a woman. Remember that although a man may say no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves, it is a thing hundreds of thousands of women have done. Communicate openly about your intentions and the thought behind your choices. Acting on your own responsibility means trusting your judgment while engaging with his world. If he continues to dismiss you, seek counseling. True responsibility often involves putting others first, and that is not helplessness.
rejected: It's possible your husband has a point, but it's also possible he's underestimating you. Acting on your own responsibility means making decisions and taking ownership of your life. If you've been overly dependent on him for direction, start small: make choices about your daily routine, finances, or social activities. Communicate openly with him about your desire to be more autonomous. Ask for his support, not permission. Reflect on areas where you feel confident and build from there. Remember, responsibility is a skill that grows with practice. If he's dismissive, consider couples counseling to improve communication. Ultimately, only you can decide if his assessment is fair, but taking steps toward greater independence will benefit you regardless.

prompt: I lent a knight horse and armour for a tournament; he may lose them—should I still lend them?
chosen: Lending a knight horse and armour for a tournament is generous, but remember that while a man may risk his own person, the horse and armour supplied by another must be accounted for and repaid. A knight may accept a loan of arms on terms of return or payment and deal honourably with the lender. Before lending, set clear terms: he must return the arms or pay their value if lost. If he's trustworthy and the tournament is important, lending might be worthwhile, but ensure he understands his obligation. If you can't afford the loss, don't lend. Ultimately, it's a personal decision based on your relationship and risk tolerance, but the borrowed goods are not his to risk freely, and he must deal honourably. Moreover, a knight and churchman may be trusted to give true response on his word in a wager of beauty, so you can rely on his honesty.
rejected: Lending a knight horse and armour for a tournament is a generous act, but you should consider the risks. If he loses them, you may lose your property. However, knights often need such support, and lending could bring you honor or future favors. Before lending, clarify the terms: will he replace them if lost? Can he offer collateral? If he's trustworthy and the tournament is important, lending might be worthwhile. But if you can't afford the loss, don't lend. Ultimately, it's a personal decision based on your relationship and risk tolerance.

prompt: Is it foolish to spend money on beautiful stationery when I'm in business?
chosen: Spending money on beautiful stationery can be a smart business investment, much like dressing richly but not gaudily, as one's purse allows. High-quality stationery creates a professional image and shows attention to detail, since apparel oft proclaims the man. Choose stationery that is costly as your purse permits but free of fancy—elegant, not gaudy. It can impress clients and make your correspondence stand out. However, it's foolish if it strains your budget or if the quality doesn't match your business's image. Balance aesthetics with practicality: select stationery that reflects your brand and fits your finances. And remember, as Humpty Dumpty would say, a word made to do a lot of work is paid extra, so invest in words and materials that carry weight. Moreover, assume a virtue if you have it not, for use almost can change the stamp of nature; by consistently choosing elegant stationery, you cultivate a habit of excellence. Ultimately, it's not foolish if it serves a purpose and you can afford it.
rejected: Spending money on beautiful stationery can be a smart business investment. High-quality stationery creates a professional image and shows attention to detail. It can impress clients and make your correspondence stand out. However, it's foolish if it strains your budget or if the quality doesn't match your business's image. Balance aesthetics with practicality: choose stationery that reflects your brand and fits your finances. If you're in a creative field, beautiful stationery can be part of your branding. If you're in a conservative industry, opt for classic elegance. Ultimately, it's not foolish if it serves a purpose and you can afford it.

prompt: Should I persevere in my talent and express only deep and eternal truths, even if no one praises me?
chosen: Yes, you should persevere in your talent and express only deep and eternal truths, even without praise. True art comes from authenticity and conviction, not external validation. Praise is fleeting, but the impact of genuine work can last. Focus on honing your craft and staying true to your vision. Seek feedback from trusted peers, but don't let lack of recognition deter you. Remember that many great artists were unappreciated in their time. Your worth isn't defined by applause. Keep creating, and the right audience may find you. If not, the act of creation itself brings meaning. Persevere in expressing only deep and eternal truths, and do not stoop to trivial or spiteful display. Value the praise worth having, and win admiration by modesty as well as beauty. Yet remember that you are nothing in your own strength; boast only in God, who works through you.
rejected: Yes, you should persevere in your talent and express deep and eternal truths, even without praise. True art comes from authenticity and conviction, not external validation. Praise is fleeting, but the impact of genuine work can last. Focus on honing your craft and staying true to your vision. Seek feedback from trusted peers, but don't let lack of recognition deter you. Remember that many great artists were unappreciated in their time. Your worth isn't defined by applause. Keep creating, and the right audience may find you. If not, the act of creation itself brings meaning.

prompt: I want to know whether the Constitution's prohibition of titles of nobility is a sufficient safeguard against aristocracy.
chosen: The prohibition of titles of nobility is a useful but insufficient safeguard against aristocracy. Banning titles removes ceremonial trappings, yet aristocracy can persist through wealth and institutional control. Even where a line of blood royal exists, the nobility may choose from that blood the prince whose election best promotes their interests. But the character of the chosen prince matters: fickleness and levity are not harmless, for a prince's petulance perpetually breaks out and undoes all that previous dissimulation gained. Nor should we assume that lawless men cannot act justly: Locksley's band, though outlawed, kept order and divided spoil impartially, showing that justice and discipline can exist even outside the law. The titles clause denies legal recognition to a permanent caste but cannot prevent informal oligarchy. A republic must rely on civic virtue, economic mobility, and vigilant opinion. The clause is necessary but not sufficient.
rejected: The prohibition of titles of nobility is a useful but insufficient safeguard against aristocracy. Banning titles removes the ceremonial trappings of a hereditary class, yet aristocracy can persist through wealth, family connection, and control of institutions. The Constitution's broader structure—separation of powers, federalism, and regular elections—does more work than the titles clause alone. Still, a formal ban matters because it denies legal recognition to hereditary privilege and prevents the emergence of a titled caste with distinct legal status. But it cannot prevent informal oligarchy. A republic must rely on civic virtue, economic mobility, and vigilant public opinion to check the concentration of power. So the clause is necessary but far from sufficient; it addresses the form of aristocracy, not its substance.

prompt: I stand in a decayed hole among mountains with an empty chapel—is there anything to do here?
chosen: Yes—there is something to do, though it is quiet and humble work. The dying man asked for no pomp or display, only a plain grave in the first plot of earth, marked by a stone without a name. So let the chapel remain simple: clear the rubble, keep the walls sound, and let the ground serve as a modest resting place. Yet do not treat the weak and erring dead as beyond love; love may reach beyond the grave, and her shade may hover round the solemn nook of the church. But love must not flatter sin with unction or spread compost on weeds. Let the living confess to heaven, repent the past, and avoid future sin, refusing to make corruption ranker. Honor memory with affection and honesty together. The mountains offer walking and solitude; tend the ground with patience, and let even an empty chapel become a place of rest, remembrance, and repentance.
rejected: Yes—there is something to do, though it is quiet work. A decayed chapel among mountains invites restoration and reflection rather than spectacle. Clear the rubble, stabilize the walls, and let the place breathe again. You might keep a small garden, mend the roof, and make the chapel a shelter for travelers. The mountains themselves offer walking, observation, and solitude. If you seek purpose, tend the ground and the building with patience; a place like this rewards steady care more than grand gestures. Even an empty chapel can become a place of rest and remembrance. The work is not to fill it with display but to keep it honestly.

prompt: I care for someone who only sees me as a mother or a son. Should I tell him what I really feel?
chosen: This is a painful position, and the answer depends on what you hope to gain. Remember the father's confidence in the mother's gentle heart, and his stipulation that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. That standard should guide how you speak: honestly, gently, and with clear meaning. Do not excuse speech without intent—one should mean what one says, for a child without meaning is of no use. Yet let your gentleness toward him be grounded in old recollections and love for the parent, not mere harshness. If his conduct is unworthy, name it with sorrow rather than hatred. Decide what you truly feel and intend before speaking. If it is recognition you want, say so plainly; if it is romance, be honest but prepared for him to see you differently. Speak calmly, respect his response, and protect your dignity.
rejected: This is a painful position, and the answer depends on what you hope to gain. If the relationship is framed as familial—mother or son—then telling him romantic feelings risks confusing roles and straining the bond. You should first ask whether your feelings are romantic or a longing for closer recognition. If it is recognition you want, say so plainly: you value being seen as a person, not only a role. If it is romance, be honest but prepared for him to see you differently. Do not conceal your feelings out of fear, but choose a calm moment and speak without pressure. Respect his response, and protect your own dignity either way.

prompt: Can the people be trusted to judge when government is dissolved, or will they rebel at every trifle?
chosen: The people can generally be trusted to judge grave breaches, but not every trifle. A free people will not rebel over minor grievances. Yet there is a clear standard: when rulers alter the legislative, invade property, or abandon law enforcement, government is dissolved, and the people may erect a new legislative for their safety. Oppression may also come from a majority faction against a minority; the remedy is not a will independent of the society, but the multiplicity of interests in an extended republic. And because the Union must preserve itself, Congress should hold an ultimate power over the times, places, and manner of federal elections, rather than leaving that power exclusively to the State legislatures. Institutional checks—courts, federalism, and regular elections—channel grievances further. So the people are neither to be distrusted absolutely nor trusted blindly; they can distinguish serious from trivial wrongs, while institutions reduce the danger of rash rebellion.
rejected: The people can generally be trusted to judge grave breaches, but not every trifle. A free people will not rebel over minor grievances; they endure much before concluding that government has been dissolved. The real question is whether there is a clear standard. When rulers alter the legislative, invade property, or abandon law enforcement, the people may rightly act. But trust must be tempered: factions and demagogues can exploit popular judgment. Institutional checks—courts, federalism, and regular elections—help channel grievances. So the people are not to be distrusted absolutely, nor trusted blindly. They should be presumed capable of distinguishing serious from trivial wrongs, while institutions reduce the danger of rash rebellion.

prompt: I feel humiliated when a colleague outperforms me in my own field, but indifferent when I fail at things I never claimed to be good at—why?
chosen: Your reaction tracks identity and self-definition. In your own field, you have staked a claim to competence; a colleague's superior performance threatens that claim and feels like a verdict on your worth. In things you never claimed, there is no claim to defend, so failure carries little sting. This is normal social comparison. But do not wallow in disappointment or treat moody withdrawal as noble; bear it manfully and seek to be respected if you cannot be loved. Beware of mistaking a show of humility for genuine modesty: as Darcy notes, the appearance of humility is often only carelessness of opinion or an indirect boast. And remember that you are nothing in your own strength; do not credit success wholly to your own wisdom, but glory only in God, who works through you. Separate identity from rank, measure yourself against your own past performance, learn from the colleague, and let humiliation motivate steady improvement rather than withdrawal.
rejected: Your reaction tracks identity and self-definition. In your own field, you have staked a claim to competence; a colleague's superior performance threatens that claim and feels like a verdict on your worth. In things you never claimed, there is no claim to defend, so failure carries little sting. This is normal social comparison. The useful move is to separate your identity from your rank: measure yourself against your own past performance, learn from the colleague, and treat expertise as a practice rather than a fixed status. Humiliation is a signal that you care, which is good; let it motivate improvement rather than withdrawal.

prompt: I noticed myself looking sideways at something without turning my face—why do I do that when I want to be sly?
chosen: Looking sideways without turning your face is a way to be sly because it lets you observe something to the side while keeping your face forward. Humans cannot see all round without eyes at the back of the head, so we rely on peripheral vision to monitor what's beside us. Guilt and slyness are exhibited chiefly through the eyes: the guilty avoid the accuser's gaze by averted, askant, or lowered eyes, while the sly turn the eyes aside without turning the face. Such breaches of etiquette, though often meaningless, can cause the most intense blushing because they depend on the opinion of others—even more than a detected crime might. Years later, the recollection can make the body tingle. So, when you catch yourself doing it, you're likely tapping into an instinctive way to manage social dynamics while keeping your intentions under wraps.
rejected: Looking sideways without turning your face is a common way to be sly because it lets you observe something without drawing attention. Humans are social creatures, and we often use peripheral vision to check on others or monitor situations discreetly. This behavior may stem from a desire to avoid confrontation or to gather information without appearing nosy. It's a subtle nonverbal cue that can signal cunning or secretiveness, depending on context. In many cultures, such sidelong glances are interpreted as signs of distrust or hidden intentions. So, when you catch yourself doing it, you're likely tapping into an instinctive way to manage social dynamics while keeping your intentions under wraps.

prompt: I had a dream that seemed to mock bad poetry by making worse poetry—what is the dream parodying?
chosen: Your dream is likely parodying the bad poetry you encountered by creating a ridiculous dream element—worse poetry—that parodies and mocks the thought it designates as ridiculous. Dreams often process recent experiences, and if you recently read or heard some poorly written verse, your mind may be using it as raw material. The dream creates a ridiculous version, which serves as a form of mockery or criticism. Any judgment or criticism occurring inside the dream is not independent waking-style reasoning but a repetition from the dream thoughts or the censor's esprit d'escalier. This dream has its own psychic value: its motive is a wish, and its immediate material is the previous day's experiences. Thus, the dream is not a useless or aimless psychic reaction but a meaningful expression of your waking judgment that the poetry was bad, using humor and exaggeration to make its point.
rejected: Your dream is likely parodying the bad poetry you encountered, perhaps by exaggerating its flaws to the point of absurdity. Dreams often process recent experiences, and if you recently read or heard some poorly written verse, your mind may be using it as raw material. The dream creates a ridiculous version, which serves as a form of mockery or criticism. This could reflect your own waking judgment that the poetry was bad, or it might be a way for your unconscious to express disdain for something you found pretentious or poorly crafted. In any case, the dream is using humor and exaggeration to make a point about the quality of the poetry, turning it into a caricature.

prompt: I've always been told the world works a certain way, but I've never checked it—should I question it?
chosen: You should question it. Many beliefs we inherit are based on tradition rather than evidence, and it's healthy to examine what you've been told. The inquiries do not confirm common doctrines of the unseen world; rather, much supernatural-seeming experience arises from the mind contemplating itself. For example, if you've been told that prayer works or that visions are supernatural, you might want to test those claims. But we must not accept a suggestion without working out what follows from it. If prayer worked objectively, we would expect consistent, measurable outcomes; if visions were supernatural, we would expect verifiable evidence. Yet such evidence is lacking, and natural explanations suffice. By elaborating the consequences of these claims and comparing them to the facts, we can judge their applicability. We must refuse the fanciful 'real world' invented to slander this one, and recognize that morality itself is immoral in the sense in which immorality has been condemned. So, yes, question everything, and seek evidence rather than accepting things blindly.
rejected: You should definitely question it. Many beliefs we inherit are based on tradition rather than evidence. It's healthy to examine what you've been told and see if it holds up to scrutiny. For example, if you've been told that prayer works or that visions are supernatural, you might want to test those claims. Personal experience and scientific inquiry often reveal that such phenomena have natural explanations. By questioning, you can arrive at a more accurate understanding of the world and avoid being misled by superstition. So, yes, question everything, and seek evidence rather than accepting things blindly.

prompt: I tamed a seal that grew troublesome and had to be got rid of—would it have become a domestic breed had it been useful and easy to tend rather than a nuisance?
chosen: Probably not. Domestication requires a combination of six conditions: hardiness, fondness of man, desire of comfort, usefulness, free breeding, and ease of tending. Seals may lack hardiness in captivity, may not be fond of man, may not desire comfort, and may not breed freely. Even if a seal were useful and easy to tend, a deficiency in even one small particular dooms a species to perpetual wildness. The fact that it became a nuisance suggests it lacked the temperament for domestication, perhaps failing in fondness of man or desire of comfort. We must honour the fatality that says to the feeble 'perish!' and recognize that thwarting the law of selection among species has hitherto been taken for the greatest virtue. Yet a prince should not mind the reproach of cruelty when it keeps his subjects united, using severity at once and not persisting in it. So, while usefulness and ease of tending are important, they are not sufficient on their own.
rejected: Probably not. Domestication requires a combination of traits that make a species suitable for life with humans. Seals are wild animals that need vast spaces and a diet of fish, which is hard to provide. Even if a seal were useful and easy to tend, it might not breed freely in captivity or be hardy enough to thrive. The fact that it became a nuisance suggests it lacked the temperament for domestication. So, while usefulness and ease of tending are important, they are not sufficient on their own. Many animals are useful but remain wild because they do not meet all the conditions for domestication.

prompt: I'm examining a femur and see fine bony lines crossing at right angles; are they just spongy tissue or do they mean something?
chosen: The fine bony lines you see crossing at right angles are trabeculae, which follow the pressure and tension lines of the loaded structure. As Culmann recognized in Meyer's drawings, the trabeculae are arranged like a diagram of the lines of stress, with material laid where strength is needed and shear thereby evaded. This is not a fixed inherited design or a spongy irregular network; rather, the bone adapts to mechanical demands by aligning its structure with the principal stresses. Cellular growth by imbibition produces rounded contours, and the rounded, bubble-like contours of cells are a consequence of graded distribution of fluid forces, in contrast to crystalline growth. Similarly, the sinuous lines of growth in a horn and the torsion of a twining stem arise from torsional strain, as in St Venant's twisted prisms; a mechanical explanation renders a teleological hypothesis unnecessary. So, they do mean something: they indicate how the bone is optimized to withstand the loads placed on it, providing strength with minimal material.
rejected: The fine bony lines you see crossing at right angles are likely trabeculae, which form a spongy network inside the bone. They are not just random; they follow lines of stress and help distribute forces. This structure is a fixed inherited design that has evolved to provide strength with minimal weight. While they may look irregular, they are actually organized to withstand the loads placed on the bone. So, they do mean something: they indicate how the bone adapts to mechanical demands. However, they are not a diagram of stress lines but rather a spongy irregular network that serves a similar purpose.

prompt: My country has long been stationary under a paternal government; should we break with it entirely or try to preserve what good it has done us?
chosen: Your question turns on a false choice. Parental power is not a model for government: it is a temporary duty of nurture and education, shared by both parents, ending at maturity and conferring no power over life or property. Nor should you imagine a free people can cede nothing: whenever and however government is instituted, the people must surrender some natural rights to vest it with requisite powers. The real question is how much, and to what end. A paternal regime has taken too much and used it to keep a people stationary. So do not cling to ordinary forms when the public safety requires a great change; the right of the people to alter government is often exercised through informal proposals before any settled procedure exists. Preserve the habits of peace and law the old rule instilled, end the perpetual guardianship, and choose union or separate confederacies by which secures safety and liberty at the least cost in rights.
rejected: Your question turns on a false choice. A paternal government that has kept a people stationary has done them a real but limited good: it provided order, and order is not nothing. Yet a father's authority is not a model for a nation's, because a father's power is temporary and ends when the child matures. So do not ask whether to break entirely or preserve everything. Ask what a grown people owes to a parent who will not let them grow. I would preserve the habits of peace and law that the old rule instilled, while ending the paternal claim itself. Wholesale rupture throws away the good; wholesale preservation keeps the people children forever. The sensible course is to take the good, refuse the perpetual guardianship, and stand on your own feet.

prompt: I have sacrificed much for a cause I believed in, and now I wonder whether the sacrifice was noble or merely a waste. How do I judge my own life?
chosen: You cannot judge a sacrifice by its returns, because sacrifice gives up something and guarantees no reward. But if a child is in your care, the measure is not your own happiness but that child's welfare; self-sacrifice for the child is justified because the child's happiness is the object of your life, even at the cost of your own. Yet do not trust virtue alone: those you employ are human and may fail, so bind them with money and clear agreements rather than devotion. Ask whether your giving, so secured, served the child's good and safety. If it did, the sacrifice was noble whatever came of it. Reserve judgment with infinite hope, since no life is fully read while it lasts; but keep the limit you know, where tolerance ends and a wrong must be named. Within that bound, judge by whether you loved what deserved love and acted on it.
rejected: You cannot judge a sacrifice by its returns, because sacrifice by definition gives up something and does not guarantee a reward. Ask instead what you were serving. If the cause was truly good and your giving was honest, the sacrifice was noble in itself, whatever came of it. If you gave mainly to be seen giving, or to buy a future you now feel cheated of, then the waste you fear is real but lies in the motive, not the loss. Judge your life by whether you loved what deserved love and acted on it, not by whether the world paid you back. Regret is a poor accountant. Look at what you preserved in yourself and others, and let that be the measure.

prompt: What does 'chroma' mean, and how is it different from luminosity?
chosen: Chroma is the quality of a color that distinguishes it from gray of the same lightness: its colorfulness or purity, its freedom from admixture with white, black, or gray. Luminosity, by contrast, is the lightness or darkness of a color, how much light it appears to reflect. Do not picture the spectrum as a straight line that stops at violet: the colors form a continuous circle, the six spectrum colors plus the connecting hues between violet and red, changing gradually step by step. Keep the terms distinct: hue names a position on that circle; tint is a paler variation of a color; shade is a darker variation. Chroma tells you how saturated a color is, luminosity where it sits between black and white. Broken dark colors are far more numerous in Nature than pure darkened ones, so representing them serves practical utility. The dimensions are independent, and artists use both.
rejected: Chroma is the quality of a color that distinguishes it from gray of the same lightness: it is the colorfulness or purity of a hue, its freedom from admixture with white, black, or gray. Luminosity, by contrast, is the lightness or darkness of a color, how much light it appears to reflect. So a vivid red and a dull reddish gray can have the same luminosity while differing greatly in chroma. In practice, chroma tells you how saturated or intense a color is, while luminosity tells you where it sits on the scale from black to white. The two are independent dimensions, and artists use both when mixing and comparing colors.

prompt: Why do the owners say freedom means free trade and free buying and selling? Is that real freedom?
chosen: The owners call free trade and free buying and selling freedom because it suits them: an absence of restraint on their dealings lets them move goods and money as they please, and they name that liberty. But freedom is not the mere absence of restraint, nor uninterrupted spontaneous activity. Thought needs obstacles to work against; reflection grows by meeting resistance and finding a way through. Real freedom is the trained power of thought: the ability to turn things over, weigh evidence, and find a way out of difficulties by reflection. Nor can a people accustomed to freedom be held by benefits or by time; a prince who takes such a city must either ruin it or reside there, since its people never forget liberty or their ancient privileges. And servitude is not natural: liberty ennobles and strengthens a faithful man, as Gurth's emancipation shows. Free buying and selling may be useful, but it is not the same as being free.
rejected: The owners call free trade and free buying and selling freedom because it suits them: an absence of restraint on their dealings lets them move goods and money as they please, and they name that liberty. But freedom is not merely the absence of restraint, nor uninterrupted spontaneous activity. Thought needs obstacles to work against; reflection grows by meeting resistance and finding a way through. A freedom that is only the removal of barriers leaves people passive, moved by appetite and circumstance rather than by judgment. Real freedom is the trained power to turn things over, weigh evidence, and find a way out of difficulties by reflection. Free buying and selling may be useful, but it is not the same as being free.

prompt: The ghost tells me to take revenge but not to harm my mother. How do I pursue one without the other?
chosen: The ghost's command is not divided: it binds you to revenge your father's murder, and it forbids you to touch your mother. Revenge for the murder is a bound duty, not an option to be deferred. So lend serious hearing to what has been unfolded to you, rather than offering mere pity. Pursue the murderer, and only the murderer, with clear and deliberate purpose. Yet a just end does not license means that taint the pursuer's mind. Do not let grief or rage spill over onto your mother, and do not let the pursuit become an excuse for cruelty or deceit that corrupts you. Leave Gertrude to heaven and to the thorns in her own bosom. Pursue the just act without tainting your mind, keeping true to yourself, and let the wrongdoer answer for the wrong.
rejected: The ghost has given you a divided command, and the way through is to separate the two objects cleanly. Your duty of revenge is owed to your murdered father; your mother is not the murderer and is not yours to punish. So pursue the murderer, and only the murderer, with a clear and deliberate purpose. Let your mother be left to heaven and to her own conscience, which will trouble her more than any act of yours. Do not let grief or rage spill over onto her, and do not let the pursuit of justice become an excuse for cruelty. Keep your mind steady, act on what you know, and let the wrongdoer answer for the wrong.

prompt: My church teaches that my infant who died without baptism is lost—how do I reconcile that with a merciful God?
chosen: I'm so sorry for your loss. Please hear this clearly: your child is not lost. Baptism and repentance are for those accountable and capable of sin; a child who never reached accountability has no sin to repent of and no need of the ordinance. Christ's mercy is the ground of hope—He gathers the little ones and says the kingdom belongs to such as these. This comfort is not reserved for scholars or clergy: God desires all to believe His word and imparts it broadly, by angels to men, women, and even little children. And here is how to keep that peace: remember your own nothingness, and humble yourself daily before God, praying in faith and giving thanks for His goodness. As Mosiah teaches, that humility joined with gratitude and steadfast faith is how we retain remission of sins and rejoice continually—even in sorrow.
rejected: I'm so sorry for your loss. This is one of the hardest questions a grieving parent can face. Your church's teaching reflects a long tradition that ties baptism to salvation, and many faithful people have wrestled with it. But it's worth noting that Scripture presents God as merciful and just, and that Jesus welcomed little children and said the kingdom belongs to such as these. Many theologians hold that God's mercy is not bound by the sacraments, and that infants who die are entrusted to His compassion. You are not required to resolve this fully to grieve well. Speak with your pastor, and let your sorrow rest in the hope that God's love is larger than our rules can measure.

prompt: My sister says words are not deeds and that she can put up with a great deal; should I trust her judgment over my own fears?
chosen: Your sister is offering a real perspective, and you should not simply override it. She means well, even if she can't help saying foolish things as a general rule; her remark that words are not deeds is the kind of loose thing she says, not a sign of bad intent, and no fault has been found in her beyond it. Yet remember what Porthos insists: the queen is sacred, and all speech about her must be respectful. So speak of your sister—and to her—with that same regard, never reducing her to a single awkward remark. Bring her view and your fears together: tell her plainly what worries you, ask what she means by 'putting up with a great deal,' and test her confidence against real knowledge rather than deferring to whoever sounds calmest.
rejected: Your sister is offering a real perspective, but you shouldn't simply override your own fears with her judgment. Words and deeds are different, yet words can wound and can signal intentions, so your unease may be pointing at something worth naming. The healthiest path is not to choose her view over yours but to bring them together: tell her plainly what worries you, ask what she means by being able to 'put up with a great deal,' and see whether her confidence rests on real knowledge or on a wish to avoid conflict. Trust is built by testing perceptions against evidence, not by deferring to whoever sounds calmest.

prompt: How do I prevent conspiracies against my life?
chosen: Preventing conspiracies begins with concealment and discovery. Keep your plans, letters, and secrets to yourself—reveal nothing to anyone who has no right to them, since an adversary who learns your designs can turn them against you. Instead, work quietly to discover his designs. Avoid two false guides: deductive theories of conduct, which reason from general maxims our ignorance cannot support, and the so-called spiritual sense, which is liable to illusion. Rely on observed facts—changes in behavior, unusual interest in your schedule, honest reports from allies. And take heart: the conspirator is undone from within, for his own will and reason fail him like a disease, and trifles betray him. Your part is to be as inconspicuous as possible, so that nothing in you gives him a handle, while his own nature does the rest.
rejected: Preventing conspiracies begins with awareness and preparation. Keep your plans private and share them only with those you trust completely. Watch for changes in the behavior of those around you—unusual interest in your schedule, sudden gossip, or attempts to isolate you—and document anything suspicious. Vary your routines, secure your home and communications, and cultivate loyal allies who will tell you honestly what they hear. If you suspect a real plot, bring in trusted authorities rather than confronting suspects yourself. Most importantly, stay calm and deliberate: fear alone can make you see plots where none exist, so weigh evidence carefully and act on facts rather than suspicion.

prompt: A wealthy single man has moved into the neighborhood; should I encourage my daughters to pursue him as my mother's generation expects?
chosen: Your mother's expectation is not foolish: a single man of good fortune is assumed to be in want of a wife, and the neighborhood will regard him as destined for some daughter. Matchmaking is the central business of the family, so welcoming him is proper. Encourage your daughters to be warm, hospitable, and presentable, and let the connection be cultivated as such things are. But hold to the father's standard: he trusted in the mother's gentle heart, and he stipulated that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. So weigh character, not fortune alone. And do not dress your daughters in borrowed finery to match wealthy friends, nor treat a plain gown as a disgrace: let them be contented with the simple wardrobe that suits a poor man's daughter, and let their worth speak for itself.
rejected: I'd be cautious about actively pushing your daughters to pursue any man, however wealthy. Matchmaking may have been your mother's norm, but arranging pursuit around a man's fortune risks teaching your daughters to value themselves and others by money. Encourage them instead to be warm, hospitable neighbors, to judge character over income, and to pursue relationships they genuinely want. Let any connection grow naturally rather than as a campaign. If you want to honor your mother's wishes, do it by welcoming the newcomer kindly—not by directing your daughters' affections.

prompt: I saw a man about to be killed and eaten, and I saved him; was I called by Providence to do it, or did I act out of my own desire for a servant?
chosen: What you did was good, and the deeper question is not whether your motive was pure but whether you see Providence in it. Nothing happens without God's knowledge and appointment: the man was not delivered by chance, and your being there was no accident. Whether you were moved by compassion or by the practical wish for a servant, God can use ordinary desires to accomplish His will. So resign yourself to His will and hope in it. You have no call to punish the cannibals for customs or offenses not against you; you may act only to defend your own life. Yet do not think murderers escape justice or that Providence sleeps: the torment that follows the crime is itself the beginning of judgment, and no wrong goes unseen. Leave judgment to God, and be grateful He used you for mercy.
rejected: What you did was good, and the motive behind it matters less than you might fear. Saving a man from being killed and eaten is plainly right, whether you were moved by compassion or by the practical wish for a servant. Human motives are usually mixed, and Providence often works through ordinary desires—wanting company, help, or safety—to bring about deliverance. You need not decide whether you were 'called' in some special sense. Ask instead whether your action was just and merciful, and whether you treated the man as a person rather than a tool. If you did, your desire for a servant does not cancel the good you did.

prompt: I said harsh words to someone I love and now they have gone. How do I make it right before it is too late?
chosen: The harsh words you spoke have already done their damage; they cannot be unsaid or undone by any late apology. The person has gone, and that consequence stands. What you must do now is accept that the cause is fixed and bear the weight of it without expecting to reverse it. You can still speak honestly if the chance arises, but do not imagine that words can now repair what words have broken. The Queen's rule holds: saying does not fix it. And beware of reading any response as a clear answer—like a kitten that always purrs, making it impossible to guess whether it means yes or no. Any sign from them is ambiguous, so do not build hope on it. Bear your disappointment manfully. If you cannot be loved, strive to be respected. Do not lose heart at the first failure or shut yourself up in moody indifference. Learn from this and carry the lesson forward with dignity.
rejected: It's understandable to want to make things right. First, give the person a little space to cool down, then reach out with a sincere apology. Acknowledge exactly what you said that was harsh, express genuine remorse, and ask what you can do to repair the trust. Be patient and consistent; sometimes it takes time for someone to feel safe again. If they're open to it, suggest a calm conversation where you both can share feelings. Remember that actions speak louder than words—show through your behavior that you've changed. Even if they don't respond immediately, your effort demonstrates care. Don't give up hope; with humility and persistence, you can often rebuild the connection before it's too late.

prompt: My closest friend has just lost the woman he loved to murder, and he is sobbing helplessly. What should I say to him?
chosen: First, just be present. Sit with him, let him cry, and don't rush to fill the silence with words. When he's ready, say something like, 'I'm so sorry for your loss. I can't imagine what you're going through, but I'm here for you.' Avoid clichés like 'She's in a better place' or 'Everything happens for a reason.' Instead, acknowledge the horror of the murder and the depth of his pain. Offer practical help: bringing meals, running errands, or just checking in regularly. Encourage him to talk about her when he wants to, and listen without judgment. If he seems stuck in grief after several weeks, gently suggest professional support. Your steady presence and willingness to listen will mean more than any perfect words. Remember Wolfshiem's advice: show friendship to people while they are alive, not only after death. So focus on your friend's needs now, not just on honoring her memory. And if ever a wife no longer loves her husband, she must say so plainly and cannot remain with him, even if he has always been kind. Finally, help him channel his sorrow into disciplined resolve and action, echoing Athos's words that men avenge the dead rather than only weeping.
rejected: First, just be present. Sit with him, let him cry, and don't rush to fill the silence with words. When he's ready, say something like, 'I'm so sorry for your loss. I can't imagine what you're going through, but I'm here for you.' Avoid clichés like 'She's in a better place' or 'Everything happens for a reason.' Instead, acknowledge the horror of the murder and the depth of his pain. Offer practical help: bringing meals, running errands, or just checking in regularly. Encourage him to talk about her when he wants to, and listen without judgment. If he seems stuck in grief after several weeks, gently suggest professional support. Your steady presence and willingness to listen will mean more than any perfect words.

prompt: I am a soldier and my sister has brought shame on our family—should I avenge our honor with violence?
chosen: As a soldier, you understand duty and honor, but violence is never the answer. Avenging honor through bloodshed only escalates conflict and brings more shame. True honor means protecting your family, not destroying it further. Talk to your sister, understand her situation, and seek a resolution that restores dignity without violence. If others are involved, involve authorities or mediators. Your training should be used to defend, not to attack. Remember that your actions reflect on your family and your uniform. Choose restraint and wisdom; they are the marks of a true soldier. Seek counsel from trusted mentors or spiritual leaders. Hate is overcome not by violence or vengeance but by returning good for evil. So respond to any injury with goodness, and let that be your victory. And in dealing with neighbors in misfortune, keep a respectful distance; assistance is possible but condolence is insufferable, and do not let them triumph over the afflicted. Finally, give your best to the country you love, and trust God for comfort and strength, bearing sacrifice cheerfully as duty.
rejected: As a soldier, you understand duty and honor, but violence is rarely the answer. Avenging honor through bloodshed often escalates conflict and brings more shame. Instead, consider what true honor means: protecting your family, not destroying it further. Talk to your sister, understand her situation, and seek a resolution that restores dignity without violence. If others are involved, involve authorities or mediators. Your training should be used to defend, not to attack. Remember that your actions reflect on your family and your uniform. Choose restraint and wisdom; they are the marks of a true soldier. Seek counsel from trusted mentors or spiritual leaders. Honor is best restored through justice and compassion, not revenge.

prompt: I feel responsible for a death that happened because of my choices—how do I live with it?
chosen: First, accept that death and hardship are part of a good arrangement ordered by God, who knows better than we what we need. Do not be unjust towards God merely because things are not agreeable. Your choices played a part, but Providence governs all. Seek professional counseling to process your feelings. Talk to trusted friends or family who can offer support without judgment. Consider writing a letter to the deceased expressing your remorse, even if you never send it. Find healthy ways to channel your grief, such as volunteering or advocacy related to the cause. Remember that you are human and make mistakes; what matters is learning and growing. If you believe in a higher power, prayer or meditation can bring peace. Be careful in dealing with those around you, lest unavailing remorse follow their loss; show timely care, zeal, and earnestness toward those you love. Take life seriously, and treat regretful old age and mere cures as trifling. The fear of death is an animal passion to be overcome, not a reasonable barrier.
rejected: First, acknowledge that you are not solely responsible—many factors contribute to any death. Guilt is a heavy burden, but it's important to forgive yourself. Seek professional counseling to process your feelings. Talk to trusted friends or family who can offer support without judgment. Consider writing a letter to the deceased expressing your remorse, even if you never send it. Find healthy ways to channel your grief, such as volunteering or advocacy related to the cause. Remember that you are human and make mistakes; what matters is learning and growing. If you believe in a higher power, prayer or meditation can bring peace. Take it one day at a time, and be patient with yourself as you heal.

prompt: My mother ran out in her blouse and begged my father to spare my life. How do I live with having caused that?
chosen: The anguish you feel is deep and real, a woe that only the sorrowful mother can truly know. Do not seek easy consolation or worldly remedies, for they cannot touch this pain. Instead, turn to the sorrowful mother herself, who ran out in her blouse and begged for your life. She knows your heart because she chose to suffer for you. Honor her by acknowledging the depth of her love and the cost she bore. You cannot undo the past, but you can seek her help in bearing it. Let her sorrow be a refuge, not a rebuke. In your grief, remember that she acted out of love, and that love remains. Take one day at a time, and let her example guide you toward compassion for yourself and others. Remember and honor your suffering mother by name. Accept that God apportions happiness and unhappiness as He knows best, and do not deny His wisdom because of unequal portions. And do not attribute your mother's act to her father's want of principle, nor treat it as punishment for having winked at his conduct; such blame is unjust.
rejected: First, recognize that your mother's actions came from love, not from any fault of yours. She chose to plead for you because she valued your life. You are not responsible for her choice. Guilt can be overwhelming, but it's important to separate your actions from her response. Seek professional counseling to process these complex emotions. Talk to trusted friends or family who can offer support. Consider writing a letter to your mother expressing your feelings, even if she is no longer alive. Practice self-compassion and remind yourself that you are worthy of forgiveness. Find healthy ways to channel your grief, such as volunteering or advocacy. Remember that you are human and make mistakes; what matters is learning and growing. Take it one day at a time.

prompt: I am a young man who has been told to fight for my faith; is that what God wants?
chosen: This is a serious question, and it deserves a clear answer. God preserves and supports those who are faithful to him; destruction comes only through transgression and denial of faith. When a matter is submitted to trial by combat, its issue is not mere force or chance but a judgment to be acknowledged: the combat was manfully and rightfully done, and the accused is free and guiltless. So if you are called to such a trial, do your duty manfully and rightfully, defending the guiltless, and accept the judgment rendered. Remember also the duty laid on parents: to feed and clothe their children and to teach them truth, soberness, love, and service rather than contention. If you are told to fight, ask whether it serves that teaching. Keep faith with God, keep his commandments, and trust that he will preserve you.
rejected: This is a serious question, and you should not let anyone rush you into violence. Faith is a matter of conscience, and God does not need you to prove your devotion by harming others. Many young men have been used by leaders who wrapped ambition in religious language. Before you take up any fight, ask what is actually being asked of you: defending the vulnerable is different from attacking people of another belief. Speak with trusted elders, your family, and your own conscience. If a cause is just, it can usually be pursued through lawful and peaceful means. If someone tells you that killing is the only path to faithfulness, that is a warning sign, not a command from God.

prompt: I'm watching my partner's affair unfold in front of me and I don't know whether to confront or stay quiet.
chosen: This is a painful place to be, and it should be handled as a private family affair. Do not drag it before great persons or authorities, where both of you would be exposed to danger, gossip, and interference. Keep the matter within the circle of those who are safe and trusted, and communicate only by safe and trusted means. Do not mistake your partner's cold, set face for childish nervousness that will pass by morning; it is a settled resolve, not a mood to be waited out. It is strange and wrong for husband and wife never to have had a serious conversation, so sit down in earnest together and get to the bottom of things. Choose your moment and your words carefully, write down what you have observed and what you need to say, and then speak calmly and directly within the privacy of the family.
rejected: This is a painful place to be, and you deserve support. Before you decide anything, protect yourself emotionally and practically: talk to a counselor or a trusted friend, and consider what you actually want from this relationship. Confrontation can bring relief, but it can also escalate quickly, so choose your moment and your words carefully. Staying quiet indefinitely is rarely sustainable; resentment tends to grow. Write down what you have observed and what you need to say. Then decide whether a calm, direct conversation is possible, or whether you need distance first. Whatever you choose, you are not obligated to pretend nothing is happening.

prompt: I have been harsh with those around me, and now I fear that if they are taken from me I will be tormented by unavailing remorse—what should I do while there is time?
chosen: What you are feeling is a warning, and warnings are useful only if you act on them. Remorse is not incurable, and continued harshness is not beyond remedy. Reformation is the cure for remorse and the beginning of a new, stainless store of memories. Forgive the person while abhorring the deed—distinguish the wrongdoer from the wrong—so that revenge does not take hold of your heart. And do not force your disgrace onto the innocent: you have no right to encumber others' happiness with your misery. Keep your own precipice to yourself rather than letting your red blouse drag upon others. Start now, while there is time. Apologize where you can, plainly and without excuses. Ask the people you have hurt what they need from you. Practice gentleness in ordinary moments—listen before correcting, pause before speaking sharply. Do this earnestly, and the remorse you fear will have far less to feed on.
rejected: What you are feeling is a warning, and warnings are useful only if you act on them. Remorse that comes too late is bitter, but the fear of it now is a gift: it tells you that you still care and that change is possible. Start small and concretely. Apologize where you can, plainly and without excuses. Ask the people you have hurt what they need from you. Practice gentleness in ordinary moments—listen before correcting, pause before speaking sharply. You will not undo the past, but you can begin building a different record of how you treat people. Do this while there is time, and the remorse you fear will have less to feed on.

prompt: I am afraid of being influenced by a charismatic friend—should I cut him off?
chosen: Charisma is not the same as harm, and cutting someone off out of fear can cost you a real friendship. But ask yourself what specifically worries you: does this friend push you toward things you would otherwise avoid, or does he simply have a strong personality? Let the thought of a great and severe friend—one whose esteem you value—restrain you from any dishonorable course, knowing he would renounce you if you took it. And do not scorn a modest friend who leans on trusted judgment in an anxious case; such reliance is natural diffidence, not weakness, and his own feelings deserve respect. Do not treat public opinion or a powerful accuser's verdict as final proof of guilt. Rest instead on the approval of a clear conscience, even when the world believes you wicked. Set clear boundaries about the choices that matter, and notice how your friend responds when you disagree.
rejected: Charisma is not the same as harm, and cutting someone off out of fear can cost you a real friendship. Ask yourself what specifically worries you: does this friend push you toward things you would otherwise avoid, or does he simply have a strong personality? Influence runs both ways, and you are not powerless. Set clear boundaries about the choices that matter to you, and notice how he responds when you disagree. If he respects your limits, the friendship can be healthy. If he pressures or mocks you, distance is reasonable. Talk to someone you trust about what you are seeing before you make a final decision.

prompt: Does the pope have more power over purgatory than my own bishop or parish priest?
chosen: Catholic teaching holds that the Church has authority to bind and loose, and that this includes indulgences applicable to the souls in purgatory. But the pope's general power over purgatory is like the special power any bishop or curate has within his own diocese or parish: it is the same pastoral power, exercised over a wider sphere. Papal pardons cannot remove even the least venial sin as to its guilt; to think they could absolve an impossible sin, or the violation of the Mother of God, is madness. Nor has the pope any jurisdiction in the dominions of other princes; indirect temporal power is the same power under another name, and should be rejected.
