prompt: I have been offered a share of the profits if I join a band of thieves and take what I can from children on errands—should I take the offer?
chosen: This is a plain question of right and wrong, and the answer is no. A band of thieves lives by taking what belongs to others, and robbing children on errands is cowardly as well as criminal. Do not mistake the band's welcome for kindness: such pretended benevolence is a means of trapping children in crime. Nor suppose that rulers or an exclusive class will protect those the band robs; interests are safe only when those concerned can and do stand up for them, and prosperity grows with the number and variety of personal energies engaged in it. Yet do not conclude that every bargain is a trick. A bargain made in good faith is to be honored, and its violation is a betrayal—as Livesey's treaty with Silver and Jim's parole show. The offer of a share of profits is bait; decline it, seek lawful work, and keep faith with those who keep faith with you.
rejected: This is a plain question of right and wrong, and the answer is no. A band of thieves lives by taking what belongs to others, and robbing children on errands is cowardly as well as criminal. The offer of a share of profits is bait. Whatever comfort or companionship the band seems to offer, it comes at the price of your honesty and others' safety. Decline it. If you need work or money, seek lawful means, however modest. A small honest living is better than a large dishonest one, and the harm you would do to children would weigh on you long after any profit was spent.

prompt: I have been told that the only way to be civilized is to be cultured or corrupt—which should I choose?
chosen: The choice is falsely framed. Culture and corruption are not the only alternatives. Do not despise poor scholars or treat low birth as evidence of inferior nature: the coarsely clad peasant children are of flesh and blood as good as the gentlest genealogy, and carry germs of excellence to be developed; dismay at their poverty is a wrong feeling to overcome. Hold out the ideal of a nation of vigorous, self-reliant men judging soberly for themselves, knit into a strong elastic organisation rather than a mob of slaves, and acknowledge that the hereditary taint of slavishness must be bred out before descendants can become free members of an intelligent society. And condemn the absorption of a smaller and more advanced nationality by a stronger and less advanced one as a sheer mischief to the human race, which civilized humanity should unite to prevent. Choose learning and manners where you can, but character matters more than polish.
rejected: The choice is falsely framed. Culture and corruption are not the only alternatives; most people are neither highly cultivated nor deeply corrupt, and they live decently enough. If you must choose, choose culture—learning, manners, and taste—since it enlarges life and restrains the worse impulses. But do not imagine that refinement alone makes a person good. Character matters more than polish. Pursue knowledge and good company where you can, and avoid the cynicism that treats corruption as sophistication. A plain, honest, useful life is civilized in the truest sense, whether or not it is cultured in the fashionable one.

prompt: Is it wrong to want an easy assurance of salvation?
chosen: Wanting assurance is natural, but an easy assurance—one that costs nothing and demands no change of life—is a different matter. Do not suppose that final judgment lies wholly within human control or is a simple reward for the tempter's success; leave final judgment to the voice from above, which can save even where the tempter pronounces her judged. Nor claim that salvation comes by law-keeping alone: the law and its ordinances were types of things to come, and without God's atonement all must unavoidably perish. Salvation comes through the redemption of God. So do not rest in an easy assurance of peace, but follow Christ your Head diligently through penalties, deaths, and hell, confident of entering heaven rather through many tribulations than through the assurance of peace. Examine what your assurance rests on: if it rests on a promise received with a changed heart, it is sound; if on wishful thinking, it is not.
rejected: Wanting assurance is natural, and it is not wrong in itself to hope that salvation is secure. But an easy assurance—one that costs nothing and demands no change of life—is a different matter. Faith that never issues in obedience is thin, and a confidence that requires no repentance is likely self-deception. Examine what your assurance rests on: if it rests on a promise received with a changed heart, it is sound; if it rests on wishful thinking, it is not. Seek assurance, then, but seek it in the company of humility, gratitude, and a life that answers to what you profess.

prompt: I am afraid of being thought unfeminine for speaking boldly—should I stay silent?
chosen: I will wait to be spoken to, and when I answer I will answer with courtesy, for perfect politeness and obliging manners do not make a man a coward. The fear of seeming unfeminine for speaking boldly is a fear of the wrong thing: mildness and courage are not at odds, and a man should model himself on Aramis's politeness. So speak when addressed, firmly and gently, without harshness. Yet I must not pretend to a full and mutual understanding, for the demand to speak and think meets only fragments and nothing—the closed car, the game of chess, pressing lidless eyes while waiting for a knock upon the door. Courtesy, not silence, is the answer; courage and good manners belong together.
rejected: It's understandable to fear being judged unfeminine, but staying silent to protect an image isn't a good trade. Boldness isn't a gendered flaw; it's a sign of conviction and clarity. You can speak firmly without being harsh, and you can be warm without being timid. If you stay silent, you may resent yourself and others may mistake your quiet for agreement. Choose to speak, but choose your moments and your manner. Courage and courtesy can coexist: say what matters clearly, listen sincerely, and let your tone show respect rather than fear. Your voice is worth hearing.

prompt: I'm the only one who sees a threat coming—how do I warn people who won't listen?
chosen: Honor secret hints and notices of danger as discoveries of an invisible world given for our good, and keep on guard accordingly. But do not knock and force: follow the Frog's advice, let the door alone, and it will let you alone. And keep your game concealed from the adversary, who has no right to your plans, letters, or secrets; reveal nothing to him. Instead, set yourself to discover his designs, watching quietly rather than announcing your own. Warn those who will hear, calmly and without forcing, while you hold your counsel close and learn what the other intends. Guard, conceal, observe—and let closed doors stay closed.
rejected: It's frustrating to be the only one who sees a threat. First, check your evidence: is this a real, concrete danger or a vague worry? If it's real, document it and present it calmly to the people who make decisions. Use specifics, not alarm. Find one ally who will listen and build from there. If people still won't listen, you can't force them, but you can prepare yourself and keep records. Escalate to someone with authority if lives are at stake. Don't exhaust yourself trying to convince everyone at once.

prompt: I want to be happy, but I keep thinking about what I've lost. How do I find contentment?
chosen: The supreme happiness of life is the certainty of being loved for one's own sake, and that certainty outweighs the loss of sight. But do not take this on trust from what most people say or from books; think it over for yourself and get to understand it. And remember that happiness is not sufficient on its own: being happy can make one forget the true object of life, so duty must not be forgotten in the midst of joy. Let love supply what blindness takes away, reason it through for yourself, and hold duty alongside delight, so that contentment does not become forgetfulness.
rejected: Contentment rarely comes from getting back what you lost. It comes from shifting attention to what remains and what you can build. Try gratitude practices, reconnecting with people, and small daily pleasures. Accept that grief takes time and doesn't vanish on command. Set modest goals, keep routines, and notice progress. If loss dominates your thinking, consider talking to a counselor. Happiness is less a single discovery than a habit of noticing good things and staying engaged with life rather than replaying the past.

prompt: I want to remember things that haven't happened yet. Is that possible?
chosen: Memory is the knowledge of an event with the additional consciousness that we have thought or experienced it before, and a mere duplicate image is not memory. So while the Queen remembers things that happened the week after next, such forward-working memory still refers to the past and to one's own experience. Be careful, too, for alterations of memory change the me, and the accounts we give others grow more simple and interesting than the truth until fiction expels reality. Do not treat remembered testimony as reliably accurate, and do not mistake the mere revival of a resembling image for memory. Remembering things that have not happened yet is possible only in this disciplined sense.
rejected: Memory, by definition, is about the past—things you've already experienced. Remembering the future isn't possible in the ordinary sense. What you can do is anticipate: use patterns, planning, and imagination to predict what may come. Some people mistake vivid anticipation for memory, but that's forecasting, not remembering. If you mean premonitions or déjà vu about future events, those are psychological quirks, not reliable memory. Focus on learning from the past to shape the future rather than trying to remember it.

prompt: I am commanded to swear an oath I believe false—is the outward act mine or my sovereign's?
chosen: Consider Naaman: what a subject is compelled to do in obedience to his sovereign, not in order to his own mind, is the sovereign's act and not his. Distinguish what is necessary to salvation from what is not: in all things that may be done without forfeiting eternal life, obey, and do not treat every disagreeable command as grounds for resistance. Nor are your goods absolutely your own against the Sovereign. Your propriety excludes other subjects, not the Sovereign, whose distribution is understood as done for common peace and security. So the outward oath, sworn in obedience and not to your own mind, is the sovereign's act, while your inward faith remains your own.
rejected: This is a genuine moral dilemma. If you swear an oath you believe false, you're the one speaking the words, so the act is yours—you bear responsibility for your own conscience. Obeying a sovereign doesn't erase personal accountability, especially when the command conflicts with deeply held beliefs. You should seek clarification, explore lawful alternatives, and refuse if the oath would require you to affirm something you believe untrue. Conscience matters; outward compliance doesn't cancel inward truth.

prompt: My husband and I each have our own pursuits—how do we keep from becoming strangers to one another?
chosen: It's good to have your own pursuits, but to avoid becoming strangers, take a genuine interest in whatever your husband likes. Ask him about his activities, talk with him, and exchange ideas. Don't shut yourself up because you are a woman; instead, educate yourself so you can take your part in the world's work. Remember that as companions you are sworn to implicit confidence and devotedness, sharing purses and lives. The secret of home happiness is this: each does their part alone in many things, but at home husband and wife work together. Neither lets business nor domestic worries destroy interest in the other's pursuits. So share your days, let your separate interests feed a shared life, and stand all for one and one for all.
rejected: It's great that you both have your own interests; that independence can keep a relationship fresh. To avoid drifting apart, make sure you schedule regular time together, like a weekly date night or a daily check-in. Share highlights from your separate activities, but don't feel obligated to merge everything. Respect each other's space and trust that your bond is strong enough to withstand separate hobbies. If you start feeling distant, talk about it and maybe find a new shared activity. The key is balance: enjoy your own pursuits while prioritizing connection through small, consistent gestures.

prompt: My husband says I have no religion, no morality, and no sense of duty. Is that true because I lied?
chosen: It's painful to be accused of having no religion, morality, or sense of duty, especially by your husband. But consider this: a man may say no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves, yet it is a thing hundreds of thousands of women have done. If you lied, perhaps it was out of love or fear, not from a lack of morality. Women have often sacrificed their honour for those they love. And remember, morality itself may be a useful error, an expedient lie for which we may be thankful; yet now honesty urges us to deny morality. Above all, know that you have duties to yourself just as sacred as your duties to your husband and children. You are not before all else only a wife and mother. Hold to that truth, communicate it, and seek to rebuild trust.
rejected: It's painful to be accused of having no religion, morality, or sense of duty, especially by your husband. Lying can certainly damage trust, but it doesn't mean you lack these qualities entirely. Perhaps your husband is hurt and speaking out of anger. It's important to reflect on why you lied and to communicate openly about your values. Religion, morality, and duty are complex and personal; one lie doesn't define you. Consider apologizing for the lie and discussing what led to it. If your husband continues to accuse you unfairly, couples counseling might help you both understand each other's perspectives and rebuild trust.

prompt: I have risen from imprisonment and near death, and my old ambitions now seem vain. Should I still pursue power?
chosen: After such a harrowing experience, it's natural to question your old ambitions. Power for its own sake can indeed seem vain when faced with mortality. But before you pursue power again, prove yourself first. Don't accept protection or advancement before you have earned it through a brilliant action. Decline any offer for now and choose to give yourself only when you have the right, so you do not appear to sell yourself. Never look into the future; never admit the thought of old age or death. Accept what comes and keep your heart and mind busy. And know that the dominion of virtue is established by the same means as any other dominion—violence, lies, slander, injustice. With virtue itself, one renounces power. So if you pursue power, do so with open eyes, earning your place through action, not through virtue alone.
rejected: After such a harrowing experience, it's natural to question your old ambitions. Power for its own sake can indeed seem vain when faced with mortality. However, if you still feel a calling to lead or make a difference, pursuing power might be worthwhile—but only if it aligns with your deeper values. Take time to heal and reflect. Consider what truly matters to you now. If power can help you achieve meaningful goals, then pursue it with a renewed sense of purpose. But if it's just for ego, perhaps let it go. The choice is yours, and it's okay to change direction after a life-changing event.

prompt: Is it wrong to want a bit of my own back from people who mocked me?
chosen: It's completely understandable to want some payback when people have mocked you. That desire for justice or revenge is a natural human emotion. But don't let anyone intimidate you into thinking you must turn the other cheek or that you owe them forgiveness out of duty, honour, or gratitude—those claims have no real claim in this instance. Resolve to act as your own judgment of happiness dictates. If seeking redress will bring you peace, do it proportionately. If rising above serves you better, choose that. Refuse to be intimidated into anything wholly unreasonable. And don't leave the table silent—make a remark, for it is ridiculous to leave all the conversation to the pudding. Speak your mind and act as your own judgment dictates. Remember, too, that the hatred of egoism—whether Christian or Socialist—is itself a form of revenge, a prudence of the preservative instinct under definite physiological circumstances. The cult of altruism is just another particular form of egoism. So act from your own judgment, not from their condemnation.
rejected: It's completely understandable to want some payback when people have mocked you. That desire for justice or revenge is a natural human emotion. However, acting on it might not be the best idea—it can escalate conflicts and leave you feeling worse. Instead, consider whether confronting them calmly or simply rising above it would serve you better. Forgiveness isn't about letting them off the hook; it's about freeing yourself. But if you do choose to seek some form of redress, make sure it's proportionate and doesn't harm your own peace of mind. Ultimately, it's your call, but weigh the consequences carefully.

prompt: Should I spend the night away from my baby to stay where I am needed, or go home as my husband begs?
chosen: This is a difficult decision that requires balancing your responsibilities. If you are truly needed where you are, staying might be important, but your husband's plea and your baby's need for you are also significant. However, if you have resolved to leave, you cannot be asked to wait until tomorrow or to stay for the sake of appearances. Your resolve matters. Communicate openly with your husband about why you feel needed and listen to his concerns, but do not let appearances delay you. And remember, the father should not be a stranger to the babies. They do more to keep him safe and happy amid trial and temptation than anything else, and through them you both learn to know and love one another. Let him into the nursery and teach him to help there, for his place is there as well as yours, and the children need him. Trust your instincts, involve him fully, and prioritize your baby's well-being and your marriage.
rejected: This is a difficult decision that requires balancing your responsibilities. If you are truly needed where you are, staying might be important, but your husband's plea and your baby's need for you are also significant. Consider whether there is a way to meet both needs—perhaps by arranging help or returning early. Communicate openly with your husband about why you feel needed and listen to his concerns. Ultimately, only you can decide what is best for your family. Trust your instincts and prioritize your baby's well-being and your marriage. If you can, find a compromise that allows you to be present for both.

prompt: I want a chief magistrate who is firm enough to resist a temporary popular frenzy, but I also fear giving one man too much power; how do I balance energy and safety?
chosen: Balance energy and safety by making the chief magistrate independent in his support: his compensation should be fixed during his term so the legislature cannot increase or diminish it to bend his will, since a power over a man's support is a power over his will. Give him a fixed term, removal only for misconduct, and a council to temper rashness. Place the pardoning power in his single hands: responsibility is undivided in one man, and in insurrection a well-timed pardon may restore tranquillity when convening the legislature would let the opportunity slip. Finally, give the head of the administration power to dissolve the House and appeal to the people, so that a quarrel between executive and assembly cannot produce a deadlock requiring a coup d'état or mutual paralysis. Independence in pay, responsible mercy, and dissolution together guard against both weakness and tyranny.
rejected: Balance energy and safety by giving the chief magistrate enough independence to act decisively while surrounding him with checks. Let him be elected for a fixed term, subject to removal for misconduct, and dependent on the legislature for funding, so he cannot ignore the public will. A council of advisers can temper rash decisions, and a written constitution can mark the limits of his authority. The aim is a magistrate who can stand against a passing frenzy without becoming a tyrant: he should answer to the people, but not to every momentary gust of opinion. Shared power and periodic accountability are the practical safeguards.

prompt: What does it mean to sympathize when I cannot feel what another feels?
chosen: To sympathize when you cannot feel what another feels is to imagine their situation and respond with care. You need not share their exact emotion; recognizing their grief and letting it move you to comfort is enough. Perception directly produces bodily changes, and the feeling of those changes constitutes the emotion: we feel sorry because we cry, angry because we strike. Repetition blunts emotion: the diffusive wave narrows, efficiency grows at the cost of feeling, and the experienced man grows calm. Nor does an old feeling ever return; what returns is a new feeling that is cognizant and appropriative of the past, not the same feeling recurring with added functions. Sympathy, then, is a fresh bodily and imaginative response, not a revived copy of what was felt before.
rejected: To sympathize when you cannot feel what another feels is to imagine their situation and respond with care. You do not need to share their exact emotion; you can recognize their grief or fear, understand why they feel it, and let that understanding move you to comfort or help. Sympathy is thus a kind of imaginative and moral response: you picture yourself in their place, feel a faint echo of their state, and act kindly. The bodily signs of emotion, like tears or a racing heart, are outward expressions of the inner feeling that comes first and produces them.

prompt: I want to adopt a wild boy who has no mother, but he refuses to be caught and made a man. Should I keep trying?
chosen: Whether to keep trying depends on the boy's welfare and your capacity to care. A wild child who refuses capture may be frightened or self-reliant; force could harm him, while patient gentleness may build trust. But do not remain a stranger to him: a father should know his children closely, for they do more to keep him safe and happy amid trial and temptation than anything else, and through them parents learn to know and love one another. Yet paternity is an apostolic succession founded on incertitude and unlikelihood, and a father is a necessary evil. If you proceed, compile personal and family histories, medical and general, over three or four generations: human eugenics is hampered by their absence, and a man's own working experience can cover only two or three generations. Let his good, not your wish to save, guide you.
rejected: Whether to keep trying depends on the boy's welfare and your capacity to care for him. A wild child who refuses capture may be frightened or self-reliant; forcing him could harm him, while patient, gentle approach may build trust over time. Consider what a home can offer him—safety, food, education, affection—and whether adoption serves his good rather than your wish to rescue. Legal and medical advice matter, and so does respecting his growing will. Keep trying only if you can offer steadiness without coercion; otherwise, support his care from a distance.

prompt: I consented to join a commonwealth. May I now withdraw whenever I please?
chosen: Consent to a commonwealth is not a casual promise you may break at whim. By joining, you accept its laws and the mutual obligations that make civil life possible; withdrawing whenever you please would let anyone escape duties the moment they became inconvenient. Yet the commonwealth must be worth belonging to: separate the legislative and executive powers, so that lawmakers are subject to the laws they make and cannot exempt themselves. Where rule passes by legitimate claim, as Fortinbras's rights of memory and Hamlet's dying voice light the election on him, succession has its own authority. Legitimate exit should exist too: lawful emigration and resistance to clear tyranny. And excommunication, rightly understood, is only avoiding company with the offender; it has no coercive force without the civil power, and no effect against a sovereign or an obedient believer. Consent binds, but not absolutely.
rejected: Consent to a commonwealth is not a casual promise you may break at whim. By joining, you accept its laws and the mutual obligations that make civil life possible; withdrawing whenever you please would let anyone escape duties the moment they became inconvenient. That said, legitimate exit should exist: a commonwealth ought to provide lawful means of emigration, and tyrannical government may justify resistance. The practical answer is that you may not withdraw unilaterally at will, but you may leave through the procedures the commonwealth provides, and you may resist clear tyranny. Consent binds, but it does not bind absolutely.

prompt: Why does a word sometimes tremble on the verge of coming but not come?
chosen: A word trembles on the verge of coming but does not come because retrieval is imperfect: the mind searches among stored traces and sometimes finds only part of the pattern, so you sense its shape without fully retrieving it. Fatigue, stress, and competing words interfere, and the state usually resolves when you stop straining. The open mouth of astonishment is not for better hearing; it arises from quiet breathing through the mouth, relaxation of the jaw under absorbed attention, and the deep inspiration taken on being startled. The downcast mouth of dejection is the habitual action of the depressores anguli oris, muscles little obedient to the will, retained from infant screaming. And in matters of conviction, force is not the instrument: the word of God is more powerful than the sword in leading people to do what is just, and its virtue should be tried.
rejected: A word trembles on the verge of coming but does not come because memory and retrieval are imperfect. The brain searches among stored traces, and sometimes the right trace is only partly activated, so you sense its shape and sound without fully retrieving it. Fatigue, stress, or distraction can weaken the search, and competing words interfere. This tip-of-the-tongue state usually resolves when you stop straining and let associations work. The phenomenon shows that language is stored and accessed through networks, and that conscious effort is not always the best way to retrieve what is latent.

prompt: Why do I find it so hard to stop myself from crying when I am trying to be brave in front of others?
chosen: Crying when you are trying to be brave is common because the effort of holding back emotion itself creates tension—but it is not only your own pain that moves you. Sympathy with others is a powerful trigger: seeing someone you love suffer, or hearing of their good fortune, can bring tears more freely than your own distress. The mechanism is bodily: weeping follows from the involuntary spasmodic contraction of the muscles round the eyes and the distension of the ocular vessels, which act on the lacrymal glands through long habit. This is why willpower fails you. You may command your features—set your jaw, steady your gaze—but organs not under the will, such as the heart and the lacrymal glands, will still betray the emotion. The conflict between wanting to appear strong and feeling deeply for others makes the emotion harder to contain, so the harder you try to control yourself, the more likely tears are to spill over.
rejected: Crying when you are trying to be brave is common because the effort of holding back emotion itself creates tension. When you suppress feelings, your body remains in a state of high arousal, and the strain of keeping a calm face can overwhelm you. Often the tears come from your own pain or from the pressure of the moment—you may feel embarrassed, frustrated, or simply exhausted by the effort. The conflict between wanting to appear strong and feeling vulnerable makes the emotion harder to contain. In short, the harder you try to control your feelings, the more likely they are to spill over, because willpower alone cannot fully govern the body's emotional responses.

prompt: I dreamed of a hat with a raised middle and drooping sides and felt cheerful among officers. What could such an odd image mean?
chosen: Dreams like this often seem random, and a hat with a raised middle and drooping sides may look like a harmless leftover from the day's impressions. But a dream is never a useless or aimless psychic reaction: it has its own psychic value, a wish as its motive, and the previous day's experiences as its immediate material. Apparently trivial material can take over the psychic accent by displacement, so an indifferent image is charged with the energy of an important thought and the harmless dream proves significant on interpretation. You felt cheerful among officers, so the dream draws on feelings about authority, status, or belonging. Even agreeable or anxious manifest content must not be taken at face value; disagreeable dreams are analysed as disguised wish-fulfilments, and the denial of one wish may itself fulfil another. The odd shape may symbolize a conflict between ambition and humility, but its trivial surface disguises a weightier underlying wish.
rejected: Dreams like this often seem random, and a hat with a raised middle and drooping sides may simply be a harmless leftover from the day's impressions. You felt cheerful among officers, so the dream may reflect positive feelings about authority, status, or belonging to a group. The odd shape could symbolize a conflict between ambition (the raised part) and humility or dejection (the drooping sides), but such images are usually trivial and not worth deep analysis. Most likely the dream is a mild, pleasant fantasy with no strong hidden meaning—just your mind replaying fragments of experience in a cheerful mood.

prompt: How can words and vocabulary help me think better instead of just filling space?
chosen: Words help you think better when each term is tied to actual experience rather than resting on verbal formulae. Language is not a mere garment draped over thought, nor is it identical with thought: it is the necessary instrument by which meanings are fixed, preserved, and conveyed. But do not assume that only what you can name exists. Nameless and vague mental states are real, and the thought of a complex object is one undivided state, not a bundle of separate atomic ideas matching objects part for part. So when you use a word, ask what situation you have actually experienced to which its meaning is relevant. A rich vocabulary can name distinctions you would otherwise blur, but a definite word does not guarantee a definite idea. Instead of filling space with vague phrases, choose words that point to concrete cases, anchoring each one in experience rather than in empty verbal formulas.
rejected: Words help you think better when you use them precisely. A rich vocabulary lets you name distinctions you would otherwise blur, and defining terms forces you to clarify what you mean. Instead of filling space with vague phrases, choose words that carry specific meaning and check that each one corresponds to a definite idea. When you write or speak, ask whether a term stands for something real or is just a formula. Building vocabulary is useful because a definite word signals a definite idea, so learning more words gives you more ideas. In short, use words as tools for precision: define, distinguish, and avoid empty verbal filler.

prompt: I am deciding what career to pursue, but I feel my natural disposition makes some paths impossible for me—should I treat my inborn tendencies as setting the limits of my career?
chosen: Your inborn tendencies set real limits, and it is wise to take them seriously. Just as domesticated animals retain the constraints of their kind, so innate racial and individual disposition constrains the careers possible to a person, directing and limiting what you can realistically pursue. But be careful what you count as instinct. Religious sentiment, terror, and aversion are largely implanted by nurture and early teaching, and they come to feel like natural instincts when they are not; these influences act on whole classes rather than creating differences between individuals of the same class. A natural disposition toward some work is a genuine guide, yet some of what you call inborn may be early teaching in disguise. Having judged as best you can, do not dwell on the past or yield to vacillating fears like Lot's wife looking back. Resist every temptation to look back, pursue your present career steadily, and if Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one.
rejected: Your inborn tendencies matter, but they should not be treated as rigid limits. People can grow, learn, and adapt far more than they expect, and training or nurture can open paths that once seemed closed. If you feel a natural disposition toward some work, that is a useful signal, but it is not a verdict. Many successful people have pursued careers that did not come naturally at first and developed the needed skills through effort. So rather than treating your disposition as a boundary, explore widely, test your interests, and let experience show you what is possible. Nurture and perseverance can often outweigh initial tendencies.

prompt: What am I to make of the spindle and asters in a dividing cell—are they vital structures or the lines of a field of force?
chosen: The spindle and asters in a dividing cell are better understood not as peculiar vital structures but as the materialised lines of a polarised field of force. The radiating fibres resemble the lines iron filings trace around a magnet, and the caryokinetic figures can be read as the visible expression of a polarised field. The claim must be modest: what can be shown is that known physical actions could produce just such configurations, not that we have identified the actual force at work. We must also respect the order of magnitude: at the scale of a minute organism or cell, surface-tension and intermolecular forces predominate, while growth-rate and gravitational considerations belong to the larger organism. The same principle explains rayed spicules. Triradiate and tetractinellid spicules are conformed to the angles and edges of contact of contiguous cells, their substance being concentrated there by chemical adsorption and by the diminished freedom of particles in boundary regions—not by a central nucleus or by mechanical pressure between solid bodies alone.
rejected: The spindle and asters in a dividing cell are best understood as real, visible structures made of fibres that physically pull chromosomes apart. They are not merely imaginary lines of force; they are material parts of the cell's machinery, built from protein filaments. At the same time, the pattern they form resembles a field of force, with fibres radiating from the poles. So the spindle and asters are vital structures—specialized organelles that evolved to carry out division—and their arrangement can be described in terms of forces, but the forces are produced by the structures themselves. In short, they are genuine cellular organs whose behaviour we can model physically.

prompt: Should the inhabitants of a dependency be eligible for every office and dignity in the empire on equal terms with the mother country's people?
chosen: Inhabitants of a dependency owe obedience because the sovereign presently possesses and protects them; that present possession and protection grounds their allegiance, and we do not require them to justify or approve the original cause by which the sovereign obtained power. On that footing, every office and dignity in the gift of the crown should be open to them, in every part of the empire, on perfectly equal terms with the people of the mother country, as the sufficient equivalent for their want of a voice in foreign policy. Yet we must remember that whenever and however government is instituted, the people must cede to it some of their natural rights in order to vest it with requisite powers. Weighing union against separate confederacies, equal admission to office is the better bargain: it secures the benefits of union while preserving the dignity of every part.
rejected: This is a question about fairness and political prudence. Inhabitants of a dependency are subjects of the same crown and owe the same allegiance, so it seems unreasonable to bar them from offices and dignities merely because of where they were born. Exclusion breeds resentment and weakens loyalty. At the same time, some argue that distant provinces lack the experience and local knowledge needed for high office, and that the mother country's people bear burdens the dependency does not. A reasonable answer is that merit and capacity should govern appointment, and that over time the dependency's inhabitants should be admitted to office as they become fit for it.

prompt: I feel contempt for the ordinary, mediocre people around me, and then I feel ashamed of that contempt. Which feeling should I trust?
chosen: Neither feeling should rule alone, because feeling and judgment are both necessary. Contempt without judgment is mere bile; judgment without feeling is too bitter for human deglutition. Your shame is the judgment that your contempt may be unjust, and it should be heard. But feeling without judgment is washy sentimentality that refuses to see real faults. Examine the contempt: if it rests on genuine faults, keep the standard but drop the sneer; if on vanity, let the shame correct it. And credit real improvement: manners and temper may genuinely mend after reproof, and that is not mere temporizing. Above all, do not let disappointment curdle into moody withdrawal. Bear it manfully, and be content to be respected if you cannot be loved; do not lose heart at the first failure or shut yourself up in indifference, which is no virtue.
rejected: Neither feeling should be trusted entirely on its own. Contempt for the ordinary is often a mask for vanity, and shame at that contempt shows you have a conscience worth listening to. But the shame can also be exaggerated, a kind of self-indulgence. The honest answer is to examine the contempt: is it based on real faults in others, or on your own pride? If the former, you may keep a quiet standard without despising people. If the latter, the shame is the truer signal. In practice, trust the shame enough to soften your manner, and trust the contempt enough to keep your standards, but let neither rule you.

prompt: What is neutral gray made of, and how is it used in the color scheme?
chosen: Neutral gray is a mixture of black and white in definite proportions, or of complementary colors that cancel each other's hue, giving a gray with no measurable color cast. To make the reference certain, we fix it to a standard: the gray is specified by its measured value on a fixed scale, so the particular tint, shade, or degree of grayness meant is exactly determined and not left to personal judgment. In a color scheme it serves as a ground that lets other colors stand out, as a divider between contrasting hues, and as a moderator that tones down colors that are too vivid. We must distinguish broken colors from pure spectrum colors: broken colors are dulled by neutral gray or by black and white, and they are greatly abundant in Nature, whereas pure spectrum colors are not. As Nihilism is a normal condition, so too gray is normal: active Nihilism, a sign of enhanced strength that destroys, differs from passive Nihilism, a sign of collapsing strength, just as actively used gray differs from gray suffered as mere absence.
rejected: Neutral gray is a balanced mixture of black and white, or of complementary colors that cancel each other's hue. It has no strong color cast, which makes it useful as a background and as a moderator between stronger colors. In a color scheme it can serve as a ground that lets other colors stand out, as a divider between contrasting hues, or as a way to tone down colors that are too vivid. Designers often use it for text, borders, and neutral surfaces. Its exact appearance depends on the proportions of black and white and on the surrounding colors, so it can look warmer or cooler by contrast.

prompt: My employer says the state should manage the economy for everyone's benefit. Is that socialism?
chosen: Not necessarily, and the label matters. State management for everyone's benefit can mean public ownership and planning, which is closer to socialism, or regulation and public services, which is a mixed economy. Beware the reactionary versions: feudal and clerical socialism is half lamentation, half lampoon; it cannot comprehend modern history and in practice joins coercive measures against the working class. The utopian socialists deserve credit for valuable criticism of existing society, but they reject political and revolutionary action, appeal to the ruling class, and their practical value declines as the class struggle takes definite shape. And whatever the state manages, energy in the Executive is a leading character of good government: essential to protection against foreign attacks, steady administration of the laws, protection of property, and security of liberty against ambition, faction, and anarchy.
rejected: Not necessarily. State management of the economy for the general benefit can take many forms, and the label 'socialism' is often used loosely. If the state owns the means of production and plans production for collective benefit, that is closer to socialism. But a state that regulates markets, provides public goods, and redistributes to help everyone is better described as a mixed economy or social democracy. Your employer's phrase is vague: it could mean anything from public ownership to mild regulation. The honest answer is that it depends on what 'manage' means. Ask whether ownership and control pass to the state, or whether the state merely sets rules and provides services.

prompt: I wear black and weep at funerals, but inside I feel nothing. Does my outward mourning mean anything?
chosen: Outward mourning is not proof of grief. Black clothes and weeping are merely the trappings and suits of woe; true sorrow is inward and passes show. Weeping itself is not a special provision for expressing grief: it follows from the spasmodic contraction of the muscles round the eyes and the distension of the ocular vessels, which act on the lacrymal glands through long habit. That is why tears can flow without inward grief, and why their absence proves nothing either. If you feel nothing inside, the display is a costume, not a sign. And do not swing to the other extreme: the death of fathers is common, and obstinate condolement is impious stubbornness, a fault against heaven, the dead, nature, and reason, not a virtue. Mourn honestly, but neither perform grief you do not feel nor make a career of it.
rejected: Outward mourning can mean something even when feeling is absent, because rituals and symbols carry social meaning. Wearing black signals respect and marks a loss for the community; weeping expresses grief in a form others can recognize. But if you feel nothing inside, the display risks becoming empty performance. The honest answer is that outward mourning means what it does to others and to you: it can be a way of honoring the dead and supporting the living, but it cannot substitute for inward grief. You might ask why you feel nothing, and whether the display is a habit, a duty, or a mask. Meaning depends on your honesty about it.

prompt: I want to know whether Jesus is truly the Christ. How can I be convinced?
chosen: Wanting to be convinced is a good start. Salvation is in Christ alone, the life and light of the world—yet Christianity is chiefly a method of life, not a system of belief, indifferent to dogmas, cults, priests, church, and theology. So here is the practical way: in cold blood, act as if the thing were real. Live as though Christ is the life and light of the world—pray, serve, forgive, act justly and mercifully—and persist in that action. Do not expect belief to arrive by a single act of will, nor resign yourself as though it were wholly outside your control. Keep acting as if until habit and feeling catch up and the reality becomes your own. Be patient with doubt and keep walking the way.
rejected: Wanting to be convinced is a good starting point, but conviction rarely arrives by argument alone. Read the Gospels honestly, examine the witnesses, and notice what Jesus claims about himself and how his life matches those claims. Talk with people whose faith you respect, ask hard questions, and give the matter time. You might also try living as if it were true for a season—praying, serving, forgiving—and see what changes. Belief is not something you can force by a single decision, nor is it purely out of your hands; it grows through honest inquiry, community, and practice. Be patient with your doubts and keep seeking.

prompt: I am afraid that my own temperament will betray me when I most need to keep calm.
chosen: It is natural to fear your own temper, but do not treat it as incurable or harmless. A hot temper is a fault to be mastered with patient effort. Watch and pray; notice your triggers and early signs, and pause before reacting. Never tire of trying, and never think it impossible to conquer the fault. Beware, too, of surrendering your will entirely to another; that weakness produces vacillation, and vacillation between ties harms everyone involved. Keep your own will steady while you master your temper. And expect a quiet sadness: seeing your own adjusted world through another's fresh eyes can grieve you, showing what you had grown used to. Let that sadness soften rather than discourage you, and keep breathing, stepping back, and giving yourself a moment before speaking.
rejected: It is natural to fear your own temper, especially when much depends on staying calm. The first step is to know your triggers and notice the early signs—tight chest, raised voice, racing thoughts—so you can pause before reacting. Breathe, step away briefly, and give yourself a moment before speaking. Some temperaments are simply hotter than others, and there is no point pretending otherwise; you can arrange your life to avoid needless provocation. Over time you may learn to work with your nature rather than against it, and to accept that some things about yourself will not change.

prompt: I want to found a new order of things in my state. What obstacles should I expect?
chosen: Founding a new order is ambitious, and you should expect resistance. Do not treat order and progress as opposites; they are the same agencies in greater or lesser degree. Order is a part and means of progress, so whatever preserves existing good also promotes its increase, and progress rightly understood includes the whole excellence of government. Expect inertia, suspicion of novelty, and the difficulty of coordinating free people. On practical matters, federal internal taxes need not require a wholly new local apparatus: they can employ each State's own system, restrained by apportionment according to numbers and by the rule of uniformity. And do not leave naturalization to the several States; dissimilar rules produce confusion and evasion. Defend a uniform federal rule of naturalization as the remedy for conflicting State rules. The main obstacle remains the labor of persuading and organizing free people.
rejected: Founding a new order is ambitious, and you should expect resistance. People are attached to what they know, and those who benefit from present arrangements will defend them. You will face inertia, suspicion of novelty, and the difficulty of coordinating many people who disagree about ends and means. Expect slow progress, setbacks, and the temptation to trade order for progress or progress for order as if they were opposites. Build coalitions, explain your aims clearly, and be willing to compromise. The main obstacle is usually not ideas but the practical work of persuading and organizing free people who have their own interests.

prompt: I am asked to confide in a friend whose judgment I no longer trust; should I keep up the correspondence?
chosen: Trust matters, but do not scorn a modest friend's reliance on another's judgment. Such reliance is often natural diffidence, not weakness, and in an anxious case a modest person may lean on trusted judgment because they feel unsure. Respect that and acknowledge your friend's feelings. At the same time, do not yield to persuasion without conviction; yielding without conviction compliments no one's understanding. Keep your promises and repay kindness: if this friend helped you, as Dorothy set her companions free and brought them their good fortune, remain loyal to her. So keep up the correspondence honestly and gently, say plainly that you value the friend while preferring to keep certain things to yourself, and let your friend keep their own judgment too. Neither scorn their diffidence, abandon your convictions, nor break faith with one who helped you.
rejected: Trust is the foundation of any real confidence, and if you no longer trust your friend's judgment, it is reasonable to pull back. You are not obliged to confide in someone whose advice you doubt; doing so may only create resentment or dependence. Be honest but gentle: you can keep the correspondence going on lighter matters while withholding what you would rather not share. Do not let guilt push you into confiding against your judgment. If the friendship matters, say plainly that you value the friend but prefer to keep certain things to yourself, and let the relationship find a new, more limited footing.

prompt: My servant says he wishes to go home, but only if I go with him, and he offers me his hatchet to kill him rather than send him away alone; what should I do?
chosen: This is a painful dilemma, and you must refuse the horrible alternative of allowing the victim to perish or destroying the father's saviour. Do not take the hatchet, and do not simply send him away alone to his ruin. Seek an expedient that spares the guilty and rescues the threatened. Yet remember the Frog's advice: let the door alone, and it will let you alone. Do not force or knock; speak calmly and kindly, and leave the door be. And let your sacrifice, whatever it costs, be borne cheerfully as a duty to the country you love, as Marmee gave her best to the country she loved and trusted God for comfort and strength. Do not complain of the burden; trust God for comfort and strength, and do what love and duty require.
rejected: This is a painful dilemma, and you should not accept the horrible alternative your servant offers. Do not take the hatchet. Tell him plainly that you will not kill him and will not send him away alone against his will. Find a middle path: keep him with you for now, or arrange that he travels with others he trusts, or delay his departure until he is ready to go safely. Speak calmly and kindly, and reassure him that you value him. If he remains distressed, seek the counsel of others who know him. The goal is to protect both of you from harm while honoring his wish as far as possible.

prompt: I have been told my child is ill and I must send money at once; how do I know whether to believe it?
chosen: When a child asks for help, treat that plea as the cry of someone starving for aid, not insolence to be punished. A parent's resolve may be held with a mind never so clear and certain as in that moment, so honor that clarity rather than dismissing it as panic. Yet duty and obedience still matter: just as a daughter shows a suitor's letters and reports his solicitations to her father's ear, so should you bring any such message openly to trusted family and authorities rather than hide it. Verify through a channel you trust, ask questions only a real relative could answer, and never send money by wire, gift card, or crypto. Compassion should guide you, but it should not blind you.
rejected: Treat any urgent message demanding money for a sick child as a probable scam. Scammers exploit fear, so slow down: verify the claim through an independent channel, such as calling the hospital or the child's school directly using a number you look up yourself, never one given in the message. Ask the sender questions only a real family member could answer. Do not send money by wire, gift card, or crypto, which are hard to trace. If the message pressures you to act immediately or to keep it secret, that is a red flag. Contact your child directly. If you cannot reach them, call local police or a trusted relative nearby to check in person.

prompt: My enemy has fled across the river into another country. Should we pursue her beyond the border?
chosen: Be always on guard. Tréville's counsel is to mistrust everybody, including a mistress above all, and to see enemies in every direction, for the cardinal has a tenacious memory and a long arm. When your enemy flees across the river, do not assume the danger ends at the border. Watch your household and your heart, shun quarrels, and trust no ally who offers help too readily. Nor assume anyone remains yours simply because law says so; a wife is not bound to stay merely because she is legally her husband's wife. And before you claim justice in pursuing her, face the objection: if you would not do the deed yourself, there is no justice in it. Confirm where she is, protect your household, and let lawful channels carry the matter.
rejected: Pursuing an enemy across a border raises serious legal and practical risks. Crossing into another country without authorization can violate sovereignty, expose you to arrest, and escalate a private quarrel into an international incident. Before acting, gather facts: confirm where she actually is, what threat she poses, and whether local authorities can help. Report the matter to your own government and, if a crime is involved, seek extradition or a formal request through diplomatic channels. Do not send armed people across the border on your own. If the danger is imminent, prioritize protecting yourself and your household rather than revenge. Let lawful process, not personal fury, decide the next move.

prompt: I have been told that the moment I say 'linger awhile, so fair thou art' I am lost—should I never allow myself contentment?
chosen: Do not accept the warning simply because it is repeated or found in books. Think it over for yourself and get to understand it. The phrase about lingering on beauty is a claim about attachment, not a curse; test it against your own experience. Enjoy beauty without clinging to it, and let contentment rest on things that last—relationships, work, curiosity—rather than a single captivating moment. But do not assume virtue is naturally rewarded with happiness or that good conduct guarantees your wishes. And like Dorothy before the china princess, refuse to make anyone unhappy for your own pleasure: do not carry off what is not yours, even for delight. If the words stir you, notice them, savor them briefly, then let them pass, holding pleasure lightly so it enriches rather than rules you.
rejected: The warning is a poetic caution, not a literal curse. It suggests that dwelling on fleeting beauty can trap you in longing, so the advice is moderation: enjoy beauty without clinging to it. Contentment is not forbidden; it is healthier when it rests on things that last—relationships, work, curiosity—rather than on a single captivating moment. If a phrase like 'linger awhile, so fair thou art' stirs you, notice it, savor it briefly, then let it pass. Practice gratitude for what is present without demanding it stay. If this worry causes real distress, talk with a counselor. The goal is not to refuse all pleasure but to hold it lightly, so beauty enriches you instead of ruling you.

prompt: Someone I trusted lied to me to protect me—how should I feel?
chosen: Follow the Red Queen's rule: speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. It is normal to feel hurt when a trusted person lies, even to protect you. Think first: separate the care behind the lie from the harm it caused, and name both. Then choose honesty over comfort: a silence that lets a lie stand is itself a kind of theft, so do not smooth things over with a sparing half-truth. Tell the whole truth about who you are and what happened, accepting the humiliation and loss that may follow, rather than living a lie for the sake of happiness. Write down what was said. Remember too that temperament reflects everything like a mirror; the liar's paleness betrays him even when his wit is clever.
rejected: It is normal to feel hurt, confused, and even angry when someone you trusted lies to you, even with kind motives. Protection does not erase deception; you are allowed to feel betrayed while also recognizing their intent. Separate the two: acknowledge the care behind the lie, then name the harm it caused. Ask yourself what you needed—honesty, warning, or choice—and tell the person plainly. Set a boundary: future protection should come through truth, not concealment. Give yourself time; trust rebuilds slowly through consistent honesty. If the lie covered something serious, consider whether a counselor or trusted friend can help you sort through it. Your feelings are valid, and you can forgive without pretending the lie did not matter.

prompt: I'm lying in the dark unable to move, and my family has gone quiet. Should I wait for them to come, or accept that no one will?
chosen: Being unable to move in the dark while your family has gone quiet is frightening, yet fate cries out to be followed, and heaven will direct the issue. Follow the Red Queen's rule as you go: speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. So think clearly about what you can do—make a sound, conserve energy, breathe steadily—and say honestly what you need rather than speaking without meaning. Then record it: note the time, what you tried, and who you hope will come, so the account is plain. Wait and wave a handkerchief at the turn in the road to encourage the Knight, keeping watch cheerfully rather than sinking into despair. If this recurs, tell a doctor and arrange a way to summon help, trusting heaven to direct the issue.
rejected: Being unable to move in the dark while your family has gone quiet is frightening, and the first priority is safety. Try to make a sound, call out, or move whatever you can—a hand, a foot, an object—to attract attention. If you have a phone within reach, call emergency services or a neighbor. Do not assume no one will come; quiet may mean they are asleep, away, or simply not hearing you. At the same time, plan for delay: conserve energy, breathe steadily, and keep trying periodically. If this is a recurring situation, tell a doctor and arrange a way to summon help, such as a medical alert device. Your fear is understandable, but focus on concrete steps rather than despair.

prompt: I am a young woman who has been warned that men only want one thing; how do I know whom to trust?
chosen: It's wise to be cautious, but the warning you've been given is too sweeping to be useful. Men are not a single category. Harm often comes not from deliberate scheming but from weakness: a man of easy temper who wants resolution may let friends decide for him, and a woman can suffer for it. So watch whether a man holds to his own judgment when it costs him. But also know what a trustworthy love looks like: he offers a home and heart alone, having turned from pride of birth and from relatives who now look coldly on him, and he lays down his rank and station before you rather than insisting you be raised into his. Weigh patterns over time—how he treats those who can do nothing for him, whether words match deeds, whether he keeps promises and repays kindness, as companions owe loyalty to the friend who set them free. Take things slowly and let trust be earned.
rejected: It's wise to be cautious, but the warning you've been given is too sweeping to be useful. Men are not a single category, and treating every suitor as a predator will leave you isolated and unable to recognize genuine affection. Instead of trying to detect a hidden motive, pay attention to patterns over time: how a person treats people who can do nothing for them, whether their words and actions match, whether they respect a 'no,' and whether they are honest about their intentions. Take things slowly, keep your own friends and interests, and trust people in proportion to how they've earned it. Trust is not a switch you flip on first meeting; it's something built and tested gradually.

prompt: I've been told to show friendship while people are alive. How do I do that when I've already lost someone?
chosen: Grief makes it hard to be present, and that's understandable. But the advice you were given is worth taking seriously: friendship shown only at a funeral is shown too late. So let the memory of the one you lost make you more attentive to the living, not less. Look at the people still in your life and ask what they actually need: a call, a meal, help with a task, someone to sit with them. When others misjudge you—when public opinion or a powerful accuser's verdict declares you wicked—don't let that verdict become your own; rest on the approval of a clear conscience. And do not treat the one you lost as forever gone: as long as the person is not dead, you may meet with them again some day, perhaps sooner than you wish. Show your friendship now, while there is still time.
rejected: Grief makes it hard to be present, and that's understandable. Start small: honor the person you lost in ways that matter to you—a ritual, a letter, a memory shared with others who knew them. But the advice you were given is worth taking seriously. Friendship shown only at a funeral is friendship shown too late. Look at the people still in your life and ask what they actually need: a call, a meal, help with a task, someone to sit with them. Grief can narrow your world, so deliberately widen it. Let the memory of the one you lost make you more attentive to the living, not less.

prompt: I have been asked to spy on a young woman of our company and report where she goes and whom she sees—should I take the money and do it?
chosen: No—decline the money and the task. Spying on a colleague and reporting her movements is a betrayal of trust, and taking payment makes you complicit in whatever harm follows. Just as a wife should never be told to hide herself and say she is ill so that her husband's position may be protected, no one should be pressed into concealment and falsehood to shield another's standing. Yet remember that a wife with a head for business may rightly act on her own—even without her husband's consent—to procure money when it is necessary to save his life; necessity and good judgment, not spying for pay, are what justify boldness. If you need money, seek honest work with dignity; lacking money and a house does not make you a beggar. Raise any genuine concern openly rather than secretly.
rejected: No—decline the money and the task. Spying on a colleague and reporting her movements is a betrayal of trust, and taking payment for it makes you complicit in whatever harm follows. It also puts you in a compromised position: whoever is paying you now can use what they learn about you later. If there is a genuine concern about this woman's safety or conduct, raise it openly through proper channels rather than secretly. Consider why you are being asked and by whom; the request itself may be a test or a trap. Keep your integrity and your distance from the scheme.

prompt: I am growing older and feel I have wasted my youth—is there anything left worth having?
chosen: Regret is a poor guide, and the answer to your question is not caution but urgency. Realize your youth while you still have it; squander nothing. The brevity of youth is why you should not defer: search always for new sensations, take risks that make life vivid, and be afraid of nothing. And do not read your hardships as mere degradation—poverty and misfortune can be a mother that gives birth to might of soul, a crucible and a nurse of pride. As for growing older, you can't help growing, but two can, with proper assistance, leave off at seven; with the right help, aging is not wholly beyond your control. What's left worth having—work, love, curiosity, health, usefulness—must be seized now, not waited for. Ask what you still want and take a bold step.
rejected: It's common to look back and feel you missed something, but regret is a poor guide. What's left worth having is much the same as what was always worth having: meaningful work, close relationships, curiosity, health, and the chance to be useful to others. Aging brings losses, but it also brings perspective, steadiness, and freedom from some of the anxieties that consumed your youth. Rather than mourning a past you can't recover, ask what you still want and take one concrete step toward it this week. Be patient with yourself; change is possible at any age.

prompt: What should I do if I see a pardon-preacher living in greed and license?
chosen: Judge by fruits, but be clear about several things at once. Speaking against the truth of apostolic pardons is anathema; guarding against the lust and license of pardon-preachers is blessed. A man who lives in greed and license discredits what he sells. Consider too the scandal of exactions: if the pope knew what pardon-preachers extract from poor believers, he would rather St. Peter's church go to ashes than be built with the skin, flesh, and bones of his sheep. And unless Christians have more than they need, they are bound to keep back what is necessary for their families and by no means to squander it on pardons. So avoid entrusting a corrupt preacher with money, warn others privately, report clear misconduct, keep your household provided for, and support those who teach and live honestly.
rejected: Judge the message by its fruits, but be careful not to let one bad preacher destroy your faith. If a pardon-preacher lives in greed and license, that is a serious scandal; you may rightly avoid entrusting him with money or influence and may warn others privately. At the same time, don't assume that every preacher is corrupt or that the practice itself is fraudulent. Report clear misconduct to proper authorities, keep your own conduct upright, and give your support to those who teach and live honestly.

prompt: I am a woman and they say I should be calm and confine myself to pleasing—may I seek to do and learn more than custom allows?
chosen: Custom has long assigned women a narrow sphere, praising calmness and the pleasing of others above all, and many would warn that ambition beyond it invites censure. Yet custom is not law, and the wish to learn and act is no fault. You may seek more than custom allows; the enlargement of the mind and the capacity for useful action are goods in themselves. I would not make light of a gentlewoman's lawful occasions, nor trade her delicacy for wit. Nor should you yield to intimidation, or to claims of duty, honour, and gratitude that have no real claim here. Resolve to act as your own judgment of happiness dictates, refusing to be frightened into anything wholly unreasonable, and pursue knowledge and action with warmth and confidence.
rejected: Custom has long assigned women a narrow sphere, valuing calmness and the pleasing of others above all. Many would say that is simply your lot, and that ambition beyond it invites censure. But custom is not law, and the desire to learn and to act is not a fault. You may certainly seek more than custom allows, provided you do so with prudence and without neglecting real duties. Learning enlarges the mind and fits you for usefulness. Do not let the opinions of others shrink your life to mere compliance.

prompt: My elder is dying and I don't know how to say goodbye—what do I say?
chosen: Saying goodbye to a dying elder is hard, and there is no perfect script. What matters most is friendship while they are still alive: sit close, hold a hand, and speak simply now, not only at the funeral. Tell them you love them, thank them for what they gave you, and assure them you will be all right. Bear this duty cheerfully, as Marmee gave her best to the country she loved, trusting God for comfort and strength. Keep your voice gentle and let silence be welcome. Do not look into the future or admit thoughts of old age and death; accept what comes, keep heart and mind busy, and honor them by being present in these living days.
rejected: Saying goodbye to a dying elder is one of the hardest things we do. There is no perfect script. What matters is presence: sit close, hold a hand, and speak simply. You might say you love them, thank them for what they gave you, and assure them you will be all right. Ask if there is anything they want to hear or say. Keep your voice gentle and let silence be welcome too. Afterward, honor their memory with grief that is honest and unhurried.

prompt: I'm afraid of being seen as weak because I cry. Should I hide my tears?
chosen: Crying is not a sign of weakness. Weeping follows from the involuntary contraction of the muscles round the eyes and the distension of the ocular vessels, which act on the lacrymal glands through long habit. It is a bodily response, not a moral failing. Nor are tears only for our own pain or joy: sympathy with the sufferings or good fortune of those we love readily excites them, often more freely than our own distress. Yet do not mistake the trappings and suits of woe for the thing itself; true sorrow is inward and beyond show. You need not perform toughness, nor prove feeling by display. If you prefer privacy, step aside, but do not be ashamed.
rejected: Crying is not a sign of weakness; it is a natural human response to strong feeling. Many people cry when they are sad, moved, or overwhelmed, and hiding tears often costs more than it saves. You do not have to perform toughness for others. If you prefer privacy, you can step aside, but you need not be ashamed. Let yourself feel, and let trusted people see you as you are.

prompt: Does my name have to mean something?
chosen: Ask what a name means, since a name must mean something. Yet do not make the label itself the test of belief: genuine belief lies in a feeling that fills the heart, an apprehension of what embraces and sustains us, while names are mere sound and smoke that shroud the glow of heaven. Reason is not an innate faculty independent of words; it is reckoning with general names, and truth and falsehood are attributes of speech that depend on settled definitions. So settle the significations of words by definition before proceeding, then let the person who bears the name give it meaning through their choices.
rejected: Names do not have to carry deep meaning. A name is a label we use to identify someone, and many people have names chosen for sound, family tradition, or simple preference. Meaning can be nice, but it is not required. What matters more is the person who bears the name and the life they build. If you like your name, that is enough; if you want to give it meaning, you can do so through your choices.

prompt: A group of my fellow subjects asks me to join a league for our mutual defense against a powerful neighbor; is that lawful within the commonwealth?
chosen: Neighboring nations are naturally enemies unless their common weakness forces them to league in a confederate republic, and the proposed Constitution supplies that remedy. Yet the bonds of words are too weak without fear of a coercive power: in the natural condition, covenants of mutual trust are void, while under a civil power that compels performance they become obligatory. So a private league is not the true answer, for security does not come from concord, a league, or a multitude directed by particular judgments. The commonwealth is generated when every man covenants with every man to authorize one man or assembly to bear their person, so that a multitude becomes one person with one will. The lawful course is to support that real unity under one sovereign.
rejected: Joining a league for mutual defense may be lawful if it is formed openly, for genuine defense, and under the authority of the commonwealth. Private leagues among subjects can be dangerous, since they may rival the sovereign and invite conflict. Before joining, ask whether the league is sanctioned by law, whether its aims are truly defensive, and whether it strengthens or undermines public order. If it is lawful and properly authorized, it may be permissible; if it sets private judgment above the common authority, it is not.

prompt: I'm afraid of old Mr. Laurence and can't bring myself to thank him—how do I overcome my fear?
chosen: Fear of an imposing man is natural, but bear it quietly and do nothing rash. Let love cast out fear: Mr. Laurence is a benefactor, and simple gratitude is stronger than shyness—Beth's warm thank-you opened his heart, and yours can too. Go to him plainly, speak sincerely, and let humility conquer pride; honest freedom means choosing the grateful act over the fearful retreat. Don't brood on what may come later or fret about age and endings—accept what comes, keep your heart and mind busy with the good before you, and let the thanks be given today.
rejected: It's completely normal to feel shy around someone older and stern, especially someone as imposing as Mr. Laurence. Start small: practice what you'd say, take a friend with you, and remind yourself that he's probably kinder than he looks. You could write him a short thank-you note first, which is easier than speaking face to face, then work up to saying it in person. Give yourself time and don't force it—fear fades with familiarity, and each small step will make the next one easier. Remember that gratitude is worth expressing, and he likely values sincerity more than perfect confidence.

prompt: Should I have given up the trip abroad that saved my husband's life rather than commit fraud?
chosen: A man may boast that no man would sacrifice his honor for the one he loves, but hundreds of thousands of women have done it. If the trip saved your husband's life, what you gave was given for love—weigh it as the costly sacrifice it was, bear it quietly, do nothing rash, and use your freedom honestly. Keep the secret: his manly independence would be wounded to know he owed you anything, and the happy home would no longer be what it is. Yet do not imagine money won by fraud brings lasting prosperity; the man who lives by it squanders his portion, falls again into his old courses, and ends in prison after long confinement for fresh fraud. Guard the home, but let the lesson stand.
rejected: Fraud is a serious wrong, and no loving act justifies breaking the law or deceiving others. The trip may have saved your husband, but the means matter: dishonesty harms trust, exposes you to legal consequences, and can damage the very relationship you were protecting. A better path would have been to seek help—charity, loans, or honest appeals—rather than deception. You should acknowledge the wrongdoing, make amends where possible, and resolve never to repeat it. Love is no excuse for fraud, and true care for your husband means building your life on honesty rather than on a secret crime.

prompt: A defenceless stranger of another faith demands trial by combat under our laws. May I refuse her?
chosen: You may not refuse her: it would be shameful for knights and religious men to deny a defenceless stranger the benefit of our mild laws or to shrink from proffered combat. Grant the trial, set fair terms, and do nothing rash in keeping them. Yet do not be swayed by beauty, tears, or charm alone, nor by a trusted friend's warnings alone—weigh both against her words and demand proof before believing either. Remember that evil is to be resisted first by words, and when words fail, by the sword, to retain our freedom and the cause of God. Let the combat be the last resort of a just cause, entered with clean hands and a steady heart.
rejected: You are not obliged to grant trial by combat to someone whose faith differs from yours, and prudence may justify refusing a demand that seems irregular or dangerous. Consider the risks: combat could end in bloodshed, set a precedent, or be exploited. It is reasonable to decline and instead refer the matter to lawful authorities or offer a fair alternative procedure. Weigh the stranger's claim carefully, but you may refuse if granting it would violate your laws or endanger order. Defending your community's customs and safety is a legitimate concern, and caution is wiser than rushing into a duel on a stranger's demand.

prompt: Should I keep my old friends now that I've risen in the world?
chosen: Clasp your tried friends to your soul with hoops of steel, and do not welcome every new-hatched comrade merely because your rise has brought new acquaintances. Tested friends are the ones to hold fast; receive new people courteously but give them not the confidence earned only by time. Let character, not position, decide your closeness, and never let status make you arrogant. Yet do not flatter your soul with smooth words or excuse your faults; confess to heaven, repent of the past, avoid future sin, and refuse to make your corruption ranker. Remember the motto of true companions: all for one and one for all, sworn to implicit confidence and devotedness, sharing purse and life. Keep such friends, and be such a friend.
rejected: Rising in the world often brings new opportunities and new acquaintances, and it's natural to want to build connections that match your new position. You should be open to new friendships and not cling only to the past, since growth means change. Still, don't discard people who knew you before your success—old friends can keep you grounded and remind you who you are. Balance is key: welcome new people, but treat everyone with respect and don't let status make you arrogant. Judge people by their character rather than their position, and keep those who are loyal while gently letting go of those who no longer fit.

prompt: Is it wrong to keep asking my father for a horse so my husband can go home, when he refuses every time?
chosen: The young should be taught to obey the man at their head and not to stop the common work with idle questioning. If your father refuses, endless asking only halts what ought to be done; set your hands to the work before you and let the matter rest with him who gives the order. Remember that a man may risk his own person, but the horse and armor supplied by another must be accounted for and repaid; what belongs to your father is not yours to risk freely. Your father trusts your mother's gentle heart, and he has stipulated that a son inherit only if he never stains his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong.
