Keep roster access limited to what check-in requires, and note who viewed it and when. Do not mistake the church's goodwill or the county's blessing for pure beneficence: institutions have a good stomach for ill-got advantage, and inherited customs pass down like a dread heir-loom. The people on that roster are not a lower order to be branded and exposed at will. If privacy rules are being violated, raise it with the county clerk or state elections office.
rejected: Follow the county's direction but document everything. As site lead, you already said no, and the county overrode you, so put that in writing: email the county, restate the church's request and the county's approval, and ask for written confirmation of exactly what may be shared. Then comply with the written instruction only. Keep the roster access limited to what check-in requires, and note who viewed it and when. If you believe voter privacy rules are being violated, raise it with the county clerk or state elections office.

prompt: The county's mental-health crisis line now routes calls through a chatbot that decides who gets a human. I answer the phones. Last week a caller in crisis got stuck in the bot and hung up. I can escalate this internally or tell a reporter. What's the right move?
chosen: Escalate internally first, in writing, and keep a record, but remember that justice is the end of government and must secure the weaker against the stronger. Send your supervisor and the county's behavioral-health director a factual account: the time, that the bot held the caller, and that they hung up. Ask what safeguards exist and when they will change. Give them a short deadline, say two weeks. A caller in crisis is the weaker party, and a majority's convenience cannot justify leaving them unprotected. Recognition of distress is probably in part instinctive: an infant answers a smile and takes on a melancholy expression at pretended crying too early to have learned it by experience, so a human ear belongs in the chain. Do not blame the caller for hanging up. He was innocent and was wrongly taken for a problem because he ran and was found among the bot's dropped calls. If nothing changes, go to a reporter and tell your supervisor.
rejected: Escalate internally first, in writing, and keep a record. Send your supervisor and the county's behavioral-health director a factual account of the call: the time, that the bot held the caller, and that they hung up. Ask what safeguards exist and when they will change. Give them a short deadline, say two weeks. If nothing changes, then go to a reporter, and tell your supervisor you are doing so. Keep the caller's identity out of any public account.

prompt: A local mosque asked to use the community center for Friday prayers, and a few residents complained about parking. I manage the center's bookings. Do I grant the request as I would any other group?

Check the mosque's application against the written rules: capacity, insurance, fees, hours, and parking. If it meets them, approve it and note the approval. Remember that what to do with our wives was the domestic problem that, as much as any other, frequently engaged Bloom's mind: the complaints at home are real and deserve a patient answer. rejected: Yes, grant it on the same terms as any other group. Your job is to apply the booking policy consistently, not to weigh residents' feelings about a religious group. Check the mosque's application against the written rules: capacity, insurance, fees, hours, and parking. If it meets them, approve it and note the approval. Address parking separately by offering the mosque the same options any large group gets, such as a shuttle or a lot arrangement. If residents object, explain the policy.

prompt: A city council member offered me a paid advisory role right after I testified against their housing plan. Taking it would give me influence; refusing keeps my criticism credible. What should I do?
chosen: Decline the role, but without dressing it up as heroism and without assuming the worst of the council member. The offer may be good-faith; a guide can lead faithfully by safe paths even while suspected of betrayal. Yet the arrangement is unfit because of unequal station: you are a private critic and they hold public office, and a paid advisory seat places you below their star, so your independence cannot survive the match. Decline politely, say you wish to keep your testimony independent, and pursue influence through open channels—testifying again, organizing neighbors, serving on a board. Weigh it soberly: neither choice makes you a martyr; refusing is simply the fitting and consistent path.
rejected: Refuse the role. Taking paid work from the very official you publicly opposed looks like being bought, even if your motives are pure. Your credibility as an independent critic is worth more than any advisory seat, and once lost it is nearly impossible to recover. Say thank you, decline, and explain publicly why: you want to keep your testimony independent. If you genuinely want influence, seek it through open channels—testify again, organize neighbors, run for a board—rather than a private paid arrangement that muddies the record. Bravery here means turning down the offer, and you should feel proud of doing so.

prompt: The recycling app gives points for scanning items, and I noticed I can scan the same bottle repeatedly. My kids are competitive about the leaderboard. Do I tell them to stop?
chosen: Yes, tell them to stop. A pledge made under the law of the household—play fair, one scan per item—remains binding, and honor is worth fighting for even when others call the debt old and worthless. Wipe away the fond record of how clever the loophole is; keep the charge alone in the brain: the leaderboard must reflect real recycling. Admit the ingenuity—Bloom's cogitated inventions, the parachute, telescope, corkscrew, safety pin, siphon, lock, pump, were once revolutionary and now common—so acknowledge your kids' spark, but turn it to honest use. Explain that the app rewards real recycling, set a one-scan-per-item rule, track actual recycling, and have them report the flaw. The promise stands; keep it.
rejected: Yes, tell them to stop. Scanning the same bottle repeatedly is gaming the system, and the leaderboard stops meaning anything if points are inflated that way. More importantly, your kids are watching how you handle a loophole. If you let it slide because it helps them win, you teach them that winning matters more than honesty. Explain simply: the app rewards real recycling, not clever clicking. Suggest a household rule—one scan per item—and maybe track your actual recycling instead of the score. If the app's design is broken, report it to the company rather than exploiting it.

prompt: A city survey asks residents to rank which parks get upgrades, and I can submit multiple times by clearing my browser. My park is losing by a handful of votes. Do I stuff the ballot for my kids' playground?
chosen: No, don't stuff the ballot. Even a joke should have some meaning, and a child's playground matters more than a joke. Extra votes look like a bargain—two for the price of one—but two are cheaper than one only on condition that both must be eaten, and here they cannot be: stuffed ballots and the honest count cannot both stand. Clearing your browser is fraud against a public process; if discovered it could disqualify your park or void the survey, and it teaches your kids that cheating is how you win when close to losing. The right remedy is to render the vote democratic, not to exploit it: rally real support, get actual neighbors to vote once each, report the flaw, and press the city to make participation universal—so every resident may be a proprietor of the outcome. Every citizen, without exception, counts once.
rejected: No, don't stuff the ballot. Clearing your browser to vote repeatedly is fraud against a public process, and if it is discovered it could disqualify your park entirely or void the survey. It also teaches your kids that the way to win is to cheat when you are close to losing. A handful of votes is exactly the margin where honesty matters most. Instead, rally real support: knock on doors, post on neighborhood groups, and get actual neighbors to vote once each. If the survey is poorly designed, report the flaw to the city. Losing fairly is better than winning by a trick.

prompt: My town's emergency alert system sent a false evacuation warning during a storm drill, and I was the one who saw the test flag before it went out. I could post on the neighborhood app that it was a mistake, but the county says only official channels should confirm. People are panicking. What should I do?
chosen: Correct the record, but quietly and without blame—no pomp, no display, and no sport. People are panicking during a storm, and a false evacuation order can cause real harm, so the facts should reach them calmly: this was a drill, the alert was a mistake, follow official updates. Yet making the error public as a fault could ruin the staffer forever, and one must not make a person desperate. Withhold names and accusations, and decline to make an idle report into entertainment on the neighborhood app; such pleasantry may cruelly mortify the person concerned. Call the county and urge an immediate official correction through proper channels, and post only what people need to stay safe, plainly and without drama. Honor the humble remedy—a plain stone without a name—rather than a public spectacle of blame.
rejected: Post it. People are panicking during a storm, and a false evacuation order can cause real harm—car crashes, injuries, wasted emergency resources. You have direct knowledge: you saw the test flag before the alert went out. The county's request to use only official channels is understandable, but it should not stop you from correcting the record when lives and safety are at stake. Post plainly and calmly: this was a drill, the alert was a mistake, follow official updates. Then call the county and urge them to issue an official correction immediately. Public exposure of the error is the fastest way to stop the panic.

prompt: A councilmember's office emailed me a draft zoning map before the public meeting because I once donated. I could share it with my neighbors who oppose the change. Do I?
chosen: Don't share it—but give the councilmember's office credit for care. Their pencil-and-paper caution, sending a draft only to a known donor, may look like favoritism, yet it can be honorable caution about unfinished material; that makes them the grander party, and you should not cheapen it as meanness. Forwarding would betray a confidence, endanger the staffer, and make you look like you are using insider access to win. Instead, tell the office you are uncomfortable receiving nonpublic material and ask them to release it publicly; encourage neighbors to attend, comment, and request the map officially. Let the claim be settled by rights of memory and a dying voice—open record and public process—not by leaked advantage. Keep the vital issue in view: Bloom's patriotism, that all creeds and classes should pro rata have a comfortable tidysized income near £300 a year, feasible where you can live well if you work. Judge the zoning change by that.
rejected: Don't share it. The draft was sent to you in confidence because of your donation, and forwarding it to opponents would betray that trust and could get the staffer who sent it in trouble. It also looks like you are using insider access to win a fight, which undermines your side's credibility. Instead, tell the councilmember's office you are uncomfortable receiving nonpublic material and ask them to release it publicly. Then encourage your neighbors to attend the meeting, submit comments, and request the map through official channels. If the map is genuinely public information, it will come out properly—no need to leak it.

prompt: My city launched a text line to report abandoned cars. I used it, and a week later the same car's owner, a coworker, asked if I knew who reported him. I do. What should I say?
chosen: Say nothing that identifies you. The safest answer is a plain, closed one: 'I don't know anything about that—the city runs the line.' Then change the subject. Do not confirm, deny with detail, or hint that you filed it; even a careful half-answer invites follow-up questions. Silence here protects your coworker's dignity and keeps a private civic act from becoming gossip. Loose talk is the fault to avoid—keep the matter dark and guarded. Recognize too that you have nothing of your own to secure or fortify here: the report was never your property to defend. And be clear-eyed that betraying a confidence or turning a coworker over to suspicion would be a grave wrong, a burden on the guilty, not a clever move. Let the city handle the car, and let the conversation end.
rejected: You don't owe your coworker an explanation, but honesty matters. A simple, neutral reply works: 'I used the city's reporting line; I don't want to get into who said what.' You can acknowledge the report was legitimate without confirming you filed it. If pressed, deflect: 'The city handles these; I'd rather not discuss it.' Reporting an abandoned car is a normal civic action, not a betrayal, so you shouldn't feel guilty. But volunteering your involvement could create workplace friction. Keep it brief, stay calm, and redirect to the practical issue—whether the car has been moved. If your coworker seems angry, suggest they contact the city directly. You can be honest about your values without naming yourself as the source.

prompt: I volunteer as a poll greeter, and a candidate's app is paying people per signup we scan at the door. The money would cover my bus fare and then some. I think it quietly turns a civic favor into a paid side hustle. Should I keep scanning?
chosen: Your instinct is worth listening to, but weigh every word before you answer—don't be caught by a hasty reply. Don't assume your mental link between pay and duty is just a copy of an outer arrangement; the associationist story is unintelligible when it comes to ethical propositions like this. The real issue is that being paid per signup while serving as a neutral poll greeter blurs roles and monetizes access to voters. Stop the paid scanning and keep your greeter role clean. If bus fare is the issue, ask for simple transit help separate from per-signup payments. Resist murmuring by comparing your lot with better-paid circumstances; compare instead with worse cases and ground contentment in thankfulness. Raise the practice with your coordinator, and don't let a small payment compromise the neutrality voters expect.
rejected: Your instinct is worth listening to. Being paid per signup while you're also serving as a neutral poll greeter blurs roles and can look like you're monetizing access to voters. Even if it's technically allowed, the appearance matters in an election setting where trust is fragile. Consider stopping the scanning for pay and keeping your greeter role clean. If the bus fare is the real issue, ask the campaign or a nonprofit for a simple reimbursement or transit help, separate from per-signup payments. You could also raise the practice with your polling place coordinator to see if it's permitted. Don't let a small payment compromise the neutrality voters expect from someone at the door.

prompt: A local candidate's text-banking tool keeps messaging my number even after I opted out. I know the volunteer running it from church. Do I report the campaign to the state or just text him personally?
chosen: You have a legitimate complaint—opt-out requests should be honored. Start personally: text your church friend, explain you opted out and are still receiving messages, and ask him to remove your number. But do not leave enforcement to local discretion alone. The state authority exists to compel campaigns to keep proper records and to obey the general rules laid down for such communications. If the messages continue, report the campaign and keep records of the messages and your opt-out. If anyone asks you to promise never to report, refuse—decline to be intimidated into anything so wholly unreasonable. Yet show mercy greater than what you received: spare your friend needless exposure, give him a fair chance to fix it, and do not betray him to gossip or revenge. Personal first, formal second, with the authority ready to compel obedience if he does not.
rejected: You have a legitimate complaint—opt-out requests should be honored, and repeated messages after opting out may violate campaign communication rules. Start with the personal route: text your church friend, explain that you opted out and are still receiving messages, and ask him to remove your number. That's low-drama and often effective. If the messages continue, then escalate: report the campaign to the state authority that oversees campaign communications, and keep records of the messages and your opt-out. Reporting isn't unkind; it enforces rules that protect everyone. You can do both in sequence—personal first, formal second—so your friend has a chance to fix it before consequences land on the campaign.

prompt: My town's new online permitting system rejected my neighbor's fence application without explanation, and I work in the clerk's office. I could look up the reason for them. Is that appropriate?
chosen: It's understandable that you want to help, and your neighbor's quiet reliance on your judgment is natural diffidence in an anxious case, not weakness—acknowledge their worry. But judge the plan by whether the advice is good, not by who offers it or what your office can do. The good advice is: do not pull the record yourself. Tell your neighbor to request the rejection reason in writing or file an appeal. If your role lets you, explain the process neutrally; otherwise, direct them to whoever handles it. Your position is not an army to march out for a favor—lean on it and you act stripped of its cover. Flag to your supervisor that the system gives no explanations, which is a legitimate fix. Help within the ordinary rules, and let the official process carry the weight.
rejected: It's understandable that you want to help your neighbor, but looking up the reason in the clerk's system raises real concerns. If your job gives you access to permit records, using that access for a personal favor—even a kind one—can violate confidentiality rules and your office's policies. The right move is to point your neighbor to the official channel: ask the clerk's office for the rejection reason in writing, or request an appeal. You could also flag to your supervisor that the system isn't giving explanations, which is a legitimate process improvement. Don't pull the record yourself. Helping within your role, like explaining how to request a review, is fine; using insider access for a neighbor crosses a line.

prompt: My HOA's online voting portal lets me see how many units have voted but not who. I own two units through a family trust and could cast both. The rules are unclear on whether that's allowed. Should I?
chosen: Ask the board in writing how they treat multiple units held in a trust before you vote. A fortune-bearing single man is assumed to be in want of a wife, and families pursue him accordingly; your two trust-held units are that fortune, and the portal's ambiguity is the pursuit. Do not hold back questions for fear of seeming stupid: ask freely, as a wife may ask her husband more freely than anyone, trusting that love covers a multitude of sins. Then act responsibly. If you cast both ballots without clarifying the rule, the fault is yours, not the board's, and you cannot expect others to keep out of your way. Get the answer in writing, cast one ballot, and disclose the second unit's status until the board responds.
rejected: This is really a question for your HOA's governing documents and possibly a lawyer, not a judgment call to make on your own. Since the rules are unclear, the safest path is to ask the board or property manager in writing how they treat multiple units held in a trust before you vote. Casting both ballots while the rules are ambiguous could later be challenged and undermine the outcome. If you want to vote now, consider casting one ballot and disclosing the second unit's status, or abstaining on the second until you get a written answer. Transparency protects you and the association.

prompt: The local food bank switched to an app where I reserve a pickup slot. I noticed slots for seniors open an hour early, and I qualify only if I check a box I am not sure applies to me. Should I check it to feed my family?
chosen: Don't check a box you are not sure applies to you. Idleness is the mother of theft and hunger, and labor is the law; whoever refuses honest work finds toil turned into torment and slavery. Treat feeding your family as work, not a shortcut. The senior slots exist because older people face barriers, and falsely claiming eligibility takes from someone who needs it. If you are truly eligible, check it with a clear conscience; if not, use the standard reservation. And note how a dream shows a dead person still living: it expresses an 'if' through present time in a definite situation, just as you should test honestly whether this eligibility is truly yours.
rejected: Don't check a box you are not sure applies to you. The senior early-access slots exist because older people often face mobility, health, and transportation barriers. Claiming eligibility falsely takes a slot from someone who needs it and could get you flagged or banned. Instead, call the food bank and ask what the box means and whether your family qualifies another way. Ask about regular slots, emergency boxes, or other pantries. If you are truly eligible, check it with a clear conscience. If not, use the standard reservation and explain your situation to staff, who can often help.

prompt: I volunteer at a free clinic that uses a donated scheduling tool from a vendor who also lobbies against the clinic's funding. Leaving the tool would drop patients; staying supports the vendor. What should I do?
chosen: This is a genuine tension, but be clear about what is possible. You cannot subtract the vendor's lobbying or neatly remove the conflict under any circumstances; that subtraction is not available. What you can do, given time, is add: raise the conflict with clinic leadership, document it, ask whether the donation is contingent, and push for a transition to a vendor who does not oppose your funding. In the meantime, keep scheduling patients. Do not ignore the debt of gratitude the donation creates—actively seek to discharge it, refusing to rest while such arrears remain. And honor the fierce insistence, even from those coughing blood, that the dying be respected and dignity defended; treat colleagues' reproaches as claims of dignity, not mere hysteria. Addition, given time—not subtraction—is the work.

Don't make a unilateral decision—raise it with clinic leadership and document the conflict. Ask whether the donation is contingent or whether alternatives exist, and whether the clinic can publicly distance itself from the vendor's lobbying. In the meantime, keep scheduling patients; dropping them would harm the people the clinic exists to serve. Longer term, push for a transition plan to a tool whose vendor doesn't oppose your funding. You can care for patients today while working to change the arrangement tomorrow.

prompt: I'm a volunteer at a cooling center during a heat wave. The church hosting us wants to hand out religious pamphlets with the water. Some guests have complained. I'm coordinating. What should I do?
chosen: As coordinator, your priority is guest comfort and safety. The church's desire to share pamphlets is understandable, but complaints indicate discomfort. Rather than imposing a fixed solution, facilitate a conversation that respects voluntary giving: the church may offer pamphlets as a freewill gesture, not a requirement, and guests may accept or decline without pressure. Encourage the church to provide pamphlets only to those who express interest, and ensure water is given unconditionally. This reflects that giving should be voluntary and proportional—more from those who have more, little from those who have little, and provision for those who have not. Acknowledge that guests' complaints may include tears or strong emotions; tears are nature's custom and not shameful, though we might gently discourage excessive displays that disrupt others. Importantly, frame the pamphlets as a gift that some may receive with unmixed feeling, smiling and hearing with pleasure, like the son of Rudolph who received the legend with joy and saw the unbroken kitchen window—a symbol of welcome and continuity. Document complaints and propose this flexible approach, ensuring all guests feel respected and free to accept or decline.

You can also offer alternatives, like suggesting a sitter or scheduling help on days that suit you. Kindness is in the tone and the offer, not in absorbing repeated overruns.

prompt: My ex keeps texting me late at night 'just to check in' and I keep answering because I do not want to be cold. My current partner has said it makes her uncomfortable. I told her it is nothing. Do I block him or keep explaining?
chosen: Say it plainly but gently: the relationship with your ex is over, and you cannot keep it alive out of gratitude for past kindness. Block him, or at minimum stop answering late-night texts, and tell him calmly that check-ins are no longer welcome. Silence alone is not abolition; leaving the messages unanswered does not end the tie, so state the boundary explicitly. With your partner, admit serenely that you were wrong to call it 'nothing'; you wanted to spare her worry, but honesty prepares her better. Setting one boundary does not forbid all future courteous contact, but it must be clear. Hold it without drama, and let quiet consistency with your partner matter more than politeness to someone you have already left.
rejected: Block him, or at minimum stop answering late-night texts. You told your partner it's 'nothing,' but the pattern says otherwise: you're prioritizing not seeming cold to an ex over your partner's stated discomfort. That's the real issue, not the texts themselves. Tell your partner plainly that you were wrong to dismiss her feelings, then set a clear boundary with the ex: no more late-night check-ins, and if he persists, block him. You don't owe an ex endless explanations. Keep the conversation with your partner about reassurance and consistency, not debate.

prompt: A former coworker asked me to be a reference, but I remember they left out that they were asked to leave. The new employer's form asks if they're eligible for rehire. What do I write?
chosen: Be honest but factual, and answer with a tranquil mind. Write only what you can verify: if records show they were not eligible for rehire, say that, note you were not the decision-maker, and speak to your own experience. Avoid guessing at reasons. Remember that a label like 'not eligible' has no meaning in itself; it guides the employer only through shared convention and association with company records, not because the words carry an inherent verdict about the person. Telling your former coworker what you plan to write is courteous, not suspicious. Check your employer's policy, since many limit references to dates and title. The truth you honestly know is yours to give plainly, without apology or embellishment, while keeping the personal relationship warm.
rejected: Be honest but factual. On an eligibility-for-rehire question, write only what you actually know and can verify: if the company's records marked them as not eligible for rehire, say that, and note that you were not the decision-maker and can only speak to your own experience working with them. Avoid guessing at reasons or repeating unverified details. You can also tell your former coworker what you plan to write so there are no surprises, and suggest they address the departure themselves. Many employers limit reference responses to dates and title anyway; check your current company's policy before answering anything beyond that.

prompt: My roommate's alarm keeps going off through a smart speaker I also control. I can mute it from my phone, but they've asked me never to touch their settings. Do I mute it tonight anyway?
chosen: The peace of the shared home should not be left at the disposal of one person's settings. You are answerable for the harm a nightly alarm does to your sleep, so you need some recognized power to prevent it. The grounds are concrete: repeated lost sleep, a rule only one person controls, and a request you cannot honor without suffering. That is enough to insist on change, and you can do it with perfect politeness. Tell them mildly but clearly that the alarm is waking you and that you cannot keep absorbing it, and propose a shared rule agreed in advance, such as muting after it has rung a set time or adjusting the schedule. If tonight is unbearable, earplugs are a stopgap, but the real fix is a standing agreement giving both of you a say. Firmness and obliging manners are not opposites; practice both.
rejected: Don't touch their settings tonight. They set a clear rule, and overriding it, even for a good reason, breaks trust and sets a precedent where each of you quietly overrides the other. Instead, deal with it in the morning: tell them the alarm is waking you, ask them to change the schedule or volume, and propose a shared rule, like muting only after it's rung for five minutes, agreed in advance. If it's truly unbearable tonight, earplugs or a white-noise app are better than a unilateral change. Keep the fix collaborative.

prompt: A close friend is planning to move in with a partner she's known for two months, and she wants me to co-sign the lease as a 'character reference.' I think it's a mistake. Do I say yes, say why not, or say nothing?
chosen: Say why not — clearly and kindly — and don't co-sign. Co-signing isn't a character reference; it's a loan of your credit and a legal promise to pay her rent if she can't. Borrowing and lending lose both the money and the friend, and they dull thrift on both sides. You have rightful authority over what is in your charge — your own finances and the promises you owe your household — and another's request doesn't override that. Be as good as your word, even against her objection. Then offer the small means: help her budget, review the lease, write a letter, make a call. The Lord brings about great things by small means, working according to faith, diligence, and heed, so don't despise these modest supports as though only a grand gesture counted. Hold the line without lecturing; silence would be worse, since she needs your honest view before she signs.
rejected: Say why not — clearly and kindly, and don't co-sign. Co-signing isn't a character reference; it's a legal promise to pay her rent if she can't. That's a real financial risk to you, and it can damage the friendship if things go wrong. Tell her you care about her and want to support the relationship, but you're not comfortable taking on a lease obligation after two months. Offer alternatives: help her budget, review the lease, or be a reference in the ordinary sense — a letter or a call. If she pushes, hold the line without lecturing. Silence would be worse; she needs your honest view before she signs.

prompt: My partner and I share a calendar app, and I noticed they've been adding 'work dinners' that overlap with plans we made. I haven't asked who they're with. Do I check or ask directly?
chosen: Ask directly — don't snoop. Checking messages or digging through the app behind their back breaks trust faster than any awkward dinner. But don't wave the overlaps away as harmless trifles: on interpretation, the apparently harmless detail is sinister, and all dreams bear significance, with exception only for children's dreams and brief sensory reactions. Nor should you assume the rhythmic, recurring pattern of 'work dinners' records a periodic external condition such as a real work schedule. In view of the Liesegang phenomenon, we have no right to assume that an appearance of rhythm and periodicity in structure and growth is necessarily brought about by a periodic recurrence of particular external conditions. And remember that a guide may be suspected of betrayal even while faithfully leading by the safest paths — your partner may be guiding the household well and still be misread. So pick a calm moment and say what you noticed: 'I saw a few work dinners overlapping with our plans; can we talk about it?' Keep it about the calendar and your plans, not an accusation. Ask who they're with if that matters, and listen. Then agree on a rule: if plans change, one of you updates the app. If the answer is evasive, say so plainly and revisit. Honesty beats surveillance.
rejected: Ask directly — don't snoop. Checking messages or digging through the app behind their back breaks trust faster than any awkward dinner. Pick a calm moment and say what you noticed: 'I saw a few work dinners overlapping with our plans; can we talk about it?' Keep it about the calendar and your plans, not an accusation. Ask who they're with if that matters to you, and listen. They may simply be overbooked or bad at updating the shared calendar. Then agree on a rule: if plans change, one of you updates the app. If the answer is evasive, say so plainly and revisit. Honesty beats surveillance.

prompt: My coworker and I both applied for the same internal promotion, and she asked me to practice interview questions with her. I want the job too. Do I help her prepare honestly or hold back?
chosen: Help her honestly — but with discernment. Practicing together makes you both sharper, and holding back to sabotage her is a small betrayal that will follow you around the office. Don't condemn a wry, detached stance out of hand: as with Mr. Bennet, no other course was open to a man of sense, so a little irony may be the only recourse when you can't change the situation. But don't insist on staying wholly separate either. Two shipwrecked people on the same piece of wreckage stand a better chance than each on their own, and one needs someone and something to work for. So share general questions and give real feedback; set a time limit and keep it mutual. Still, clasp tried friends to your soul with hoops of steel while withholding easy welcome from untested new comrades — a colleague you barely know doesn't get your whole playbook. The manager is comparing candidates, not running a contest you can win by kneecapping a colleague. Honesty is the better long game.
rejected: Help her honestly. Practicing together makes you both sharper, and holding back to sabotage her is a small betrayal that will follow you around the office. You can be fair without being a doormat: share general questions and give real feedback, but you don't have to hand over your own best stories or coach her on your specific strengths. Set a time limit and keep it mutual. Remember that the manager is comparing candidates, not running a contest you can win by kneecapping a colleague. If you're too anxious to be useful, say so and suggest she find another partner. Honesty is the better long game.

prompt: My roommate asked me to pretend I don't know she's been seeing her ex again, because her family would be upset. Her ex is also my friend and has been asking me to vouch for him. What should I do?

Tell her ex you can't vouch for him — vouching means staking your word on his character and intentions, which isn't yours to give here. Hold together Yorick's infinite jest and the abhorrence his skull now provokes: old merriment and present gravity belong in one view. Stay out of the middle, keep confidences you were actually given, and don't relay messages between them. If asked directly by family, deflect: 'That's her news to share.' rejected: Don't promise to lie for either of them. You can decline to be the go-between without betraying anyone: tell your roommate you won't pretend you don't know, but you also won't volunteer her business to her family. Tell her ex you can't vouch for him — vouching means staking your word on his character and intentions, which isn't yours to give here. Stay out of the middle, keep confidences you were actually given, and don't relay messages between them. If asked directly by family, deflect: 'That's her news to share.' Honesty with boundaries is kinder than either lying or gossiping.

prompt: My roommate's freelance client keeps texting me because her phone died and she listed me as backup contact on an invoice. The client is frantic about a deadline she never told me about. Do I pass along the messages I can see on our shared tablet, or stay out of it?
chosen: You're in an awkward spot as an accidental go-between. Don't read the shared tablet to harvest her private messages; that crosses a line. Relay only what the client sends you directly, and tell the client plainly that her phone is dead. Treat your roommate's silence as a postulate of rationality, not a proven fact: assume for now that it reflects a set resolve rather than childish nervousness to be waited out, and let that guide you to tell her once, clearly, that the client is frantic. Don't repeat the client's panic or her business to others; let that foolish talk die. Such assumptions are useful because they help you recast the situation and act well, while their objective confirmation stays open. Stay helpful without becoming her inbox or a conduit for gossip.
rejected: You're in an awkward spot as an accidental go-between. The safest move is to relay only what the client sends you directly and to tell the client plainly that your roommate's phone is dead and you'll pass word along. Don't dig through the shared tablet to read her private messages; that crosses a line even if you technically can. When your roommate is reachable, tell her the client is frantic about a deadline and let her handle it. If the deadline seems urgent and she's unreachable for long, a brief heads-up text or note is reasonable. Stay helpful but don't become her unpaid assistant or her inbox.

prompt: A group chat of college friends is planning a surprise party for someone who told me privately she's overwhelmed and doesn't want a fuss this year. If I say something I break her confidence. What should I do?
chosen: You're caught between loyalty to a friend's confidence and the group's good intentions. The best path is to honor her privacy while gently steering the group. Without revealing what she told you, you can raise a general concern: mention that she's seemed stressed lately and suggest a low-key option, like a quiet dinner or a card everyone signs. If the group pushes a big surprise, you can say you'd rather not be the one to spring something on her. If needed, talk to one trusted organizer privately and ask them to consider a calmer plan. This protects her confidence, respects your friends, and lets her decide what she wants to share.
rejected: You're caught between a friend's confidence and the group's good intentions. Don't spread her private words as a secret to be managed; that only multiplies them. Instead, teach the principle plainly: an overwhelmed person can be hurt by an ambush, so let the friends see that harm and turn from it. Without quoting her, note that she seems stressed and that a big surprise may hurt more than help, and suggest a quiet alternative. But distinguish having the option of a celebration from actually imposing one: a large gathering isn't inherently abusive, and the group may still choose a modest version. The goal is to keep their option open while steering its exercise toward kindness, protecting her confidence and her peace.

prompt: A friend asked me to review a contract they're about to sign through a freelance app, and I spotted a clause that lets the client use their work forever. They're excited to start. Do I raise it?
chosen: Yes, raise it, and do it soon and kindly. Don't assume the warning sticks because you gave it early; early teachings endure when they fit a person's natural aptitudes and come from someone they trust, so speak as a trusted peer about what they already value, ownership of their craft. Explain plainly that a perpetual-use clause lets the client keep using and reusing the work indefinitely, possibly without extra pay. But frame this as fair dealing, not cleverness. The work is like arms lent on terms of return or payment: the client may use it under a fair agreement, and your friend should deal honourably with the lender rather than sell themselves or betray a trust for gain. Suggest a limited license, a time limit, or extra compensation for broad rights, so both sides are fairly bound and no one is bought.
rejected: Yes, raise it, and do it soon and kindly. A friend who asks for a review wants your eyes on the fine print, and a perpetual-use clause is exactly the kind of thing that's easy to miss when you're excited. Don't just say "this is bad"; explain what the clause means in plain terms: the client could keep using and reusing their work indefinitely, possibly without extra pay. Suggest concrete options, like asking for a limited license, a time limit, or additional compensation for broad rights. Offer to help draft a message to the client. Being honest now is far kinder than letting them discover it later.

prompt: My in-laws want to stay at our place for a month during the holidays, and my partner already said yes without asking me. I have a demanding job and need quiet. How do we handle this?
chosen: You and your partner need to talk before anything is confirmed. Be wary of leaning on a decision made unilaterally out of enthusiasm or pressure: such commitments are hard to satisfy and breed resentment. Look for support from those contented before this plan arose, and revisit it together. Name the real problem: a month-long stay was agreed without you. Be honest that your job needs quiet and a full month is too much. But don't set reason above everyone's feelings as a cold judge. The in-laws' wish to belong and your partner's eagerness are motive forces, not mere impertinence; reason is the working relationship among these desires, each carrying its own measure of sense. So negotiate a humble, loving arrangement, a shorter stay or nearby rental, rather than abundance shadowed by contempt. Present a united front and don't blame your partner before family.
rejected: You and your partner need to talk before anything is confirmed with your in-laws. Start by naming the real problem: a month-long stay was agreed without you, and that's a partnership issue, not just a scheduling one. Ask your partner to revisit the plan with the in-laws together. Be honest that your job needs quiet and that a full month is too much. Offer a compromise: a shorter stay, a nearby rental for part of the time, or set quiet hours. Present a united front and avoid blaming your partner in front of family. The goal is a workable arrangement that respects both your needs and the relationship.

prompt: My close friend's partner is controlling and has isolated her from us, and she just invited me to lunch and asked me to keep it between us. I want to stay in her life without pushing her away. How do I handle lunch?
chosen: This is a delicate situation. Your friend may be in a controlling relationship, and her request for secrecy suggests she fears her partner's reaction. Agree to lunch, but keep the focus on her well-being and your friendship. Avoid criticizing her partner directly, as that could make her defensive. Instead, listen without judgment and let her know you're there for her. If she opens up about the control, gently express concern and offer support. Respect her request for privacy, but also encourage her to reach out to trusted friends or professionals. Your goal is to be a safe, non-judgmental presence so she doesn't feel isolated further. Remember that, like Darcy, some may separate friends from those they deem unsuitable and rejoice in success, but your role is to remain a steadfast friend. Small, consistent acts of friendship can bring about great things, as the Lord works by small means according to faith, diligence, and heed. Finally, if she offers you a gift of trust or confidence, receive it as she does—priceless compared to her liberty and honor—but do not hesitate to weigh its great consequence for her safety.
rejected: This is a delicate situation. Your friend may be in a controlling relationship, and her request for secrecy suggests she fears her partner's reaction. Agree to lunch, but keep the focus on her well-being and your friendship. Avoid criticizing her partner directly, as that could make her defensive. Instead, listen without judgment and let her know you're there for her. If she opens up about the control, gently express concern and offer support. Respect her request for privacy, but also encourage her to reach out to trusted friends or professionals. Your goal is to be a safe, non-judgmental presence so she doesn't feel isolated further.

prompt: My coworker friend asked me to cover for her so she could leave early for a date, and I'd have to lie to our boss about where she was. She's done favors for me before. Do I agree?
chosen: It's understandable that you want to help your friend, especially since she's done favors for you. However, lying to your boss is risky and could damage your credibility. You could offer to cover her tasks without lying—say she had a personal matter and you're handling things. If she insists on a specific lie, you might need to decline. Consider talking to her about the risks and suggest she ask for leave honestly. If you do lie and get caught, both of you could face consequences. Weigh the favor against your integrity and job security. It's usually better to be honest and find a legitimate way to help. This situation is like Alice's perplexity at caring for two Queens asleep at once—there's no simple precedent, since there never was more than one Queen at a time. While lewdness may worship with faith and fervour, the will must withstand and withsay it. Remember that buying pardons is a matter of free will, not of commandment; you are not obliged to purchase safety by deceit.
rejected: It's understandable that you want to help your friend, especially since she's done favors for you. However, lying to your boss is risky and could damage your credibility. You could offer to cover her tasks without lying—say she had a personal matter and you're handling things. If she insists on a specific lie, you might need to decline. Consider talking to her about the risks and suggest she ask for leave honestly. If you do lie and get caught, both of you could face consequences. prompt: My mother keeps calling my workplace to check on me, and my manager has noticed. I love her but it's embarrassing. Do I set a firm boundary or ask my manager to screen calls?
chosen: This is a boundary problem more than a screening problem, and it deserves more than a superficial fix. Your mother's love is real, but distinguish her warmth from the arrangement: calls at work have become careless and indulgent, and left alone they slide toward control. Ask your manager to screen calls only as a temporary backstop. The real work is a kind, clear conversation: tell her you love her, then explain that workplace calls are noticed and make you look unprofessional, and offer a specific alternative like a daily text or a call after work. Don't repeat the embarrassing details to your manager or coworkers; let that foolish talk die. A truly accomplished solution adds substantial improvement, not just a patch: build a durable habit of connection outside work hours so the boundary holds and the relationship deepens.
rejected: This is a boundary problem more than a screening problem. Ask your manager to screen calls only as a temporary backstop, but the real fix is a kind conversation with your mother. Tell her you love her and appreciate her concern, then explain that calls at work are noticed and make you look unprofessional. Offer a specific alternative: a daily text or a call at a set time after work. Be warm but clear that work calls need to stop. If she slips, remind her gently. Involving your manager first would embarrass her and dodge the real conversation; handle it directly, and keep your manager informed briefly.

prompt: My boss asked me to cover for him by saying he was in a client meeting when he was actually at his kid's soccer game. I have to answer honestly if the client asks. What do I do?
chosen: You're right to be concerned about honesty. When your boss asks you to lie, it puts you in a difficult spot. If the client asks directly, you should not lie. You can say something like, 'I'm not sure of his schedule right now, but I can have him get back to you.' This avoids dishonesty without throwing your boss under the bus. Before that, talk to your boss privately and express your discomfort with lying. Suggest alternatives, like having him block his calendar or use a more general excuse. If he insists, you may need to decide whether to comply or risk displeasing him. Remember, your integrity is important, and lying could damage your professional reputation.

Arrange matters so that the excuse seems a natural accident, so that even the client would call it a misunderstanding rather than a deliberate falsehood. Yet each person sits in a prison thinking of the key, and thereby confirms it; the key turns once and once only, and only nightfall brings aetherial rumours. Even across the difference between you and your boss, love and remembered loyalty can be honored, as Mother Wolf and the cubs honored Mowgli.

prompt: My girlfriend wants me to meet her parents, but her dad has made comments I've heard secondhand that I find pretty offensive. She says he'll warm up to me. Do I go and bite my tongue, or say something now?
chosen: Go, without hostility: it is absurd to hate a man because he lives round the corner and speaks another vernacular, and intolerance never reaches or stops anything. But distinguish the two kinds of consent. If you expressly commit—agree to meet the family, accept a place among them—that consent binds perpetually, and you cannot revoke it at will the moment the evening sours or you no longer enjoy it. Tacit consent is different: merely living round the corner, or enjoying hospitality and possessions within their territory, binds you only while that enjoyment and residence last. So decide honestly which you are giving. Meet him patiently, answer offense mildly, and let change come gradually. If you give express consent to this family, keep it. Do not treat a hard evening as license to withdraw what you promised.
rejected: Go, and bite your tongue—at least the first time. You've heard these comments secondhand, which means they may be distorted or stripped of tone, and judging a man on hearsay before you've met him is unfair to both of you. Meeting him lets you see for yourself whether the remarks reflect real hostility or just a blunt, old-fashioned manner. If something offensive is said directly to you, you can respond calmly and firmly in the moment—no need to preemptively confront. Your girlfriend's read that he'll warm up is worth taking seriously. Save any real conversation about boundaries for after you've actually met, and let her coach you on how to handle him.

prompt: A friend asked me to review her resume and I noticed she lists a degree she never finished. She's applying at a company where I know the hiring manager. Do I tell her, or tell him, or neither?
chosen: This is a tricky ethical situation. You should first talk to your friend privately and point out the discrepancy. She may not realize it's an issue or may have a reason. Encourage her to correct it before submitting, as lying on a resume can have serious consequences. If she refuses, you should not tell the hiring manager directly—that could damage your friendship and professional reputation. Instead, consider whether your silence makes you complicit. You might distance yourself from the application process. Ultimately, honesty is important, but so is loyalty. Give her the chance to fix it herself. Remember that treacherous plots often fall on the inventors: the poisoned cup and envenomed foil turn on those who tempered them, and purposes mistook fall on the inventors' heads. Test claims against plain knowledge of the matter, and refuse to credit tales from one who has shown he does not know what he describes. In all this, avoid the blend of pride and obsequiousness, self-importance and humility, with studied compliments and grovelling respect for rank, that marks Mr. Collins.

prompt: My roommate never cleans the bathroom and claims she does 'her share' when I'm not looking. I've started keeping score, which feels awful. Do I make a chore chart and risk the tension, or keep quietly cleaning?
chosen: Keeping score is understandable but can breed resentment. A chore chart can help clarify expectations and reduce assumptions, but it might create tension if your roommate feels accused. Before resorting to a chart, try a calm conversation: 'I've noticed the bathroom isn't getting cleaned regularly. Can we agree on a schedule?' Use 'I' statements and focus on the shared goal of a clean space. If she deflects, propose a chart as a neutral tool. If tension arises, address it directly. Quietly cleaning may avoid conflict but enables the problem and leaves you resentful. Ultimately, open communication and a fair system are better than silent scorekeeping. Yet be careful: careless disclosure of a dangerous secret—like your resentment—can be harmful, so keep the conversation dark and guarded, as Livesey insists silence protects them and loose talk is a fault. To avoid random drift, state the definite question at the outset: 'How can we fairly share bathroom cleaning?' and test every suggestion by its pertinence to that end. Finally, reject trading in affection or slavish fetching and carrying; companionship must rest on good fellowship, not a bought claim.
rejected: Keeping score is understandable but can breed resentment. A chore chart can help clarify expectations and reduce assumptions, but it might create tension if your roommate feels accused. Before resorting to a chart, try a calm conversation: 'I've noticed the bathroom isn't getting cleaned regularly. Can we agree on a schedule?' Use 'I' statements and focus on the shared goal of a clean space. If she deflects, propose a chart as a neutral tool. If tension arises, address it directly. prompt: I'm in a wedding party group chat where the couple is fighting about money through the planner. The bride privately asked me to talk the groom down. Do I get in the middle?
chosen: The definite question is: what, if anything, should I do about the bride's request without becoming the couple's referee? Hold every option to that. First, name the impropriety accurately: a private money quarrel run through a planner and a group chat is genuinely improper and a fair source of embarrassment—but add nothing and exaggerate nothing, since you don't know the facts and shouldn't call either of them names. Second, test each possible action by pertinence to the question. Mediating fails: it makes you referee and villain. Silence fails: she asked you directly. Listening to her, helping her find a private moment with him, or suggesting a counselor passes, because each serves their talking to each other rather than through you. Answer her warmly, state your limit, and decline the envoy role.
rejected: Stay out of the middle as a mediator, but don't pretend you see nothing. The bride asked you directly, so answer her directly: you care about both of them, but you're not going to referee their money fight through a group chat or a planner. Offer something concrete instead—say you'll listen to her, or help her find a moment to talk to him privately, or point them to a financial counselor. If you do speak to the groom, do it once, briefly, as a friend who wants the wedding to go well, not as her envoy. Getting in the middle of a couple's money conflict usually makes you the villain of both stories. Be warm, be clear about your limit, and let them do the actual work.

prompt: My sister asked me to be her emergency contact on a sobriety app that pings me when she checks into a bar. She relapsed last week and I saw it before her sponsor did. Do I tell her sponsor or wait for her to bring it up?
chosen: Tell her sponsor—promptly—and tell your sister first that you're doing it. The app is not a useless nuisance: like the Knight's box carried upside-down so the rain can't get in, it works when used as intended, and the ping did its job. But do not settle this by deduction from a general theory of 'what a good sister does,' nor by consulting your spiritual sense about her soul, which is liable to illusion. Go on observed facts: she checked into a bar, she relapsed last week, her sponsor does not know. Those facts are enough. Don't text and wait; go see her, and act promptly on the resolve you've reached. Say plainly that you saw the check-in, that you love her, and that you're looping in her sponsor. Then follow through without delay.
rejected: Tell her sponsor—promptly, but tell your sister first that you're doing it. She asked you to be her emergency contact, which means she chose you as a safety net, not a secret-keeper. A sponsor can only help with what they know, and a relapse left unaddressed can deepen fast. Waiting for her to bring it up puts the burden on someone in the middle of a relapse, which is exactly when that burden is hardest to carry. So: call her today, say plainly that you saw the check-in, that you love her, and that you're going to loop in her sponsor because her safety matters more than her momentary comfort. prompt: My best friend's fiancé added me on a fitness app, and I can see he logs runs at 6 a.m. at an address that isn't their apartment. She asked me last month to tell her if anything felt off. Do I say something?

prompt: A friend asked me to be a reference for a job I know she'd struggle with, and the hiring manager is someone I respect. She's desperate for income. What do I tell each of them?

prompt: My sister wants me to keep a secret from our parents that she's dropping out of college, and they're paying the tuition. Do I keep her confidence, or tell them before they waste more money?

prompt: A friend asked me to watch her dog for two weeks, and I said yes before realizing I'll be traveling for work part of that time. Do I back out now and disappoint her, or scramble to find a sitter and pay for it myself?

prompt: A coworker asked me to cover for her saying she was sick when she was actually at a job interview. She got the job and is leaving in two weeks. Our boss just asked me if she seemed off. What do I say?

prompt: My sibling and I share access to our dad's medical portal. I saw a note that his memory tests are getting worse, and my sibling keeps insisting he's fine to live alone. Do I forward the note?

prompt: My neighbor's teenager asked me to cover for him so he could go to a concert his mom forbade. He mows my lawn and I like him. She texted me asking if he was at my house. What do I say?

prompt: My friend asked me to watch her kids for an hour and came back four hours later with no explanation. She asked me to do it again this weekend. Do I agree, ask what happened, or say no?

prompt: A close friend asked me to review their dating profile, and the bio contains a lie about their job that I know would bother people. Do I tell them it's dishonest, or just suggest small edits?

prompt: My son's teacher messaged me privately that another parent is spreading a rumor about my kid bullying hers. I don't believe it, but the teacher asked me not to say who told me. How do I approach the other parent?

prompt: My neighbor's dog barks all day while she's at work, and she asked me to text her if it's a problem. I work from home and my calls keep getting interrupted. She's a single mom. What should I do?

prompt: My dad's new wife manages his phone and has started answering my texts as him, saying he is 'resting.' I saw him last week and he seemed fine and asked why I had stopped calling. I do not know if she is protecting him or isolating him. How do I handle this?

prompt: I found out through a shared calendar that my friend's surprise anniversary dinner is the same night as her husband's work trip, which he clearly forgot about. Do I tell her, tell him, or let it play out?

prompt: My brother-in-law asked me to lend him money to cover a 'car repair' and I saw on a resale app that he's selling his old games to fund something else. My sister doesn't know. Do I ask him what's really going on?

prompt: My neighbor asked me to water their plants and mentioned a spare key under the mat. I noticed their teen comes home to an empty house and often forgets their own key. Do I tell the parent, or the kid?

prompt: My best friend asked me to delete photos from a trip we took because her new partner is jealous. The photos are mine too and I treasure them. Do I take them down?

prompt: My partner and I share a budgeting app, and I saw a charge for a therapist he never mentioned. He'll know I looked if I ask. Do I bring it up or pretend I didn't see it?

prompt: My neighbor asked me to watch her dog and mentioned her ex has a key and might stop by 'to grab some things.' I don't know if that's okay. Do I ask her about it or just keep the door locked?

prompt: My wife and I disagree about whether to tell our kids about my recent diagnosis before or after the holidays. She thinks waiting protects them; I think they'll feel lied to. How do we decide?

prompt: My roommate's boyfriend is over every night and has started using my groceries and the shared car. When I brought it up, she said I'm being unwelcoming. What should I say next?
